We wish to object to the erection of the BESS development on land at [PLACE] for the following reasons: 1. Increased risk of road traffic collisions for vehicles entering and leaving the proposed development (50 mph road). NOTE: Many vehicles drive at speeds far in excess of this. 2. The development will be very close to housing - particularly houses in [PLACE] at approx 50m range - which, in the event of an explosion and fire and subsequent release of toxic fumes, is far too close. The most hazardous gases released from lithium-ion batteries to air is Hydrofluoric acid. Inhalation of a just a few ppm of HF can have serious toxic effects. It readily penetrates the skin and accidental dermal exposure has caused death in humans. This risk is unacceptable. 3. Disruption to surrounding area during hook-up to the national grid. 4. Environment disruption to local area: Lithium-ion batteries have a limited life-span and their disposal is a serious problem. The toxic metals contained in them can contaminate water supplies and ecosystems if they leach out of landfill sites. 5. Fire raising and vandalism is a fairly common occurrence at the [PLACE] which is in very close proximity to [PLACE] - clearly, this behaviour creates further risk to the BESS. 6. There are many hazards associated with lithium-ion battery storage: Inadequate temperature control within the containers can lead to thermal runaway; a chain reaction resulting from a damaged battery releasing heat with risk of fire, explosion and release of highly toxic gases. Clearly, this presents risk to the safety and health of nearby residents. 7. Risk associated with failure of remotely operated control system, slowing down emergency response. 8. Scientific papers state repeatedly that the research area of lithium-ion battery toxic gas emissions needs considerable more attention to mitigate the associated risks. Until these risks have been robustly mitigated, the location of BESS facilities should be restricted to areas far from dwellings and other highly populated areas, thus reducing the risk to as low as reasonably practical. 9. There are serious difficulties associated with extinguishing lithium-ion battery fires. The 2020 BESS fire in [PLACE] took over 30hrs to extinguish. Fires can re-start hours or even days after they have initially been extinguished. There have been over 65 BESS fires worldwide since 2017 ([LINK]) - this does not include fires that occurred in transit. 10. Noise level: We understand that the developer intends to erect a noise suppression (acoustic) fence as there will be a level of background noise from the air conditioning system within the BESS containers. However, sound is omnidirectional so unless the whole storage facility was enclosed the noise level will not be adequately reduced. The tonal buzzing and humming resulting from the high voltage electrical equipment onsite will be offensive to people living nearby. 11. Re-sale of housing in [PLACE] would be adversely affected. Many people would not entertain the thought of buying a house beside a 49 MW BESS for all the reasons listed above.

Basic work should include reviewing prevailing wind direction and impact of local topography on how toxic fumes may travel and accumulate. East of the site: to the east of the proposed site there are a group of houses in a shallow valley a few hundred meters (and further to east [PLACE]). Two important factor to bear in mind are, firstly, that the smoke fumes produced by these sorts of fires are denser than air and will sink down when the smoke cools. Secondly, the terrain between the proposed site and [PLACE] is a valley - if the wind was from the west (one of the principal wind directions) this would have the effect of funnelling the smoke along the valley towards the town, rather than allowing the smoke to dissipate. Placing a BESS next door to the sub-station will create a continuous "industrial ribbon," severely eroding the character of a rural setting. Overconcentration of infrastructure The proximity of this site to [PLACE] is a clear addition of industrial infrastructure to a greenfield site. As such it has a cumulative and detrimental effect on the character of the area. One industrial site should not be an excuse to allow more development, this is not a policy and should not be an excuse to give planning permission. We wish to object to the erection of the BESS development on land at [PLACE] for the following reasons: 1. Increased risk of road traffic collisions for vehicles entering and leaving the proposed development (50 mph road). NOTE: Many vehicles drive at speeds far in excess of this. 2. The development will be very close to housing - particularly houses in [PLACE] at approx 50m range - which, in the event of an explosion and fire and subsequent release of toxic fumes, is far too close. The most hazardous gases released from lithium-ion batteries to air is Hydrofluoric acid. Inhalation of a just a few ppm of HF can have serious toxic effects. It readily penetrates the skin and accidental dermal exposure has caused death in humans. This risk is unacceptable. 3. Disruption to surrounding area during hook-up to the national grid. 4. Environment disruption to local area: Lithium-ion batteries have a limited life-span and their disposal is a serious problem. The toxic metals contained in them can contaminate water supplies and ecosystems if they leach out of landfill sites. 5. Fire raising and vandalism is a fairly common occurrence at the [PLACE] which is in very close proximity to [PLACE] - clearly, this behaviour creates further risk to the BESS. 6. There are many hazards associated with lithium-ion battery storage: Inadequate temperature control within the containers can lead to thermal runaway; a chain reaction resulting from a damaged battery releasing heat with risk of fire, explosion and release of highly toxic gases. Clearly, this presents risk to the safety and health of nearby residents. 7. Risk associated with failure of remotely operated control system, slowing down emergency response. 8. Scientific papers state repeatedly that the research area of lithium-ion battery toxic gas emissions needs considerable more attention to mitigate the associated risks. Until these risks have been robustly mitigated, the location of BESS facilities should be restricted to areas far from dwellings and other highly populated areas, thus reducing the risk to as low as reasonably practical. 9. There are serious difficulties associated with extinguishing lithium-ion battery fires. The 2020 BESS fire in [PLACE] took over 30hrs to extinguish. Fires can re-start hours or even days after they have initially been extinguished. There have been over 65 BESS fires worldwide since 2017 ([LINK]) - this does not include fires that occurred in transit. 10. Noise level: We understand that the developer intends to erect a noise suppression (acoustic) fence as there will be a level of background noise from the air conditioning system within the BESS containers. However, sound is omnidirectional so unless the whole storage facility was enclosed the noise level will not be adequately reduced. The tonal buzzing and humming resulting from the high voltage electrical equipment onsite will be offensive to people living nearby. 11. Re-sale of housing in [PLACE] would be adversely affected. Many people would not entertain the thought of buying a house beside a 49 MW BESS for all the reasons listed above.

target_text: Grid scale Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) should form part of FRS planning in accordance with arrangements required under section 7(2)(d) of the Fire and Rescue Services Act (2004). Site Specific Risk Information (SSRI) should be made available to crews in the form of an effective Emergency Response Plan. Details of any site access arrangements, such as key codes, should be provided to the FRS. Information required as early as possible from the applicant /developer/designer/manufacturer etc., to allow an initial appraisal of the BESS to be made. This information should be provided to the FRS (via the Local Authority Planners in the first instance), with appropriate evidence provided to support any claims made on performance, and with appropriate standards cited for installation. Such information should also be made available to FRSs for inclusion in Site Specific Risk Information (SSRI) records. System design and construction Information required: 1. The battery chemistries being proposed (e.g. Lithium-ion Phosphate (LFP), Lithium Nickel Manganese Cobalt Oxide (NMC)). Because: a. Battery chemistries will directly affect the heat released when a cell goes into thermal runaway2 b. Battery chemistries will influence vapour cloud formation. 2 [LINK] robles.pdf c. An understanding of the battery chemistry is useful when requesting scientific advice during an incident. 2. The battery form factor (e.g. cylindrical, pouch, prismatic) 3. Type of BESS e.g. container or cabinet 4. Number of BESS containers/cabinets 5. Size/capacity of each BESS unit (typically in MWh) 6. How the BESS units will be laid out relative to one another. 7. A diagram / plan of the site. 8. Evidence that site geography has been taken into account (e.g. prevailing wind conditions). 9. Access to, and within, the site for FRS assets 10. Details of any fire-resisting design features 11. Details of any: a. Fire suppression systems b. On site water supplies (e.g. hydrants, EWS etc) c. Smoke or fire detection systems (including how these are communicated) d. Gas and/or specific electrolyte vapour detection systems e. Temperature management systems f. Ventilation systems g. Exhaust systems h. Deflagration venting systems 12. Identification of any surrounding communities, sites, and infrastructure that may be impacted as a result of an incident. Testing Details of any evidence based testing of the system design should be requested, for example, results of UL 9540A testing. Design Design features should be made clear. These may include: - Rack layout and setup - Thermal barriers and insulation - Container layout and access arrangements Detection and monitoring An effective and appropriate method of early detection of a fault within the batteries should be in place, with immediate disconnection of the affected battery/batteries. This may be achieved automatically through the provision of an effective Battery Management System (BMS) and/or a specific electrolyte vapour detection system. Should thermal runaway conditions be detected then there should be the facility in place for the early alerting of emergency services. Detection systems should also be in place for alerting to other fires that do not involve thermal runaway (for example, fires involving electrical wiring). Continuous combustible gas monitoring within units should be provided. Gas detectors should alarm at the presence of flammable gas (yes/no), shut down the ESS, and cause the switchover to full exhaust of the ventilation system3. Sensor location should be appropriate for the type of gas detected e.g. hydrogen, carbon monoxide, volatile organic compounds. External audible and visual warning devices (such as cabinet level strobing lights), as well as addressable identification at control and indicating equipment, should be to linked to: 1. Battery Management System (when a thermal runaway event is identified) 2. Detection and suppression system activation This will enable first responders to understand what the warning is in relation to. This will aid in their decision-making. Suppression systems Suitable fixed suppression systems should be installed in units in order to help prevent or limit propagation between modules. Where it is suggested that suppression systems are not required in the design, this choice should be supported by an evidence based justification and Emergency Response Plan that is designed with this approach in mind (for example, risk assessed controlled burn strategies, and external sprinkler systems). Whilst gaseous suppression systems have been proposed previously, current research indicates the installation of water based suppression systems for fires involving cell modules is more effective. The installation of gaseous suppression systems for electrical fires that do not involve cell modules may be appropriate but should be built into a wider suppression strategy. FM Global cite the following reasons for not recommending gaseous protection systems4: 1. Efficacy relative to the hazard. As of 2019, there is no evidence that gaseous protection is effective in extinguishing or controlling a fire involving energy storage systems. Gaseous protection systems may inert or interrupt the chemical reaction of the fire, but only for the duration of the hold time. The hold time is generally ten minutes, not long enough to fully extinguish an ESS fire or to prevent thermal runaway from propagating to adjacent modules or racks. 3 FM Global (2017) Property Loss Prevention Data Sheets: Electrical Energy Storage Systems, para. 2.5.5.2 4 FM Global (2017) Property Loss Prevention Data Sheets: Electrical Energy Storage Systems, para. 3.3 2. Cooling. FM Global research has shown that cooling the surroundings is a critical factor to protecting the structure or surrounding occupancy because there is currently no way to extinguish an ESS fire with sprinklers. Gaseous protection systems do not provide cooling of the ESS or the surrounding occupancy. 3. Limited Discharge. FM Global research has shown that ESS fires can reignite hours after the initial event is believed to be extinguished. As gaseous protection systems can only be discharged once, the subsequent reignition would occur in an unprotected occupancy The choice of a suppression system should be informed by liaison with a competent system designer who can relate the system choice to the risk identified and the duration of its required activation. Such a choice must be evidence based.5 Any calculations for sufficient water supply for an appropriate suppression system will need to be completed by a competent person considering the appropriate risk and duration of any fire. Water run-off and potential impact on the environment, along with mitigation measures, should be considered and detailed in the Emergency Response Plan. Lack of sufficient water supplies at a particular site location should not be considered as the basis for a suppression system choice. Such an approach could result in potentially ineffective and/or dangerous system designs. Deflagration Prevention and Venting BESS containers should be fitted with deflagration venting and explosion protection appropriate to the hazard. Designs should be developed by competent persons, with design suitability able to be evidenced.6 Exhaust systems designed to prevent deflagration should keep the environment below 25% of Lower Explosive Limit (LEL). Flames and materials discharged as a result of any venting should be directed outside to a safe location and should not contribute to any further fire propagation beyond the unit involved or present further risk to persons. The likely path of any vented gasses or materials should be identified in Emergency Response Plans to reduce risk to responders. Explosion/deflagration strategies should be built into the emergency plan such that responders are aware of their presence and the impact of their actions on these strategies.7 Where emergency ventilation is used to mitigate an explosion hazard, the disconnect for the ventilation system should be clearly marked to notify personnel or first responders to not disconnect the power supply to the ventilation system during an evolving incident.8 5 NFPA (2023) Standard for the Installation of Stationary Energy Storage Systems, para C.3 6 BS EN 16009:2011 Flameless Explosion Venting Devices; BS EN 14373:2021 Explosion Suppression Systems; BS EN 14797:2007 Explosion Venting Devices. 7 UL FRSI (2020) Four Firefighters Injured in Lithium-ion Battery Energy Storage System Explosion – [PLACE], pp. 47-49 8 NFPA (2023) Standard for the Installation of Stationary Energy Storage Systems, para G.1.4.3.3. Access Site access Suitable facilities for safely accessing and egressing the site should be provided. Designs should be developed in close liaison with the local FRS as specific requirements may apply due to variations in vehicles and equipment. This should include: - At least 2 separate access points to the site to account for opposite wind conditions/direction. - Roads/hard standing capable of accommodating fire service vehicles in all weather conditions. As such there should be no extremes of grade. - A perimeter road or roads with passing places suitable for fire service vehicles. - Road networks on sites must enable unobstructed access to all areas of the facility. - Turning circles, passing places etc size to be advised by FRS depending on fleet. Access between BESS units and unit spacing In the event of a fire involving a BESS unit, one of the primary tactics employed will be to prevent further unit to unit fire spread. Suitable access for firefighters to operate unimpeded between units will therefore be required. This should allow for the laying and movement of hose lines and, as such, access should be free of restrictions and obstacles. The presence of High Voltage DC Electrical Systems is a risk and their location should be identified. Exclusion zones should be identified. A standard minimum spacing between units of 6 metres is suggested9 unless suitable design features can be introduced to reduce that spacing. If reducing distances a clear, evidence based, case for the reduction should be shown. Any reduction in this separation distance should be design based by a competent fire engineer. There should be consideration for the fire separation internally and the total realistic load of fire. Proposed distances should be based on radiant heat flux (output) as an ignition source. The [ORGANIZATION] does not support the stacking of containers/units on top of one another on the basis of the level of risk in relation to fire loading, potential fire spread, and restrictions on access. Distance from BESS units to occupied buildings & site boundaries Individual site designs will mean that distances between BESS units and occupied buildings/site boundaries will vary. Proposed distances should take into account risk and mitigation factors. However, an initial minimum distance of 25 metres is proposed prior to any mitigation such as blast walls. Reduction of distances may be possible in areas of lower risk (e.g. rural settings). Where possible buildings should be located upwind. 9 FM Global (2017) Property Loss Prevention Data Sheets: Electrical Energy Storage Systems, para. 2.3.2.2 Site Conditions Sites should be maintained in order that, in the event of fire, the risk of propagation between units is reduced. This will include ensuring that combustibles are not stored adjacent to units and access is clear and maintained. Areas within 10 metres of BESS units should be cleared of combustible vegetation and any other vegetation on site should be kept in a condition such that they do not increase the risk of fire on site. Areas with wildfire risk or vegetation that would result in significant size fires should be factored into this assessment and additional cleared distances maintained as required. Water Supplies Water supplies will depend on the size of the installation. In the majority of cases, initial firefighting intervention will focus on defensive firefighting measures to prevent fire spread to adjacent containers. As a result, proposals for water supplies on site should be developed following liaison with the local fire and rescue service taking into account the likely flow rates required to achieve tactical priorities. This should also take account of the ability of/anticipated time for the fire and rescue service to bring larger volumes of water to site (for example through the provision of High Volume Pumps). IP ratings of units should be known so that risks associated with boundary cooling can be understood. As a minimum, it is recommended that hydrant supplies for boundary cooling purposes should be located close to BESS containers (but considering safe access in the event of a fire) and should be capable of delivering no less than 1,900 litres per minute for at least 2 hours. Fire and rescue services may wish to increase this requirement dependant on location and their ability to bring supplementary supplies to site in a timely fashion. Water supply for any automatic suppression system will be covered by the relevant standard/design depending on which system chosen as appropriate for the risk. For manual water, amounts should come from performance based requirement rather than a reference to a code, unless it can be proven that the code specifically covers BESS. Regarding water storage tanks, volumes will again need to be informed on a performance-based need. Isolation points should be identified. Any static water storage tanks designed to be used for firefighting must be located at least 10 metres away from any BESS container/cabinet. They must be clearly marked with appropriate signage. They must be easily accessible to FRS vehicles and their siting should be considered as part of a risk assessed approach that considers potential fire development/impacts. Outlets and connections should be agreed with the local FRS. Any outlets and hard suction points should be protected from mechanical damage (e.g. through use of bollards). Consideration should be given, within the site design, to the management of water run-off (e.g. drainage systems, interceptors, bunded lagoons etc). Signage Signage should be installed in a suitable and visible location on the outside of BESS units identifying the presence of a BESS system. Signage should also include details of: - Relevant hazards posed - The type of technology associated with the BESS - Any suppression system fitted - 24/7 Emergency Contact Information Signs on the exterior of a building or enclosure should be sized such that at least one sign is legible at night at a distance of 30 metres or from the site boundary, whichever is closer10. Adherence to the Dangerous Substances (Notification and Marking of Sites) Regulations 1990 (NAMOS) should be considered where the total quantity of dangerous substances exceeded 25 tonnes. Emergency Plans Site operators should develop emergency plans and share these with the Fire and Rescue Service. These include: A Risk Management Plan should be developed by the operator, which provides advice in relation to potential emergency response implications including: - The hazards and risks at and to the facility and their proposed management. - Any safety issues for firefighters responding to emergencies at the facility. - Safe access to and within the facility for emergency vehicles and responders, including to key site infrastructure and fire protection systems. - The adequacy of proposed fire detection and suppression systems (eg., water supply) on-site. - Natural and built infrastructure and on-site processes that may impact or delay effective emergency response. An Emergency Response Plan should be developed to facilitate effective and safe emergency response and should include: - How the fire service will be alerted - A facility description, including infrastructure details, operations, number of personnel, and operating hours. - A site plan depicting key infrastructure: site access points and internal roads; firefighting facilities (water tanks, pumps, booster systems, fire hydrants, fire hose reels etc); drainage; and neighbouring properties. 10 NFPA (2023) Standard for the Installation of Stationary Energy Storage Systems, para G.1.4.2.1.1 - Details of emergency resources, including fire detection and suppression systems and equipment; gas detection; emergency eye-wash and shower facilities; spill containment systems and equipment; emergency warning systems; communication systems; personal protective equipment; first aid. - Up-to-date contact details for facility personnel, and any relevant off-site personnel that could provide technical support during an emergency. - A list of dangerous goods stored on site. - Site evacuation procedures. - Emergency procedures for all credible hazards and risks, including building, infrastructure and vehicle fire, grassfire and bushfire Environmental impacts Suitable environmental protection measures should be provided. This should include systems for containing and managing water runoff. System capability/capacity should be based on anticipated water application rates, including the impact of water based fixed suppression systems. Sites located in flood zones should have details of flood protection or mitigation measures. Recovery The operator should develop a post-incident recovery plan that addresses the potential for reignition of ESS and de-energizing the system, as well as removal and disposal of damaged equipment.11 11 FM Global (2017) Property Loss Prevention Data Sheets: Electrical Energy Storage Systems, para. 2.8.2.3

In Scotland, a cumulative effects objection to a planning application refers to the concern that the combined impact of a proposed development, along with existing or planned developments, will negatively affect the area. Key aspects of a cumulative effects objection in Scotland: Combined Impacts: The core of the objection is that the development, considered alongside other existing or proposed developments, will create a greater negative impact than the sum of the individual impacts. Relevant Considerations: This can include issues like: 1. Environmental Degradation: Increased pollution, habitat loss, or strain on natural resources. 2. Infrastructure Strain: Overburdened roads, inadequate parking, or strain on utilities. 3. Impact on Local Character: Changes to the visual landscape, loss of green space, or alteration of the area's identity. 4. Loss of Amenity: Increased noise, traffic, or other disruptions to residents' quality of life. Importance of Cumulative Effects Assessment (CEA): Scottish planning policy increasingly emphasizes the need for CEA to assess the combined impacts of multiple developments. The Fire Safety Strategy refers to [ORGANIZATION] Grid Scale BESS Planning Guidance which has been developed by the National Fire Chiefs Council of the United Kingdom and provides guidance regarding the reduction of risk as reasonably practical regarding public safety and emergency responders at BESS sites. The [ORGANIZATION] guidelines recommend a water supply to the site that can deliver 25000 gallons/hour for a minimum period of 2 hours. Given the recognition that large amounts of water would be discharged in the event of a large fire occurring, there appears to be no apparent provision regarding retention of the contaminated runoff water either by ponding or bunding around the site. (Also see comments regarding the Ecological Impact Assessment below.) Additionally permitting a large-scale fire to simply ‘burn off’ in a controlled manner would result in the discharge of toxic fumes and chemicals into the surrounding area which, given the close proximity of housing and businesses, would endanger the occupant’s health and damage the environment. There is no mention in the Fire Strategy document regarding the adjacent water treatment works which is located extremely close to the proposed site or any risk to that property and any employees on that site should a major incident occur at the BESS site. The water treatment works represent a substantial part of the infrastructure of the City of [PLACE]. Whilst mention is made of some aspects of a Risk Assessment plan and Emergency Response plan as detailed in the [ORGANIZATION] Guidelines, there are obvious omissions in the Fire Strategy document. This leads to a conclusion that this proposed Fire Strategy has not been fully explored by partner agencies particularly Scottish Fire and Rescue Service. It is suggested that full consultation should occur at the earliest opportunity and, in any case, prior to any considerations regarding the development as proposed by this company. (Note: [ORGANIZATION] Grid Scale Battery Energy Storage System Planning Guidance is available from the National Fire Chiefs Council. New South Wales Planning (2011), Hazardous Industry Planning Advisory Paper No 2 Fire Safety Study Guideline.) iv Whilst reference is made to NFPA855 it should be noted that since its introduction in 2021 there have been several fires relating to BESS sites in the USA. Available information indicates that 7 of these fires related to equipment less than 1 year old. The latest incident occurring on 15 May 2024 in San Diego. These incidents indicate that despite the safety offered by NFPA855 current BESS sites still present a risk of fire during operation. Ecological Impact Assessment The impact assessment correctly identifies the local Non-statutory Designated Sites including the [PLACE] located 295 metres from the proposed development. Whilst the assessment concludes there would be no adverse effects to any of these sites, it fails to take regard of the impact where, as stated in the Fire Strategy document, there would be deployment of a water deluge to extinguish a fire on the site. Such a deluge system would result in a substantial production of contaminated runoff water. This could be as much as 25000 gallons/hour until the fire is extinguished if the Grid scale Battery Energy Storage Systems guidance by the National Fire Chiefs Council is applied. There is no provision for such a quantity of contaminated runoff water being retained on site by either ponding or bunding. No reference is made regarding the [PLACE] downstream where the river meets the sea. Given the potential for a substantial quantity of contaminated runoff water in the event of a fire and given the lack of apparent planning to retain such water on site it seems inevitable the runoff would find its way into the [PLACE] and downstream to the potential detriment of wildlife in and around the river. Wildlife located in that area includes various birds, otters and common seals the latter of which frequently swim upstream. (See comments in the Flood Risk Assessment and Surface Water Drainage Strategy below). (Note that the State of Victoria (County Fire Authority) (2023), Design Guidelines and Model Requirements: Renewable Energy Facilities provides in depth guidelines regarding fire safety and methods of dealing with contaminated fire water runoff.) Additionally see New South Wales Planning (2011), Hazardous Industry Planning Advisory Paper No 2 Fire Safety Study Guideline.) Flood Risk Assessment and Surface Water Drainage Strategy The Flood Risk Assessment focuses on surface water drainage based on available existing data relying on current available data and states – ‘This surface water drainage strategy will seek to mimic the existing runoff regime and ensure that there is no increase in peak discharge from the impermeable areas on Site. This will be achieved through the installation of a gravel trench along the southern boundary of the BESS infrastructure.’ The drainage strategy makes no allowance for large amounts of contaminated runoff water from any firefighting at the site if no retention measures are provided for such water. Additionally, the strategy states - ‘In the low probability event of an exceedance of the infiltration basin, water would overtop and follow the local topographic gradients southwards, through the grounds of the [PLACE] and towards the [PLACE]. This exceedance flow follows the existing route of overland flow and is away from the areas of the Site where battery storage and DNO compounds are proposed, and is away from the majority of Scottish Water infrastructure.’ Given the substantial runoff of contaminated water required to control the ‘burn off’, the lack of on-site retention facilities or consideration of sewerage drainage together reinforce the shortcomings identified in the Ecological Impact Assessment. It is hoped that, given the issues identified above and the lack of consultation with the relevant emergency services that this development is not progressed. I would add that I am fully supportive of the drive towards green energy and net zero. However, there is a need for full regulation particularly of BESS developments to ensure the safety of local communities. There is a growing understanding that large BESS sites should not be located close to occupied dwellings given the potential safety risks. There is a great deal of research on the subject and regretfully details of safety failures in that industry which reinforces the need for full regulation of this type of project.

I am submitting these comments on behalf of the [ORGANIZATION]. The proposed development has already been subject to three consultation events, held in [PLACE]. In addition the developer of the proposed facility and their consultant attended a [ORGANIZATION] meeting on 28th April 2025 to present the scheme and answer any question of the Council. As a result of feedback from the consultation events the applicants have altered the location of the access to the proposed development to minimise the impact of construction and operational traffic. In addition the applicant has increased the height of bunding around the site and increased planting of native trees. The proposed development is consistent with the National Planning Framework's (NPF4) policies on tackling climate change (Policy1), implementing net zero (Policy 2), tackling biodiversity (Policy 3), impact on local landscape (Policy 4), impact on historic assets or places (Policy 7), promotion of renewable energy development (Policy 11), mitigation of flood risk (Policy 22) as well health and safety (Policy 23) and rural development (Policy 29). In addition the development appears to be consistent with the relevant policies of the [PLACE] Local Development Plan - development in the countryside (Policy R2), Layout, Sitting and Design (Policy P1), hazardous, potential polluting developments and contaminated land (Policy P4), impact on natural heritage (Policy E1) and on landscape (Policy E2), renewable energy (policy C2) and flood risk (Policy C4). Although the application appears to be consistent with the policy framework. The Community Council has a number of concerns: 1. The applicants state that they will sign up to a decommissioning and restoration programme when the facility reaches the end of its operation life of around 40 years. This would be achieved through a suitably worded planning condition. Given the various uncertainties in business it perhaps would be better if the applicant were required to post a financial bond equivalent to the anticipated decommissioning and restoration costs.This could be used if for any reason e.g. the applicants were to sell the site or become insolvent. 2. There are 6 proposed developments of this nature in the wider [PLACE] area. We appreciate that the reasons for this is the nearby junction of two High Voltage power lines and a major electricity substation. However the [ORGANIZATION] is concerned that we are seeing the creeping industrialisation of an attractive rural area and this is occurring without any strategic policy framework being developed by the local planning authority. Perhaps [ORGANIZATION] should be looking at the cumulative impact of these (and potentially other additional) developments and setting limits on what the area can accommodate. In our view the applicant has provided all the information required to enable the Community Council to reach a view, they have also shown themselves willing to alter their plans to address the concerns of local people - increasing the height of the bund and increased tree planting to screen the development and altering the access road to alleviate local traffic. The development may bring local construction jobs but there are unlikely to be many permanent jobs created. The development is generally in a logical location for such a facility, close to a major substation and High Voltage power lines and will complement the Scottish Government's push towards net zero and sustainable energy. On balance the [ORGANIZATION] recommendation is not to object to this application but to ask [PLACE] County, if they approve this application, to pursue an appropriate financial bond from the projects developers to ensure that the funding for decommissioning and restoration are available when the project reaches the end of its lifespan. In addition [ORGANIZATION] wishes to express their concern to [ORGANIZATION] at the number of similar development being proposed in this area and the need for an assessment of the cumulative impact of these developments and to develop a strategic framework for the consideration of future similar development.

The area enjoys a serene environment with low ambient noise. - The operational noise from the substation will contribute a constant background noise with this noise being more pronounced during periods of reduced ambient noise, such as late hours of the day and night. - Construction Noise will involve heavy machinery, excavation activities, and heightened vehicle traffic, all of which will cause temporary increase in noise levels to the area. - It is very concerning how close this is to residential homes, especially to several newly constructed residential properties. During construction there will be a notable escalation in traffic, especially HGV's transporting materials and equipment. This poses considerable hazards to road safety. - Unsuitable road conditions. This is a narrow single-track road with passing places at farm/property entrances and will also deteriorate these roads causing further impairment. - Safety - the heightened presence of HGV traffic raises safety for residents/pedestrians along the route. Two homes facing the road have young children and most homeowners have dogs with the road to the woods walked numerous times during the day. 4: Energy Storage: There is no justification that further BESS are required to meet local area grid needs, or to achieve ESO short- or long-term national projects. To meet Scotland 2030 and 2045 net zero targets, energy storage of up to 6.4MW and 7.6MW are required. However, in the Department of Energy Security and Net Zero data end of Oct 2024, there are 304 energy storage applications or in the planning totaling 21GW which is three times the 2045 target. 5: Flood ground: The application site is situated on flood prone ground, demonstrated by SEPA as having a High Likelihood (10%) of annual surface flooding, with severe flooding and run off from this site being evidenced and recorded within the past two years alone. Also as stated the noise levels will not be masked by the trees for a number of years until they grow to a good height to help mask noise - report states 15 years!!. Cultural Heritage - The [PLACE] The development site is situated within the broader context of [PLACE], a site of national heritage and royal significance. The proposed facility shows disregard for the royal heritage associated with the Castle, which is linked to HM Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother. The developer's assertion that there will be 'no harm' is based on assumptions rather than concrete evidence, potentially underestimating the negative effects on one of Caithness's most significant heritage assets. Tourism and the Rural Economy The economy of [PLACE] is closely tied to its pristine landscapes, peaceful environment, and rich cultural heritage. Tourism plays a vital role in driving the local economy, supporting small businesses, hospitality services, craft industries, and historic sites. The region's allure is rooted in its rugged natural beauty, coastal vistas, and historical landmarks, notably [PLACE], a popular destination for numerous visitors each year. It also falls short in conducting thorough site surveys, which is in violation of the nature-positive principle outlined in NPF4 Policy 3 and the obligations of the EU Habitats Directive. Furthermore, the proposal not only threatens biodiversity and the landscape but also makes unsubstantiated claims of being environmentally friendly. It lacks evidence of nature restoration, biodiversity net gain, or responsible land use practices. The EcIA fails to provide a concrete and measurable plan to showcase any positive impacts on biodiversity. Industrialisation of Prime Agricultural Land The proposed development would result in the permanent sterilisation of 5.5 hectares of productive farmland in an area where agriculture has long been the cornerstone of rural livelihoods and land stewardship. The installation of hardstanding, impermeable surfaces, high-voltage equipment, and fencing would render the land unsuitable for food production, grazing, or biodiversity enhancement. Industry experts have observed that these systems can produce constant background noise and tonal disturbances that are more disruptive than their decibel levels suggest, especially in quiet rural areas. The BS4142:2014([PLACE]:2019) standard acknowledges the increased annoyance caused by tonal noise in peaceful environments, which has not been adequately addressed in the assessment. Furthermore, there is a lack of effective measures to mitigate issues such as nighttime security lighting, disruptions during the construction phase (including dust, traffic, and noise), and the long- term deterioration of residential living conditions. The serene visual environment of the area is complemented by its peaceful soundscapes, a crucial aspect that appears to have been overlooked in the assessment. Moreover, the OBSMP fails to address the heightened fire risk posed by the facility's rural location. Lithium-ion battery energy storage systems (BESS) are susceptible to prolonged, serious fires, which in a low-resource area like this could have catastrophic consequences for life, property, and agricultural land. These risks must not be overlooked for the sake of convenience. Summary This proposal is of an industrial scale, lacking concrete justification, and fundamentally incompatible with the setting of a protected royal heritage site, local land use, and the planning principles outlined in NPF4 and HEPS. am writing to formally object to the proposed large-scale battery storage development at [PLACE]. Fire and Safety Risks Large battery storage facilities carry a well-documented risk of thermal runaway, fire, and toxic smoke. Given the scale of the proposed installation, any incident could pose a significant danger to nearby homes, businesses, emergency responders, and the wider environment. It is unclear whether sufficient fire suppression measures, emergency response plans, and access routes have been fully assessed or agreed with local fire authorities. 2. Proximity to Residential Properties The proposed development is in close proximity to residential areas. This raises concerns regarding public safety, constant industrial presence, visual dominance, and long-term health impacts. Residents should not be exposed to increased risk or anxiety due to the siting of a high- risk industrial facility near their homes. 3. Noise and Disturbance Battery storage sites operate continuously and rely on cooling systems, transformers, and inverters that generate noise both day and night. This would adversely affect residential amenity, particularly during night-time hours, and may exceed acceptable background noise levels. 4. Visual Impact and Character of the Area The scale, height, and industrial nature of the development would significantly harm the visual character of the area. The site would be out of keeping with its surroundings and would negatively affect landscape quality, local views, and potentially property values. 5. Environmental and Ecological Concerns The development may result in habitat loss, increased surface water runoff, and pollution risks from battery chemicals in the event of leakage or fire. The long-term environmental consequences, including decommissioning and disposal of batteries, have not been convincingly addressed. 6. Lack of Demonstrated Local Benefit There appears to be limited direct benefit to the local community, while the risks and negative impacts are borne almost entirely by nearby residents. Thank you for considering my objection.

The Acoustic Design Specification summarises the night time operation at 33dB(A) (precisely the Target Noise Level set by [ORGANIZATION]), +5dB compared to the background noise level, with an uncertainty of +/-3dB (i.e. as much as +8dB due to uncertainty). The report also notes, that under the guidance “A difference of around +5 dB is likely to be an indication of an adverse impact, depending on the context”, while also that “A difference of around +10 dB or more is likely to be an indication of a significant adverse impact, depending on the context.”. I do not consider an adverse impact to be acceptable for those in the community who will be most affected, especially not without further mitigations for those closest being detailed in the proposal. 4. Safety The current location is the worst possible from a safety perspective. Local firefighters have confirmed that current policy with BESS fires is to leave it to burn: this would mean an extensive evacuation of most of the community, including the main shelter at the Community Centre given prevailing wind. There exists the possibility of production of Hydrofluoric Acid in a Lithium-Ion BESS fire and the location proposed would mean this could affect large areas of the community, including the Doctors Surgery and the Primary School. This is unacceptable exposing the community to needless risk while better options exist elsewhere. UK National Fire Chiefs Council document Grid Scale Battery Energy Storage System planning – Guidance for FRS details the required information for proper consideration of such developments and much of this, including emergency planning, is missing from this application. It cannot be consented in its current form given its proximity to residences, a playpark, businesses, the Primary School, and major routes into and out of the community. 5. Future of the site and impact wider ecosystem Especially in the event of accident what assurances exist that the site can be returned to prime arable land? What drainage exists for emergencies other than dumping contaminated water in [PLACE]? Is there any information about the acoustic impacts on protected species such as bats? None of this is clear from the application and unless these questions are answered the longer term impact of this development on the environment of our community may be tremendous. I do not support these applications by [ORGANIZATION] on behalf of [ORGANIZATION] and [ORGANIZATION]. Please take account of my concerns and objections in your consideration of this application.

Approving an industrial battery facility in such close proximity to a Royal heritage site based on speculation, inadequate evidence, and flawed policy implementation is unacceptable. Furthermore, the BESS is being put forward without a defined local or national strategic framework dictating suitable locations for such developments. The rationale behind selecting this rural site over brownfield or industrial alternatives remains unexplained. The absence of strategic siting criteria leaves rural communities in Scotland susceptible to unplanned industrial proposals that erode landscape quality and cohesion. Concerns are also raised regarding the understated risks to local residents and the wider community in the event of a fire or other incident at the site. Of utmost concern is the potential impact on the setting and experience of [PLACE], a significant and symbolic heritage asset in Scotland. The [PLACE], a cherished retreat of the late Queen Mother and a landmark recognized across the Commonwealth, has had its setting meticulously preserved for generations. Allowing a BESS facility in close proximity risks commercializing and devaluing the legacy of this royal site. Such a decision carries international visibility and could have lasting repercussions on Scotland's planning credibility and tourism appeal. Landscape and Visual Impacts The proposed location is situated in a vast, open landscape with expansive views over [PLACE]. Even with the addition of vegetation, this area is not suited for accommodating large-scale energy infrastructure without significantly altering its natural character. The project would introduce industrial elements such as hard boundaries, metal fencing, and 6-metre structures into a serene rural environment, with numerous residents living just a short distance from the entrance. The resulting impact is neither justified nor adequately mitigated. Community Consultation and Consent Process The BESS proposal advanced to the consent stage without affording local residents and community groups a meaningful opportunity to influence or raise objections. Consultation efforts were inadequate, poorly publicized, and disconnected from other developments in the area. The community affected by this proposal deserves a fair chance to voice their opinions on whether industrial energy infrastructure is suitable for their surroundings. By sidestepping local planning procedures and directly approaching the Scottish Government’s Energy Consents Unit, the application has marginalized the community's ability to influence the decision-making process. Residents, who will bear the consequences of this development, have been left with minimal opportunity to impact the final outcome. Projects of such significant local consequence should involve genuine community engagement in decision-making, rather than being relegated to mere footnotes in the realm of energy infrastructure. Harm to Tourism and Rural Economy [PLACE] is renowned for its expansive horizons, tranquillity, and unspoiled rural charm, qualities that are becoming increasingly scarce and precious. These scenic vistas appeal to hikers, cyclists, artists, and eco-tourists. The large-scale energy industrialization plans, which include battery storage facilities, jeopardize the distinct allure of the area and threaten the future of the local economy reliant on sustainable, rural tourism. Fire and Safety Risks From Battery Infrastructure Large lithium-ion battery storage systems pose well-documented fire hazards. Although rare, these incidents can be severe, challenging to put out, and dangerous to nearby individuals, animals, and emergency services. The developer has not provided a comprehensive emergency response plan or addressed how rural firefighting resources would handle a battery fire. Given the site's proximity to woodlands and peat, a fire in the Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) could potentially lead to a rural wildfire disaster. The rural location implies a delayed emergency response time and insufficient firefighting capabilities. The potential risks to life, property, and the environment should not be ignored for the sake of convenience. Impacts from Noise: Flooding and Site Hazards Serious concerns have been raised regarding the adequacy of the noise impact assessment that has been submitted for the proposed [PLACE] Battery Energy Storage System (BESS). The assessment has been criticized for its lack of transparency, failure to consider the specific site conditions, and the absence of the necessary level of independent scrutiny required for a development of this scale in a rural and heritage-sensitive location. The current assessment is deemed inadequate, and the proposal is deemed unsuitable for the site due to the inevitable acoustic impacts it would bring. Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) facilities are known to produce continuous operational noise from various equipment such as cooling fans, HVAC systems, transformers, inverters, and fire suppression systems. Experts in the industry have pointed out that these systems can generate tonal noise and persistent background hums that are more intrusive than indicated by their decibel ratings, especially in quiet rural environments with minimal background noise. Tonal noise, recognized under BS4142:2014 ([PLACE]:2019), is considered a "penalized" noise type due to its heightened impact on residential amenity. In tranquil settings like [PLACE], even moderate industrial noise can cause significant disruption. The submitted report appears to overlook the importance of the area's auditory tranquillity, which is as crucial as its visual appeal. Moreover, the application fails to adequately address historical surface flooding issues. The construction of impermeable infrastructure like container bases and access roads is expected to increase surface runoff, potentially elevating the risk to nearby properties. This raises serious concerns about local water management and flood resilience. Road Network and Inadequate Access Infrastructure The location is accessed via narrow, unclassified rural roads that are currently under pressure from agricultural and residential activities. The introduction of construction traffic, heavy machinery, and ongoing maintenance vehicles would lead to congestion, road surface deterioration, and potential risks to local residents and livestock. The applicant has not provided sufficient evidence of how they plan to effectively handle the higher volume of traffic on roads that were not intended for industrial purposes. Threat to Local Wildlife and Habitats The area forms a diverse landscape of pasture, hedgerows, and woodland edges that provide habitats for various bird species, small mammals, and invertebrates. However, there has been no comprehensive ecological evaluation released for the BESS project, only a superficial assessment influenced by the developer's perspective. The introduction of concrete surfacing, fencing, artificial lighting, and vegetation removal would result in an ecological void within the surrounding ecosystem. This goes against the nature-positive planning principle outlined in NPF4. Grid Expansion and Landscape Fragmentation The proposed Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) would solidify the presence of high-voltage energy infrastructure in this area of [PLACE]. With the establishment of a battery installation, switching station, and turbines, it establishes a precedent that simplifies the case for more pylons, substations, and transmission lines. This gradual process of industrial expansion progressively breaks up a previously cohesive rural environment, eroding its distinctive qualities, compromising its environmental and cultural heritage, and reducing its worth for generations to come. Absence of Environmental Impact Assessment Despite the size and characteristics of the proposed BESS, a comprehensive Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) has not been conducted. Considering the potential for substantial effects on the landscape, heritage, biodiversity, noise levels, and overall infrastructure, an EIA would typically be required for a project of this nature. The lack of a mandatory EIA is a significant deficiency in environmental assessment and compromises the transparency and effectiveness of the planning procedure. No Long Term Decommissioning or Restoration Plan The candidate has not presented a definitive long-term plan for the decommissioning, restoration, or safety measures of the site once the BESS reaches the end of its operational lifespan. In the absence of concrete restoration guidelines and financial guarantees, there is a potential for the site to be abandoned with deteriorating infrastructure, environmental contamination, or perpetual maintenance responsibilities long after the energy benefits have ceased. Industrialisation of Prime Agricultural Land The proposed BESS would be constructed on land that has historically been utilized for productive agriculture, cultivating crops such as oats for an extended period. The establishment of the BESS, involving structures, fencing, roadways, and related infrastructure, would result in the permanent conversion of valuable farmland. This conflicts with national planning goals aimed at promoting sustainable rural land utilization. Once the development is completed, the land will no longer be available for future agricultural purposes or to contribute to food security. NPF4 Policy 1 emphasizes the importance of sustainable land use and climate resilience. Therefore, the conversion of prime agricultural land for industrial purposes contradicts these objectives and jeopardizes local food security. Summary This project is situated in close proximity to a small rural village without any evident public benefit, thereby contravening the principles of environmental justice and democratic planning. The Council's own guidance acknowledges the "particular sensitivities in this location," which remain unaddressed. Despite its industrial scale, the project offers no discernible advantages to the community, such as local employment opportunities, infrastructure enhancements, or revenue sharing. Consequently, it falls short of the standards outlined in the Scottish Planning Policy (SPP) and the [PLACE] Council's Community Benefit Policy for Renewables. The absence of a community vote, referendum, or popular petition in support of this development raises concerns about the legitimacy of the decision-making process. Consultation efforts have been minimal and largely ineffective, disregarding clear opposition from local residents. A project with significant implications for daily life, health, heritage, and land should not be imposed without genuine, proactive, and locally endorsed consent. This development lacks such consent. It contradicts the core values of sustainability, place-based decision-making, heritage preservation, and rural fairness outlined in NPF4. The project is clearly disproportionate and unsuitable for its surroundings, posing a permanent threat to the local landscape and the historic rural character of [PLACE], a site of national significance. Approving an industrial battery installation in such close proximity to a Royal heritage site based on speculation, inadequate evidence, and flawed policy implementation is unacceptable.

My family and I live at the above address, an historic former hunting lodge registered with [PLACE]. Our land includes registered ancient woodland with legally protected wildlife species present. Our home lies less than 1 km (approx. 700m) from the proposed development site and I therefore believe our concerns should be taken very seriously when considering approval of this application! Fire Safety – the anxiety and fear created by the prospect of living near one of these dangerous installations is very real. The developer states that they “WILL” produce an emergency response plan before construction begins, i.e. they haven’t actually produced one yet – this is completely unacceptable and alone is grounds to reject this application! There is no mains water at this site, no pressurised hydrants available, is a considerable distance from any local fire- stations, (retained service in [PLACE] is 16 miles and manned station in [PLACE] is 30 miles) only has one main access into the site for use by emergency services, there are no stated plans on how contaminated water will be contained and not allowed into the neighbouring burn that flows to [PLACE] and the [PLACE] and the site is surrounded by flammable woodland. The applicant stated at their consultation that fires would be left to burn out BUT copious amounts of water are still required to cool the thermal runaway reaction and stop the fire spreading to neighbouring containers and potentially exploding - The [ORGANIZATION] 2023 Guidance advises that sites should be capable of delivering no less than 1,900 litres per minute for at least 2 hours, where will all this water come from? They also said that toxic fumes “should disperse” before reaching neighbouring properties, including ours, but what about our prevailing westerly winds? – this is just not acceptable! A full and detailed fire safety plan should be in place BEFORE this application is even considered. Protected wildlife – Considering the size and scale of this development and its rural location, it is very disappointing that an EIA has not been compulsory! The developer states that pre-construction surveys WILL be carried out i.e. have NOT be completed yet and this again is grounds for this application to be refused! Previous surveys carried out for a wind farm, the substation and cable connections confirmed the presence of protected species including otters, badgers, pine martins and water voles, as well as red squirrels and mountain hare and there may well be bats there too. There is also the birdlife that is regularly observed in this area including the locally nesting osprey, golden eagle, red kites that nest in our garden, golden plover, merlin, hen harrier and greylag geese. It is NOT acceptable that this applicant be granted permission to develop a site that could potentially destroy the habitats of legally protected species and then only investigate their presence after permission is granted – this should and must be a requirement BEFORE the application is considered. This goes against NPF4 policy 1 – tackling the nature crisis and policy 4 - natural places. Trees – The Scottish Government policy is opposed to permanent removal of woodland for the purposes of conversion to another land use unless it would achieve significant public benefits, which this development will not. There is also an area of ancient woodland (Scots pine) identified on this site – who will be responsible for its protection? NPF4 also supports protecting, enhancing and improving woodlands. Need – this tiny community has ALREADY had 3 x up to 50MW battery storage facilities approved – [PLACE] Battery Storage ref: [APPLICATION_CODE], [PLACE] Wind farm Ext 11 including battery storage ref: [APPLICATION_CODE] and [PLACE] including battery storage ref: [APPLICATION_CODE]. Cumulative impact – the area surrounding this proposed development already has a great deal of energy related infrastructure – [PLACE] Wind Farm, plus extension 1, [PLACE], upgraded 132KV pylon line, [PLACE] plus [PLACE] Wind Farm Ext 2, [PLACE] and [PLACE] BESS also consented but not yet built and another wind farm at [PLACE] proposed. This area has already done its fair share for renewable energy. We are being unfairly targeted due to our sparce population and our voices are not being heard – this is undemocratic. A Plume Assessment be carried out.The aim of the plume assessment is to understand possible impacts of the BESS Compound on the nearby receptors in an emergency situation; primarily the emergency responders and those in the surrounding area such as workers or local residents. EIA: Environmental Impact Assessment Examples, Methods & Steps When a project, policy change, or event has a chance of impacting any part of an environment or ecosystem, it’s important to do an environmental impact assessment (EIA). Not only is an EIA screening the responsible way to proceed with a project or plan, but it’s also often required by law to ensure that human interventions won’t cause undue harm or irreversible damage to the environment. An environmental impact assessment example would be the need to assess what a new manufacturing facility in a region means as far as air quality, water quality, noise pollution, ecosystem upset, and more. An environmental impact assessment project will look for effects, both positive and negative, on things like air and climate, land, water, ecology and biodiversity, and human environment. Is it not important that an EIA is carried out so as to ascertain the prevention of the contamination of drinking water for a community. Despite the challenges of environmental impact assessment in developing countries, the results can mean the difference between life or death. For example, in an underdeveloped community with rich natural resources, environmental impact assessment meaning can be the halt of a project that would ruin farmland and thus the community’s ability to thrive. An environmental impact assessment example will generally categorize impacts as: - Air and Climate: This includes things like air quality, health implications, ecosystem impacts, contributions to climate change, etc. - Land: This includes the use of non-renewable resources, changes to land morphology, impacts to historic or cultural sites, etc. - Water: This includes impacts on local drinking water, sustainability, the effect of local use for irrigation and other activities, health implications, etc. - Ecology & Biodiversity: This includes the importance of biodiversity value, both terrestrial and marine, economic use to the community, ecosystem well-being, etc. - Human Environment: This includes things like light and noise pollution, community safety, employment opportunities, community value creation, etc. - designing for location weather – consideration should be given to how weather at the selected battery site may impact operating capabilities or asset degradation. Obvious examples include ambient temperature and how this might change over time (including the impacts of climate change and the possibility of extreme heatwaves). This could impact asset operation and cooling requirements. Other considerations include locations near the coast, where coastal ‘salt air’ can accelerate corrosion. target_text: I object to the proposed Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) development near [PLACE] due to serious concerns regarding emergency response, public safety, and the suitability of local infrastructure to support such an industrial project in a rural setting. 1. Inadequate Emergency Access and Response Times The site is located in a remote, rural area where access roads are narrow, often single-track, and prone to becoming impassable during winter conditions due to snow and ice. Emergency services would face significant delays in reaching the site, particularly during a fire or other hazardous incident. Given that lithium-ion battery fires are extremely difficult to extinguish and can burn for extended periods, a delayed response could have catastrophic consequences - not only for the site itself but also for nearby properties, livestock, and natural areas such as the adjacent [PLACE]. 2. Unmanned Site Increases Risk Once operational, the BESS facility will be unmanned, meaning early detection and immediate response to incidents will not be possible. Without on-site personnel, a fire or hazardous material event could go unnoticed until it is already out of control. There is no indication of how the site will be monitored, who will be responsible for initiating emergency protocols, or how local residents will be informed in the event of an incident. No evacuation plans or livestock safety measures have been disclosed. 3. Risk to Rural Infrastructure and Residents The surrounding infrastructure - including local roads - is not designed to accommodate the heavy industrial traffic required for construction, maintenance, or emergency services. These roads are used daily by pedestrians, cyclists, and horse riders from the nearby villages. Increased HGV traffic poses a safety risk to residents and damages rural roads not built for such load-bearing use. There is also no indication of how road damage (e.g. potholes, surface wear) will be repaired or funded, and no commitment to limit construction traffic during [PLACE] runs or peak pedestrian hours. 4. Lack of Emergency Planning or Public Assurance Crucially, no emergency response plan has been made publicly available. Residents living near the site deserve to know what protections are in place in the event of fire, chemical leak, explosion, or flooding. Has the local fire service been consulted? What are their capabilities for responding to a lithium-ion fire in such a remote location? Without this information - and without credible reassurances - this proposal is unsafe and ill-suited to the local context. Conclusion This BESS project introduces unacceptable risk to a rural area without the infrastructure, services, or emergency provisions necessary to manage such a high-hazard development. Until safety, access, and emergency planning concerns are fully addressed and communicated, this development should not be permitted to proceed.

The conversion from agricultural land to an industrial facility will irreversibly change the character of the area. Its proximity to the substation does not justify such a transformation, which will be visibly and experientially intrusive to residents and visitors. 3. Unassessed Noise Impact The noise emissions from this development will be variable and dependent on load and operational conditions. Assessment should consider original baseline levels before the substation was introduced, and should evaluate cumulative noise from all adjacent infrastructure. Residents already report stress due to unresolved powerline noise - further disturbance will compound this issue. 4. Fire Risk and Emergency Preparedness Lithium-ion battery fires are notoriously difficult to manage and cannot be extinguished by conventional means. Given the site will not be permanently staffed, it is unclear how emergency services would respond, particularly in winter when roads are often impassable. Risks to nearby woodland, livestock, and rural homes have not been adequately accounted for. 5. Water Contamination and Flood Risk Fire suppression efforts would introduce contaminated water into an environment where residents rely on private wells and local watercourses. The proposed SUDS pond, situated on an elevated site, increases the risk of pollution entering aquifers and burns. With more frequent extreme weather events, overflow is a real concern. Consultation with SEPA appears absent. 6. Construction and Road Impact Significant disruption is expected during the construction phase, especially to narrow rural roads used daily by residents, walkers, and cyclists. No clear traffic impact assessments or mitigation plans have been shared for [PLACE], [PLACE], or surrounding routes. The impact on domestic properties adjacent to the access point has not been addressed. 7. Biodiversity and Protected Species The proposed site borders sensitive ecological areas such as the [PLACE], where several badger setts and ground-nesting birds have been identified. There is no clear evidence of recent ecological assessments or consultation with relevant conservation bodies such as the Badger Trust or [ORGANIZATION]. The potential impact on bats has also been overlooked. 8. Visual Appearance and Design Control Though the developer claims the battery units will be coloured to suit the landscape, there are no binding conditions to ensure this will be upheld. Past experience with similar developments suggests this may not be enforced, leading to an eyesore in what is currently an unspoiled area. 9. Restoration and Developer Responsibility There is no plan for site rehabilitation, no soil baseline data, and no mechanism to ensure land restoration. Developers of similar projects have sold them post-approval, raising accountability concerns. An ESCROW fund for environmental recovery should be a non-negotiable requirement. 10. Cumulative Impact on Community Wellbeing The local population has already endured years of disruption from adjacent energy infrastructure. This development will only intensify noise, traffic, and stress, further diminishing the health and quality of life of residents. The area is also an important recreational space for nearby communities - its degradation will be widely felt. 11. Absence of Community Benefit It is troubling that no community benefit is proposed, particularly given the long-term impact and scale of the development. This omission highlights a lack of local engagement or responsibility toward the communities affected. Conclusion Given the risks to public safety, environmental harm, disruption to rural life, and lack of community gain, this proposal is fundamentally unsuitable for this location.
