I am writing to formally object to the proposed [PLACE] Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) development due to its significant risks to public safety, environmental integrity, and the well-being of our local community. While energy storage infrastructure is an important part of the transition to renewable energy, this particular development raises serious concerns that must be addressed before proceeding. Public Safety Risks One of the most pressing concerns is the risk of fire and thermal runaway associated with lithium-ion battery storage facilities. Such incidents can result in uncontrollable fires, toxic smoke emissions, and potential explosions, posing a serious threat to residents, emergency responders, and local infrastructure. Given the remote nature of the site, it is unclear whether emergency services would have the necessary resources to contain a large-scale fire, further exacerbating the danger. Environmental and Health Concerns The potential for toxic contamination from battery leakage or fire incidents is another major issue. Hazardous chemicals, including heavy metals and electrolytes, could leach into the soil and nearby water sources, endangering local ecosystems and water supplies. Additionally, noise pollution from battery cooling systems, inverters, and maintenance operations could have a lasting impact on the well-being of residents and wildlife in the area. Impact on Landscape and Community This development threatens to disrupt the natural beauty and character of [PLACE]. The large industrial-scale infrastructure required for the BESS will significantly alter the landscape, affecting tourism, property values, and the overall quality of life for those living nearby. The long-term consequences of such an installation have not been adequately addressed, and the lack of community consultation raises concerns about transparency and fairness in the planning process. Conclusion Given these risks, I urge the planning authority to reject this proposal or, at the very least, require a thorough independent assessment of the safety, environmental, and community impacts before proceeding. Alternative locations, stricter safety regulations, and enhanced community engagement should all be considered before granting approval. I strongly oppose the [PLACE] BESS development in its current form and ask that my objection be formally recorded.

[PERSON] [PLACE] To: [ORGANIZATION] Re: Objection to Proposed Battery Energy Storage Facility - [PLACE]; Planning Reference: [APPLICATION_CODE] (or [APPLICATION_CODE]) Dear Sir/Madam, I am writing to formally object to the proposed development of a 49.9 MW battery energy storage system (BESS) at [PLACE] (postcode [PLACE]), under the above planning reference. 1. Fire and Public Safety Risks The scale of the proposed lithium-ion battery installation presents a serious fire risk. Should thermal runaway occur, fires can release toxic gases such as hydrogen fluoride and dioxins. A fire scenario could affect nearby residents, including myself, within minutes. The proximity of local housing and lack of adequate local fire & rescue emergency response capacity within our area - combined with the difficulty of containing such fires - makes this an unacceptable risk. Our local community already has first hand experience of a large scale incident caused by fire at the [PLACE] BESS site in February 2025. There are real risks with capacity to respond to incidents of these nature as surrounding fire service facilities are operated by retained fire fighters and which may not have the experience or training to deal with large scale battery fires. 2. Environmental Contamination and Water Run-Off The risk of contaminated water run-off entering nearby burns or private boreholes is alarming. Large volumes of water may also be required in the event of a fire. If run-off containment fails, this could pollute downstream supplies, threatening wildlife and residents who like myself who rely on private water sources. 3. Noise and Amenity Impacts The facility will operate continuously and house a number of cooling units. These are expected to generate a constant humming noise, especially during energy discharge events. This will severely impact the rural tranquillity that residents currently enjoy. I am particularly concerned about the 24/7 nature of the operation and how it will affect quality of life, mental health, and sleep, especially for my children and neighbours. 4. Traffic and Road Safety The proposal would lead to a significant increase in vehicle movements - potentially hundreds per day during the construction period. This is unsuitable for our narrow rural roads. Increased heavy goods traffic poses real safety risks and would cause road degradation and disruption to our local community. 5. Landscape and impact on local Wildlife This industrial-scale development is entirely out of character with the surrounding countryside. The development risks habitat loss for local species, including badger sets, roe deer, foxes, and birdlife. No amount of screening will adequately mitigate the visual or ecological impact. 6. Planning Process and Environmental Impact Assessment It is deeply concerning that an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) was not required for this proposal, despite its scale and the clear risk to public health and the environment. This appears to contravene the precautionary principle. The local community has also not been adequately consulted or informed about the cumulative impact of all the multiple BESS sites which are progressing through planning on a project by project basis in out local area. Multiple sites are progressing in and around the [PLACE] area without any joined up thinking on how much battery storage is required within our local area. 7. Benefits to local community I note that the developer has shared no information on the benefits this scheme would bring to the local community either during construction and once operational. A multi-million pound development like is required to detail the additional social value which will be achieved and its impact on local job creation and benefits to our local economy. Once operational, there has also not been any community legacy benefits stated which would share any value of hosting battery storage with our local community. Conclusion For all the reasons above, I strongly urge you to refuse this planning application. The proposed development poses an unacceptable risk to public safety, the environment, local amenity, and the rural character of the surrounding area of [PLACE] and [PLACE]. Until a full environmental and safety assessment has been undertaken, and all risks transparently addressed, this application must not proceed.

I wish to submit a formal objection to the proposed Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) development near [PLACE]. My concerns focus on the potential for fire hazards, water contamination, and the lack of environmental safeguards, particularly regarding local watercourses and consultation with SEPA. 1. Severe Fire Risk in a Rural, Unmanned Location Lithium-ion battery systems are known to pose a significant fire risk. These fires can be extremely difficult to control and often burn for many hours or days. As this site will be unmanned during its operational phase and located in a rural area with limited access, emergency response may be delayed, especially in adverse weather when local tracks are often snowed in or impassable. There is currently no publicly available emergency response plan. This absence is particularly concerning for residents who live in close proximity to the site, as well as for nearby agricultural operations and the adjacent mature woodland. Questions remain unanswered: What are the emergency response times? Has the fire service been consulted? Who will coordinate road access during an emergency? 2. Contaminated Fire Suppression Water and Impact on Watercourses In the event of a fire, the water used to suppress it will become heavily contaminated with toxic chemicals. This runoff poses a direct threat to local watercourses, aquifers, and private wells used by residents. Given the elevated position of the site, any overflow from the fire suppression effort or the planned SUDS (Sustainable Urban Drainage System) pond will drain into surrounding water systems. This includes a burn that flows into [PLACE] and feeds nearby private supplies. No detailed plan has been provided to contain or treat contaminated water before it enters the natural environment. This is an unacceptable risk. 3. Inadequate Drainage and Risk of SUDS Pond Overflow The proposed SUDS pond is positioned on sloped ground, increasing the risk of overspill, especially during heavy rainfall or storm events. Planning documents describe the site as "stormproof," yet in recent years there has been increasing evidence of severe weather and localised flooding - including reports from 2023 of flood damage to homes near the affected burn. The pond is designed to allow soak-away into surrounding soil, but this raises serious questions about groundwater contamination, especially with no buffer zone from the natural hydrological systems. There is also no clear information on how the pond will be maintained or monitored over time. 4. Lack of SEPA Consultation and Environmental Oversight It is unclear whether SEPA (Scottish Environment Protection Agency) has been meaningfully consulted in the assessment of water risks. Given the potential impact on watercourses, private water supplies, and flood management, it is imperative that SEPA's input be obtained and published before any approval is considered. The lack of transparency around this consultation suggests that water safety risks have not been adequately evaluated, nor mitigation plans robustly designed. Conclusion This application introduces substantial, unmanaged risk to the local environment through fire hazards, inadequate emergency access, and the threat of contaminated water reaching sensitive local ecosystems. Without a detailed fire response plan, flood prevention strategy, and proper environmental oversight by SEPA, this proposal is not fit for approval. I strongly urge [ORGANIZATION] to refuse this application unless these critical concerns are fully addressed with public input and the cooperation of the relevant emergency and environmental authorities.

While I do not live locally, I am deeply concerned about the wellbeing of those who do live close to these developments. Fire Risk & Emergency Response Lithium-ion battery fires are difficult to control and highly toxic. This site is unmanned, rural, and prone to winter inaccessibility. No emergency plan has been provided-have fire services been consulted? The SUDS pond, on elevated ground, risks overflowing during storms or fire. Has SEPA reviewed this? Hazardous Materials Large volumes of hazardous substances will be stored on-site. Lack of Accountability There is no robust plan to restore the land once operations cease. Developers often sell such projects on-who is responsible long-term? An escrow fund should be mandatory to guarantee site restoration. Given the risks and lack of proper national regulation, developments like this should not be approved-especially when they impact people living so close, with no meaningful protection in place.

I wish to submit a formal objection to the proposed Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) development near [PLACE]. My concerns focus on the potential for fire hazards, water contamination, and the lack of environmental safeguards, particularly regarding local watercourses and consultation with SEPA. 1. Severe Fire Risk in a Rural, Unmanned Location Lithium-ion battery systems are known to pose a significant fire risk. These fires can be extremely difficult to control and often burn for many hours or days. As this site will be unmanned during its operational phase and located in a rural area with limited access, emergency response may be delayed, especially in adverse weather when local tracks are often snowed in or impassable. There is currently no publicly available emergency response plan. This absence is particularly concerning for residents who live in close proximity to the site, as well as for nearby agricultural operations and the adjacent mature woodland. Questions remain unanswered: What are the emergency response times? Has the fire service been consulted? Who will coordinate road access during an emergency? 2. Contaminated Fire Suppression Water and Impact on Watercourses In the event of a fire, the water used to suppress it will become heavily contaminated with toxic chemicals. This runoff poses a direct threat to local watercourses, aquifers, and private wells used by residents. Given the elevated position of the site, any overflow from the fire suppression effort or the planned SUDS (Sustainable Urban Drainage System) pond will drain into surrounding water systems. This includes a burn that flows into [PLACE] and feeds nearby private supplies. No detailed plan has been provided to contain or treat contaminated water before it enters the natural environment. This is an unacceptable risk. 3. Inadequate Drainage and Risk of SUDS Pond Overflow The proposed SUDS pond is positioned on sloped ground, increasing the risk of overspill, especially during heavy rainfall or storm events. Planning documents describe the site as "stormproof," yet in recent years there has been increasing evidence of severe weather and localised flooding - including reports from 2023 of flood damage to homes near the affected burn. The pond is designed to allow soak-away into surrounding soil, but this raises serious questions about groundwater contamination, especially with no buffer zone from the natural hydrological systems. There is also no clear information on how the pond will be maintained or monitored over time. 4. Lack of SEPA Consultation and Environmental Oversight It is unclear whether SEPA (Scottish Environment Protection Agency) has been meaningfully consulted in the assessment of water risks. Given the potential impact on watercourses, private water supplies, and flood management, it is imperative that SEPA's input be obtained and published before any approval is considered. The lack of transparency around this consultation suggests that water safety risks have not been adequately evaluated, nor mitigation plans robustly designed. Conclusion This application introduces substantial, unmanaged risk to the local environment through fire hazards, inadequate emergency access, and the threat of contaminated water reaching sensitive local ecosystems. Without a detailed fire response plan, flood prevention strategy, and proper environmental oversight by SEPA, this proposal is not fit for approval. I strongly urge [ORGANIZATION] to refuse this application unless these critical concerns are fully addressed with public input and the cooperation of the relevant emergency and environmental authorities.

I write to object to the proposed Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) development on the following grounds: 1. Public Safety and Hazardous Materials The presence of hazardous substances in lithium-ion batteries introduces a significant risk. There is no evidence that COMAH regulations have been consulted, nor any indication of coordination with the [ORGANIZATION]. The absence of an emergency response plan, especially given the site's remote, unmanned status, raises serious safety concerns. 2. Landscape and Character Degradation The area in question is part of a valued rural landscape described by the applicant's own assessment as "well settled, wooded, and attractive." The conversion from agricultural land to an industrial facility will irreversibly change the character of the area. Its proximity to the substation does not justify such a transformation, which will be visibly and experientially intrusive to residents and visitors. 3. Unassessed Noise Impact The noise emissions from this development will be variable and dependent on load and operational conditions. Assessment should consider original baseline levels before the substation was introduced, and should evaluate cumulative noise from all adjacent infrastructure. Residents already report stress due to unresolved powerline noise - further disturbance will compound this issue. 4. Fire Risk and Emergency Preparedness Lithium-ion battery fires are notoriously difficult to manage and cannot be extinguished by conventional means. Given the site will not be permanently staffed, it is unclear how emergency services would respond, particularly in winter when roads are often impassable. Risks to nearby woodland, livestock, and rural homes have not been adequately accounted for. 5. Water Contamination and Flood Risk Fire suppression efforts would introduce contaminated water into an environment where residents rely on private wells and local watercourses. The proposed SUDS pond, situated on an elevated site, increases the risk of pollution entering aquifers and burns. With more frequent extreme weather events, overflow is a real concern. Consultation with SEPA appears absent. 6. Construction and Road Impact Significant disruption is expected during the construction phase, especially to narrow rural roads used daily by residents, walkers, and cyclists. No clear traffic impact assessments or mitigation plans have been shared for [PLACE], [PLACE], or surrounding routes. The impact on domestic properties adjacent to the access point has not been addressed. 7. Biodiversity and Protected Species The proposed site borders sensitive ecological areas such as the [PLACE], where several badger setts and ground-nesting birds have been identified. There is no clear evidence of recent ecological assessments or consultation with relevant conservation bodies such as the Badger Trust or [ORGANIZATION]. The potential impact on bats has also been overlooked. 8. Visual Appearance and Design Control Though the developer claims the battery units will be coloured to suit the landscape, there are no binding conditions to ensure this will be upheld. Past experience with similar developments suggests this may not be enforced, leading to an eyesore in what is currently an unspoiled area. 9. Restoration and Developer Responsibility There is no plan for site rehabilitation, no soil baseline data, and no mechanism to ensure land restoration. Developers of similar projects have sold them post-approval, raising accountability concerns. An ESCROW fund for environmental recovery should be a non-negotiable requirement. 10. Cumulative Impact on Community Wellbeing The local population has already endured years of disruption from adjacent energy infrastructure. This development will only intensify noise, traffic, and stress, further diminishing the health and quality of life of residents. The area is also an important recreational space for nearby communities - its degradation will be widely felt. 11. Absence of Community Benefit It is troubling that no community benefit is proposed, particularly given the long-term impact and scale of the development. This omission highlights a lack of local engagement or responsibility toward the communities affected. Conclusion Given the risks to public safety, environmental harm, disruption to rural life, and lack of community gain, this proposal is fundamentally unsuitable for this location. I urge the Council to reject the application unless all these matters are fully addressed and resolved through meaningful consultation.

I am writing to formally object to the above planning application. I am a long-term resident of the area, having lived at [PLACE] with my family since 1991. My parents, now elderly, continue to live here, and I am deeply concerned about the risks this development poses to their health, safety, and quality of life. This proposal is one of six separate BESS applications currently under consideration within a small area around [PLACE]. Yet there appears to be no assessment of the cumulative effects on our community. That in itself is deeply troubling. My objections are as follows: 1. Fire Risk and Emergency Response Lithium-ion battery fires are notoriously difficult to control, as seen in the recent incidents at [PLACE] and [PLACE]. These fires are capable of reigniting, producing toxic smoke, and burning for days. The proposal fails to explain how such an incident would be managed on this rural site, which lacks the infrastructure and proximity to emergency services. Most importantly, there is no public evacuation plan - yet residents like my elderly parents may have limited mobility. We need clarity on how people in their position would be safely informed, assisted, and protected in an emergency. 2. Water Supply for Firefighting The village of [PLACE] does not have a mains water supply, raising serious concerns over how a fire could be effectively tackled. The application does not provide any detail on water storage volumes, sourcing, or whether boreholes could compromise local private water supplies, which my family relies on. 3. Environmental Pollution from Fire Water Run-Off Fire suppression water is often contaminated with harmful chemicals. Without proper containment, this could easily enter the local water table or the burn that flows into [PLACE], putting both human and environmental health at risk. This is particularly serious for homes with private wells. 4. Noise Impacts Cooling units, inverters, and transformers produce continuous operational noise. As a quiet rural area, any new noise sources must be assessed against baseline levels before the substation was built - and must also factor in the noise from the five other proposed BESS facilities. Living close by, this noise will affect our daily lives and long-term well-being. 5. Construction Traffic and Access Concerns This development would lead to significant disruption during construction, especially from heavy goods vehicles and daily movements of large construction crews. Our roads are narrow and not designed for this level of industrial traffic. As a resident of [PLACE] Avenue, I worry about the safety of my elderly parents and other vulnerable people walking or driving on these single lane roads, especially given limited visibility and lack of pavements. 6. Decommissioning and Land Restoration There are no guarantees in the proposal for how the site will be properly decommissioned after the 25-year operational period. Concrete bases, cables, and other infrastructure may remain unless a fully costed restoration plan and secured fund are in place. Without this, the land could be left permanently damaged. In conclusion, this development is completely unsuitable for a rural residential area. The lack of emergency planning, the risks to water and air quality, and the unacceptable disruption to residents - particularly to vulnerable people like my elderly parents - make this proposal deeply inappropriate. I strongly urge [ORGANIZATION] to reject application [APPLICATION_CODE] in the interest of protecting residents, safeguarding our environment, and preserving the character of our community.

My objections are based on the following material considerations: 1. Environmental and Wildlife Concerns The site lies adjacent to a diverse and thriving wildlife area, home to local bee hives, swans, deer, foxes, and many other species. This ecosystem is not only important for biodiversity but is also a source of pride and enjoyment for the community. Bats, bees, and birds, in particular, are vulnerable to disturbance from noise, electromagnetic interference, and changes to their habitat. Under the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981, these species are protected, and any harm or disruption could constitute a legal offence. I urge the Council to ensure that a full ecological and biodiversity assessment is conducted and made public before this application is considered further. 2. Noise Pollution and Impact on Quality of Life Battery storage systems generate continuous low-frequency hums from inverters and cooling systems. In a peaceful, rural setting such as [PLACE], even moderate levels of industrial noise can disrupt residents' daily lives, impact mental wellbeing, and erode the tranquil enjoyment of the countryside. This development would fundamentally alter the area's character and diminish the quality of life for those who spend time here. 3. Fire and Safety Risk BESS facilities carry serious fire and explosion risks due to thermal runaway-a chain reaction in lithium-ion batteries that can cause uncontrollable fires. Once ignited, such fires can burn for days and are extremely difficult to extinguish. More troubling is the release of toxic gases during these events, including: Hydrogen fluoride (HF) - corrosive and lethal even at low exposure, Hydrogen cyanide (HCN) and carbon monoxide (CO) - both highly toxic, Volatile organic compounds (VOCS) harm air quality, soil, and water. Previous incidents, such as the [PLACE] explosion (2019) and the Moorabool fire in Australia (2020), demonstrate the dangers of these facilities. Any fire would severely risk local residents, wildlife, and farmland. 4. Incompatible Use of Land and Loss of Natural Beauty [PLACE] is part of a cherished landscape, used daily by walkers and families who appreciate its open views and peaceful environment. It is entirely inappropriate to industrialise a location so closely tied to local identity and community wellbeing. The proposal is completely out of character with the surrounding rural setting and offers no meaningful benefit to the local community. 5. Impact on Property Value and Insurance The presence of large-scale industrial infrastructure in a rural area may negatively impact property values. 6. Carbon Emissions and Supply Chain Impact While the intention behind BESS facilities is to support renewable energy, the overall carbon cost of manufacturing, transporting, and installing lithium-ion batteries is significant. A full life-cycle carbon impact assessment should be required, especially considering the environmental costs of extracting raw materials and shipping components internationally. In summary, this proposal threatens the unique rural character, biodiversity, and wellbeing of the [PLACE] area. It is poorly suited to its location, introduces avoidable risks, and offers little to no benefit to the local community. I respectfully urge the Council to reject planning application [APPLICATION_CODE].

My objections are based on the following material considerations: 1. Environmental and Wildlife Concerns The site lies adjacent to a diverse and thriving wildlife area, home to local bee hives, swans, deer, foxes, and many other species. This ecosystem is not only important for biodiversity but is also a source of pride and enjoyment for the community. Bats, bees, and birds, in particular, are vulnerable to disturbance from noise, electromagnetic interference, and changes to their habitat. Under the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981, these species are protected, and any harm or disruption could constitute a legal offence. I urge the Council to ensure that a full ecological and biodiversity assessment is conducted and made public before this application is considered further. 2. Noise Pollution and Impact on Quality of Life Battery storage systems generate continuous low-frequency hums from inverters and cooling systems. In a peaceful, rural setting such as [PLACE], even moderate levels of industrial noise can disrupt residents' daily lives, impact mental wellbeing, and erode the tranquil enjoyment of the countryside. This development would fundamentally alter the area's character and diminish the quality of life for those who spend time here. 3. Fire and Safety Risk BESS facilities carry serious fire and explosion risks due to thermal runaway-a chain reaction in lithium-ion batteries that can cause uncontrollable fires. Once ignited, such fires can burn for days and are extremely difficult to extinguish. More troubling is the release of toxic gases during these events, including: Hydrogen fluoride (HF) - corrosive and lethal even at low exposure, Hydrogen cyanide (HCN) and carbon monoxide (CO) - both highly toxic, Volatile organic compounds (VOCS) harm air quality, soil, and water. Previous incidents, such as the [PLACE] explosion (2019) and the Moorabool fire in Australia (2020), demonstrate the dangers of these facilities. Any fire would severely risk local residents, wildlife, and farmland. 4. Incompatible Use of Land and Loss of Natural Beauty [PLACE] is part of a cherished landscape, used daily by walkers and families who appreciate its open views and peaceful environment. Impact on Property Value and Insurance The presence of large-scale industrial infrastructure in a rural area may negatively impact property values. 6. target_text: Planning Application Reference [APPLICATION_CODE] I submit the following formal objection to the proposed Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) development on the basis that the application, in its current form, does not adequately address key feasibility, environmental, and planning policy considerations. A detailed review of the submitted documentation identifies substantive deficiencies across multiple disciplines - including grid connection feasibility, cumulative development impacts, environmental risk assessment, drainage and water environment protection, landscape character and visual amenity, ecological safeguarding, and decommissioning strategy. These deficiencies raise significant questions regarding the deliverability of the scheme and its compliance with relevant local and national planning policies, including those relating to sustainable development, protection of designated sites, and mitigation of cumulative environmental effects. From a technical perspective, the absence of essential baseline assessments, inconsistent supporting documentation, and a lack of secured mitigation measures represent material planning risks that must be resolved prior to any consent being considered. Transmission Entry Capacity (TEC) Register This BESS site is not listed on the TEC Register, which is managed by National Grid ESO. The TEC Register comprises projects that have secured a connection to the electricity transmission network, and inclusion on this register is a critical step in the process of connecting to the grid and becoming operational. Without a connection agreement, the feasibility of this site should be seriously questioned, as there is currently no requirement for it to connect to the [PLACE]. No grid connection route The proposed site is located approximately 5 kilometers from the [PLACE]. However, the planning application does not provide clarity on how the site will be connected to the grid. This ambiguity raises concerns about the potential need for the installation of 5 kilometers of overhead cabling in the future. Furthermore, there are currently no wayleave agreements in place with the surrounding landowners. Given the scale of this development, it is imperative that this issue is addressed as a fundamental consideration in the construction planning process. Cumulatively the total BESS sites in planning for the [PLACE] totals near 766MW. This particular application stands out as an outlier, both in terms of its distance from the substation and its proposal to locate the facility in a rural agricultural setting with limited existing infrastructure. Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) The EIA Screening Opinion Response issued by [ORGANIZATION] on July 8, 2024 (ref: [APPLICATION_CODE]), stated that an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) would not be necessary for the proposed development. However, considering the close proximity of the site to the Site of Special Scientific Interest ([PLACE]) [PLACE], I am deeply concerned that an EIA is not included in the planning application process. The lack of a comprehensive environmental assessment raises serious concerns regarding the potential negative impacts on the local ecosystem and biodiversity. The EIA Screening Opinion Response document highlights several points that must be taken into account in the planning application - Section 1 (b) - "There are not other consented Battery Energy Storage Systems in close proximity". There are currently another 5 sites, totalling over 766MW within 5km radius of the [PLACE]. These are approved/in construction and in pre application status. These applications should be considered as a cumulative due to the industrialised nature on the village of [PLACE], homesteads, and residential housing. Section 1 (c) - "There are no statutory designated sites for nature conservation of international importance ([PLACE], SPA, Ramsar) within a 15km buffer. [PLACE] which is a site of specific scientific interest ([PLACE]), is located 500 metres to the east of the proposed site. The area is designated for its basin fen habitat, which is one of the largest and least disturbed in northeast Scotland. Mitigation will be required to contain surface runoff through creation of attenuation features" Surface runoff must be contained via attenuation features, this should be suitable for any contaminates or spillages on site. This design requires approval that the burn south of the site is suitable for discharge. This should be agreed and have appropriate approval & licensing, currently this is listed as only a possible solution for developer and full design analysis has not taken place. Section 1 (f) - "In case of thermal runaway, the proposal will be designed in line with the BESS guidance from National Fire Chiefs Council. The proposal will incorporate 2 separate access points to the battery infrastructure and an access network capable of accommodating any vehicle without obstruction. Spacing of BESS containers will be approximately 6m subject to confirmation of final design. A sufficient water supply will also be provided within the proposed design." Only one access point to the site is provided, with road width of 4m. If access point is blocked from [PLACE] road, there is no secondary access point considered. Tree Felling In terms of the access, it requires the removal of eight to ten mature trees from a line of mainly beech trees located to the north of the [PLACE]. LCT 23 specifically references policy woodlands and shelter in the landscape appraisal notes. Part of the character of LCT 23 are the numerous groups/line of trees. The trees to the north of the [PLACE] therefore form part of the landscape fabric of this LCT. The proposed development will require a material break in the tree line and the loss of mature/semi-mature trees. This is a partial loss of landscape fabric and increases the local impact on landscape character. In most circumstances, if an Applicant were proposing to remove such trees for development it would have to be last resort and having considered all the alternatives. The choice of access has increased the adverse effects of this development and proposes to lead to a loss of landscape fabric. The photomontage from viewpoint 1 may not be an accurate depiction of the localised impact that this development will have on the landscape character at this location. The total quantity of trees to clear area for the access road or for site visibility cannot be determined from the document TREE_SURVEY-11556676. Tree 50 is shown in Appendix A to be retained however is listed in trees to be felled. These inconsistencies suggest that the planning application may not adequately consider the environmental impact of the proposed development, particularly in relation to tree preservation and biodiversity. It is alarming that important trees highlighted in the tree management report conflict with the high- level detail in the Appendix. This raises serious concerns about the potential loss due to administration errors and leave ambiguity to the total loss of felled trees along the [PLACE]. Landscape and Visual Impacts The landscape and visual impacts have been understated in the landscape appraisal. The choice of photomontage locations has not fully represented the receptors. The first point to note is that this is character references. All landscape character types reference farming. It is clear that this part of [PLACE] represents open countryside which is primarily characterised by farmland and some elements of woodland. Water Suds Drainage The Public Consultation Boards at event three ( Appendix X of PRE APPLICATION CONSULTATION REPORT-11556654) the site plan does not show any SuDS/attenuation pond. However within planning application, document SITE_PLAN-11586460 the outfall from SuDS pond is identified South of the site. The developers have designated this location as a suitable discharge point; however, the FLOOD_RISK_AND_DRAINAGE_STATEMENT-11556666 indicates that further investigation is required to determine if it can be utilized as an outfall. Consequently, there may be no established discharge rate or licensing agreements in place. It is essential that these agreements are finalised to ensure a controlled release that protects the existing local drainage system. Given the site's proximity to the [PLACE] [PLACE], it is crucial that these matters are resolved prior to granting planning consent to allow for thorough analysis. As a consultee SEPA have not reviewed this application as it falls below the threshold for site specific advice, this is concerning the outfall is not considered with respect to the affect it may have on local area & [PLACE]. Light Pollution Document - OUTLINE_BATTERY_SAFETY_MANAGEMENT_PLAN-11556653 "Sufficient lighting will also feature on the site; however, the lighting will be operated manually by staff on-site to limit light pollution in the area. Therefore, minimising the impact on the local ecosystem, residential properties and other stakeholders. In the event of a fault leading to an emergency, the lighting will be switched on automatically as part of the emergency protocols." - There is no information on the location and type of lighting installed on the site, it is mentioned within the construction documents as a temporary measure. This information is required to fully assess the risk of light pollution to the local residents to ensure it is kept to a minimum when in operation. Document - PLANNING_DESIGN_AND_ACCESS_STATEMENT-11556650 "No permanent security lighting is proposed as part of the Proposed Development, however there will be motion sensored / user operated lighting for personnel attending the specific onsite associated infrastructure." - I would like to raise a concern regarding the proposed lighting for the site. It is unclear where the lighting will be installed, and this aspect should be thoroughly considered during the application process to mitigate any potential disturbance to the nearby residential properties. Currently, the area experiences minimal light pollution, and it is essential to specify both the type and location of the proposed lighting to ensure that it does not adversely impact the surrounding community. Decommissioning Section 1 (c) of EIA screening document - "BESS schemes can be easily decommissioned and land restored to its previous use. This will be confirmed through a decommissioning strategy." No decommissioning strategy is included within the planning application for review and appraisal by [ORGANIZATION]. All structures should be temporary for the 40 year life cycle however site images of DNO Control room show structure to be made of red brick material sitting on solid base. No information is given on the material of the base; are foundations required for this structure? Customer switch room also appears to be sitting on grey foundation block with no details of material. Use of materials such as concrete should be minimal and avoided. To remove ambiguity this material should be listed within the application as a consideration to how it will be decommissioned and returned to original condition after 40 years. During consultations, no foundations were shown in planned views of the site. Conclusion On balance, the current application is incomplete, insufficiently evidenced, and fails to demonstrate that adverse environmental and amenity effects can be avoided, reduced, or mitigated to an acceptable level. I therefore recommend that [ORGANIZATION] refuse the application in its current form. Any resubmission should be supported by a comprehensive, policy-compliant evidence base, including full cumulative environmental assessment, confirmed grid connection arrangements, detailed drainage and access design, and robust mitigation secured through enforceable planning conditions.

retrieved_examples.text: [PLACE], [PLACE] 12 August 2025 Dear Sirs, APPLICATION AT FAIRFIELD, INVERURIE [PLACE] [APPLICATION_CODE] INSTALLATION OF BATTERY ENERGY STORAGE SYSTEM (BESS) WITH AN INSTALLED CAPACITY OF [PLACE] AND ASSOCIATED INFRASTRUCTURE Key Issues Landscape and Visual Impacts The landscape and visual impacts have been understated in the landscape appraisal. The choice of photomontage locations has not fully represented the receptors. Photomontage 5 is not reflective of the visibility of the BESS development and associated access infrastructure from the north. The viewpoint is at an oblique angle. Another key point in relation to the images is that these have been produced at 90 degrees and therefore they tend to over play the wider context in which the viewpoint sits and that is reflective of the horizontal scale of the photomontages. In real life, the infrastructure will look larger and will not be seen in as broad a context. This is a matter that needs to be carefully evaluated in placing weight on the visualisations. It is important that any value judgements are made from using the material at the locations. Furthermore, in respect of viewpoint 1, it is anticipated that some of the trees shown in the photomontage may not be actually retained after the access arrangements have been implemented. There are a number of mature tree removals which are required to facilitate the access. Another key aspect in considering the landscape and visual impact is the impression given with the application papers is that in order to produce an impact that may be unacceptable, it would have to be a significant one in Environmental Impact Assessment terms. That is simply not the threshold which is applied in the context of planning. In particular, the vast majority of planning applications that are refused for landscape and visual reasons are not development which would give rise to significant environmental impact. That is an important consideration when it comes to applying policy. In terms of landscape character, the application sits within two landscape character types within [PLACE]. The start of the access and the [PLACE] is located within the LCT 23 which is the farmed basin. The battery element of the development sits just north of the boundary in LCT 19 which is the farmed rolling ridges and hills. It is this landscape character type in which the greatest visibility of the proposed development is to be found and in particular, this is to be found to the north. The landscape and visual appraisal also makes reference to landscape character LCT 32 which extends further north beyond LCT 19 and is the LCT 32, farmed and woodland river valleys. The first point to note is that this is character references. All landscape character types reference farming. It is clear that this part of [PLACE] represents open countryside which is primarily characterised by farmland and some elements of woodland. In terms of the access, it requires the removal of a significant number of mature trees from a line of mainly beech trees located to the north of the [PLACE]. LCT 23 specifically references policy woodlands and shelter in the landscape appraisal notes. Part of the character of LCT 23 are the numerous groups/line of trees. The trees to the north of the [PLACE] therefore form part of the landscape fabric of this LCT. The proposed development will require a material break in the tree line and the loss of mature/semi-mature trees. This is a partial loss of landscape fabric and increases the local impact on landscape character. In most circumstances, if an Applicant were proposing to remove such trees for development it would have to be last resort and having considered all the alternatives. The choice of access has increased the adverse effects of this development and proposes to lead to a loss of landscape fabric. The photomontage from viewpoint 1 is not an accurate depiction of the localised impact that this development will have on the landscape character at this location. The description of LCT 19 is of a rural agricultural landscape with rolling topography and hill slopes being characteristic. The location of the BESS development on lower ground immediately below sloping ground to the north means it will be overlooked from the higher ground. The loss of landscape character from views from the north will be particularly prominent. This reflects the fact that there will be a visible linear access road from the [PLACE] to the BESS. The BESS landscape treatment with bunds and planting will, by its very nature, inevitably look like an intrusion into the landscape. It is almost impossible to mitigate effects from looking down onto the development. The development is entirely alien to the LCT 19. The Planning Design and Access Statement summarises the development as approximately 22 BESS containers with the dimensions set out in paragraph 3.2. These dimensions are slightly larger than a standard container. How would a proposed storage depot for 22 containers be considered in landscape and visual terms? The simple answer to that question is that it would not be permitted. Furthermore, the decision to locate such a proposal in open agricultural land would be considered wholly unacceptable. There is no difference in looking at the BESS development in the same location. Even if you were choosing to locate such a development in this general vicinity, it would make far more sense to locate it closer to the [PLACE] where it would not be overlooked and the bunding would effectively potentially mitigate views into the development itself. This is important as at times when considering such matters, basic planning principles are not properly considered. Simply put, this is an inappropriate location for such a development. There is no existing infrastructure which it relates to. It is simply a location in open countryside. This does in fact contrast with many other of the BESS proposals which propose to access [PLACE]. Most of these are located in close proximity to existing electrical overhead and ground-based infrastructure. This is relevant when coming to consider the overall suitability of this site for this type of development. There is an inherent conflict in promoting this type of development in this location. In terms of the visual impact, it is understated in the appraisal and particularly the choice of viewpoints has been poor. There is no viewpoint due north of the proposed development. This would reveal the true impact that the development would have on the visual amenity to the north of the proposed development. In essence, this would disclose an obvious man-made track running southwards for a considerable length and thereafter culminating in an obvious artificial man-made structure with battery storage infrastructure visible. It is this type of viewpoint which would illustrate the true incongruous nature of the development location. It is simply not understood why viewpoint 5 has been selected when, in terms of the ZTV heat map with Screening Effect of Woodland (figure3), the full development is not visible. Why was a location with a "deeper red to the north" not shown. Policy Analysis The key policies relative to the Application Before going on to consider the policy matters, it is perhaps important to also set out the cumulative context to this Application. The [PLACE] area has seen considerable development pressure. Planning Application [APPLICATION_CODE] for the installation of a BESS of [PLACE] has been granted Planning Permission. It is understood that amendments to this Planning Permission have been sought and a new submission is currently under consideration under Application Ref: [APPLICATION_CODE]. Furthermore, a Planning Application for a further BESS scheme of [PLACE] under reference [APPLICATION_CODE] is now under construction and a further Application was granted for a BESS under reference [APPLICATION_CODE]. In addition, a further Section 36 Application for a BESS of 500MW has been submitted to the Energy Consents Unit, described as "land west of [PLACE]". These sites are located in much closer proximity to the sub-station. These developments are all located in closer proximity to the sub-station and that reflects the nature and character of existing infrastructure in and around the sub-station. This includes the sub-station itself and substantive overhead electrical infrastructure as well. This reflects that this Application is an outlier both in terms of its distance to the sub-station, but also in terms of its proposal to locate it in a rural agricultural setting with more limited infrastructure context. NPF4 Policy 1 - in terms of NPF4, key policies that are potentially applicable in the context of a BESS scheme in broad terms are policies 1, 2 and 11. In terms of Policy 1, there is general support responding to the climate and nature crisis. One of the ways of responding is through energy infrastructure associated with Policy 11. However, to claim strong support for Policy 1, the Applicant would have to be able to demonstrate how this particular development contributes to the reduction in greenhouse gas emissions. The development does not exceed 50MW and is therefore not national development. It is therefore major development. In terms of NPF4, this does not have in-principle support. Policy 2 - Policy 2 deals with climate mitigation and adaption. In terms of climate mitigation, developers are required to assess the carbon contributions that the proposed development would give rise to. Policy 2 has recently been supported by further guidance issued by the Scottish Government in relation to its application. It is suggested that, on any reading, the onus is on the Applicant to set out an assessment of greenhouse gas emissions. It is clear from the guidance that this applies to all forms of development and also includes, for example, renewable energy development. If there were existing methodologies for demonstrating the issue, then they should be used. Alternatively, it is recommended that general methodologies be applied. The Applicant has not included this information and, as a consequence, the Application cannot be said to be in accordance with Policy 2. Policy 2 stated in the following terms: "Development proposals will be sited and designed to minimise lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions as far as possible". In the context of battery storage schemes, proximity to the sub-station will be a measure of this. The longer the distance from the sub-station, the greater the losses of electricity through the cables. This policy therefore strongly supports a location in as close a proximity to the sub-station as possible. In addition, it would also seek to minimise other infrastructure such as the extent and length of access road and the need to carry out earth works such as bunding. There is no evidence that the Applicant has not had regard to Policy 2 in formulating the relevant proposals. Policy 11 - general policy Energy Policy 11 is also clearly relevant to the consideration of a battery scheme. The policy provides general support for a range of technologies which also includes battery storage. Sub-paragraph (e) provides a range of topic matters that have to be considered. Finally, in terms of the overall decision making, significant weight is to attach to the contribution that the development will make either to renewable energy generation targets, or greenhouse gas emission reduction targets. The development is not renewable energy generation and therefore the only weight that can be in support of a BESS scheme is the greenhouse gas emissions reductions. At no point has the Applicant sought to quantify these and therefore no weight can be attributed in the balance to that. In addition, in terms of the design of the scheme, sub-paragraph (e) identifies that there are a range of factors that parties should take into account in formulating such projects and, in particular, project design and mitigation have to demonstrate how impacts are addressed. In terms of sub-paragraph (2), it is considered that this Application has not adopted an appropriate design. The choice of access location through a tree line is wholly inappropriate and should not have occurred. Furthermore, the choice of location which is a design consideration. It should not have selected a site in the open rural countryside which has no equivalent infrastructure in place already. Furthermore, the impact on trees also specifically has to be considered in the context of the Application. Policy 6 - the loss of trees is addressed in NPF4 by Policy 6. Sub-paragraph 3 of Policy 6 states that adverse impacts on individual trees of higher biodiversity value would not be supported unless appropriate mitigation measures are identified. In the context of the current Application, there can be no mitigation for the removal of the trees to the north of the [PLACE] because they are required to facilitate the access and also maintain the visibility for the access. Against that background, it is clear that the current design, as promoted by the Applicant, is not consistent with the policy outcomes anticipated by Policy 6. In particular, the existing trees are not being protected and this design choice is contrary to policy. [PLACE] Local Development Plan In addition to NPF4, the [PLACE] Local Development Plan also incorporates policies which are relevant. In terms of Policy P1, the LDP promotes high quality places and recognises the importance of good design. The choices made by the Applicant in respect of the design of this Application do not accord with those principles and, in particular, the access arrangements run entirely contrary to the concept of good design and would be contrary to Policy P1. In terms of Policy E1 on natural heritage, the removal of the trees associated with the access do not accord with policy. In particular it will fragment habitats and have adverse impacts upon the site's environmental quality. In terms of Policy E2 on landscape, the access arrangements are clearly contrary to the thrust of the objectives. In particular, the trees will be lost are part of the landscape fabric. It was the choice of the Applicant to select an access through these trees and the loss would have an adverse impact on landscape fabric. It therefore could not be said that the development in terms of the location, scale and design is of a high standard. Policy E3 - forestry woodland - the woodland loss is not consistent with the aims and objectives of the policy. Higher quality trees would be lost to the access. Providing planting around the BESS does not compensate for this loss of landscape fabric, nor the quality of the existing trees. RD1 - Policy RD1 states that the Councill will only allow development "if it is located and designed to take advantage of, or incorporate the services, facilities and infrastructure necessary to support it". Such matters may include "sustainable transport linkages and supporting infrastructure, facilities for alternatively field vehicles, road access, waste management provision or to supply waste water connections and treatment and other elements as may be appropriate in the circumstances". In the context of this BESS, it is not well located relative to the sub-station. It is critical infrastructure to which it requires to connect into. The alternative Applications which have come forward are far better located and would not require such extensive connection works. Policy C2 - Policy C2 provides the relevant policy in relation to battery storage. It supports developments which are "in appropriate sites and of appropriate design". As identified in the above, it is submitted that this Application Site is wrong in that it is in open rural countryside and, in addition, the design is wholly inappropriate in that the access has chosen to go through a mature line of trees which form part of the landscape fabric of the area. It then lists the range of factors which can be taken into account. This includes the adverse environmental ones and also the positive ones regarding greenhouse gas emissions. As stated above, the Applicant has not set out in any meaningful way how the Application proposals will contribute. Finally - Is there really a need for this development? The Applicant's justification for the project is contained in paragraph 2.2.2 of the Planning Design & Access Statement. This just states that the Applicant has studied the information provided by DNOs for this type of project. [PLACE] is one of these locations, therefore suggesting demand for the proposed development. That is the only site-specific policy that is referenced. The Planning Design & Access Statement goes on to analyse general policy support in Section 5 and references in support the Clean Power 2030 Action Plan at paragraph 5.4.9. It references positive comments about the general need for storage across the whole of the UK. What the Applicant fails to do is to point out that within the Action Plan the requirement for battery storage is not a general one and is one which is tied to grid location. In terms of the 2030 Action Plan, it was also accompanied by a connections reform annex "which has been updated". This provides estimates of generation required for particular technologies. The Applicant quotes from the general figures but does not drill into the subsequent information which gives information on breakdowns of technologies required by 2030. This Application is a distribution connected scale of development. This identifies that for 2030 across the whole of the distribution networks of [ORGANIZATION] and Scottish Hydro Electric Power Distribution (SHEPD) some 900MW is required. [PLACE] alone has received connection requests for over 700MW to date. [ORGANIZATION] and SHEPD have received applications for over 8GW in total so there is only a demand for around 10% of applications. Only the most suitable sites should be selected. [PLACE] is certainly not in this category as the points raised in this letter demonstrate. I earnestly request that this planning application is refused. [PERSON]

I am writing to formally raise objections to the Section 36 planning application put forward by [ORGANIZATION] ([ORGANIZATION]) for the proposed Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) development situated to the north of [PLACE], near [PLACE]. The project aims to establish a 100 MW lithium-ion battery facility on currently unused agricultural land, along with associated transformers, fencing, lighting, fire infrastructure, and drainage. My objection is centred on the significant risks that the development presents to public safety, the local environment, and community welfare. These risks encompass fire and contamination hazards, potential harm to biodiversity, degradation of the landscape, disruption to traffic flow, and inadequate emergency preparedness. The planning documentation provided by the developer lacks the necessary technical specifications, safety measures, and compliance with policies essential for the responsible implementation of an energy project of this magnitude. Each part of this objection articulates specific reasons why the application falls short of meeting the criteria outlined in the National Planning Framework 4 (NPF4) and the [PLACE] Local Development Plan. These reasons include deficiencies in consultation, the absence of ecological protections, a lack of assessment of cumulative impacts, and a failure to address the entire lifecycle of hazardous infrastructure. I strongly recommend that the planning authority rejects this application in its entirety. Environmental and Ecological Impact The development site is located in a rural farmland area surrounded by hedgerows, marshy grassland, and drainage features that provide support to wildlife and contribute to the local ecological network. It is in close proximity to the [PLACE] and encompasses habitats recognised for their biodiversity value, including waterlogged ground and species-rich grass margins. However, the ecological assessments that have been submitted are incomplete and crucial seasonal survey data has been omitted. Key assessments such as bat roost evaluations, dusk or dawn emergence surveys, monitoring of badger activity, and studies on amphibians have not been carried out during the appropriate seasons. These assessments are standard requirements under the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 and the Nature Conservation (Scotland) Act 2004 when potential habitats are impacted by development. The absence of this data means that the developer cannot accurately claim to comprehend or address the ecological risks associated with the proposal. The site is set to be significantly covered with containerised battery units, impermeable roads, fencing, firewater tanks, and related infrastructure, leading to the permanent loss of semi-natural grassland and the fragmentation of hedgerow corridors. This will eliminate foraging and commuting paths for protected species like bats and birds. While the planting of replacement hedgerows is presented as a biodiversity enhancement, no Biodiversity Net Gain (BNG) calculation has been provided, and there is no proposed habitat management or monitoring plan. According to National Planning Framework 4 Policy 3, developments must enhance biodiversity and prevent harm to existing natural assets. [PLACE] Local Development Plan Policy PV7 mandates the protection and mitigation of priority habitats and species. Unfortunately, this proposal fails to meet either standard. The lack of comprehensive survey work, habitat destruction, and inadequate mitigation measures render it environmentally unsound. There is a risk of long-term ecological deterioration in an area that supports farmland species and local biodiversity. Cumulative Impact The [PLACE] area has emerged as a significant hub for energy infrastructure projects, encompassing large substations, overhead transmission lines, solar developments, and various proposals for Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS). The addition of a 17-acre BESS to the existing cluster of industrial energy assets is expected to intensify the physical, environmental, and psychological pressures on the local community. Despite the presence of other approved or pending developments within a 1 km radius, the current application lacks a cumulative impact assessment. There is no consideration given to how the simultaneous construction, noise emissions, lighting, fire risk, and traffic volumes from multiple projects will be managed. This fragmented approach to development neglects to address the overall impact of infrastructure saturation on the land, wildlife, and residents of [PLACE]. Concerned residents have highlighted issues regarding the industrialisation of the area and the combined effects of these proposals on mental well-being, safety, and environmental standards. It is imperative for the planning authority to evaluate not only the repercussions of this individual development but also its contribution to a broader trend of encroachment and disruption. Policy 29 of the National Planning Framework 4 stipulates the necessity of considering cumulative effects in decision-making processes. The absence of such an assessment represents a significant oversight. Approving this development without a comprehensive overview would further exacerbate the disproportionate and unsustainable strain on this rural community. Increased Traffic and Infrastructure Strain The construction of the Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) would entail almost 900 Heavy Goods Vehicle (HGV) movements over a 12-month period, with peak daily traffic reaching up to 1 large vehicles. These vehicles will navigate narrow rural roads not originally intended for heavy industrial traffic, such as [PLACE] and the surrounding local road network, which are currently shared by [PLACE] transport, agricultural vehicles, cyclists, and pedestrians. Despite the presence of multiple other energy projects proposed or already in progress in the vicinity, there has been no comprehensive assessment of the cumulative traffic impact. The planning application lacks any proposed mitigation measures, such as road reinforcement, visibility enhancements, or traffic diversion plans. Additionally, there is no specified construction delivery schedule to avoid peak traffic hours, and no road safety assessment has been provided. The proposed BESS construction also poses a threat to [PLACE], a popular walking and cycling route that passes near the site. The establishment of the construction compound and access roads is anticipated to cause disruption, visual obstructions, and potential safety risks for path users. No temporary diversion or strategy to safeguard the path has been outlined. According to NPF4 Policy 13, infrastructure should be designed to minimise impacts on local networks and ensure safety for all users, a criterion that this application fails to meet. Without adequate transport planning, this development could lead to road deterioration, heightened collision risks, and prolonged disruption to the community and local access rights. Community Wellbeing, Mental Health, and EMF Concerns The proposed development in the vicinity of [PLACE] raises significant concerns beyond physical risks and environmental impacts, particularly regarding community wellbeing and mental health. The area is already facing pressure from various energy projects, and the introduction of another large-scale, high-risk facility is causing considerable stress and anxiety among residents. Concerns about potential battery fires, pollution, explosions, and toxic smoke are not merely hypothetical, as similar risks have been observed at comparable sites globally. Local residents have voiced worries about the psychological impact of residing near such infrastructure, especially when it is inadequately understood and regulated. The sense of being surrounded by hazardous industrial developments can lead to enduring fear, disrupted sleep patterns, and diminished trust in public decision-making processes. The absence of a Health Impact Assessment accompanying the application is troubling. There is a failure to acknowledge the psychological strain that prolonged proximity to a high-risk site can impose, particularly in rural areas where quality of life hinges on peace, safety, and environmental stability. This oversight is particularly concerning for families, elderly residents, and individuals already grappling with mental health conditions. Furthermore, concerns have been raised about potential exposure to electromagnetic fields (EMFs) emanating from the site's electrical infrastructure, such as transformers and underground cabling. While EMF levels may comply with accepted thresholds, the lack of transparent monitoring or public information contributes to local unease. Perceived risk can be as detrimental to wellbeing as physical exposure, especially when residents feel excluded from the planning process. National Planning Framework 4 Policy 23 mandates that developments safeguard health, wellbeing, and safety, encompassing mental health and quality of life, not solely physical risk. The absence of any wellbeing assessment or mitigation strategy further highlights the applicant's disregard for the local population. Summary The application is fundamentally flawed as it does not address or mitigate the serious risks linked to large-scale lithium-ion battery storage. The planning documents lack essential information concerning fire safety, pollution control, waste management, biodiversity, and community health. The consultation process was insufficient, and the proposal does not adhere to the standards set out in National Planning Framework 4 or the [PLACE] Local Development Plan. If approved, this development would industrialise a rural landscape, compromise local wellbeing, strain emergency services, and create lasting environmental issues. It does not exemplify responsible energy infrastructure and does not serve the public interest. Therefore, it should be rejected.

Formal Objection to Planning Application [APPLICATION_CODE] - [PLACE] Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) To: [ORGANIZATION] From: [PERSON] Address: [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE] Date: 22/04/2025 Subject: Objection to the Siting and Scale of the Proposed Battery Energy Storage System at [PLACE], [PLACE] ([APPLICATION_CODE]) I wish to formally object to the proposed installation of a [PLACE] Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) at [PLACE], [PLACE]. This objection is based on the proposal's scale, siting, safety risks, landscape and ecological impacts, and serious procedural and factual gaps across the application. It is submitted in line with the planning framework and public interest obligations of National Planning Framework 4 (NPF4). 1. Scale Expansion Without Re-Consultation The number of battery containers has increased from 10 (as stated during public consultation) to 22, as confirmed in application documents. This more than doubles the scale of the proposed infrastructure without updated consultation, environmental assessment, or noise and visual impact reassessment. 2. Green Belt and Landscape Character Harm The proposed site lies within the Green Belt and the Coastal Agricultural Plain (LCT 17). The area is characterised by openness, tranquility, and visual coherence. All homes in [PLACE] are single or 1.5-storey, making them more sensitive to visual intrusion. The Landscape and Visual Appraisal admits theoretical visibility from the [PLACE] - contradicting earlier claims that the development would be fully screened. Previous developments in this are were refused on the basis of impact to landscape setting important to the maintain the integrity of the landscape setting between [PLACE] and the shire. This is in clear conflict with NPF4 Policy 4 (Natural Places) and Policy 8 (Green Belt). 3. Flood Risk Contradictions The Flood Risk and Drainage Statement claims the site is outside designated flood zones. However, SEPA maps clearly show both surface water and fluvial flood risk within 25 metres of the site boundary. No buffer analysis or exceedance modelling is provided. This contradicts the requirements of NPF4 Policy 22 (Flood Risk and Water Management). Additionally, the proposal involves significant land levelling, infrastructure foundations, and trenching for underground cabling. The site is within Carbon and Peatland Class 4 - indicating the potential presence of carbon-rich or ecologically sensitive soils. The development does not adequately assess the impact on soil stability, structure, or long-term degradation, nor does it propose mitigation. This represents a further breach of NPF4 Policy 5 (Soils), which seeks to minimise disturbance and protect Scotland's valuable soil resources. The Flood Risk and Drainage Statement claims the site is outside designated flood zones. However, SEPA maps clearly show both surface water and fluvial flood risk within 25 metres of the site boundary. No buffer analysis or exceedance modelling is provided. This contradicts the requirements of NPF4 Policy 22 (Flood Risk and Water Management). 4. Ecological Oversights: Red Squirrels and Bats Red squirrels are known to use the development site as a movement corridor between nearby woodlands. Bats are also active in the area. Despite this: - No bat activity surveys were conducted. - No mitigation for red squirrel connectivity is included in the CEMP. - Does not consider any potential impacts to nearby burns in the area. - Not clear if impacts to protecting the area of woodland have been clearly understood in terms of proximity and root protection. These omissions contradict NPF4 Policy 3 (Biodiversity) and Policy 4 (Natural Places) and protecting woodland. 5. Transport Network Misrepresentation The BESS connects onto a stretch of [PLACE] that is not a quiet rural road. It is a heavily used route with multiple nearby junctions, none of which are assessed in the Transport Statement. Further: - There is a quarry to the northeast of [PLACE], raising the likelihood of additional HGV traffic through unsuitable routes. - Local roads include single-track stretches and are not designed for increased HGV traffic. - This is an area of repeated accidents which do not appear to have been addressed in the roads officer's response despite being identified in the transport appraisal by the developer. This undermines the conclusions of the Construction Traffic Management Plan. 6. Community and Child Safety Risks The Outline Battery Safety Management Plan does not address: - Emergency planning for nearby homes (especially those with children); - Risks from toxic gas release (e.g. hydrogen fluoride); - Fire response and light/noise stress during an emergency; There is no defined evacuation plan or coordination strategy for affected residents, in breach of NPF4 Policy 1 (community wellbeing). 7. Underground Cabling - Confirmed, But Needs Conditioning Underground cabling is mentioned in application documents for both internal connections and the grid export route. However: - The grid route is not mapped; - There is no assessment of flood zones, community land, or habitat impacts along the route. This commitment should be secured as a planning condition if fully understood to have no negative impact. 8. Cumulative Impact: Adjacent Quarry Proposal ([APPLICATION_CODE]) The same landowners have submitted a parallel planning enquiry for sand and gravel extraction immediately adjacent to the BESS site. This introduces unassessed risks: - Cumulative traffic impacts from quarry and BESS construction HGVs; - Worsened landscape and visual intrusion beyond what was assessed in the LVA; - Ecological fragmentation of woodland corridors used by protected species. There is no cumulative impact assessment, despite the potential for both projects to proceed concurrently. 9. Operational Incompatibility: Excavation Next to BESS Excavation and battery storage are incompatible adjacent land uses in a community setting. Risks include: - Ground vibration affecting battery integrity and control systems; - Disruption to fire suppression and monitoring infrastructure; - Dust contamination and altered drainage stability; - Increased likelihood of thermal runaway, equipment failure, or hazardous emissions. None of these risks are assessed in the safety documentation, breaching NPF4 Policy 11 (resilient energy infrastructure). 10. Regulatory Threshold Concerns: [PLACE] Limit This proposal is deliberately set at [PLACE] - just below the 50MW threshold that would trigger enhanced regulatory scrutiny under the Electricity Act and National Infrastructure planning regime. Given the scale of infrastructure (22 battery containers and 11 inverters), it is not clear how the operators will ensure the site remains permanently under this threshold. Each battery container model referenced in the documents (e.g. Sungrow PowerTitan 2.0) is capable of delivering between 1.5MW and 2.5MW of power. With 22 containers and 11 inverters, it is technically feasible for the installation to exceed 50MW if not deliberately limited. The application does not provide sufficient technical detail or verifiable mechanisms (such as fixed output capping or regulator oversight) to demonstrate long-term compliance with the sub-50MW capacity claim. This raises concerns of future expansion, cumulative risk, and a potential attempt to avoid more robust oversight. Given the sensitive setting - including residential proximity, flood zones, and ecological corridors - the proposal should be subject to higher regulatory scrutiny regardless of nominal capacity, and any permission granted should include strict monitoring and output enforcement conditions. Requested Actions Given the above, I respectfully request that this application be refused.

[PERSON] [PLACE] [EMAIL] [PHONE] 08.02.2025 [APPLICATION_CODE] Installation of Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) with installed capacity of [PLACE] and Associated Infrastructure. I am writing to object to the planning application submitted for the Installation of Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) with installed capacity of [PLACE] and Asociated Infrastructure to land north east of the [PLACE]. The proposed project poses a risk of irreversibly changing the character of the area while also placing unjustifiable burdens on the community. This objection articulates why the application should be declined, drawing upon its inconsistencies with planning regulations, environmental standards, and community welfare. 1: Loss of Landscape Character and Visual Amenity: The proposed BESS presents a significant encroachment upon the landscape of the area of [PLACE], known for its expanses of farmland. The industrial aesthetic of this development is poised to dominate the surrounding setting, resulting in irreversible harm to its visual charm. Noteworthy aspects regarding the visual impact encompass: - Prominence on the Horizon: The BESS's visual presence will be pronounced from houses nearby and from the busy road. The proposed alleviation strategies like tree plantations and bundling fall short in adequately concealing the development. The inadequacies in the proposed screening measures serve to compound apprehensions, as they neglect to comprehensively mitigate the extent of the visual encroachment. The proposed bund is 3m high to the front and only 1m high at the side. As the field is at an angle then the 1m high bund will not screen the facility from people travelling east on the road or from houses at [PLACE] or [PLACE] as the field cuts in front of the house and so It should therefore be at least 3m on both sides. There is no evidence that any brownfield sites have been looked into. - Accumulative Visual Impact: The BESS, will give rise to an industrialised environment that starkly contrasts with the rural surroundings. 2: Significant Noise Pollution for Local Residents The operation and construction of the BESS are expected to generate significant noise levels, thereby disrupting the peace and tranquillity of the rural area. Specific concerns to the projected noise disturbances are as follows: - Operational Noise: The transformers and cooling systems of the BESS are anticipated to emit continuous background noise, which will be most noticeable during the quieter periods of the day and night. - Construction Noise: The construction phase is expected to involve the use of heavy machinery, excavation activities, and increased vehicle traffic, all of which will contribute to temporary yet considerable noise pollution. - Proximity to Residences: The proximity of several residential properties to the proposed site implies that the noise pollution will directly and materially impact the quality of life for these residents.
