As previously stated the bund needs to be at least 3m on both sides and not just the front to help with noise. Also as stated the noise levels will not be masked by the trees for a number of years until they grow to a good height to help mask noise - report states 15 years!!. This really is not a solution to the documented problems with noise that these batteries create. For the residents affected, the persistent noise pollution is perceived as a substantial deterioration of their living environment in the long term. 3: Facilitating Future Industrialisation by Setting Precedent The endorsement of the proposed BESS poses a substantial risk of establishing a hazardous precedent for heightened industrialisation of rural regions with subsequent developments likely to ensue upon approval of this application. - Erosion of Rural Identity: Sanctioning this project would convey the message that rural landscapes are dispensable in favour of industrial imperatives, establishing a concerning standard for other communities throughout Scotland. 4: Lack of consideration and mitigation against fire risk and the resulting contamination of local watercourses, land and ecosystems: - The dangers BESS present to both human health and the environment are known, there exists a serious risk of hazardous substance release, air pollution, pollution to a local water course, carbon rich roils, and other sensitive ecosystems. The proposed strategy for firewater runoff is noted as 'Full Containment' within the attenuation pond, however this mistakenly only considers [ORGANIZATION] guidance calling for 2 hours of water supply for initial firefighting intervention for defensive measures, to try and prevent fire spread to adjacent containers. [ORGANIZATION] guidance goes on to state that there is currently no way to extinguish a BESS fire, and that they can reignite hours after the initial event is believed to be extinguished. - Should even a single BESS container go on fire, they will require to be quenched for days, or simply left to burn out as witnessed during BESS fires recently in the UK and globally. The proposal suggests that local waste disposal companies would be employed to cope with the level of contaminated runoff in the event of a larger fire, as if such vehicles could even approach a lithium ion fire site considering the level of heat, toxicity and danger to life, makes a complete mockery of this strategy. The reality is, that in the event of a larger fire, contaminated runoff would inevitably flow into the local watercourse, poisoning the adjacent marshland and streams all the way down to the coast with devastating effect. - There exists a real danger of any fire to spread to adjacent forestry, woodland and hedgerows, with potential to escalate risking local properties and life. - [ORGANIZATION] states in their brochure that a Fire Risk Management Plan would be prepared in consultation with Regional Fire and Rescue Services but I see no evidence of this. 5. The application does not consider the full extents of the BESS through to grid connection, with excessively large site footprint: - This application is only for the BESS site, excluding the grid connection from roadside to the substation, raising the question as to how this further energy infrastructure will be routed, above or below ground and following what route. If it is now to be connected to the proposed Hurly substation at [PLACE] then this would be between 7 -11 miles away depending on the route. If it is to be connected to the existing small substation at [PLACE] then this is still about 2 miles away! - The site boundary 'Option Plan' under application is also excessively large considering the BESS footprint, leaving opportunity for the developer to push the BESS closer to local residence and / or apply for future extensions. 6. Road Safety and Construction Logistics - Raises significant safety and logistic concerns for local roads and the very busy [PLACE]. - From the south transporting materials will require the use of the central reservation which is too narrow to safely accommodate large vehicles. For vehicles approaching from the north, there is no slip road, creating high risk of accidents on an already hazardous turn as the lorries would need to come to a complete stop on the [PLACE] to take the turn off - Tight corners and the narrow busy single track road off the [PLACE] are unsuitable for heavy goods vehicles. - 20 vans and 1 HGV travelling on that road every day for around 6 months until construction ends is a lot of extra traffic on an already busy single track road with no dedicated passing places, 7. The proposed development will have a damaging impact on the landscape, character of the area and community, especially considering the cumulative impact of all other power generating facilities in the Community area: This proposed BESS site, is situated on a quiet greenfield site, on rural farmland that is encircled by residential properties and is placed at a significant distance from the substation which would result in roads being dug up for miles. On the other hand 2 x BESS have already been approved at the [PLACE] Site: [APPLICATION_CODE] (NW of West Bendings) approved 29/06.23 and [APPLICATION_CODE] ([PLACE]) approved 19/09/23 and a further 2 storage facilities being subject of proposal of applications notice: [APPLICATION_CODE] and [APPLICATION_CODE] also very close to the [PLACE]. In these cases it makes sense to have them here as they are close to the [PLACE] so very easy to connect without digging up field and roads and there is only one house close by at [PLACE], the home owner has a financial interest in the BESS and therefore he is reaping the financial rewards but not inflicting noise, visual impact, stress and worry about potential fires giving off toxic fumes and impacting on their everyday lives on anybody else. There is also one already approved Northwest of [PLACE], [PLACE] ([APPLICATION_CODE]. A further BESS in the area should therefore not be considered as essential infrastructure within this area. If this should go ahead it will set a precedent for individuals, who do not live in an area, to buy up land and offer to the energy companies for financial gain with no thought to the changes in the rural landscape or the people they are inflicting this on. There is no evidence of a site suitability assessment against alternative sites in the area to demonstrate why such greenfield land development is justified, especially considering potential for brownfield development in this area. According to the Department for Energy Security & Net Zero database at end of October 2024, there are already 304 energy storage applications under construction or in the planning system, totalling approximately 21GW excluding those co-located with renewable energy generation; approximately Three (3) times the 2045 target. Within the [PLACE] catchment area and including the CKD community, there is currently 102MW of intermittent renewable energy generation online or awaiting construction, that could benefit from energy storage backup. Within the same area code, there is currently 130MW of BESS approved and awaiting construction; that leaves 28MW of excess energy storage capacity already due to come online. This local overcapacity (combined with national capacity well on the way to far exceed 2045 targets), demonstrates that no further BESS sites are necessary and should not be considered as 'essential infrastructure' within this area - The proposed development will be visually imposing and will cause constant noise pollution during construction and the lifetime of the BESS; bringing detrimental social impact for the community and risking impact on local protected wildlife species. - From an economic standpoint, the development offers minimal benefits to the local community. The short-term nature of construction jobs, coupled with potential losses in agricultural land, underscore the disproportionate burden imposed on the local area. ¿ In terms of policy compliance, the application deviates from [ORGANIZATION] Local Development Plan and does not align with the principles of the National Planning Framework 4 (NPF4). It prioritises industrial expansion over sustainability, community well-being, and environmental conservation. These shortcomings are exacerbated by a lack of robust mitigation measures, casting doubt on the project's ability to operate without causing lasting harm. This BESS project establishes a risky precedent for rural industrialisation, jeopardising not only this area but also other rural communities in Scotland. Approving this development would suggest that community needs and rights can be overlooked in favour of industrial ventures, contrary to the principles of a Just Transition and equitable energy development. The approval of this application would set a precedent, that will result in BESS applications being installed throughout this area, regardless of site suitability and the negative impact they have on the community. 9. Selecting the Site The process of selecting the substation site has been marred by fundamental flaws, including a lack of transparency and a failure to consider alternative locations that could mitigate environmental and social impacts. [ORGANIZATION] states that "proximity to grid connection sites are chosen near substations for easy grid connectivity with minimal environmental disruption" and " use of brownfield or previously developed land is the preference to minimise the impact on undeveloped or agricultural land". I feel they have not followed their own ethos in this case as do not seem to have considered other suitable land. 10. Flood Prone Risk - The application site is situated on flood prone ground, demonstrated by SEPA as having High Likelihood (10%) of annual surface flooding, with severe flooding and run off from this site being evidenced and recorded with the past two years alone; The developer dismisses this flood risk along with accuracy of SEPA data, their proposal could increase flood vulnerability in this area, and alternative lower risk locations have not been considered. Flooding run off goes into the local watercourse as well as neighbouring marshland with underlying carbon rich peat bog, then onwards to [PLACE] and [PLACE]; this is important to note when considering pollution risks. - National and local Planning Policies do not permit development in flood risk areas, unless this is for Essential Infrastructure where location is required for Operational Reasons. Protected Species The NESBREC Report confirms Common Toad, Pine Martens, Water Vole, Brambling and Barn Owls in very close proximity to the site. The loss of agricultural land is particularly troubling, as it signifies a permanent reduction in the region's capacity to support sustainable agriculture and food production. Key issues like visual impact, noise pollution, traffic disruptions, and safety risks during construction and operation remain insufficiently resolved, leaving residents exposed to significant and prolonged disturbances. I strongly urge [ORGANIZATION] to reject this proposal outright. I am writing to object the Installation of Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) at land to North East of [PLACE], [APPLICATION_CODE]. Firstly, my objection in general terms is the further industrialisation of rural areas and the impact on an agricultural area that already has significant Energy infrastructure. Currently it is not possible to look in any direction from this area without seeing excessive amounts of windmills and pylons (both at land and at Sea). By approving this BESS within this area it will present a further huge impact on our natural countryside, wildlife, and prime agricultural land. If approved it will be adding more industrial infrastructure to an already industrially congested rural area and potentially setting precedence for even more future industrial development of a rural setting. This is wholly unacceptable to anyone who values our countryside and the well-being of its residents and inhabitants. Below I lay out more pointed reasons that I object this development. Each of these objections has merit individually and collectively. NON-ESSENTIAL INFASTRUCTURE We are already 3x above the 2045 target for net zero in the area so this is not a required facility. Within the [PLACE] catchment area there is currently 102MW of intermittent renewable energy generation online or awaiting construction, that could benefit from energy storage backup. Within the same area code, there is currently 130MW of BESS approved and awaiting construction; that leaves 28MW of excess energy storage capacity already due to come online. This local overcapacity (combined with national capacity well on the way to far exceed 2045 targets), demonstrates that no further BESS sites are necessary and should not be considered as 'essential infrastructure' within this area. As non-essential infrastructure, building this BESS will in fact be in conflict with any Green Agenda or Policy as we will be destroying natural land and expending resource and creating pollution on a scheme that provides Zero benefit due to overcapacity in supply. The environmental impact of manufacturing all items that would be installed at this site must be considered along with the destruction of agricultural land. Also, the civil engineering work utilising plant and equipment, transportation, construction of access roads, installation of foundations, and all building activities associated with the placement of these units which is not required. Where this BESS would connect to the grid, and the distance between this site and the grid connection, also has to be considered in the context of Non-Essential Infrastructure (See INADEQUATE LOCATION below) FLOOD CONCERNS The land is in a flood prone area as advised by SEPA. It has a high likelihood (10%) of annual surface flooding. Severe flooding and run off can regularly be witnessed in the area of the proposed BESS (as anyone who uses this road can confirm). The run off from [PLACE] and its natural reservoirs is significant, especially after periods of sustained rain, significant down pours, or during winter when the ground is frozen and impermeable. It is generally understood and accepted that these conditions will only get worse due to climate change and predicted weather patterns - so we can anticipate that flooding will be worse than historically experienced. When flooding does happen then any contamination will leak into the [PLACE] which will damage our wildlife, pollute the water and cause significant negative effects. Further consideration should also be made of the nearby area that these waters discharge into the sea: [PLACE] is an [ORGANIZATION] [PLACE] and any potential contamination could have a significant detrimental effect on the birdlife. Thermal runaway is a major health risk for our local community and wildlife. Current policies do not permit development in flood risk areas unless for essential infastructure. As previously noted, this is not essential due to the overcapacity of BESS. However, taking this out of the equation, there has been no valid points raised as to why this location is the most appropriate for linking to a substation that is miles away, taking up prime agricultural land, invading an area thriving with wildlife and surrounded by residential properties. There is also no clarity provided for this development on how this BESS would be connected to the substation - several miles of ditches and cabling adding to the Net Positive impact of a site that simply is not required? There are two main areas relating to my flood concerns. The first is natural flooding (which already occurs on a regular basis), and the second is flooding in a fire scenario where, as has been experienced elsewhere, substantial amounts of water have to be used over extended periods of time to control battery fires. INADEQUATE LOCATION It is understood the location of this application is a considerable distance from the substation that it is being connected to. Although nothing in the application states where this is actually being connected to? Therefore, a report should be commissioned into where this is being connected to and how they propose to do this without causing unjustifiable disruption and damage. At the initial consultation it was advised that it is due to be connected to [PLACE] and this location was carefully considered due to the close proximity to [PLACE]. The location of [PLACE] substation, which is now the presumed substation due to initial plans with [PLACE] not going ahead, is between 7.4 miles and 11 miles away depending on the route they take. Therefore, requiring major disruption to our local community during the digging to allow the cables to be placed in the ground. This road is a [PLACE] bus route and if closed is going to impact our children getting to [PLACE], along with locals getting to work and going about their daily routine. This route would need to cross the [PLACE] and would cause significant disruption to place significant quantities of cabling all this way along single track roads. It is hard to justify that this scheme and location has any logical or reasonable benefit in reaching net zero. Common sense determines that if this development is absolutely necessary, then a location near the substation is the right thing to avoid disruption to roads, noise pollution from diggers, air pollution and emissions from construction plant running in excess due to the distance required to be dug up, disruption to countryside digging up verges and therefore disturbing wildlife which may inhabit these areas. There is simply no logic that can reasonably support this as a reasonable chosen location for a BESS. I would request that a report is commissioned into why this is even considered an appropriate location, and seek clarity on the connection point to the grid which appears to be a substantial distance away? ACCESS ROAD CONCERNS Another major concern is that having the stated 21 vehicles and one HGV per day accessing the site on multiple occasions for an extended duration. Plus the cranes etc that will inevitably be involved with construction activity and loading and offloading of battery and associated units. The road is already in very poor condition (probably due to the flooding mentioned above). It has significant pot holes which get very deep very quickly due to wash out. What measures would be taken to ensure the condition of this road is not worsened by the increased volume of traffic during construction, and what will be done to ensure the road is returned to its current condition (or better) after construction There is no slip off from the [PLACE] to turn onto the single carriageway road and this is extremely dangerous for a car, having more and larger vehicles turning off is definitely going to increase the risk of a road traffic accident HGV type vehicles will need to come to an almost complete stop on the duel carriageway before turning off due to the tightness of the turn off. Knowing the behaviours of drivers on this fast stretch of road will most definitely cause accidents. Equally heading North and turning onto the [PLACE], the middle area at the intersection, that does not even fit a car comfortably, will be so dangerous for a HGV. Heading South will be HGVs turning into a Major Road without the benefit of any slip road to gain speed. CLOSE PROXIMITY TO HOMES & NATURAL RESOURCE This proposed area is encircled by properties who will all be directly impacted by the building of this BESS. The noise and light pollution emitted from it will be significant due to how open this area is. If it was to go on fire this would be a major concern for loss of property, loss of woodland, loss of protected wildlife, and health complications. Situated right next to woodland which is currently being replanted, and being in such a windy spot, this could get out of control very quickly. Recent fires of battery storage have proven that they will burn for days. The toxic chemicals leaked from this are a massive health concern for nearby residents and wildlife and these concerns also need to be considered as part of the Planning consideration. FIRE RISK As well established by media reports BESS carry significant risk of substantial fire. The fumes from a thermal runaway can be fatal to anyone present, including first responders. Via the Media we are also advised that such fires burn for at least a few days until it has burnt out. Given the proximity to houses this is not an acceptable scenario. The proposed plan states that there will be a pond, however, this only has enough to provide initial firefighting for 2 hours. The [ORGANIZATION] guidance states that there is no way to extinguish a BESS fire so it is difficult to understand how the pond is deemed adequate and simply increases the concern of local residents of an uncontrolled fire scenario. NOISE IMPACT The noise impact assessment needs to be reviewed and reconsidered as it appears to be inadequate and contains anomalies which are neither explained nor understood. Within the Report itself it states that the findings were considered unusual. It is also understood that the noise surveys were not carried out at all property locations adjacent to the site (i.e. [PLACE]). With these anomalies and omissions it is clear that a proper noise assessment has not been conducted and the proposer has not determined any level of suitability and acceptability. FLAWS IN DESIGN/LAND OWNERSHIP ERROR On the Planning application there is a proposed cut off ditch at the opposite site of the field to the access road. It is not clear what this entails? Clarity is required to determine what the intent is here. Also for your info and consideration it appears there are more than one land owners in this area, which conflicts with the proposal. The corner of the field closest to [PLACE] (approx. 0.5 acre in size) is actually not owned by the current landowner, as presented on the documentation, who is proposing to lease land for the BESS development. Therefore the proposer is misrepresenting the ownership and right to lease the land. It is likely that if this development is given the go ahead, and that area above is impacted, then legal issues could arise as ownership of lands has not been truly represented in the application? PRIME AGRICULTURAL LAND This field is currently farmed and is prime agricultural land. Once this site is changed to cater for a BESS, it is stated it will be returned to its natural farming state after use. Consideration needs to be taken as to the validity of this statement as it is not understood, or explained, how they would get this back to it's natural farming state once un-natural and harmful chemicals and construction materials had been present (especially in the aftermath of a fire scenario). VISUAL IMPACT As stated in the application the development will present a moderate to major visual impact on [PLACE]. That is not an acceptable situation for the residents, nor should it be for the decision makers within the Planning Dept. This rural area is already heavily congested with large amounts of Masts and windmills. RISK TO SPECIES The local area is home to pine marten, common toad, European water vole, and two species of owl. By allowing this BESS we would be disturbing and damaging the natural habitat of species that we should be trying to protect. OTHER SIGNIFICANT CONSIDERATION Although the following may not be wholly relevant to this particular Planning Application it cannot go un-noted that the entire concept of BESS Development is very poorly considered, fundamentally flawed, and wholly inadequate to the best interest of the country as a whole. There appears to be no consolidated Plan or consideration as to where and how many BESS are being built, and these things are becoming so numerous that they are having a detrimental impact on rural areas. I have no doubt that at a point in the future this whole topic will become a source of National shame and scandal in the way it is being handled by both National Government and Local Councils. BESS developments are not adequately controlled and are being allowed to be developed in existing agricultural areas and destroying the natural footprint of this land, industrialising rural areas. The huge and unrealistic money being paid for the BESS developers to lease this land is many many times more than the actual value of the land. The BESS sites are often located miles from the asset they will connect to, thus introducing further excessive infrastructure and destruction to achieve connection to the Network and generating significant costs that would not normally be regarded as economical. All these costs will have to be recovered and it will be the consumers who have to face the bill. Once the general public realise what is going on and are faced with large bills to pay for the excessive expenditure of these developments I imagine the roof will come off, and the decision makers such as yourselves who facilitated and approved this will be held accountable. Why can BESS units not be located at existing sites, such as within the footprint of existing windmills, where infrastructure has already been installed and exists - thus significantly reducing the cost and the damage to existing green spaces. I would appreciate these points to be put forward for objection.

target_text: To whom it concerns, I object to the Battery Energy Storage System. Apart from the fact that this area of [PLACE] has alreday been subjected to more than its fair share of battery developments and associated risk, this site is adjacent to to a Site of Special Scientific Interest that needs to be protected from potential contamination. Whilst the drainage plan does address potential fire situations, it only considers contaminated water entering the SUDS pond. There is no consideration of an impermeable membrane as proposed at other BESS site to prevent ground contamination. It states that a flow control device "can" be closed off to cut off the drainage from the wider water environment but does not state why this might be required. The risk of chemical contamination is deliberately not made clear. There are further statements about exact arrangements established at detailed design. I agrue that due to the [PLACE], the exact arrangements are crucial to the decision for approval or otherwise. This cannot be left till detailed design and must be made clear before approval is granted. I note that there is 180,000litre tank for cooling water on site. Firstly, a Scottish Fire and Rescue Fire pump vehicle has the capacity to pump around 2000 litres per minute. So in the event of a fire, a single pump will empty the tank in 90 minutes. It is well documented that a lithium battery will burn for much longer than 90 minutes. What happens after the 90 minutes and the tank is empty? Further, when water is stored there is generally biological growth in the water, which chokes pipes, valves and pumps. There are 2 ways to prevent it, flow through and agitation or chemical biocide. Since there is no proposal for flow through or agitation, I assume that biocide will be used. Use of biocide in such quantities adjacent to a [PLACE] can lead to devasting effects. I did ask the company personnel at the public engagement sessions about this, and they freely admitted thay had no clue about this. They were planning consultants and no idea about operation of the site and considered any chemical use to be an operational issue. Again, I argue that adjacent to a [PLACE], this is a material issue that needs to be ironed out before approval is granted.

retrieved_examples.text: I wish to submit a formal objection to the proposed Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) development near [PLACE]. My concerns focus on the potential for fire hazards, water contamination, and the lack of environmental safeguards, particularly regarding local watercourses and consultation with SEPA. 1. Severe Fire Risk in a Rural, Unmanned Location Lithium-ion battery systems are known to pose a significant fire risk. These fires can be extremely difficult to control and often burn for many hours or days. As this site will be unmanned during its operational phase and located in a rural area with limited access, emergency response may be delayed, especially in adverse weather when local tracks are often snowed in or impassable. There is currently no publicly available emergency response plan. This absence is particularly concerning for residents who live in close proximity to the site, as well as for nearby agricultural operations and the adjacent mature woodland. Questions remain unanswered: What are the emergency response times? Has the fire service been consulted? Who will coordinate road access during an emergency? 2. Contaminated Fire Suppression Water and Impact on Watercourses In the event of a fire, the water used to suppress it will become heavily contaminated with toxic chemicals. This runoff poses a direct threat to local watercourses, aquifers, and private wells used by residents. Given the elevated position of the site, any overflow from the fire suppression effort or the planned SUDS (Sustainable Urban Drainage System) pond will drain into surrounding water systems. This includes a burn that flows into [PLACE] and feeds nearby private supplies. No detailed plan has been provided to contain or treat contaminated water before it enters the natural environment. This is an unacceptable risk. 3. Inadequate Drainage and Risk of SUDS Pond Overflow The proposed SUDS pond is positioned on sloped ground, increasing the risk of overspill, especially during heavy rainfall or storm events. Planning documents describe the site as "stormproof," yet in recent years there has been increasing evidence of severe weather and localised flooding - including reports from 2023 of flood damage to homes near the affected burn. The pond is designed to allow soak-away into surrounding soil, but this raises serious questions about groundwater contamination, especially with no buffer zone from the natural hydrological systems. There is also no clear information on how the pond will be maintained or monitored over time. 4. Lack of SEPA Consultation and Environmental Oversight It is unclear whether SEPA (Scottish Environment Protection Agency) has been meaningfully consulted in the assessment of water risks. Given the potential impact on watercourses, private water supplies, and flood management, it is imperative that SEPA's input be obtained and published before any approval is considered. The lack of transparency around this consultation suggests that water safety risks have not been adequately evaluated, nor mitigation plans robustly designed. Conclusion This application introduces substantial, unmanaged risk to the local environment through fire hazards, inadequate emergency access, and the threat of contaminated water reaching sensitive local ecosystems. Without a detailed fire response plan, flood prevention strategy, and proper environmental oversight by SEPA, this proposal is not fit for approval. I strongly urge [ORGANIZATION] to refuse this application unless these critical concerns are fully addressed with public input and the cooperation of the relevant emergency and environmental authorities.

Objections - Proposed Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) Development - [PLACE] I would like to lodge the following objections to the above-mentioned development: 1. The proposed location is too close to existing and planned domestic housing. Large scale battery energy storage systems are a fundamental part of the UK's move towards a sustainable energy system and represents relatively new technology. There have been several major failures in systems worldwide with the most serious resulting in thermal runaways. In this case, the short timeframe limited the community’s ability to fully digest and respond to the proposals. I respectfully request that the planning authority take these issues into account and ensure that proper consultation standards are upheld before any further consideration is given to this application. 1 The application’s reference to a 400MW capacity is misleading. The proposed battery energy storage system has a total energy capacity of 800MWh over two hours, equating to a nominal output of 400MW per hour. However, battery systems typically operate at 85–90% round-trip efficiency, meaning that to deliver 800MWh of usable energy, the system would actually need to store and process approximately 890–940MWh. This additional energy demand, due to efficiency losses, increases the system’s environmental and operational impact. The application should reflect these real-world performance characteristics to provide a more accurate representation of the development’s scale and implications. - Blue bars represent the consistent usable output of 800 MWh. - Red bars show the increasing input energy required as efficiency decreases: - At 90% efficiency, ~889 MWh is needed. - At 87.5% efficiency, ~914 MWh is needed. - At 85% efficiency, ~941 MWh is needed. This clearly illustrates how efficiency losses significantly increase the installed capacity above the two hour supply to nearly 1Gw. 2 The location plan submitted with application [APPLICATION_CODE] clearly indicates site access from the west, via [PLACE]. Local residents deserve a clear explanation of this apparent discrepancy, and at the very least, a pause in the planning process until the matter is fully clarified. 3 The application inaccurately describes the proposed site as being located within an area of "felled forestry." In reality, the 9.9-hectare site is not felled land but has been recently replanted with new woodland. This mischaracterisation of the site’s current condition is misleading and should be corrected in the application documentation. 4 The [PLACE] and [PLACE] originate on or near [PLACE] and flow into the [PLACE], while the [PLACE] and [PLACE] run south into [PLACE] priority catchment. The proposed [ORGANIZATION] BES 400MW site sits directly on the watershed dividing these two sensitive areas. This location poses a significant environmental risk. Any accidental release of pollutants—such as fuel, oil, chemicals from battery storage systems, or construction runoff—could enter surface water systems and impact both catchments. These watercourses ultimately feed into the [PLACE] and [PLACE], both of which are designated priority catchments due to their ecological and public water supply importance. Despite this, the application contains no reference to either the [PLACE] or [PLACE] catchments, nor does it assess the potential for cross-catchment contamination. Given the scale of the proposed development and the sensitivity of the surrounding hydrology, this omission is unacceptable. Both rivers must be protected from industrial pollution, and the risks associated with this site demand thorough hydrological assessment and mitigation planning before any approval is considered. 5 While the application addresses surface water and notes a low risk of flooding, it makes no mention of groundwater. However, the presence of year-round water in existing ditches and ponds at [PLACE], along with the use of private wells in the area, clearly indicate a consistent groundwater source originating from [PLACE]. This omission raises concerns about the adequacy of the hydrological assessment. 6 The proposed locations of the fire water tank and the 1,900-litre attenuation pond—both situated to the north of the site’s sole access route—raise serious safety concerns. In the event of a fire, emergency vehicles would be required to drive through the central access road, potentially flanked by burning battery compounds, in order to reach the water supply needed to suppress the fire and cool adjacent units. Their poor condition poses serious safety risks—not only for construction operations but also for local residents who rely on these routes daily. The planning application fails to address these issues entirely, which is a significant oversight and further reason the proposal should not proceed. 9 Fire Risk and Environmental Containment Concerns Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) fires—particularly those involving lithium-ion batteries—can reach extremely high temperatures due to thermal runaway. Individual cells may reach 500°C to 700°C, and in large-scale incidents, temperatures can exceed 1,000°C, especially in cascading failures. These temperatures are capable of: - Melting structural and containment materials, - Releasing flammable and toxic gases, - Generating intense radiant heat that can ignite nearby structures or vegetation. target_text: The siting of the plant in this location is contrary to the council’s land categorisation within the Local Development Plan. Industrial scale commercial development is inappropriate on designated greenbelt. There is a significant allocation of land in the LDP to support the development of renewable energy and developments should be focussed in that area or other brownfield or industrial sites. 2. While Part 2, Section 11 of NPF4 states that “LDPs should seek to realise their area’s full potential for electricity and heat from renewable, low carbon and zero emission sources by identifying a range of opportunities for energy development”, it also states that “Development proposals will only be supported where they maximise net economic impact, including local and community socio-economic benefits such as employment, associated business and supply chain opportunities.” The local benefits of this type of proposal will be minimal, with the construction likely to be undertaken by specialist outside contractors and minimal manual intervention required in the operation of the site. It is therefore unlikely that there will be any direct benefit to the local communities. 3. NPF4 also states that “In considering these impacts, significant weight will be placed on the contribution of the proposal to renewable energy generation targets and on greenhouse gas emissions reduction targets”. While battery storage in the right location undoubtedly has its place in the wider energy system, it is questionable whether this site has a specific impact on emissions reductions targets or that it supports renewable energy development. The energy stored will be taken from the grid rather than from a direct zero-emissions source and will therefore be the standard grid- mix at any given point. It is essentially a trading mechanism for buying at periods of low use and selling when prices are high. 4. The prominent location on the approach to [PLACE] is inappropriate for this scale of development and the proposed mitigations to the visual impact do not seem to be sufficient. Given that there is no grid connection point locally (as confirmed via Scottish Power Energy Network’s Distributed Energy Heat Maps [LINK] ). Other more suitable locations closer to the connection point should surely be given priority consideration? 5. The proposals do not comply with guidance issued by the National Fire Chiefs Council ([LINK]). Specifically, the plan does not include at least 2 separate access points to the site to account for opposite wind conditions/direction. 6. The plan shows an attenuation pond at northeast corner with a controlled outlet to existing burn and then to the [PLACE]. It is unlikely that this attenuation pond would be sufficiently large enough to deal with the water run-off in the event of a fire on site, meaning that there is a significant risk of a contamination event on the [PLACE], directly threatening biodiversity and water quality. 7. The impacts on the local road and active travel networks are likely to be significantly impacted both during construction of the facility itself and in the laying of cables required to get to the required grid connection point. The strength of feeling locally in relation to this proposal is clear from the number of objections submitted. While battery storage has its place in the wider energy system, it is critical that this is not to the detriment of local landscapes and character.

Given that [PLACE] is a conservation village, with historic mills and renowned for its greenery and cycling opportunities, it is inconceivable as to how the proposed development would not cause such significant loss of character. The proposal would be an industrial site, filled with shipping containers emitting humming noises. This would equate to gross vandalism if the project is approved. The applicant has stated that there will be 12 months of road disruption while the area is prepared and these units are installed. This not only will impact on [PLACE] residents for a prolonged period of time (the queues at the [PLACE] at rush hour frequently extend up the [PLACE] towards [PLACE]) but due to the access roads vicinity to the [PLACE] is likely to impact on the [PLACE] (where the queues at rush hour can extend back 3⁄4 mile directly along this sites northernmost border). This is likely to lead to increased crashes at an already dangerous roundabout that sees frequent accidents. The applicant has also stated in their transport statement section 6.8 that "vehicle parking for site workers during all stages of construction and operation will be accommodated on site with no vehicles allowed to park or wait on the adjoining road network during any stage of the development". However for the first two months, before any groundwork has taken place there will be no on site parking. This raise the question of where these workers are going to park as there is no space for parking in the vicinity surrounding low Borland. Will this mean there are increased cars parking in [PLACE] and [PLACE]? This itself is likely to contribute to road safety issues in the wider community. [PLACE] descends from [PLACE] towards [PLACE]. I have concerns that this means this industrial installation encompassing will be highly visible from the road for every [PLACE] resident that travels down the [PLACE] every day. The applicant plans to put the access road directly opposite a [PLACE] which is so listed because it is an example of a late 18th or early 19th century farmhouse. Part of the charm of any listed building is the setting within which it resides. An access road to an industrial unit directly opposite this markedly changes this setting. At the second public consultation the attendees were told that there would be 16 BESS units in the form of standardized shipping containers. It is therefore disappointing to note that along with the 16 6.06 x 2.9 m standard shipping containers there will also be 8 larger 12.16 x 2.44m shipping containers marked as 'PVC'. I would have concerns that this project would impact on their habitat as well as the security lights disturbing their natural behaviours. To what extent will the bats echolocation etc be impacted upon by the noise pollution created by these units? The applicant states that they are not putting in any noise mitigation. I have major concerns about allowing a limited company with no liability to construct a BESS. This response has been prepared on the premiss that the proposals are unacceptable and the writer objects to the development in the strongest terms. It is acknowledged that renewable energy is essential for maintaining a reliable, ecological source of electricity, which will gradually mitigate the need for other, more polluting, forms of production, such as gas, coal, and nuclear. It is recognised that the physics of producing electricity using, for example, wind energy results in spikes of supply, which do not correspond with demand times and that storage is required to smooth out the availability of electricity for consumers. What is not accepted is the justification for locating such a facility on greenfield land, immediately beside dwellings and land where livestock is being raised. This response looks at the documents compiled by [ORGANIZATION] and their team. It raises concerns, highlights relevant issues and poses questions, to which written responses are required. SUBMITTED DOCUMENTS This response is based on the majority of the documents submitted. Those referred to appear to have most relevance to the arguments being presented. Battery energy storage facility with associated infrastructure, substation, security fencing, CCTV, security lighting and landscaping on land near [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE] (Grid Reference: X 251181, Y 674239) This is an overarching, introductory document and so more general observations of the proposals and questions have been included here. LOCATION The document implies that the site is in a remote location. It does not mention the residential properties that lie immediately adjacent to the development site, which will be severely impacted by the proposals. Why can the facility not be located on brownfield, formerly industrial land where this type of use is established? It is understood the grid infrastructure, located adjacent to the facility, will NOT be used for the distribution of the electricity being stored here; instead, the [PLACE], some 30km to the north east will be used ([ORGANIZATION] Consultants’ website “Why was this Location Chosen?”). So, there is no practical reason why the development needs to be on this particular greenfield site. VISUAL IMPACT The site is located in open countryside, so will be highly visible from near and far views to the detriment of the area. The site is on sloping exposed ground, which ensures the views to the site are maximised. No amount of screening planning will prevent this, in the short to medium term. OTHER DETRIMENTAL IMPACT Sound - Please confirm the source of sound and the sound levels that will be produced from the facility. Local residents would expect a zero-decibel impact at their property, given the rural nature of the setting. Wildlife Habitat - The development will destroy 29 hectares (or 36.2 hectares, according to the [ORGANIZATION] Consultants’ website) of natural habitat and farmland; more if road widening goes ahead. This alone is reason to force the developers to seek out an urban brownfield site for this facility. Global loss of habitat is not being taken seriously enough and the reduction in wild places and biodiversity will have direct consequences for humanity, if this is not halted now. Walking interest - The immediate area of the site is a place of significant walking interest, with the site bounded on three sides by core paths and with many other routes of access to and around the surrounding countryside and the [PLACE] including the long distance route, the [PLACE], which goes along the eastern boundary of the proposed development. Pre-historic rock art - The proposed development impacts on one of the densest and most accessible accumulations of pre-historic rock art in Scotland’s central belt. The proposed development site at [PLACE] has seven cup and ring marked rocks along the boundary, and 9 more within 250m of the boundary. The [PLACE], which is one of the most important and most extensive pieces of prehistoric rock art in Scotland lies only 500m from the boundary of the development. The site dominates the Neolithic landscape of [PLACE] and would significantly impact on the setting of the stones. SCALE The development is of a scale inappropriate to its location. How was the scale of this development established? HEALTH and SAFETY Fire - Any outbreak of fire at the facility will be a significant hazard to health, directly from heat and flame but perhaps more significantly from the dangerous pollutants that will be released should fire take hold. Ground Contamination - Any leakage from the batteries will contaminate the surrounding land. Leaching of leaked chemicals/toxins to adjacent properties will present risk to life/health. Provide written confirmation that there are no such risks from the installation and that the ground can be given back to farming or other natural rural uses once the site is abandoned. Air contamination - Do the batteries issue any fumes or gases in operation. It is assumed that any malfunction of the batteries or damage to their containment will result in the release of toxic chemicals into the airborne environment. COSHH Regulations. Please provide a written report on all chemical substances used within the battery storage units. Any contamination of the environment, as a result of the development, will affect the health and wellbeing of local residents and the flourishing wildlife here. Risks for vandalism/terrorism. - The rural nature of the site means that supervision and security will be difficult to control and any unwanted events will lack the rapid response that could be put in place within a more urban setting. ROADS and ACCESS [PLACE] is a winding, single track road with poor surface and a steep gradient. It is wholly unsuited to this type of development. The traffic generated by both construction works and the operation of the facility will be extremely hazardous for local users. To increase the width of the road would be detrimental to the rural character of the area, would destroy habitat and reduce biodiversity. The gradient and topography will not result in a road which is safe for all users. [PLACE] is a fast commuter route and the access point, where [PLACE] joins this is already hazardous, given its close proximity to the blind corner to the west. Adding large construction vehicles and increased traffic during operation of the site is likely to exacerbate accident rates here, significantly. Historic Environment Desk-based Assessment “The available archaeological records suggest that there is some limited potential for the survival of prehistoric period remains within the study site. The study site is likely to have remained in agricultural use through the medieval and post-medieval periods. It is possible that buried remains relating to medieval or early post-medieval agriculture, such as ploughing or field boundary features, could survive, but these would be considered to be of negligible significance.” The study, which resulted in these conclusions was desk-based, so it cannot be stated, at this stage, that any remains would be of “negligible significance”. The presence of the nearby [PLACE] and Neolithic – Bronze Age Cup and Ring markings alone must raise concerns whether this site is suitable for development. Other historic features and events are noted within the study site. The quantity of notes of historical interest within and surrounding the study site requires that a full scheme of site investigation works be carried out, both at application stage and ongoing during installation. It seems highly probable that further examples of significant heritage value would be destroyed, should the development be allowed to progress to site. Item 5.2.7 makes reference to the views to the site, which will be possible from local landmarks but that “the proposals would have no significant impact upon the setting of this part of the WHS”. This cannot be for the applicant to decide and must be independently and impartially assessed. Even if the battery storage units can be installed without any disruptive excavation being carried out, potential leakage from the batteries will contaminate sub-surface archaeology. NOTE other documents submitted make reference to cut and fill operations, which would destroy any archaeology in the affected area. The conclusion to this report focuses on designated heritage, however it is the undiscovered archaeology that must be identified and protected here. The report highlights human activity across the site, continuously, from the earliest times. Another site with less historic interest should be considered. Photographs - The photos annexed to this document show clearly the site’s elevated and prominent position. It has commanding views out to the city and surrounding countryside, so views to the site will be equally clear. Notice to the Scottish Ministers. to construct and operate a battery energy storage facility. The Notice describes the development as: “.battery energy storage facility with associated infrastructure, substation, security fencing, CCTV, security lighting and landscaping” The visual impact of security fencing surrounding the site will be inappropriate and out of keeping in a rural area. Security lighting cannot be entertained in a rural area. Light pollution will have a detrimental impact on the amenity and wellbeing of local residents. Further, lighting of this type is known to have a detrimental effect on night-flying creatures like bats. The light alters their flight paths and interferes with their feeding patterns. [ORGANIZATION] [ORGANIZATION] has been appointed to act on behalf of the developer, [ORGANIZATION]. Their website contains a section, titled “How will the local community benefit from this proposal?” This goes on to explain “The proposed battery storage facility will benefit UK consumers as a whole by facilitating the supply of low-cost, low carbon electricity on the national grid.” In fact, [ORGANIZATION] are unable to state ANY benefits to the local community from this development. Pre-application Consultation Report - [ORGANIZATION] No comment at this stage. Design and Access Statement (DDA) - [ORGANIZATION] The Introduction (item 1.4) makes reference to: “Policy 14 of the National Planning Framework 4 (NPF4) states how the planning system should “encourage, promote and facilitate well designed development that makes successful places by taking a design-led approach and applying the Place Principle.” Annex D of NPF4 then lays out the ‘Six Qualities of Successful Places’, with quality number 2 ‘Pleasant’ emphasising the importance of creating “attractive and welcoming” places which mitigate against noise, air and light pollution, as well as avoiding undesirable features.” This is indefensible. There is not a single instance, in this development, where “design” can be seen to have been used. The battery facility will be a scar on the landscape; its location and topography will exacerbate its inappropriate scale and the batteries themselves are industrial in nature. The site enclosure and floodlighting will be reminiscent of a high security institution. (item 1.5) Place Principle. Whilst public consultation has taken place, this has only alerted the local community to the blight to the countryside and their lifestyle, which is proposed here. Property values will be destroyed and the rural amenity local people have enjoyed, will be removed. Discussions with local people cannot and will not result in this development becoming acceptable. The very nature of the proposal is so alien to this place that no amount of “tweaking” will resolve concerns. (item 2.1) The Site. The DDA states the facility will connect to the grid via [PLACE] and [PLACE] substations. This is different to the information on AAH’s website (see above) but nevertheless, these substations are remote from this site, reinforcing the suggestion this location is not critically important to the functioning of the grid feed-in. (item 2.3) Flooding. Please confirm if the SEPA records, referred to, factor-in climate change? SEPA is updating their data, currently, to reflect climate change and this often results in a very different picture for sites where a low risk was indicated previously. NPF4 recommends that no development should take place on land at risk of flooding and certainly, where electricity and hazardous chemicals are involved, this must surely be avoided completely. NOTE Raising of equipment to avoid flooding will only increase the visual impact of the proposals. (item 3.4) Sustainability. This development is not sustainable if leakage from batteries renders the land barren and unusable for future generations and these risks have not been explored, fully. (item 3.5) Mitigation. How will the loss of natural habitat be mitigated? Were the development located on brownfield land, this would not be an issue. (item 3.7) Planning. Since this application will be determined by the Scottish Ministers and NOT the local planning authority, please confirm how the planning system will form part of this process? (item 3.8 and 3.0) Planning Policy and Guidelines. Whilst relevant policies are identified, the DDA does not delve into these nor expand on how the proposals comply. With regard to Policy 1, this only considers renewable energy installations to be appropriate “in principle”. It is worth exploring, too, whether the proposals do, in fact, constitute a renewable energy development or rather, is battery storage an adjunct to that industry, which comes with a host of issues, which need to be overcome. Not least of these are the visual impact implications and risks to health and wellbeing. (item 4.4) Temporary development. Please clarify the finite lifespan of the development. (item 5.3) Scale. The size of the development is stated as filling the land available. This is not a calculated justification for the proposals scale. It is noted in 5.7 the scale is required for viability, however the measure of this is not stated. (item 5.11) States the development is of an appropriate scale. This is the opinion of the applicant and therefore cannot be taken at face value. Comparing the proposals with other land uses in the vicinity demonstrates clearly how out-of-scale this development will be in this location, where other structures comprise dispersed single houses and farm buildings. (Image 5.1) Proposed Layout. The proposed site access is too far up [PLACE], meaning construction and then operating vehicles will clash with other road users over a greater length of road than is necessary. Far more information is required on proposed screening, by way of planning and bunding. There is no key provided to accompany the layout. (item 5.15) Access and security. The measures described will be completely out of character here. Widening the road, as described, will destroy natural habitat and is likely to encourage joy-riders in this remote location. There is no description of the boundary fencing proposed in this document but the pole-mounted CCTV cameras and security lighting suggest a grim and hostile appearance, which is unacceptable. (item 5.17/ 5.18) Landscaping. Please explain how the introduction of c. 30 Ha of battery storage along with a high security enclosure and lighting will “preserve and enhance the existing landscape features.” The retention of hedgerows will not compensate for the destruction of a large swath of natural land where ground-dwelling plants and animals reside. (item 5.19) Appearance. The overall appearance of the proposed development will NOT be “.sympathetic and in keeping with the surrounding context”. This is simply not true and it defies understanding how [ORGANIZATION] can promote this view. (items 5.2 – 5.23) Access. The disruption that will be caused to local residents during the 24-month construction phase is unacceptable. (item 6.2) Carbon reduction. This is acknowledged as vital to the future of the planet but if a natural and wild place needs to be destroyed to facilitate this, what’s the point? What are we saving the planet for? Outline Safety Management Plan - [ORGANIZATION] (item 1.5) The battery technology system to be employed has not been chosen yet, so this document is irrelevant, other than it flags up there ARE risks to those, out-with the site, to: - Fire - Explosion - Release of harmful gases The document states that detection and suppression systems will be put in place but by the time an alert is raised, the accident has already happened. All the systems do is attempt to minimise its impact. This is not acceptable to adjacent property owners; indeed, the release of harmful gases could affect those living remotely to the site too. Noise Impact Assessment – Professional Consult As noted previously, local neighbours should expect a zero decibel effect from the development. Landscape and Visual Impact Assessment - [ORGANIZATION] No further comment at this time. Landscape Proposal Drawings - [ORGANIZATION] Drwg No APA-PL-01 Whilst the proposed tree planting is welcomed, the size of tree specimens proposed (6080cm) is inadequate. The mitigating effect of the new woodland will not be established for 15-20 years, which is not acceptable. Heavy standards should be used throughout and a programme of maintenance and replacement put in place from the outset. Consideration should be given to bunding between new planting and the battery storage containers. Transport Statement – [ORGANIZATION] 21,190 two-way vehicle trips during construction is unacceptable. Six-day working week is unacceptable. The impact on other road users during construction is unacceptable. Danger to other road users from construction traffic is too great. Preliminary Ecological Appraisal – [ORGANIZATION] Concerns about impact on ecology noted elsewhere. Access Gate and Fencing (drawing) - [ORGANIZATION] The appearance of this style of fencing is unacceptable in this location. A boundary fence location plan is required. Any fencing required must be located to the inside of any landscape buffer. Appendix B2 Accurate Visual Representation and Methodology Slide Viewpoint 8 – Year 1 demonstrates clearly the extremely adverse visual impact presented by this elevated site. According to the subsequent slide, it will take 15 years for the screening planning to have its proper effect. This is not acceptable. LIDAR data is limited and the visuals produced using LIDAR are not useful representation of actual situations. CONCLUSION Until the advent of NPF4, Development in the countryside came under the utmost scrutiny and an assumption against development was made in most cases. The new guidelines, which seem to favour developments such as this; where a “green” or “sustainability” label can be attached, appear to attract no such attention. Indeed, they are encouraged without the usual means of recourse. However, due care must be exercised by any local authority that supports such a venture. This is unknown and untried territory with both real and perceived levels of risk to health and life, not to mention the impact the development will have on the visual amenity of this beautiful rural area and the lives of the families who live here. The [ORGANIZATION] website tries to justify the use of agricultural land as follows: “The draft National Policy Statement for Renewable Energy (EN-3) confirms that Agricultural Land Classification (ALC) should not be the predominant test in site selection.” This conflicts strongly with the overarching principles of NPF4, which promotes the protection of natural habitat and creation of places where biodiversity can thrive as being of paramount importance in planning decision-making. It appears these sentiments have been lost in our eagerness to embrace renewable energy systems, at all costs.

[ORGANIZATION] Planning Services By E-Mail: [EMAIL] 23rd May 2024 Dear Sir/Madam, Objection to Application Reference [APPLICATION_CODE] for "Construction and Operation of a 40 MW Battery Energy Storage Facility together with Associated Infrastructure, Substation, Security Fencing, CCTV, Security Lighting and Landscaping" As a concerned resident of [PLACE], I am writing to formally object to planning application [APPLICATION_CODE]. The proposal to construct and operate a 40 MW battery energy storage facility at the "Land East of Site of [PLACE] G76 0DN" raises several significant issues that, in my opinion, should lead to the refusal of this application. ### Impact on Historic Assets The proposed development will negatively impact the [PLACE] Category C Listed Building, and no measures have been proposed to mitigate this harm. This is in direct conflict with NPF4 Policy 7 and LDP2 Policy D15, which mandate the protection and enhancement of historic assets. The development risks causing irreversible damage to our heritage, which is unacceptable. ### Green Belt and Landscape Concerns The site is within the Green Belt, and this development does not comply with NPF4 Policy 8 and LDP2 Policy D3, which only support renewable energy developments in such areas. Since the facility will store rather than generate renewable energy, it fails to meet these criteria. Furthermore, the landscape will suffer considerable visual harm, both immediately and over the long term, conflicting with NPF4 Policy 14. The mitigation measures proposed, such as planting, are insufficient to offset this damage. ### Environmental and Health Risks There are serious environmental health and safety concerns associated with this project. The presence of a high-pressure gas main on the site poses significant risks, particularly in the event of a fire. The applicant has not consulted with the Fire and Rescue Service or conducted a thorough risk assessment, as recommended by government guidelines on grid-scale electrical energy storage systems. This oversight conflicts with NPF4 Policy 23, which aims to protect people and places from harm. Additionally, the expected increase in noise levels without adequate mitigation measures will adversely affect local residents, violating LDP2 Policy E5 and NPF4 Policy 23. ### Biodiversity and Greenfield Land Issues The application fails to demonstrate any contribution to enhancing biodiversity, as required by NPF4 Policy 3. The Preliminary Ecology Report provides no substantial evidence of planned biodiversity improvements. Furthermore, the development is proposed on a greenfield site, contrary to NPF4 Policy 9, which discourages development on such sites unless explicitly supported by the LDP, which in this case, it is not. ### Decommissioning and Site Restoration No decommissioning or restoration plan has been presented, nor are there funds safeguarded for this purpose, which is a requirement under NPF4 Policy 11. The absence of such plans raises concerns about the long-term impacts and future use of the site after the facility's operational life ends. ### Principle of Development Finally, the principle of development itself is flawed. The applicant has not justified why this specific Green Belt location is essential, nor have they provided evidence that alternative sites were considered and found unsuitable. This lack of justification conflicts with NPF4 Policy 8. Additionally, the proposal does not align with NPF4 Policy 11's support for renewable, low-carbon, or zero-emission technologies, as the facility itself does not generate renewable energy. Given these substantial conflicts with key planning policies, I strongly urge [ORGANIZATION] to refuse planning application [APPLICATION_CODE]. The proposed development poses significant risks to our environment, heritage, and community, and does not align with the strategic objectives of our local and national planning frameworks.

Installation of a grid battery energy storage facility (up to 40 mw) with associated development Land at [PLACE], [PLACE] Ref. no. [APPLICATION_CODE] I object to the above planning application for the following reasons: 1. Location in a Green Belt zone - when other more appropriate sites are available: The proposed development would sit in a Green Belt zone. Development can be permitted in Green Belt land if there is an overriding environmental need and there is no other suitable option. That is not the case here as there are many other possible and more appropriate sites. The use of 2.1 hectares of natural protected space in a predominantly residential zone, for heavy industrial purpose, is highly inappropriate and cannot be justified by a bogus claim that this is the only possible space for this development. 2. Impact on a nearby conservation area: The site is not only located in an environmentally valuable area of ever decreasing [PLACE] land but it is in close proximity to [PLACE] which is rich in bio diversity. Developments of the boundaries of such a rich bio diverse area will be impacted by any inappropriate and damaging development on the boundary area. Further loss of trees will add to the damaging impact. 3. Health and Safety risk during transport of battery units to site: Transport of the battery units to the site will pose risks to people and the environment as they would have to be transported through numerous residential areas in the city and they are classified as 'dangerous goods'. This is not a one-off risk since the batteries have a limited life (5-15 years) and would need to be replaced with ongoing risks to people and the environment during transport of replacement units. 4. Health and Safety risk to nearby residents during operation of the facility: Further Health and Safety concerns include the risk of 'thermal runaway' which has been identified by the UK government as a key failure of these storage systems and which, they caution, can lead to significant hazard to the surrounding environment. Thermal runaway can lead to fire, explosion and release of toxic gasses or water run-off. This is not a risk which the nearby residents should be exposed to, and for which [ORGANIZATION] has a duty to ensure they are not exposed to. (Risk cited in Gov UK guidance published 18th April 2024). The aftermath of any leakage or fire at such a site and cleanup costs, which could extend beyond the site and incur cost for the local authority, is very considerable. 5. Noise and disturbance during the construction phase of the facility and during the operational phase: Although the developer states sound proofing will be provided there is no assurances or guarantee that this will not have an impact on residents and wildlife. This is a peaceful and tranquil area and in certain weather conditions noise will travel very far and will have an impact well beyond the site. Finally, the developer uses the argument that building a Battery Energy Storage Facility is an environmentally good thing to do. In an appropriate site, where there is no impact on people or the environment, this is a reasonable premise. However, destroying valuable and protected greenbelt land within [PLACE] to achieve this completely negates any environmental benefit and I argue on this basis that this application must be rejected.

target_text: Firstly, the planning application should be refused as it is clearly and inherently unsafe to site such an industrial facility at this location. The [PLACE] area is a major cycling destination, with the cycle lanes from [PLACE] over the [PLACE], and past [PLACE] to link up with the [PLACE] cycle routes being particularly popular. In addition, I, and others, cycle commute from [PLACE] into work in [PLACE] and elsewhere. Both myself and other cycle commuters and leisure cyclists extensively use the [PLACE] at [PLACE], which passes adjacent to the proposed site of the BESS and includes the proposed entrance / exit to it. Of my journey into work that includes [PLACE] city centre, in my view, by far the most dangerous part of my journey is the part on either side of the [PLACE], including the part of the road adjacent the proposed site and the entrance/exit to the facility. The Belle Criag is so busy and traffic so fast at commuting time that trying to cross the roundabout on bike via the road at commuting times would be a death wish, so the only real option is to use the underpass, which is accessed by a lead in path. In order to access the underpass access path going Northbound, it is necessary to pull out into the middle of the road significantly in advance of the access to the underpass access path entrance in order to avoid getting dangerously boxed in by much faster moving overtaking traffic, usually roughly right at the location of the proposed access to the BESS site. Having the access at this section, just where you want to pull out into the middle of the road / outside of the lane would simply add another danger / hazard to be aware of at an already dangerous traffic location, and puts additional burden on cyclists to be aware of not just traffic quickly approaching behind and in front of them, but also potentially coming out of the access to the BESS site as well. In addition, it is usually necessary to sit stationary in the middle of the road waiting to turn right onto the underpass access path whilst fast moving traffic passes on both sides.During construction, there will be large, wide lorries bringing battery units and other construction materials to the site. This represents an unacceptably increased risk to stationary cyclists who will be right at the outside of their lane, adjacent the white lines dividing the lanes, trying to turn right onto the underpass access. Furthermore, for cyclists travelling southbound towards [PLACE], the are trying to merge off the shared use path from the underpass back onto [PLACE] [PLACE] in the zone leading up to the proposed BESS site access. In addition to cyclists, pedestrians and joggers on the well used path that runs along [PLACE] [PLACE] between [PLACE] would be at additional risk due to construction and maintenance traffic going into and out of the BESS site over the foot path. This is in addition to the normal road traffic, which often is accelerating hard off the [PLACE] heading towards Eagelesham, and having trucks and other industrial traffic leaving and accessing the BESS site so close to the roundabout represents an additional road hazard.
