Adverse cumulative impacts of industrialization of this whole area of which this plant, if built will form a component. Adverse effects on tourism which is a vital source of income in [PLACE]. This proposed BESS is in close proximity to another site designated for a sub station. This level of industrialization is entirely unwelcome and completely unacceptable to the residents of this scenic coastal village and for people in [PLACE] as a whole, who enjoy visits there. This particular application is for a very large BESS. BESS are very problematic because the safety aspects are not assessed before planning consent is granted. Safety aspects are relevant to site selection and design and should be considered BEFORE an application is granted. All hazards should be declared, assessed and properly mitigated in an application. This has not been done here.

Planning Reference No. [APPLICATION_CODE] I wish to object to the above planning application for the following reasons: 1. The proposed development would be totally contrary to the [PLACE] Local Development Plan. The area is designated Green Belt. 2. It would be detrimental to the rural aesthetics of the surrounding area and totally inappropriate in an area of natural beauty. 3. It would have a negative impact on local wildlife. 4. There is a major concern regarding the risk of a future fire and proximity to domestic property. There would be potential contamination from leaking batteries subsequent to any fire, eg. water polluted with hydrochloride acid reaching the [PLACE]. 5. There are significant concerns regarding the effect on traffic. During development and future access there is a proposed entry gate on [PLACE]; a narrow, already busy bus and commuter route. Combined with a very congested [PLACE] particularly at peak times, traffic increase will become intolerable. Apart from driver frustration there is the increased risk to public safety. 6. There is no perceived benefit whatsoever to the communities of [PLACE].

My objections are based on the following material considerations: 1. Environmental and Wildlife Concerns The site lies adjacent to a diverse and thriving wildlife area, home to local bee hives, swans, deer, foxes, and many other species. This ecosystem is not only important for biodiversity but is also a source of pride and enjoyment for the community. Bats, bees, and birds, in particular, are vulnerable to disturbance from noise, electromagnetic interference, and changes to their habitat. Under the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981, these species are protected, and any harm or disruption could constitute a legal offence. I urge the Council to ensure that a full ecological and biodiversity assessment is conducted and made public before this application is considered further. 2. Noise Pollution and Impact on Quality of Life Battery storage systems generate continuous low-frequency hums from inverters and cooling systems. In a peaceful, rural setting such as [PLACE], even moderate levels of industrial noise can disrupt residents' daily lives, impact mental wellbeing, and erode the tranquil enjoyment of the countryside. This development would fundamentally alter the area's character and diminish the quality of life for those who spend time here. 3. Fire and Safety Risk BESS facilities carry serious fire and explosion risks due to thermal runaway-a chain reaction in lithium-ion batteries that can cause uncontrollable fires. Once ignited, such fires can burn for days and are extremely difficult to extinguish. More troubling is the release of toxic gases during these events, including: Hydrogen fluoride (HF) - corrosive and lethal even at low exposure, Hydrogen cyanide (HCN) and carbon monoxide (CO) - both highly toxic, Volatile organic compounds (VOCS) harm air quality, soil, and water. Previous incidents, such as the [PLACE] explosion (2019) and the Moorabool fire in Australia (2020), demonstrate the dangers of these facilities. Any fire would severely risk local residents, wildlife, and farmland. 4. Incompatible Use of Land and Loss of Natural Beauty [PLACE] is part of a cherished landscape, used daily by walkers and families who appreciate its open views and peaceful environment. It is entirely inappropriate to industrialise a location so closely tied to local identity and community wellbeing. The proposal is completely out of character with the surrounding rural setting and offers no meaningful benefit to the local community. 5. Impact on Property Value and Insurance The presence of large-scale industrial infrastructure in a rural area may negatively impact property values. 6. Carbon Emissions and Supply Chain Impact While the intention behind BESS facilities is to support renewable energy, the overall carbon cost of manufacturing, transporting, and installing lithium-ion batteries is significant. A full life-cycle carbon impact assessment should be required, especially considering the environmental costs of extracting raw materials and shipping components internationally. In summary, this proposal threatens the unique rural character, biodiversity, and wellbeing of the [PLACE] area. It is poorly suited to its location, introduces avoidable risks, and offers little to no benefit to the local community. I respectfully urge the Council to reject planning application [APPLICATION_CODE].

I wish to formally object to the above planning application on the following grounds: 1. Lack of Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) The application fails to include a full Environmental Impact Assessment, despite the site's proximity to a Site of Special Scientific Interest ([PLACE]). This omission is unacceptable given the potential risks to protected habitats and local biodiversity. A development of this scale demands rigorous environmental scrutiny. 2. Cumulative Industrialisation of the Area This proposed development would be the sixth BESS installation within a 5km radius. The cumulative impact of these facilities is transforming the rural character of the [PLACE] area into an industrial zone. The planning authority must consider the broader implications of over- concentration. The visual, noise, and environmental stress on the local community. 3. Inadequate Water and Drainage Management There is no evidence of agreed drainage or discharge systems. Without established plans, the risk of uncontrolled water runoff poses a significant threat to the [PLACE] and existing local water management infrastructure. 4. Insufficient and Unsafe Road Access The proposed access point lacks detailed construction methodology and may require the removal of mature trees. Additionally, the absence of a secondary access route raises serious safety and emergency response concerns. 5. Unclear Grid Connection Proposals The application provides no detail on how the facility will connect to the grid. This uncertainty raises the possibility of unplanned, visually intrusive overhead cabling or other disruptive infrastructure. No necessary consents or agreements appear to be in place. 6. Contradictory Tree Felling Information The documentation contains conflicting information regarding tree removal, creating confusion over the true environmental and visual impact. This lack of clarity undermines trust in the application and suggests potential misrepresentation of the scheme's scope. 7. Unaddressed Noise Pollution No noise mitigation measures have been proposed. Given the operational nature of a BESS facility, the likely noise from cooling systems and inverters could significantly disturb nearby residents and local wildlife, particularly in such a rural setting. 8. Fire Safety Hazards Battery storage systems carry inherent fire risks. The proposed site's proximity to the [PLACE] increases the danger of wildfire spread, toxic smoke release, and long-term ecological damage. No detailed fire risk assessment or emergency response plan has been provided. 9. Visual Impact and Inadequate Screening The planned tree removal, coupled with unclear protections for screening vegetation, will make the facility highly visible from local viewpoints. This visual intrusion is unacceptable, especially given the rural, scenic character of the area. 10. Foundation and Structure Concerns The inclusion of solid concrete foundations for some buildings contradicts the previously stated intention to use temporary container-style units. This raises serious questions about the project's permanence and the long-term environmental implications-none of which were addressed during public consultations. 11. Absence of a Decommissioning Strategy There is no proposed decommissioning plan, which is essential for a project of this nature. Without clear commitments to dismantling, site restoration, and long-term environmental protection, the risk of leaving a derelict industrial site post-operation is high. Conclusion: In light of these unresolved issues-particularly the environmental, safety, and cumulative impacts-I urge the planning authority to reject this application until the concerns above are fully addressed through rigorous assessment, transparent documentation, and meaningful community consultation.

[APPLICATION_CODE] | Installation of Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) with an Installed Capacity of [PLACE] and Associated Infrastructure I wish to object to the above planning application on the following grounds: 1. The effect of hazardous substances contained within the BESS batteries. 2. The change in character of the landscape namely industrialisation of agricultural land. 3. The variation of the noise level depending on the BESS configuration and set-up for example if all battery sites are offloading to the gird at the same peak time. 4. The acoustic impact especially the consideration of all sites operating together in addition to the proposed sites. 5. The fire risk in that it is not possible to extinguish a lithium-ion battery fire in conjunction with the apparent lack of emergency plan for the residents who live adjacent to the site especially as there has already been a battery fire on or close to the site. 6. The substantial risk of flooding subsequent to any fire suppression in addition to any toxic run- off into neighbours' water supplies and the local burns, and rivers. 7. The significant and unprecedented (for this area) disruption caused by construction especially due to single-track roads and the subsequent impact on adjacent domestic residences and the wider environment. 8. The visual impact of stark contrasting BESS storage against the environment. 9. The apparent lack of guarantees concerning the restoration of the land to its original state at the end of project. 10. The impact on the health of the community especially due to the prior construction noise and traffic from the substation, grid stability facility and BESS sites during the last five years.

target_text: I am writing with an objection to Application Reference [APPLICATION_CODE] for “Construction of a 40 MW battery energy storage facility together with associated infrastructure, substation, security fencing, CCTV, security lighting and landscaping.” I live in the conservation [PLACE] and will be impacted negatively by this site. I object to this planning application. I believe that it will. - Detract from the entrance to a conservation village - Have a significant visual impact on the community that will not be appeased by the planting - Cause significant disruption between [PLACE] during the construction period affecting public transport, transportation to schools and affecting commuting in and out of the village on an already busy road - Cause noise pollution with a continual humming noise that will affect the enjoy-ability of the landscape - Pose a fire risk – if a fire occurs this will risk damaging the environment particularly the nearby river and risk the health of nearby residents - Increase the risk of road traffic accidents particularly with the position of the planned access road. - Cause light pollution with the security lights that are being installed - Increase the risk of flooding with the ground compaction from the construction equipment - Affect the ability for people to walk and cycle past during construction and affect the enjoyment of the path for walkers and cyclists in the longer term due to its appearance and noise - Decrease the biodiversity and affect wildlife in the area. Please see below for further details: [PLACE] Local Development Plan 2 (March 2022) - Policy D1: Placemaking and design states that the development “should not result in a significant loss of character to the surrounding area” and “be appropriate to its location”. An industrial site full of shipping containers is neither in keeping with the character of the area or appropriate for this location. - Strategic policy 1 (development strategy) of ERC’s local development plan 2 states that the council’s approach is to protect and enhance the green belt and landscape. This project does not do this – it will have negative impacts on the unique identity of [PLACE]. This policy also states that features of historic interest (such as a listed building which is directly opposite the large opening of the access road) should not be adversely impacted upon. A development such as this would negatively impact on this. This policy also comments on the skyline. Currently we have a beautiful skyline as you leave [PLACE] looking down towards [PLACE] with [PLACE] in the distance – this will be tarnished with this development. - The applicant states in their full planning application that “the green belt location is essential due to its location within a viable radius of the grid connection point at [PLACE] and the lack of availability of suitable sites within the intervening land area” but what they don’t mention is that this site is almost 4 miles away from the [PLACE]. I find it hard to believe that there is no brownfield site (or closer greenfield that is within the [ORGANIZATION] development plan) within a 4 mile radius of [PLACE]. They mention that “higher land values in urban areas can make this type of development. unviable and undeliverable” – essentially they do not wish to eat into profits by paying the prices of what more appropriate land is worth. - Policy D9: Access of ERC’s local development plan 2 (LDP) states the council will protect, promote, and extend existing and proposed active travel. Core path E15 runs immediately adjacent to this site. Once past the planted trees at the underpass, the hedgerow is lower than eye-line for the entire length of this field and the site will emit a humming noise. This is hardly promoting encouraging people to walk between [PLACE]. In addition during the 12 months of construction the ability to walk this path will be severely hampered. - [ORGANIZATION] are developing strategic cycle corridors including one starting at [PLACE] running to [PLACE]. The applicant intends to connect to the substation in [PLACE] by underground cabling which at the public consultations I was led to believe would involve digging up the road. I would worry about the impact this would have on this cycle corridor – if this development progresses after the cycle paths are put in will this involve them digging up the majority of this path as utilities will go under the cycle paths/pavements? Even if this development goes ahead before the cycle paths are in place it is yet another utility company that may need to access the cabling for maintenance once they are in place with resultant damage to cycle paths. - The applicant is repeatedly trying to sell this project as renewable in their application. Renewable energy encompasses wind and solar energy which may feed into how the electricity is generated but it will be electricity from the overall grid and therefore while it may benefit energy security for the country it is not particularly green. Road Safety Issues - The applicant proposes to move both the bus stop at [PLACE] north towards the [PLACE]. They have not said by how much. This will mean the already busy exit from [PLACE] is likely to be hampered further by the bus service to [PLACE] stopping closer to the roundabout. Bus users will be at increased risk of accidents. There is no acknowledgment that bus users heading in the [PLACE] direction use the opposite side of the road and currently stand directly opposite the bus stop in [PLACE] – an inlet that is protected from cars. There would be no safe place for a pedestrian to stand on the north travelling side of the road if the bus stop was moved - The applicant proposes to move the streetlight north. This streetlight was put in a couple of years ago with the intention of lighting the road at the area where three driveways exit onto [PLACE] and has made this stretch of road significantly safer. Moving the street light, with no disclosed plans as to how far will increase the risk of an accident from cars leaving these exits due to poor lighting. - The applicant has stated that there will be 12 months of road disruption while the area is prepared and these units are installed. This not only will impact on [PLACE] residents for a prolonged period of time (the queues at the [PLACE] at rush hour frequently extend up the [PLACE] towards [PLACE]) but due to the access roads vicinity to the [PLACE] is likely to impact on the [PLACE] (where the queues at rush hour can extend back 3⁄4 mile directly along this sites northernmost border). This is likely to lead to increased crashes at an already dangerous roundabout that sees frequent accidents. - The large volume of mud that will be deposited during construction, and transported towards the roundabout is also a significant concern. This is likely to make the road slippery in the wet and increase the risk of accidents. - The applicant has also stated in their transport statement section 6.8 that “vehicle parking for site workers during all stages of construction and operation will be accommodated on site with no vehicles allowed to park or wait on the adjoining road network during any stage of the development”. However for the first two months, before any groundwork has taken place there will be no on site parking. This raise the question of where these workers are going to park as there is no space for parking in the vicinity surrounding low Borland. Will this mean there are increased cars parking in [PLACE] and [PLACE]? This itself is likely to contribute to road safety issues in the wider community. - The proposed access road entrance is just over the brow of the hill on exiting from the [PLACE] and will not be visible to traffic until almost upon the entrance, thus creating a blind summit. - It's important to note that a planning application for a church dwelling diagonally opposite this proposed development on the other side of the roundabout was recently declined in part because of concerns over road safety. In that instance the plan for the entrance to the had been moved closer to [PLACE] by not much less than what is proposed here. Visual Impact - [PLACE] descends from [PLACE] towards [PLACE]. I have concerns that this means this industrial installation encompassing will be highly visible from the road for every [PLACE] resident that travels down the [PLACE] every day. - The units being placed are shipping containers and painting them green or grey is going to have minimal impact on hiding them. - The visualisations provided are frankly misleading. The water tank is incorrectly sized – its plan states it is 4 metres tall therefore should be one of the highest buildings on site – yet it is shown on the visualisations as smaller than the BESS units at 2.9 metres. For example a picture taken at [PLACE] at [PLACE] is not representative of the majority of the communities view and has been taken behind a hill. In one case they have specifically stood behind a tree to take a photo (VP01)! The picture at the underpass has been taken through the trees – move 10 metres uphill beyond this point and this creates an entirely different vista – with direct views over the hedgerow onto the installation. There is no picture that demonstrates the vast majority of the communities view point on a daily basis– just above the mid Borland turn off where you descend from [PLACE]. (attach pic) - The hedgerows planned are double root stock being planted in two rows. The applicant has stated it will take 15 years for these to reach the height of the perimeter fencing of 2.4metres (no mention of reaching the 2.9m height of ) - There is also a water tank planned for the closest aspect to [PLACE] road which on the plans will measure 4 metres tall by 5 metres wide. This is not adequately represented on the visual impact (viewpoint 7 – year 1). In addition the CCTV poles with security lighting will never be obscured. This will be a massive eyesore for anyone travelling down [PLACE] towards [PLACE] - The plans are for the batteries to be raised up on concrete pads on top of a permeable under-layer and the area needs to be flat and high enough due to the fact that they have admitted that this is waterlogged site (which will be compounded by the heavy plants compacting the soil on the site.) By the time the permeable road and the concrete pads are installed it seems highly likely that a degree of land raising will have occurred. - The applicants are not taking into consideration any form of shielding the appearances from the [PLACE] side, relying on the existing tress that are not on the land that they will be leasing. There are two large gaps that view into the field from the [PLACE] in a location where slow/standstill traffic is often present. In the winter the existing trees offer no shielding and even in summer there would be a direct line of sight towards the BESS units and their ancillary structures through the gaps. - The applicant plans to put the access road directly opposite a [PLACE] which is so listed because it is an example of a late 18th or early 19th century farmhouse. Part of the charm of any listed building is the setting within which it resides. An access road to an industrial unit directly opposite this markedly changes this setting. - The European landscape convention in there document Guidelines for landscape and visual impact assessment (GLVIA3), as quoted in the landscape and visual appraisal report state that “landscape is an area, as perceived by people, whose character is the result of the action and interaction of natural and/or human factors” they go on to say “character is not just about the physical elements and features that make up a landscape, but also embraces the aesthetic, perceptual and experiential aspects of the landscape that make different places distinctive. it concerns more than simply the appearance”. Essentially in applying this statement to the [PLACE] community who pride themselves on being a conservation village, the impact of this very visible development to the community, will be sorely felt. - At the second public consultation the attendees were told that there would be 16 BESS units in the form of standardised shipping containers. It is therefore disappointing to note that along with the 16 6.06 x 2.9 m standard shipping containers there will also be 8 larger 12.16 x 2.44m shipping containers marked as ‘PVC’. They have been disingenuous regarding this. - The applicant has asked for permission to undertake ‘micrositing’ by up to 25 metres from the original position. This means that, because they are limited by the pylons and high pressure gas pipeline that converge on the east border of the site, the realistic position change they can make is to move the containers closer to [PLACE]. Environmental Considerations - The flow of the water run off travels from the middle of the western border of the site directly under the proposed placement of the batteries to the north-eastern most tip and then drains into the [PLACE]. In the event of a fire if any water was applied due to the permeable under-layer the water, now contaminated with hydrofluoric acid, would drain into one of Glasgow’s major rivers causing significant environmental impact. There is a large site of special scientific interest ([PLACE]) of ancient woodland on the eastern side of the river at [PLACE]. - Bats roost in the tress in the surrounding area. The ecological report confirms that this is likely in 4 of the trees surrounding the site and residents have confirmed that bats reside within the area. I would have concerns that this project would impact on their habitat as well as the security lights disturbing their natural behaviours - The preliminary ecological appraisal states that the current landscape is of low ecological value but could recommended three measures to enhance the biodiversity. The three recommendations (development of a SUDS pond, creation of a herptile hibernaculum and creation of species rich native grassland that have been suggested) have not been taken on by the applicant and therefore what they are proposing reduces the ecological value of the site rather than adding to it. - The access road once the site is operational appears to have no gate planned at [PLACE]. As this is an unmanned site, and with no gate barring access I believe that it will be very easy for fly tipping to occur on this road especially in relation to the ease of access form the [PLACE] and the fact that that design of the access road will allow easy access for large vehicles. Fire Safety - The applicant states that following the public consultations that “the issues raised are addressed in full in the technical reports”. One such issue that was raised continually and noted by them in section 4.2 in their public consultation documentation was the fire safety risk and therefore its disappointing that the planners have made no such attempt to involve the fire and rescue service in Scotland at this stage. The “Health and safety in Grid Scale Electrical Storage Systems” guidance published by the UK government online on the 18th April 2024 states that as a stakeholder the fire service should be consulted at the design and planning stage. - The applicant makes no note of the type of lithium ion batteries (e.g lithium ion phosphate (LFP); Lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide (NMC)) that they plan to place on the site. They state that they could use a “variety of battery solutions”. However, the “Health and Safety in Grid scale electrical energy storage systems” published in April 2024 by the UK government state it is important at the design stage to know which type of lithium battery is proposed as this will impact on the fire and rescue services fire fighting strategy and therefore the applicant should be stating what they intend to use so the correct risk mitigations can be included at the design phase. - [ORGANIZATION], the national fire chiefs council and most recently the UK government in April 2024 has stated that there should be at least two access roads to battery energy storage systems so chemical fires can be targeted no matter what the wind direction and in case one becomes obstructed or inaccessible. This is clearly not within these plans. - [PLACE] have recommended that appropriate turning circles for fire engines are in place and access to an external fire hydrant that has the capability of delivering 1900 litres of water per minute for at least 2 hours. It seems unlikely that the fire hydrant at [PLACE] would be able to supply this. - The applicant states that “where water based suppression systems are installed, firewater containment facilities will be provided to ensure firewater run off does not leave the site.such as directing firewater to an appropriate retention facility.which may include collection for off site treatment”. However when BESS fires have occur they are protracted events ([PLACE], [PLACE] 2020 required defensive fire fighting for 59 hours). If there was a fire at this development, assuming that 1900 litres of water was being delivered per minute for this time period that would create a total of 6.7 million litres of water. This is enough to fill 2.5 Olympic sized swimming pools. There is no space on this site to house this size of a containment facility. The alternate is that the firewater run off would be directed immediately into the [PLACE] leading to irreparable damage to a major river in [PLACE]. - The design is poor from a fire safety point of view. A circular access road goes round all of the BESS units. If one of these units goes on fire then fire engines will have to drive past the units and turn into the prevailing wind to attempt to fight the fire. They will not be able to get to the water tank (if this is planned to be the source for fire fighting – its unclear what the water tanks role is) which is placed at the most westerly point of the site. - In a Freedom of information request to Scottish Fire and Rescue service ([ORGANIZATION]) (issued on 4th April 2024) on exploring there preparedness to combat BESS fires in Scotland it was reported that the working group looking at BESS developments has been disbanded at present and it is unclear if there is any documentation that explicitly explains how to manage a BESS fire in Scotland. The plan to wait until planning permission is granted before putting in an Emergency Response Plan is hardly reassuring to a community that has repeatedly voiced concerns over fire risk. - The applicant repeatedly in their “Outline Safety Management Plan” will not commit to what type of technology they will use and thus what fire suppression systems they will put in place and what emergency plans are required. The applicant is likely to argue that they will look at these issues at the detailed design stage but since the mitigations they are putting forward as possibilities do not seem to be feasible, I do not think it is appropriate that they use sweeping statements about mitigations they cannot fulfil. - The applicant has stated there are safety systems in place to mitigate against fires. Despite these sort of systems being in place there are numerous records of these fires occurring (e.g [PLACE], [PLACE]; [PLACE], USA and [PLACE], Australia). - In the event of a fire the hazardous gases that are produced could travel to nearby residential properties. Bearing in mind the nature of many of the old buildings in the conservation village, with numerous houses having chimneys and older style windows and doors, I would have concerns that the advice that is usually issued in these circumstances of “keep your windows and doors closed” is less effectual. In the event of a prevailing wind these gases would be blown directly onto the [PLACE] again increasing the risk of road traffic accident and would cause protracted disruption as one of the main trunk roads in the [PLACE] area would need to be closed. Excess Noise Levels - The applicant states that they are not putting in any noise mitigation. The batteries omit a continual humming noise due to the need for air conditioning units to cool them. [PLACE] is used heavily by people walking between [PLACE] as well as cyclists using the road to head primarily towards the windfarm. These developments will be audible for these area users. When the council are trying to encourage the use of walking and cycling a development that will deter this goes against ERC’s policies. Light Pollution - The applicant plans to put in put in three 4 metre tall posts that will house CCTV and security lighting. They state that “it will not be illuminated at night time other than by intruder activated security lighting. The ecological report states that a 10cm gap should be left on the perimeter fence so that badgers can get onto the site. This space would allow relatively large sized animal onto the site which could trigger the lights. In addition bats and owls fly in the area and I would be concerned that they would trigger the security lights frequently. Poor Design and Materials - Despite this being a 4 hectare site this choice of location is a poor choice of site as there is a high powered gas mainline pipe running at the southern tip of the site which is severely impacting on where these units can be sited within the field. There is also overhead pylons to the north. Both of these structures mean there is only a triangle in the centre of the field where the shipping containers can be placed with the larger side running adjacent to [PLACE]. The applicant has asked for ‘micrositing’ up to 25metres. As the current layout plans to put the site as far to the east as possible it means that if they do intend to use ‘micrositing’ the only way they will be able to move is to the west.closer to [PLACE]. - The applicant plans to use lithium ion batteries. It should be noted that there are other types of batteries that are infinitely safer to use in grid systems. Vanadium redox batteries can remain discharged indefinitely without any damage, they have no noise or emissions, have a longer discharge/charge cycle life so would not need to be replaced as frequently as 7 years like these lithium ion batteries and are non flammable. They are of course more expensive. - There is a watercourse running adjacent to the western border of the site. As the applicant has highlighted, on the other side of the road there is a high risk of flooding and it has been known to cause flooding onto [PLACE] road in the past (a retaining wall had to be rebuilt as flooding destroyed this a few years ago). This area drains directly into the water course just before the location where the access road is proposed. The access road will directly run across this watercourse and the applicant has not included as part of the planning application a definitive plan as to how this will be addressed instead proposing some options of what could be done – a ford (impractical with the 5 foot drop from the road to the field directly into the stream) or culverting the water through what would be an approximately 30 metre pipe to cover the width of the access road at that point (risk of blockage and opening up questions as to how this will be maintained). - The access road is depicted on the drawings to have a wide mouth opening which starts at the current bus stop and extends to the middle of the driveway at [PLACE] before eventually tapering to the 3 metre wide access road that they state in their plans. This opening is around 25 metres and highlights the difficulty they will have in manoeuvring these large containers around a greater than 90 degree angle (essentially turning back on themselves) onto the site both during construction and every 7 years for the sites 40 year lifespan. - The applicant makes very little mention of how they will connect to the [PLACE] within the documents submitted. They informed us at the public consultation events that the plan would be to connect via underground cabling along the main road via [PLACE] to the substation greater than 4 miles away. By having it this far away from the grid there is an approximately 10% loss of transmission each way. This is of no concern to the applicant as they will still make substantial profits from the electricity they do store and sell back to the grid but if Scotland as a nation is going to be sensible about how they manage BESS developments then at this early stage in this technology we should not be locating these installations at the limit of their viability (which is 5 miles) and picking sites which maximise their potential. Figure 1: The image red circle illustrates the area which is closer to the [PLACE] than this choice of site. Yet the applicant claims there are no brownfield sites that would provide a more suitable location - The applicant makes mention of the fact that this is a waterlogged site and as such this is likely to be worsened by compaction of the soil when construction commences. Concerns over this Type of Company I have major concerns about allowing a limited company with no liability to construct a BESS. The public consultations were done on behalf of [ORGANIZATION] by [ORGANIZATION] (as detailed in the newspaper article on page 6 of the [ORGANIZATION] public consultation report). All three of these companies have the same director. It concerns me that this current organisation is a limited company. Unless they have personal guarantees they are able to walk away from any venture at any stage with no comeback. Bearing in mind the equipment being placed is potentially dangerous, if they did choose to abandon the site at any stage after the ground was dug who would take responsibility for a now brownfield site that may require decommissioning of hazardous materials, would it be the Scottish government, [ORGANIZATION] themselves or the land owner? NPF4 policy 11 states that project design and mitigation will demonstrate that they can “guarantee availability of finances” around site restoration plans. As this would in 40 years time I would be keen to know how this could be guaranteed with such a volatile group of companies. [ORGANIZATION] has no experience in the installation of BESS developments and neither does [ORGANIZATION]. I look forward to hearing from you in due course. [PERSON] [PLACE] 44 [PLACE] [PLACE] G76 0AS

I am writing to formally raise objections to the Section 36 planning application put forward by [ORGANIZATION] ([ORGANIZATION]) for the proposed Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) development located to the north of [PLACE], near [PLACE]. The development aims to establish a 100 MW lithium-ion battery facility on presently undeveloped agricultural land, along with associated transformers, fencing, lighting, fire infrastructure, and drainage. My objection is centred on the significant risks that the development poses to public safety, the local environment, and community well-being. These risks include fire and contamination hazards, potential damage to biodiversity, landscape deterioration, traffic disruption, and inadequate emergency planning. The planning documents submitted by the developer lack the necessary technical detail, safety strategy, and adherence to policies required for responsible energy development of this magnitude. Each section of this objection highlights specific reasons why the application does not meet the criteria set out in the National Planning Framework 4 (NPF4) and the [PLACE] Local Development Plan. These reasons include shortcomings in consultation, the absence of ecological safeguards, failure to conduct a cumulative impact assessment, and neglect in addressing the complete lifecycle of hazardous infrastructure. I strongly urge the planning authority to reject this application in its entirety. Deficiencies in the Consultation Process The applicant's engagement with the local community was deemed as limited and insufficient. Only two public drop-in sessions were conducted, with notably low attendance and minimal feedback. Many residents did not receive adequate notice or subsequent communication. Crucial design details, such as fire safety systems, access routes, and layout alterations, were not disclosed during the consultation period. There is no documentation of substantial interaction with emergency services or public health authorities, and no further consultation took place once major aspects of the proposal were finalised. Essential safety and environmental issues highlighted by the community remain unaddressed. This approach falls short of meeting the requirements set out in National Planning Framework 4 Policy 12, which stipulates early and effective community engagement in significant infrastructure projects. It also does not comply with the UK's commitments under the Aarhus Convention, which ensures public access to environmental information and involvement in decision-making processes. The consultation procedure failed to ensure transparency, neglected to engage affected stakeholders adequately, and prevented the public from fully assessing or responding to the development's risks. As a result, it is considered a significant deficiency in the application. Environmental and Ecological Impact The development site is located in a rural farmland area surrounded by hedgerows, marshy grassland, and drainage features that provide support to wildlife and contribute to the local ecological network. It is positioned near the [PLACE] and encompasses habitats recognised for their biodiversity value, such as waterlogged ground and species-rich grass margins. However, the ecological assessments that have been submitted are incomplete and do not include essential seasonal survey data. No assessments have been carried out for bat roosts, dusk or dawn emergence surveys, monitoring of badger activity, or studies on amphibians during the appropriate seasons. These are standard requirements outlined in the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 and the Nature Conservation (Scotland) Act 2004 when development impacts potential habitats. The absence of this data means the developer cannot accurately claim to comprehend or mitigate the ecological risks associated with the proposal. The site is set to be significantly covered with containerised battery units, impermeable roads, fencing, firewater tanks, and related infrastructure, leading to the permanent loss of semi-natural grassland and the fragmentation of hedgerow corridors. This will eliminate foraging and commuting routes for protected species like bats and birds. While the planting of replacement hedgerows is presented as a biodiversity benefit, no Biodiversity Net Gain (BNG) calculation has been provided, and there is no proposed habitat management or monitoring plan. According to National Planning Framework 4 Policy 3, developments must enhance biodiversity and prevent harm to existing natural assets. Similarly, [PLACE] Local Development Plan Policy PV7 mandates protection and mitigation for priority habitats and species. Unfortunately, this proposal fails to meet either standard. The lack of survey efforts, habitat loss, and speculative mitigation render it environmentally unsound and pose a risk of long-term ecological degradation in an area that supports farmland species and local biodiversity. Risk of Battery Failures and Fire Hazards The proposed Battery Energy Storage System would utilise lithium-ion technology, known for its significant and well-documented fire and explosion risks stemming from the potential of thermal runaway. These fires are intense, self-sustaining, and emit highly toxic smoke and contaminated firewater. Past incidents at similar BESS sites worldwide have led to prolonged fires, public health advisories, and emergency evacuations. Despite these recognised hazards, the application lacks a formal Fire Safety Management Plan. While the site plans include a firewater pump house and tank, there is no indication of capacity modelling, hazard containment design, or coordination with the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service ([ORGANIZATION]). The Pre-Application Consultation report reveals that [ORGANIZATION] did not respond to the applicant’s email inquiry, with no subsequent follow-up or evidence of collaborative emergency planning. Moreover, the application overlooks crucial aspects such as fire scenario modelling, toxic plume dispersion assessments, emergency access planning for responders, community evacuation protocols, and firewater containment and pollution control measures. In the event of a fire, suppression water could become contaminated with lithium salts, acid gases, heavy metals, and fine particulates. Without engineered containment systems like bunds, spill basins, or diversion channels, this runoff could endanger the surrounding land, drains, and the [PLACE], particularly given the sloping terrain of the site and its proximity to surface water features. This absence of fire safety and environmental protection planning violates NPF4 Policy 23, which mandates development to protect human health and manage risks. It also disregards national guidance from the National Fire Chiefs Council ([ORGANIZATION]), which categorises BESS sites as high-hazard and calls for site-specific risk management. Without robust fire planning, this development poses an unacceptable risk to local residents, first responders, and the environment. Proximity to [PLACE] – Water Contamination Risk The development site is situated next to the [PLACE], a small yet ecologically significant watercourse running along the southern boundary of the proposed Battery Energy Storage System. The land slopes downwards towards the burn, which raises concerns about the potential for surface runoff, pollutants, or firewater from the development to enter the waterway. During regular operations, the site is expected to generate runoff from paved areas and electrical infrastructure, carrying oils, chemicals, and particulate matter. Of greater concern is the risk of a battery fire, which could lead to the production of large quantities of contaminated firewater. This firewater typically contains hazardous compounds like lithium, cobalt, nickel, and hydrogen fluoride, posing acute dangers to aquatic life and downstream land users. While the application includes a firewater tank and a basic drainage plan, it lacks a specific strategy for containing firewater or spills. There are no bunds, interceptor tanks, or environmental protection measures outlined to prevent polluted water from reaching the [PLACE]. The Flood Risk Assessment also notes that parts of the site are within or close to a surface water flood zone, heightening the risk of off-site contamination during heavy rainfall or fire incidents. No hydrological modelling or pollution pathway assessment has been provided to show how the burn would be safeguarded in case of a fire, chemical spill, or drainage system failure. This absence of preventative infrastructure goes against environmental protection obligations set out in national planning policy and Scottish water regulations. Considering the potential irreversible harm that a single contamination incident could cause, coupled with the lack of credible protective measures from the applicant, the proposal poses an unacceptable risk to the local water environment. Failure to Collaborate with Emergency Services Despite the high-risk nature of the proposed development, there is no evidence of meaningful consultation or joint planning with emergency services. The Pre-Application Consultation Report confirms that the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service ([ORGANIZATION]) was contacted once via email but did not respond. No further action was taken to engage them, and no formal agreement or operational plan has been submitted. Battery energy storage systems require specialised emergency response procedures, as fires involving lithium-ion technology cannot be extinguished with standard methods and may reignite repeatedly. Responders need site-specific information, including containment strategies, ventilation risks, access protocols, and toxic gas exposure plans, none of which has been developed or shared. There is no evidence of collaboration with [ORGANIZATION], the [ORGANIZATION], or any local emergency planning authorities. The application includes no evacuation plan for nearby residents, no identification of exclusion zones, and no assessment of how local emergency services would safely access or control a major incident on site. This lack of preparation not only places the public and responders at risk but also contradicts key principles of safe infrastructure planning. It breaches NPF4 Policy 23, which demands that public safety be at the core of energy infrastructure decisions, and it fails to meet expectations set out in national emergency preparedness guidance for hazardous facilities. In the absence of any coordinated emergency response plan, the proposal is incomplete and cannot be responsibly approved. Landscape and Visual Impact The proposed Battery Energy Storage System is set to significantly transform the rural landscape to the north of [PLACE]. Currently an open farmland with extensive views across the surrounding countryside, the development plans include the installation of rows of metal battery containers, security fencing, lighting columns, and industrial infrastructure, resulting in a permanent and visually intrusive presence. The Landscape and Visual Impact Assessment submitted by the applicant recognises that the project would have a substantial visual impact within a 250-metre radius, remaining visible from nearby residential areas, roads, and public rights of way, including [PLACE]. Photomontages illustrate that the site would continue to be highly visible to nearby receptors, particularly to the north and northwest, even five years after completion. Furthermore, the project would introduce new sources of light pollution to an area known for its dark night skies. The proposed security lighting and motion-activated CCTV systems would operate continuously, affecting neighbouring residences and nocturnal wildlife. The absence of a lighting impact assessment and a control strategy to minimise glare, sky glow, or light spill is noted. The proposed development would alter the visual and sensory characteristics of the area from rural to industrial, impacting landscape quality, recreational value, and local identity in a lasting manner, as the changes are expected to endure for 40 years. This proposal is in conflict with National Planning Framework 4 Policy 4 and Policy 6, which emphasise the importance of developments respecting landscape character and maintaining high-quality environments. The developer has not presented sufficient evidence on how these adverse effects would be mitigated or justified. Given the unacceptable scale and permanence of the visual impact in this rural setting, it is recommended that consent for the project be withheld on this basis. Cumulative Impact The [PLACE] area has emerged as a significant hub for energy infrastructure projects, encompassing large substations, overhead transmission lines, solar developments, and numerous Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) proposals. The addition of a 17-acre BESS to the existing cluster of industrial energy assets would intensify the physical, environmental, and psychological strains on the local community. Despite the proximity of other approved or pending developments within a 1 km radius, the current application lacks a cumulative impact assessment. There is no consideration of how concurrent construction activities, noise levels, lighting, fire hazards, or traffic flow will be coordinated. This fragmented approach to development overlooks the overall implications of infrastructure saturation on the land, wildlife, and residents of [PLACE]. Local residents have expressed significant apprehensions regarding the industrialisation of the area and the combined effects of these proposals on mental well-being, safety, and environmental standards. It is imperative for the planning authority to evaluate not only the repercussions of this individual project but also its contribution to a broader trend of encroachment and disturbance. Policy 29 of the National Planning Framework 4 clearly stipulates the necessity of accounting for cumulative effects in decision-making processes. The absence of such an assessment represents a crucial oversight. Sanctioning this development without strategic supervision would reinforce an inequitable and unsustainable strain on this rural community. Noise Pollution Battery Energy Storage Systems produce continuous operational noise from inverters, transformers, and cooling equipment. This noise, which is low-frequency, can easily travel in open rural areas, particularly at night when ambient noise levels are low. Over a 40-year period, nearby homes could be subjected to a constant mechanical hum. The Noise Impact Assessment provided with the application is deemed inadequate as it lacks a comprehensive baseline survey of current background noise, detailed modelling of low- frequency sound, and an assessment of nighttime impacts on residents and wildlife. These shortcomings are worrying, especially in light of previous noise complaints linked to the neighbouring [PLACE]. Furthermore, there is no operational noise management plan, post-consent monitoring strategy, or commitment to taking corrective action if noise levels exceed acceptable limits. This deficiency leaves nearby residents vulnerable to potential disturbances. Noise pollution can have serious health consequences, including sleep disturbances, heightened stress levels, and long-term cardiovascular effects. It can also disrupt foraging and breeding behaviours in nocturnal species like bats and owls, which are found in the vicinity. The Alpacas at [PLACE] could also be significantly impacted as they communicate through humming. According to National Planning Framework 4 Policy 23, developments must safeguard health and wellbeing by implementing effective noise management practices. This proposal falls short of meeting this standard. The absence of reliable noise data, coupled with the likelihood of substantial disturbances, constitutes a key reason for rejecting the proposal. Increased Traffic and Infrastructure Strain The development of the BESS will necessitate approximately 900 Heavy Goods Vehicle (HGV) movements over a span of 12 months, with peak daily traffic reaching up to 15 large vehicles. These vehicles will traverse narrow, rural roads not originally intended for heavy industrial traffic, including [PLACE] and the surrounding local road network, which are currently shared by [PLACE] transport, agricultural vehicles, cyclists, and pedestrians. Despite the presence of multiple other energy projects either proposed or already in progress in the vicinity, there has been no comprehensive assessment of the cumulative traffic impact. The planning application lacks any proposed mitigation measures, such as road reinforcement, visibility enhancements, or traffic diversion plans. Furthermore, there is no outlined construction delivery schedule or strategy to avoid peak traffic hours, and no road safety assessment has been provided. The proposed development also exerts strain on [PLACE], a cherished walking and cycling route that runs near the site. The construction compound and associated access roads are anticipated to cause disruptions, visual obstructions, and potential safety risks for users. There is no provision for temporary diversions or safeguarding strategies for the path. In accordance with NPF4 Policy 13, infrastructure should be designed to minimise impacts on local networks and ensure safety for all users. Regrettably, this application falls short of meeting these standards. Without adequate transport planning, this project poses risks of road damage, heightened collision probabilities, and sustained disruptions to the community and local access rights. Waste Management and Decommissioning The planning application does not outline a clear strategy for the long-term management of hazardous waste or the safe decommissioning of the site following its 40-year operational lifespan. Throughout this period, the BESS facility will amass a significant volume of materials necessitating specialist disposal, such as lithium-ion battery modules, electronics, fire suppression systems, and contaminated infrastructure. There is no mention of waste tracking or handling procedures in the application. The applicant has not specified licensed disposal facilities capable of handling lithium-ion components, nor have they provided a plan for monitoring the chemical stability of batteries at the end of their life. This omission raises serious concerns about the safe treatment and removal of hazardous materials that could remain reactive or flammable long after deactivation. Moreover, the proposal lacks a decommissioning plan. There is no commitment to remove foundations, cabling, or underground infrastructure, nor has there been an assessment of potential soil contamination or the need for remediation. The absence of a restoration scheme or financial bond to ensure decommissioning places the responsibility for future clean-up on the landowner or the public. According to NPF4 Policy 22, energy developments must demonstrate full lifecycle responsibility, including sustainable decommissioning. This application falls short of that standard. Without a robust waste and end-of-life strategy, the risk of environmental damage and long-term neglect is unacceptably high. Security and Terrorism Risk The proposed development is situated in a small area that already accommodates a growing cluster of nationally significant energy infrastructure, such as substations, overhead lines, and other Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) projects, all linked to the wider transmission network. The concentration of these assets in one location raises serious concerns regarding national security and vulnerability to physical or cyber threats. BESS facilities are known targets for sabotage due to their ability to disrupt electricity supply and their use of flammable, reactive materials. However, the application lacks a security risk assessment, threat modelling, and evidence of consultation with Police Scotland’s Counter Terrorism Security Advisors or other relevant agencies. Although drawings show perimeter fencing and CCTV, these measures are deemed insufficient deterrents and not commensurate with the strategic importance of the site. There is no cybersecurity plan for remote monitoring systems, intrusion detection network, or emergency response procedure for malicious incidents. Given the growing national focus on infrastructure resilience, the absence of a threat analysis is a significant shortcoming. Approving this application without a comprehensive security and risk mitigation plan would introduce an unnecessary vulnerability into Scotland’s energy system and place nearby communities at an unacceptable level of risk. Community Wellbeing, Mental Health, and EMF Concerns The proposed development near [PLACE] raises significant concerns beyond physical risks and environmental impacts, particularly regarding community wellbeing and mental health. The area is already facing pressure from multiple energy projects, and the introduction of another large-scale, high-risk facility is causing stress and anxiety among residents. Real concerns about battery fires, pollution, explosions, and toxic smoke have been observed at similar sites globally, heightening fears among locals. Living near such infrastructure, which is poorly understood and regulated, can lead to persistent fear, sleep disturbances, and a loss of trust in public decision-making processes. The absence of a Health Impact Assessment with the application is worrying, as it fails to acknowledge the psychological impact of long-term proximity to a high-risk site, especially in rural areas where quality of life depends on peace, safety, and environmental stability. This omission is particularly concerning for families, elderly residents, and individuals with existing mental health conditions. Additionally, worries about potential exposure to electromagnetic fields (EMFs) from the site's electrical infrastructure, without transparent monitoring or public information, add to local unease. National Planning Framework 4 Policy 23 mandates that developments safeguard health, wellbeing, and safety, including mental health and quality of life considerations, not just physical risks. The lack of a wellbeing assessment or mitigation strategy further highlights the applicant's disregard for the local population. Summary The application in question is significantly flawed as it does not adequately address or mitigate the substantial risks associated with large-scale lithium-ion battery storage. The planning documents lack essential details concerning fire safety, pollution control, waste management, biodiversity, and community health. The consultation process was deemed inadequate, and the proposal does not adhere to the standards set by the National Planning Framework 4 or the [PLACE] Local Development Plan. If this development is approved, it would industrialise a rural landscape, compromise local wellbeing, strain emergency services, and create enduring environmental liabilities. It fails to represent responsible energy infrastructure and does not align with the public interest. Therefore, it should be rejected. Personal Comments We request a moratorium on this and all other renewables infrastructure proposals in Scotland's highlands. A pause in developments will allow time to assess and address the cumulative impact of this, and similar proposals. These are damaging communities and their environments in an unsustainable way. The human toll also involves the developing socioeconomic disaster which is witnessed in our excessively high energy bills and excessive tax hikes: this developing Scottish community-poverty scandal is due to the nationally significant government actions subsidising power companies at public expense. We are forced to pay government back for this folly of theirs. We cannot afford any further renewables developments. Stop and reassess these damaging issues. Then start to plan a way forward. Government is forgetting, in their rush, to properly devise a real workable plan for this industry. It should not be based on, and led by, power company revenue and profits.

It should also be noted that there are two SSSIs in the vicinity of the proposed BESS and a SPA. There appears to be no assessment of the impact of the proposed BESS on the SSSIs and it is not clear whether NatureScot has been consulted. Noise It is noted from the noise impact assessment that the review was carried out only of residential properties within 500 metres of the proposed BESS. That assessment excluded [PLACE] and [PLACE], as well as excluding any noise impacts on [PLACE] more generally. [PLACE] water supply It is noted from the hydrogeological risk assessment that although the private water supply which services [PLACE] lies down-catchment of the proposed BESS facility, it lies on the opposite side of [PLACE] reducing the likelihood of groundwater continuity and that the risk of contamination of the private water supply is low to moderate as the site of the proposed BESS facility will be lined to prevent infiltration. This response has been prepared on the premiss that the proposals are unacceptable and the writer objects to the development in the strongest terms. It is acknowledged that renewable energy is essential for maintaining a reliable, ecological source of electricity, which will gradually mitigate the need for other, more polluting, forms of production, such as gas, coal, and nuclear. It is recognised that the physics of producing electricity using, for example, wind energy results in spikes of supply, which do not correspond with demand times and that storage is required to smooth out the availability of electricity for consumers. What is not accepted is the justification for locating such a facility on greenfield land, immediately beside dwellings and land where livestock is being raised. This response looks at the documents compiled by [ORGANIZATION] and their team. It raises concerns, highlights relevant issues and poses questions, to which written responses are required. SUBMITTED DOCUMENTS This response is based on the majority of the documents submitted. Those referred to appear to have most relevance to the arguments being presented. Battery energy storage facility with associated infrastructure, substation, security fencing, CCTV, security lighting and landscaping on land near [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE] (Grid Reference: X 251181, Y 674239) This is an overarching, introductory document and so more general observations of the proposals and questions have been included here. LOCATION The document implies that the site is in a remote location. It does not mention the residential properties that lie immediately adjacent to the development site, which will be severely impacted by the proposals. Why can the facility not be located on brownfield, formerly industrial land where this type of use is established? It is understood the grid infrastructure, located adjacent to the facility, will NOT be used for the distribution of the electricity being stored here; instead, the [PLACE], some 30km to the north east will be used ([ORGANIZATION] Consultants’ website “Why was this Location Chosen?”). So, there is no practical reason why the development needs to be on this particular greenfield site. VISUAL IMPACT The site is located in open countryside, so will be highly visible from near and far views to the detriment of the area. The site is on sloping exposed ground, which ensures the views to the site are maximised. No amount of screening planning will prevent this, in the short to medium term. OTHER DETRIMENTAL IMPACT Sound - Please confirm the source of sound and the sound levels that will be produced from the facility. Local residents would expect a zero-decibel impact at their property, given the rural nature of the setting. Wildlife Habitat - The development will destroy 29 hectares (or 36.2 hectares, according to the [ORGANIZATION] Consultants’ website) of natural habitat and farmland; more if road widening goes ahead. This alone is reason to force the developers to seek out an urban brownfield site for this facility. Global loss of habitat is not being taken seriously enough and the reduction in wild places and biodiversity will have direct consequences for humanity, if this is not halted now. Walking interest - The immediate area of the site is a place of significant walking interest, with the site bounded on three sides by core paths and with many other routes of access to and around the surrounding countryside and the [PLACE] including the long distance route, the [PLACE], which goes along the eastern boundary of the proposed development. Pre-historic rock art - The proposed development impacts on one of the densest and most accessible accumulations of pre-historic rock art in Scotland’s central belt. The proposed development site at [PLACE] has seven cup and ring marked rocks along the boundary, and 9 more within 250m of the boundary. The [PLACE], which is one of the most important and most extensive pieces of prehistoric rock art in Scotland lies only 500m from the boundary of the development. The site dominates the Neolithic landscape of [PLACE] and would significantly impact on the setting of the stones. SCALE The development is of a scale inappropriate to its location. How was the scale of this development established? HEALTH and SAFETY Fire - Any outbreak of fire at the facility will be a significant hazard to health, directly from heat and flame but perhaps more significantly from the dangerous pollutants that will be released should fire take hold. Ground Contamination - Any leakage from the batteries will contaminate the surrounding land. Leaching of leaked chemicals/toxins to adjacent properties will present risk to life/health. Provide written confirmation that there are no such risks from the installation and that the ground can be given back to farming or other natural rural uses once the site is abandoned. Air contamination - Do the batteries issue any fumes or gases in operation. It is assumed that any malfunction of the batteries or damage to their containment will result in the release of toxic chemicals into the airborne environment. COSHH Regulations. Please provide a written report on all chemical substances used within the battery storage units. Any contamination of the environment, as a result of the development, will affect the health and wellbeing of local residents and the flourishing wildlife here. Risks for vandalism/terrorism. - The rural nature of the site means that supervision and security will be difficult to control and any unwanted events will lack the rapid response that could be put in place within a more urban setting. ROADS and ACCESS [PLACE] is a winding, single track road with poor surface and a steep gradient. It is wholly unsuited to this type of development. The traffic generated by both construction works and the operation of the facility will be extremely hazardous for local users. To increase the width of the road would be detrimental to the rural character of the area, would destroy habitat and reduce biodiversity. The gradient and topography will not result in a road which is safe for all users. [PLACE] is a fast commuter route and the access point, where [PLACE] joins this is already hazardous, given its close proximity to the blind corner to the west. Adding large construction vehicles and increased traffic during operation of the site is likely to exacerbate accident rates here, significantly. Historic Environment Desk-based Assessment “The available archaeological records suggest that there is some limited potential for the survival of prehistoric period remains within the study site. The study site is likely to have remained in agricultural use through the medieval and post-medieval periods. It is possible that buried remains relating to medieval or early post-medieval agriculture, such as ploughing or field boundary features, could survive, but these would be considered to be of negligible significance.” The study, which resulted in these conclusions was desk-based, so it cannot be stated, at this stage, that any remains would be of “negligible significance”. The presence of the nearby [PLACE] and Neolithic – Bronze Age Cup and Ring markings alone must raise concerns whether this site is suitable for development. Other historic features and events are noted within the study site. The quantity of notes of historical interest within and surrounding the study site requires that a full scheme of site investigation works be carried out, both at application stage and ongoing during installation. It seems highly probable that further examples of significant heritage value would be destroyed, should the development be allowed to progress to site. Item 5.2.7 makes reference to the views to the site, which will be possible from local landmarks but that “the proposals would have no significant impact upon the setting of this part of the WHS”. This cannot be for the applicant to decide and must be independently and impartially assessed. Even if the battery storage units can be installed without any disruptive excavation being carried out, potential leakage from the batteries will contaminate sub-surface archaeology. NOTE other documents submitted make reference to cut and fill operations, which would destroy any archaeology in the affected area. The conclusion to this report focuses on designated heritage, however it is the undiscovered archaeology that must be identified and protected here. The report highlights human activity across the site, continuously, from the earliest times. Another site with less historic interest should be considered. Photographs - The photos annexed to this document show clearly the site’s elevated and prominent position. It has commanding views out to the city and surrounding countryside, so views to the site will be equally clear. Notice to the Scottish Ministers. to construct and operate a battery energy storage facility. The Notice describes the development as: “.battery energy storage facility with associated infrastructure, substation, security fencing, CCTV, security lighting and landscaping” The visual impact of security fencing surrounding the site will be inappropriate and out of keeping in a rural area. Security lighting cannot be entertained in a rural area. Light pollution will have a detrimental impact on the amenity and wellbeing of local residents. Further, lighting of this type is known to have a detrimental effect on night-flying creatures like bats. The light alters their flight paths and interferes with their feeding patterns. [ORGANIZATION] [ORGANIZATION] has been appointed to act on behalf of the developer, [ORGANIZATION]. Their website contains a section, titled “How will the local community benefit from this proposal?” This goes on to explain “The proposed battery storage facility will benefit UK consumers as a whole by facilitating the supply of low-cost, low carbon electricity on the national grid.” In fact, [ORGANIZATION] are unable to state ANY benefits to the local community from this development. Pre-application Consultation Report - [ORGANIZATION] No comment at this stage. Design and Access Statement (DDA) - [ORGANIZATION] The Introduction (item 1.4) makes reference to: “Policy 14 of the National Planning Framework 4 (NPF4) states how the planning system should “encourage, promote and facilitate well designed development that makes successful places by taking a design-led approach and applying the Place Principle.” Annex D of NPF4 then lays out the ‘Six Qualities of Successful Places’, with quality number 2 ‘Pleasant’ emphasising the importance of creating “attractive and welcoming” places which mitigate against noise, air and light pollution, as well as avoiding undesirable features.” This is indefensible. There is not a single instance, in this development, where “design” can be seen to have been used. The battery facility will be a scar on the landscape; its location and topography will exacerbate its inappropriate scale and the batteries themselves are industrial in nature. The site enclosure and floodlighting will be reminiscent of a high security institution. (item 1.5) Place Principle. Whilst public consultation has taken place, this has only alerted the local community to the blight to the countryside and their lifestyle, which is proposed here. Property values will be destroyed and the rural amenity local people have enjoyed, will be removed. Discussions with local people cannot and will not result in this development becoming acceptable. The very nature of the proposal is so alien to this place that no amount of “tweaking” will resolve concerns. (item 2.1) The Site. The DDA states the facility will connect to the grid via [PLACE] and [PLACE] substations. This is different to the information on AAH’s website (see above) but nevertheless, these substations are remote from this site, reinforcing the suggestion this location is not critically important to the functioning of the grid feed-in. (item 2.3) Flooding. Please confirm if the SEPA records, referred to, factor-in climate change? SEPA is updating their data, currently, to reflect climate change and this often results in a very different picture for sites where a low risk was indicated previously. NPF4 recommends that no development should take place on land at risk of flooding and certainly, where electricity and hazardous chemicals are involved, this must surely be avoided completely. NOTE Raising of equipment to avoid flooding will only increase the visual impact of the proposals. (item 3.4) Sustainability. This development is not sustainable if leakage from batteries renders the land barren and unusable for future generations and these risks have not been explored, fully. (item 3.5) Mitigation. How will the loss of natural habitat be mitigated? Were the development located on brownfield land, this would not be an issue. (item 3.7) Planning. Since this application will be determined by the Scottish Ministers and NOT the local planning authority, please confirm how the planning system will form part of this process? (item 3.8 and 3.0) Planning Policy and Guidelines. Whilst relevant policies are identified, the DDA does not delve into these nor expand on how the proposals comply. With regard to Policy 1, this only considers renewable energy installations to be appropriate “in principle”. It is worth exploring, too, whether the proposals do, in fact, constitute a renewable energy development or rather, is battery storage an adjunct to that industry, which comes with a host of issues, which need to be overcome. Not least of these are the visual impact implications and risks to health and wellbeing. (item 4.4) Temporary development. Please clarify the finite lifespan of the development. (item 5.3) Scale. The size of the development is stated as filling the land available. This is not a calculated justification for the proposals scale. It is noted in 5.7 the scale is required for viability, however the measure of this is not stated. (item 5.11) States the development is of an appropriate scale. This is the opinion of the applicant and therefore cannot be taken at face value. Comparing the proposals with other land uses in the vicinity demonstrates clearly how out-of-scale this development will be in this location, where other structures comprise dispersed single houses and farm buildings. (Image 5.1) Proposed Layout. The proposed site access is too far up [PLACE], meaning construction and then operating vehicles will clash with other road users over a greater length of road than is necessary. Far more information is required on proposed screening, by way of planning and bunding. There is no key provided to accompany the layout. (item 5.15) Access and security. The measures described will be completely out of character here. Widening the road, as described, will destroy natural habitat and is likely to encourage joy-riders in this remote location. There is no description of the boundary fencing proposed in this document but the pole-mounted CCTV cameras and security lighting suggest a grim and hostile appearance, which is unacceptable. (item 5.17/ 5.18) Landscaping. Please explain how the introduction of c. 30 Ha of battery storage along with a high security enclosure and lighting will “preserve and enhance the existing landscape features.” The retention of hedgerows will not compensate for the destruction of a large swath of natural land where ground-dwelling plants and animals reside. (item 5.19) Appearance. The overall appearance of the proposed development will NOT be “.sympathetic and in keeping with the surrounding context”. This is simply not true and it defies understanding how [ORGANIZATION] can promote this view. (items 5.2 – 5.23) Access. The disruption that will be caused to local residents during the 24-month construction phase is unacceptable. (item 6.2) Carbon reduction. This is acknowledged as vital to the future of the planet but if a natural and wild place needs to be destroyed to facilitate this, what’s the point? What are we saving the planet for? Outline Safety Management Plan - [ORGANIZATION] (item 1.5) The battery technology system to be employed has not been chosen yet, so this document is irrelevant, other than it flags up there ARE risks to those, out-with the site, to: - Fire - Explosion - Release of harmful gases The document states that detection and suppression systems will be put in place but by the time an alert is raised, the accident has already happened. All the systems do is attempt to minimise its impact. This is not acceptable to adjacent property owners; indeed, the release of harmful gases could affect those living remotely to the site too. Noise Impact Assessment – Professional Consult As noted previously, local neighbours should expect a zero decibel effect from the development. Landscape and Visual Impact Assessment - [ORGANIZATION] No further comment at this time. Landscape Proposal Drawings - [ORGANIZATION] Drwg No APA-PL-01 Whilst the proposed tree planting is welcomed, the size of tree specimens proposed (6080cm) is inadequate. The mitigating effect of the new woodland will not be established for 15-20 years, which is not acceptable. Heavy standards should be used throughout and a programme of maintenance and replacement put in place from the outset.
