Consideration should be given to bunding between new planting and the battery storage containers. Transport Statement – [ORGANIZATION] 21,190 two-way vehicle trips during construction is unacceptable. Six-day working week is unacceptable. The impact on other road users during construction is unacceptable. Danger to other road users from construction traffic is too great. Preliminary Ecological Appraisal – [ORGANIZATION] Concerns about impact on ecology noted elsewhere. Access Gate and Fencing (drawing) - [ORGANIZATION] The appearance of this style of fencing is unacceptable in this location. A boundary fence location plan is required. Any fencing required must be located to the inside of any landscape buffer. Appendix B2 Accurate Visual Representation and Methodology Slide Viewpoint 8 – Year 1 demonstrates clearly the extremely adverse visual impact presented by this elevated site. According to the subsequent slide, it will take 15 years for the screening planning to have its proper effect. This is not acceptable. LIDAR data is limited and the visuals produced using LIDAR are not useful representation of actual situations. CONCLUSION Until the advent of NPF4, Development in the countryside came under the utmost scrutiny and an assumption against development was made in most cases. The new guidelines, which seem to favour developments such as this; where a “green” or “sustainability” label can be attached, appear to attract no such attention. Indeed, they are encouraged without the usual means of recourse. However, due care must be exercised by any local authority that supports such a venture. This is unknown and untried territory with both real and perceived levels of risk to health and life, not to mention the impact the development will have on the visual amenity of this beautiful rural area and the lives of the families who live here. The [ORGANIZATION] website tries to justify the use of agricultural land as follows: “The draft National Policy Statement for Renewable Energy (EN-3) confirms that Agricultural Land Classification (ALC) should not be the predominant test in site selection.” This conflicts strongly with the overarching principles of NPF4, which promotes the protection of natural habitat and creation of places where biodiversity can thrive as being of paramount importance in planning decision-making. It appears these sentiments have been lost in our eagerness to embrace renewable energy systems, at all costs.

[ORGANIZATION] Planning Services By E-Mail: [EMAIL] 23 May 2024 Dear Sir/Madam, Objection to Application Reference [APPLICATION_CODE] for "Construction and operation of a 40 MW battery energy storage facility together with associated infrastructure, substation, security fencing, cctv, security lighting and landscaping" [ORGANIZATION] has been instructed on behalf of our clients to prepare this letter of objection on behalf of those who will be impacted by planning application reference [APPLICATION_CODE] at the "Land East of Site of [PLACE]". The proposed development provides for the "Construction and operation of a 40 MW battery energy storage facility together with associated infrastructure, substation, security fencing, cctv, security lighting and landscaping". Those submitting this letter in objection to application reference [APPLICATION_CODE] do so on the basis that the proposed development conflicts with the policies of the Development Plan. For the avoidance of doubt, the development plan comprises the [PLACE] Local Development Plan 2 (LDP2) which was adopted on the 31st March 2022 and the National Planning Framework 4 (adopted February 2023). Where there is tension between the LDP2 and NPF4, the most recent Plan carries supremacy. The LDP2 was prepared with the emerging NPF4 (at the time) and there is little tension between the Plans, and none that bear relevance to this objection. The following topic areas will be explored below Principle of development; Landscape and design; Historic assets; and, Environmental Health, Health and safety We have identified conflicts with the following policies of the Development Plan. There are no material considerations that outweigh the conflicts given the harm identified. On the contrary, there are material considerations that outweigh the benefits of the proposed development. As such, and in accordance with Section 38(6) of the Planning and Compulsory Purchase Act 2004 and Section 37(2) of the Town and Country Planning Act (Scotland) 1997, the development proposal should be refused. Conflict is clearly identified with the following Development Plan policies: NPF4 Policy 4 Biodiversity Policy 7 Historic Assets Policy 8 Green Belts Policy 9 Brownfield, vacant and derelict land Policy 11 Energy Policy 14 Liveable Places Policy 23 Health and Safety LDP2 Policy D1: Placemaking and Design Policy D3: Green Belt and Countryside around Towns (CAT) Policy D14: Management and Protection of the Built Heritage Policy D15: Listed Buildings Policy E5: Noise Impacts We identify the conflict with these policies through our discussion of the topic areas below. Further, the proposed development is in conflict with the "Health and safety in grid scale electrical energy storage systems" government guidance published on the 18th April 2024. The paper can be found here: [LINK] and-safety/health-and-safety-in-grid-scaleelectrical-energy-storage-systems-accessible-webpage. Principle of Development Green Belt. Renewable Energy Development? Summary: The proposed development is not a renewable energy development and so it conflicts with NPF4 Policy 11 and LDP2 Policy D3. For clarity, the proposed development is for a 40mW battery energy storage facility and ancillary development. The proposed development will not generate electricity. There is no air/sun/water driven energy generating facility proposed as part of this development. At Section 1.3 of their Design and Planning Supporting Statement (DPSS) the applicant's planning consultant introduces the proposed development as: S1.3 "The proposed development would allow electricity from the national grid to be stored in batteries at times of low demand and then exported back to the grid at times of high demand." At Section 3.26 of the same document a table is presented. The applicant describes the development in the final row of the table as: S3.26, Table, Final Row: "The proposed development is an energy storage facility" At Section 5.5 of the same document the proposed development is described as: S5.5: "[.] a backup supply to the National Grid and allows for balancing of the network when there is an excess or a shortage of electricity to ensure a constant energy supply, particularly with the increase in renewable energy sources as part of the move to a low-carbon economy." [our emphasis]. The proposal is therefore very clearly merely a means of electrical energy storage (generated by any means) and not a renewable energy generator. Yet the applicant champions the proposed development's renewable energy credentials. The "Need" section (at DPSS S5.4 - 5.5) and "Principle of Development" section (at DPSS S5.12 -5.14) stem from a supposed baseline that this proposed development is a renewable energy development. It is not. The LDP2 and NPF4 identify what renewable energy development is for the applicant and so it is not clear on what basis they can consider battery storage to be renewable energy. Borrowing from a policy that will be discussed in due course, NPF4 Policy 11 on Energy supports all forms of renewable, low carbon and zero emission technologies including battery storage. However it does not set out that battery storage is a renewable energy technology, rather that it belongs to the group of "renewable, low carbon or zero emission". The objector in this case wholly accepts that battery storage is a low carbon technology - but it is not a renewable energy development on its own. The site is within the Green Belt, therefore NPF4 Policy 8 on Green Belts is particularly relevant. Policy 8 is explicit that development in the Green Belt will only be supported if, among other things, it belonged to "minerals operations and renewable energy developments". It is important to remember that the proposed development does not generate any renewable energy, and its purpose is purely to support the national grid where the energy is supplied by any variety of sources, potentially including coal, oil and gas produced domestically or imported. There is no indication that the battery storage would only be charged by renewable energy generators, or even that it would facilitate any specific renewable energy developments. It may be charged with any energy provided via the grid. Had the Policy 8 sought to support battery storage, low carbon, or zero emission development in the Green Belt then it would have said that - yet it does not. The policy is explicit that renewable energy developments are acceptable developments in the Green Belt. The proposed development is battery storage, and directly in conflict with Policy 8. Equally, LDP2 Policy D3 on Green Belt and Countryside around Towns is explicit that developments will be supported in principle where they are for, among other things, renewable energy, however this proposal is not. Returning to Policy 11, the proposed development can be supported by NPF4 because it is a form of energy storage. However, such developments can only be supported where impacts on: individual dwellings; landscape and visual receptors; the historic environment are considered, and only where the development proposal examines the future decommissioning of the development (we deal with this latter point below). Biodiversity Summary: The proposed development does not appear to provide any contribution to the enhancement of biodiversity as required by NPF4 Policy 3. It is a requirement for development proposals to contribute to the enhancement of biodiversity. This is set out in NPF4 Policy 3a and the development proposals do not appear to offer, with the exception of a single sentence at the end of the supporting Preliminary Ecology Report, any tangible evidence that biodiversity enhancements will be provided by the proposal. NFP 4 Policy 3b requires development proposals for major development to demonstrate that they will conserve, restore and enhance biodiversity, however no evidence of this has been provided by the applicant. On that, the proposal as read simply does not comply with NPF4 Policy 3. Site Specific Assessment and Greenfield Land Summary: No assessment has been carried out to identify that land beyond the Green Belt is unsuitable and that only land within the Green Belt is suitable for this proposed development, in breach of NPF4 Policy 8. The proposal is on a greenfield site which is not supported by NPF4 Policy 9. NPF4 Policy 8 requires that reasons are provided as to why a Green Belt location is essential and why it cannot be located on an alternative site outwith the Green Belt. The applicant's Design and Planning Supporting Statement has not provided or alluded to any technical drawings or papers that establish why this specific site was chosen for this application. One would have expected to see a map or plan identifying which sites were being pursued at the onset of the project, and why the other land parcels have been discounted. This might be similar to how a sequential test would be carried out, concluding on this site being the most appropriate notwithstanding its Green Belt location. The applicant has not sought to produce any evidence for this, other than throwaway lines that the site needs a willing landowner (DPSS S5.24; S5.28), a general proximity within a viable grid connection (DPSS S5.25), a need for this development to be in a rural location (DPSS S5.26). A justification for this is further set out at Section 5.26 setting out: S5.26 "As grid connection points tend to be focused around significant population centres such as [PLACE], suitable locations for BESS within viable distances to grid connection points will often be within the designated green belt which surrounds such conurbations". It cannot be accepted that, merely because Battery Storage developments may be better suited to rural locations, that means that Green Belt locations are the only suitable sites for such developments. Without any tangible evidence to the contrary, the proposed development is further in conflict with Policy 8. Further, NPF4 Policy 9 provides that proposals on greenfield sites will not be supported unless the site has been allocated for development or the proposal is explicitly supported by policies in the LDP. The land is not allocated for development, nor does the LDP explicitly support the development proposal at this Green Belt location. On that, this proposal conflicts with NPF4 Policy 9. Decommissioning and Site Restoration Summary: No indicative or detailed decommissioning or restoration plan is proposed, and funds are not shown to be safeguarded in breach of NPF4 Policy 11. NPF4 Policy 11 requires that the applicant addresses proposals for decommissioning and safeguarded or guaranteed finances to implement these plans. There is absolutely no evidence that these matters have been considered. No decommissioning plan has been proposed in either a full or indicative layout, and no evidence that finances have been guaranteed or safeguarded has been provided. This is a conflict with NPF4 Policy 11. Landscape and Design Summary: Even after 15 years of planting growth there is still recognised harm to the landscape, in breach of NPF4 Policy 14, and LDP2 Policy D1 and Policy D3. Furthermore, the design of the proposed development invites risk and harm and does not represent good placemaking and design in conflict with LPD2 Policy D1. Landscape NPF4 Policy 14 on Liveable Places explains that, regardless of scale, development proposals will be designed to improve the quality of an area whether in urban or rural locations. The submitted Landscape and Visual Appraisal speaks of a construction phase, and operation phase. The construction phase will have moderate negative impacts and moderate adverse effects on the rural countryside. The proposal suggests that mitigation can be incorporated through planting. Therefore in the operation phase, the assessment focuses on the impacts in year 1 and year 15, where the planting is fresh and mature respectively. Year 1 is put forward by the applicant as having a slight negative and minor adverse impact on the landscape. Figure 1 below illustrates this 'slight negative and minor adverse impact'. One cannot reasonably consider that this only 'slight' and instead this this represents significant harm to the landscape. At year 15, shown below at figure 2, the LVA continues to document a slight negative and minor adverse impact. That means that even after 15 years (of what it supposed to be a 40 year development) there is still harm. Of the eight viewpoints where data is provided for assessment, the LVA reports there is high sensitivity from viewpoint 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8, or in other words, all 8 viewpoints of high sensitivity will receive harm. These images clearly show the harm of the development on the quality of the area. Furthermore, the landscape here is open and the proposed mitigation will substantially 'close off' the existing views. Therefore it is clear that the proposed development will cause landscape visual harm from the outset, and then for 15 years while the planting is establishing, and even after then, it will still cause harm. It cannot therefore be said to improve the quality of the area, in breach of NPF4 Policy 14. The Report of Handling for application reference [APPLICATION_CODE] regarding the "Erection of church building and dwellinghouse with associated accesses and associated works" was issued in 2024 and this regards land only ~250m north of this proposed development. In that case, for a church and a dwellinghouse, Officers' professional conclusion was that: "In terms of the whole development, the proposal would lead to the loss of a highly visible part of the green network close to a principal road junction. This would be to the detriment of the overall integrity of the green network and would detract from the character and amenity of the area and would be contrary to Policy 20 of NPF4 and Policy D4 of LDP2." Notwithstanding that the application site in this case is not in the green network, the same themes of detracting from the character and amenity of the area do carry through, and conflict with policy D1 (Placemaking and Design) and policy D3 (Green Belt and Countryside around Towns (CAT)) of LPD2. Design The proposed indicative drainage layout (drawing no. 137-DR-IN-1001) states plainly that the entrance road will be by a culvert or a ford over the existing water course. The scale of the plan is difficult to extract topographical data from, however it does appear to recognise that there is approximately a 5ft sheer drop to the water course. The plan is marked "For Approval" which suggests it may not have had final sign-off. That would make sense as a crossing with a 5ft drop does not seem like good design. It appears that the plans fail to note this would still be a 5ft drop on either side once the road was cut through the hedge to provide the access. This drop would require a slope which would presumably completely cover the road culvert. In addition, if this water course was damaged a public health concern would emerge. That is because it holds the outflow from the septic tank of the 2 neighbouring residential properties, which is shown as a high flood risk zone in the SEPA maps. The septic tank drains through the culvert under the road, directly to the area of the proposed entrance road and there is no recognition of that in the applicant's submission. The surface water runoff pond is listed on the drawing as a possible water supply for fire emergencies - this pond is more than 5m below the BESS site and has no access without passing the battery storage site as there is no other access point. This is clearly not a feasible water source in case of emergency as it is reasonable to consider the access may become obstructed. On this, the design of the proposed development conflicts with LDP Policy D1. Historic Assets Summary: The proposed development causes unmitigated harm on the [PLACE] Category C Listed Building and no mitigations have been designed or proposed to alleviate that harm, contrary to NPF4 Policy 7 and LDP Policy D15. The proposed development will impact on Category C listed buildings. The application is accompanied by a Historic Environment Impact Assessment (HEIA). The figures up to 3b inclusive are blank and show nothing. Under the section "Potential Indirect Impacts of the Proposal" (S82 - 86) the document states at S82: "The grouped components of the Battery Energy Storage System have the potential to generate a significant adverse effect on the setting of historic environment sites within the study area and, reasonably, on significant designated sites within its immediate visual envelope taken to be a distance of up to 1km from the outer boundary of the Study area." The HEIA sets out that mitigation measures will only include archaeological works investigations, and no mitigation is offered which might offset harm to the heritage assets. NPF4 Policy 7 on Historic Assets and Places requires that where impacts cannot be avoided that they should be minimised. The proposed development therefore only offers harm to the assets and no demonstration regarding how the harm has been minimised has been put forward by the applicant. LDP Policy D14 seeks to safeguard, preserve and enhance built heritage and is clear that proposals likely to affect these assets will not be supported. LDP Policy D15 requires that new development is appropriate to the character and appearance of a listed building and its setting, and the proposed development therefore conflicts with these policies. Further, it is local knowledge that the [PLACE] listed building does not have foundations. However the proposed development requires the relocation of bus stops and works at the [PLACE] road to create an access directly opposite the heritage asset. There is no evidence that these considerable works will not cause any shift in the land, which has the potential to be exceptionally damaging to the heritage asset due to its lack of foundation. Without evidence to the contrary, it cannot be claimed that the proposed development will ensure the heritage assets are safeguarded, preserved and enhanced, contrary to LPD Policy D14. Environmental Health, Health and Safety Summary: The proposed development conflicts with LDP Policy E5 and NPF4 Policy 23 regarding an increased level of noise without mitigation that will contribute to an unacceptable impact on amenity. There is a gas mains pipeline within the redline boundary of the site, and the proposal further conflicts with NPF Policy 23 with regards to safety, and fire safety in particular. The policy requires development proposals to consider the associated risks of and potential impacts of the proposal and the gas pipeline, however the development proposal apparently has no recognition of good fire practice and does not consider the potential impacts of the proposal or the pipeline. The Government has published guidance for this type of development during the planning stage, which although is not part of the development plan, does form a material consideration. The proposed development does not accord with this guidance. Noise LPD Policy E5 on Noise Impacts says the impact of noise will be taken into account when assessing relevant development proposals, particularly those that are close to or could become a source of noise. In this case, the existing noise baseline is not presently at an unacceptable level however the proposed development will contribute to more noise. The NIA sets out that, at Section 5.1.8 that with mitigation, the rated level of noise generated will be less than +4dB above the typical daytime and night-time background sound level and that level of noise is not unacceptable. It is not immediately clear what the increased noise level will be with mitigation though and it is clear from the development proposals that no mitigation has been proposed. It stands to reason then, that without mitigation the proposed development may have an unacceptable impact on the residential receptors. Even if mitigation had been proposed with regards to the decibel level, battery storage areas require significant cooling machinery to maintain stable temperatures which include air conditioning units that emit an irritating acoustic tonality. This type of noise is very different to people making garden chatter and will be relentlessly irritating to the nearby residential receptors. NPF4 Policy 23 and LPD2 Policy E5 do not accept development proposals where unacceptable noise impacts are imposed, particularly on residential receptors. On that, without mitigation, the proposed development conflicts with the NPF4 Policy 23 and LDP Policy E5. Fire, Health and Safety The purpose of NPF4 Policy 23 is to protect people and places from harm. The site occupies a high pressure gas main, and the development comprises a proposed development which, in the event of a fire, is particularly hazardous. Policy 23 sets out development proposals within the vicinity of a major accident hazard site or major accident hazard pipeline (because of the presence of toxic, highly reactive, explosive or inflammable substances) will consider the associated risks and potential impacts of the proposal and the major accident hazard site/pipeline of being located in proximity to one another. The Design and Planning Supporting Statement does not refer to the "Health and safety in Grid Scale Electrical Storage Systems" guidance published by the UK government online on the 18th April 2024: [LINK] and-safety/health-and-safety-in-grid-scaleelectrical-energy-storage-systems-accessible-webpage While this document is not adopted planning policy, it does represent a material consideration. That document is very clear the fire service should be consulted at the design and planning stage as an important stakeholder. Section 1.1 states: "The complexity of the landscape, with a plethora of standards (some with overlapping requirements), can be a barrier to the development of BESS in line with appropriate regulations and health and safety (H&S) standards. This highlights the need for robust, clear guidelines for grid-scale battery systems so that all stakeholders can understand good-practice and are implementing the correct health & safety measures throughout the BESS lifecycle." It would appear that the applicant has no contact with Scottish Fire and Rescue service, and they state they will create an emergency response plan during the detail design phase, post planning. However, section 3 is clear the guidance has been prepared for the Design & Planning stage, so it is inappropriate to defer contact to a post consent phase. At Section 3.1, the guidance advises that: "There should be a full consideration of risks including, but not limited to, accidental or intentional damage and natural phenomena and security. Note that risk assessments should be bidirectional - i.e., include both risks to the project and from the project. The planning process should assess the following risks and describe how the credible worst case has been mitigated.". However no risk assessment has been provided by the applicant. The guidance is explicit at 3.1.1 that: "Due to the potential hazards to the surroundings of any BESS, careful considerations must be made as to its location to determine the risks that the storage proposes. With lithium-based technologies, thermal runaway is a key failure mode which can lead to hazards to the nearby environment. Thermal runaway can be caused by a wide variety of internal and external factors, including physical damage, misuse, aging and fluctuating temperatures outside of the safe temperature range. Thermal runaway can lead to: Fire Explosion release of toxic gases or water run-off These hazards pose a serious risk to the immediate vicinity of any BESS, which places an emphasis on the consideration of site location." On that, the potential risks are matters that are advised to be examined at the planning stage and in this development proposal, there has been no examination. Section 3.2.2.2 on "Monitoring, fire detection and suppression" further reinforces the need for "Engagement with the Fire and Rescue Service at this stage of development will also enable fire suppression systems to be aligned with a wider firefighting strategy." however again it is important and a material consideration to recognise that no contact has been made with the fire service. At Section 3.3.1 the guidance sets out: "Studies and risk assessments for the local ecosystems must be considered in site proposals, as the release of potentially harmful gases and chemicals could cause irreparable damage to the nearby environment. [13]". However, consistently, no emergency plan has been put forward by the applicant, and the site proposes to drain directly into the white cart water source. With regards to site layout, Section 3.4 explains that the layout of proposed site is key to its safety, with regard to mitigating the effects of fire and in ensuring access for staff and emergency services. Under "emergency scenarios" the guidance considers how emergency responders, such the Fire and Rescue Service or paramedics, can obtain access to and move around the site in the event of a fire or other emergency. The guidance is clear that emergency response arrangements and preparedness plans should be developed as early as possible and considered at every stage of the development. It is important that the site has more than one access - however this proposed development only has one access which does not conform to the guidance's advice on design. On a lack of evidence to the contrary, it appears then the developer has not made any attempt to involve the fire and rescue service in advance of submitting this application, or perhaps they did however the response was not what the developer would like to publish. It is recognised that at S1.7 of the Design and Planning Supporting Statement, the applicant's planning agent has stated: "The current design has been drawn up to be as flexible as possible to allow for a variety of battery solutions for this 40 MW scheme" This all appears to have been written without sight of the "Health and Safety in Grid scale electrical energy storage systems" noted above wherein it is put forward that it is important to understand what specific form of battery technology is being proposed as this is directly important for fire and rescue services. Given there is an added threat at this site, i.e. a gas pipeline, any risk and consequence of fire is presumably greater and it is disconcerting that the developer has been entirely unspecific on this matter. On this, it appears that the applicant has not considered the associated risks and potential impacts of the proposal as required by the NPF4. As such, the proposed development conflicts with NPF4 Policy 23.

My family and I live at the above address, an historic former hunting lodge registered with [PLACE]. Our land includes registered ancient woodland with legally protected wildlife species present. Our home lies less than 1 km (approx. 700m) from the proposed development site and I therefore believe our concerns should be taken very seriously when considering approval of this application! Fire Safety – the anxiety and fear created by the prospect of living near one of these dangerous installations is very real. The developer states that they “WILL” produce an emergency response plan before construction begins, i.e. they haven’t actually produced one yet – this is completely unacceptable and alone is grounds to reject this application! There is no mains water at this site, no pressurised hydrants available, is a considerable distance from any local fire- stations, (retained service in [PLACE] is 16 miles and manned station in [PLACE] is 30 miles) only has one main access into the site for use by emergency services, there are no stated plans on how contaminated water will be contained and not allowed into the neighbouring burn that flows to [PLACE] and the [PLACE] and the site is surrounded by flammable woodland. The applicant stated at their consultation that fires would be left to burn out BUT copious amounts of water are still required to cool the thermal runaway reaction and stop the fire spreading to neighbouring containers and potentially exploding - The [ORGANIZATION] 2023 Guidance advises that sites should be capable of delivering no less than 1,900 litres per minute for at least 2 hours, where will all this water come from? They also said that toxic fumes “should disperse” before reaching neighbouring properties, including ours, but what about our prevailing westerly winds? – this is just not acceptable! A full and detailed fire safety plan should be in place BEFORE this application is even considered. Protected wildlife – Considering the size and scale of this development and its rural location, it is very disappointing that an EIA has not been compulsory! The developer states that pre-construction surveys WILL be carried out i.e. have NOT be completed yet and this again is grounds for this application to be refused! Previous surveys carried out for a wind farm, the substation and cable connections confirmed the presence of protected species including otters, badgers, pine martins and water voles, as well as red squirrels and mountain hare and there may well be bats there too. There is also the birdlife that is regularly observed in this area including the locally nesting osprey, golden eagle, red kites that nest in our garden, golden plover, merlin, hen harrier and greylag geese. It is NOT acceptable that this applicant be granted permission to develop a site that could potentially destroy the habitats of legally protected species and then only investigate their presence after permission is granted – this should and must be a requirement BEFORE the application is considered. This goes against NPF4 policy 1 – tackling the nature crisis and policy 4 - natural places. Trees – The Scottish Government policy is opposed to permanent removal of woodland for the purposes of conversion to another land use unless it would achieve significant public benefits, which this development will not. There is also an area of ancient woodland (Scots pine) identified on this site – who will be responsible for its protection? NPF4 also supports protecting, enhancing and improving woodlands. Need – this tiny community has ALREADY had 3 x up to 50MW battery storage facilities approved – [PLACE] Battery Storage ref: [APPLICATION_CODE], [PLACE] Wind farm Ext 11 including battery storage ref: [APPLICATION_CODE] and [PLACE] including battery storage ref: [APPLICATION_CODE]. These are all within a few miles of this proposed development. We do NOT need ANOTHER huge 200MW battery storage facility within our small rural community! In addition, a FOI request regarding BESS (via EIA, Scotland, no. [APPLICATION_CODE]) states that Scotland will need 6.2GW of BESS (output) by 2030 and 7.1GW by 2050 yet the Renewables Database published by DESNEZ to October 2024 shows a total of 21GW already approved or in operation – ie 3 TIMES the requirement to be installed in Scotland by 2050 – we do NOT NEED any more! Cumulative impact – the area surrounding this proposed development already has a great deal of energy related infrastructure – [PLACE] Wind Farm, plus extension 1, [PLACE], upgraded 132KV pylon line, [PLACE] plus [PLACE] Wind Farm Ext 2, [PLACE] and [PLACE] BESS also consented but not yet built and another wind farm at [PLACE] proposed. This area has already done its fair share for renewable energy. We are being unfairly targeted due to our sparce population and our voices are not being heard – this is undemocratic. In addition, the bigger picture of all these developments combined is not being considered e.g. whilst [ORGANIZATION] claim they will use trees to screen this development, [ORGANIZATION] say they will need to fell the very same trees for a potential wind farm grid connection for the proposed [PLACE] wind farm! [PLACE] wind farm will also need a connection to the substation so this development could actually conflict with the connection of other renewable energy projects. Inappropriate size for the location – this 200MW development is HUGE, covering an 18.3 ha site with up to 72 battery containers that will be seen from the surrounding hillsides, plus the [PLACE] and main route to the west, if the existing tree cover intended for screening is not properly managed and preserved. Such a huge facility should not be subjected on such a small rural community – this is the wrong development in the wrong place. No local socio-economic benefit – NPF4 policy 11(C) Energy states that there must be economic benefit to the local area by way of employment, associated business and supply chain opportunities. All the developer is offering is to work with local schools to encourage careers in STEM and renewable energy. This is simply a PR exercise promoting their own company and has no direct benefit to communities whose schools are already well equipped and actively promoting STEM related careers, without the need for developer involvement. There are no community benefit funds going to be paid, there are not going to be any employment opportunities apart from possible short-term work during the construction phase, the energy being stored will not be for local community use but instead transported south to areas of greater need, no reduction in electricity prices for this community that is hosting all the infrastructure. This does NOT comply with NPF4 policy 11. Poor Community Consultation and Engagement – at the local consultation events the developer had poor quality maps, was unable to answer very basic questions, had failed to advertise in the most popular local paper leaving many locals unaware, and demonstrated very little local knowledge and research including other battery storage facilities that have already been approved. They appeared uninterested in community feedback and the events seemed to be the opportunity to simply tick boxes for the planning process. Their online information and promotional material were also very poor quality. Precedent for future development – if this facility is granted planning permission, where will it end? Will the substation need to be further extended? Yet more pylon lines be built? We have enough infrastructure already! Proximity to homes – this development lies less than 300 meters from a residential property and family home and less than 1km (approx. 700m) from ours. Facilities like these should be developed on brown field sites, closer to the area where the energy is actually needed. Impact on people – whilst these developments are being targeted in rural locations with low populations, the reality is that people living in the vicinity are suffering a high level of mental anguish and worry regarding how such a development will affect their health and wellbeing. It is stated that there will be 5.1m lights that not only will be seen from great distances but will have a negative impact on the dark skies that are enjoyed locally. How much noise will be produced? How thorough are the surveys conducted on the impact all this will actually have on the local residents? Access / traffic – the amount of traffic, noise, pollution and disturbance this development will generate will have a significant impact on local residents during the 2 years of construction and the [PLACE] has become busier in recent years with the promotion of the [PLACE] route. They state in their application that this access has been used previously during wind farm construction – this is completely untrue! When E-ON applied for planning permission to build [PLACE] they had intended to use the [PLACE] for access to the site but the [ORGANIZATION] insisted that access be via the more appropriate [PLACE] instead, NOT at [PLACE]. No contribution to the climate emergency – the majority of the public “believe” this development will store renewable energy from the neighbouring wind farms and therefore make a contribution to net zero targets and saving the planet. However, these batteries will be charged when energy is at it’s cheapest, usually in the middle of the night when the wind isn’t blowing and the sun isn’t shining, directly from the grid, therefore having a high percentage of fossil fuels, NOT renewables. This stored energy will then be sold back to the grid at peak demand when the prices are at their highest. This is PURELY about the applicant making profits through arbitrage as they are energy traders. Planning policy – whilst NPF4 supports the development of renewable energy generation, this is NOT energy production, but storage, and NOT storage of renewables but simply energy trading using the grid. NPF4 policy 11 Energy does support battery storage but ONLY where they maximise net economic impact, and in this case, with no direct benefit to the local community, this development does not meet the aims of NPF4. In addition, it does not demonstrate the enhancement of biodiversity stated in policy 3 of NPF4. It appears that the land they intend to regenerate would be replanted anyway as part of the tree management plan already in place, and this would therefore NOT constitute enhancement and should not be supported on this basis. Benefit vs environmental damage – stating the size of a battery storage facility in MW is very misleading and should be MWh. This development will result in tree removal, damage and removal of carbon storing peat, destruction of wet heathland, wildlife (including protected species) and habitats, permanent and irreversible affect on visual amenity and for what gain? This facility, as confirmed by the applicant, will store energy that will last for a maximum of just 2 hours!! Does the gain outweigh the destruction? Mitigation measures – the developer plans to use existing trees for screening and also do compensatory planting. However, it is unclear whether they intend planting trees further up the hill, which is unlikely to produce good quality woodland due to the poor soil quality, or on the land where felling has already taken place, and will therefore be due for replanting anyway, so will NOT be compensatory. Any compensatory planting and existing trees being used for screening should either be under developer ownership or managed by a 3rd party to ensure they are maintained for their intended purpose. As mentioned above, it looks like existing trees planned to be used for screening are under threat from other renewable developments so should not be relied upon. Adverse impact on landscape – the sheer number of energy developments in this small community has had a huge affect on the landscape of this beautiful glen which in turn affects tourism and the local business that depend on it. This HUGE industrial development with fencing and floodlighting will have a significant visual impact on the surrounding landscape. Flooding – the landslip scars on the hillside above the proposed development are lasting evidence of the horrific flooding of 2017 and the impact potential flooding would have on this project does not seem to have been fully investigated or addressed. How “Green” is this development? – whilst the obsession to hit net zero targets continues the environmental impact during the manufacture of these lithium-ion batteries seems to be ignored – what about the mining of the rare metals? The significant emissions during the manufacturing process? The use of forced labour and abuse of human rights? The hazardous processes and chemical used in manufacture and the inability to recycle? Just because these do not occur on our shores does not mean they are not negatively contributing to the very climate crisis we are supposed to be tackling. There are significant environmental impacts arising throughout the lifecycle of battery storage systems, from raw material extraction to end-of-life disposal. Key issues include resource depletion, greenhouse gas emissions, and pollution from mining activities. The applicant – whilst the history of the developer is not taken as a material consideration, morally and for due diligence their background should be! [PERSON] (a former banker energy trader) was the co. founder of Bulb that went bust leaving a taxpayer bailout of £6.5bn. He then set up a holding company [ORGANIZATION] in Dec 2020. Under this holding company each of the [ORGANIZATION] sites have been set up as separate limited companies. [ORGANIZATION] was only incorporated in Nov 23 so no Companies House filing to date. The company does not have a long history of battery storage expertise and R&D, but energy trading. I am EXTREMELY concerned about the impact and safety of this proposed development in such close proximity of my home for all the reasons listed above and therefore request that permission be refused.

1. This objection has been prepared in respect of the repeat proposal for the [PLACE] Battery Storage development, [ORGANIZATION] planning application reference [APPLICATION_CODE]. The objection has been prepared by [PERSON] M behalf of the [ORGANIZATION]. 2. The instructions in this case have been issued by the Committee members of the Community Council. The Community Council strongly objects to the proposed development. No formal community meetings were held, but the Community Council contacted approximately 40 neighbours around the proposed development site and all were opposed to the planning application proposals. 3. This application is an identical repeat of the previous battery storage application reference [APPLICATION_CODE]. The community council submitted an objection to that application in August 2021. The application was subsequently refused. As the application is identical and as the supporting visualisations are identical this objection incorporates much of the text of the original objection but is updated, in particular to take account of NPF4, but also to refer to other community concerns. 4. The relevant experience of [PERSON] was set out in the original objection and is not repeated here. 5. The application is proposing an industrial development on agricultural land in a rural location. It would appear that the planning application site has been chosen simply because it is available. Up to 36 storage containers (reduced from up to 50 from the last application but with the same installed capacity) would be set out on the site and surrounded by what is described as low level fencing and landscaping. The output for the proposed facility is quoted as [PLACE] (as with the first application), suspiciously just below the Electricity Act S36 limit of 50MW installed capacity. However, there is no figure given for the storage capacity in terms of how much power can be released before the storage is drained. 6. The application Supporting Statement confirms that the proposal is an energy storage facility and that it is not a form of electrical generation infrastructure. However, the use of the word “storage” is misleading as is the claim for the development being high tech when referring to batteries connected to the UK grid. The implication is that electricity from uncontrollable variable generating sources such as wind farms can be stored at times of surplus and released at times of deficit to balance supply and demand. However, looking at similar proposals throughout Scotland, the size of batteries being installed and the capacity of schemes being planned are only well suited to provide seconds/minutes of grid stability. Proposals such as the [PLACE] battery storage facility are simply too small to balance supply and demand over longer periods of an hour or more. These important and material electrical engineering issues are simply not addressed in the Statement. 7. It is noted that all of the chapters on the Supporting Statement appear to have been written by the same person rather than by separate independent experts. This reduces the weight that can be placed on their conclusions. 8. In terms of the grid connection to the [PLACE] it is understood that the applicants do not control the land that would be needed to deliver this connection. Without demonstrable control over that land the application is once again simply wasting everyone’s time and money. 9. Section 6 of the Statement repeats the earlier assessment of landscape and visual effects alongside addressing the reasons for refusal. The assessment is considered to be insufficient given the highly visible location. It remains the case that only 4 viewpoints are provided in the application material and these do not appear to be to any particular technical specification. Some comments are provided below: a. VP 1 – [PLACE] – this viewpoint, 400m to the south of the application site, significantly underplays the likely visual effect from the 3m high containers, the 4m high fencing and the new landscaping all of which would be a new and alien feature in the view b. VP 2 – to the north of the site – it is not at all clear that the application proposals have been properly scaled in this montage from a location that is just 100m from the site boundary c. VP 3 – [PLACE], 500m to the north of the site – it is unclear what this landscape and visual effects this is meant to show as the written assessment advises that there would be no visibility of the proposal from this location d. VP 4 – [PLACE] to [PLACE], 800m north west of the site – again it is unclear what effects this viewpoint is meant to be illustrating as there would be no visibility 10. In summary there are, therefore, effectively only two viewpoint illustrations that show effects that would appear to be underassessed. As with the first application a much more comprehensive LVIA, including viewpoints that look down into the site from higher elevations and wirelines of the predicted outlook from nearby residential properties, should have been requested from the applicants. 11. Noise is an issue of concern to the local residents as there are already very numerous instances when there is noise impact from the existing substation. Indeed, that noise effect is the subject of ongoing monitoring. There is therefore now a prospect of further noise intrusion. 12. Beyond the above issues it is not considered that it is necessary to set out a detailed rebuttal to every part of the application Supporting Statement (and the associated figures). The primary reason for that is that this is a very poorly chosen location with that choice, poor though it might be, not being justified in the application documentation either in terms of the site itself or in terms of alternatives. That alone should lead to rejection of the proposal. 13. There is some concern around the current legal standing of the applicant company. That is not directly a material planning consideration, but it does mean that a very careful approach is needed in providing for decommissioning at any stage in the life of the project. It is suggested that this should be secured by way of a Section 75 Agreement so that the provisions are binding on both current and future landowners. 14. In recent years it has been realized that the risk of fire from this type of battery storage is a potentially serious hazard that could impact on the local community. That should be taken into consideration by the Council when assessing the application. 15. It is of particular interest for this proposal in this locality since it is well known that the mains water pressure is low, and it is unclear if there would be sufficient water pressure for the [PERSON] to tackle a major fire outbreak. 16. It is considered important to address the potential local and wider cumulative effects in a separate section of the objection prior to considering the assessment of the proposal in terms of the Development Plan. 17. At a local level the localities around [PLACE] are facing the prospects of multiple OHL proposals, new electrical substations and expanded substations. The proposed battery storage facility will be yet another renewable energy development to add to the mix. The Council is asked to consider the local cumulative effects and come to the conclusion that they add to the case for the rejection of this particular proposal. 18. At a wider level there seems to be a considerable number of battery storage planning acts applications and S36 applications coming forward throughout [PLACE] with no overall planned co-ordination and no consistent consideration about how electricity will reach and be transmitted from these disparate sites. The Council is asked to take a clear stance against this proliferation of unplanned proposals. 19. It is noted that the Flood Management Team has objected to the proposal on flood risk grounds. It is also noted that the Transport Planning Team have objected to the application on the basis of the increased use of the current minor road access with the [PLACE]. These considerations should lead to the refusal of the application. 20. This is a planning application for an industrial development in a rural location in the [PLACE] hinterland and, therefore, the correct approach to assessing the detailed acceptability or otherwise of this proposal is through the consideration of the relevant policies in the Development Plan (and then material considerations). 21. With the adoption of the National Planning Framework 4 (NPF4) it is now necessary to consider the proposal in the light of the relevant national planning policies. 22. The relatively generic text in the Regional Spatial Strategy for the North (pages 25, 26 and 27 of NPF4) lists renewable energy generation and transmission as one of the priorities whilst recognising the area’s exceptional assets and natural resources. However, this broad brush generic statement of spatial planning priorities cannot then translate directly across to an approval for any specific project in any specific location. The various relevant policies in NPF4 still have to be applied. NPF4 is very clear on this aspect. 23. Therefore, for battery storage developments of this scale the location specific and project specific policy assessments from NPF4 still have to address the key question as to whether or not this is the right development in the right location. To do that requires the consideration of NPF4 Policies as addressed in the following paragraphs. 24. Policy 1 (tackling the climate and nature crises) is an overarching policy that requires that significant weight is given to these two issues when considering development proposals. In relation to this Policy there is ample evidence that the proposal will cause some harm to nature through effects on bird species, and habitat displacement. Furthermore, the applicants can point to no evidence that the project, on its own or in combination with other projects, will have any verifiable and measurable beneficial effect on climate. The proposal, therefore, has no demonstrable beneficial effect on climate but an adverse effect on nature (that is not offset by any net biodiversity gain) and so the proposal fails to demonstrate compliance with the terms of this overarching policy test. 25. For the application the non significant effects for the various biodiversity considerations are predicated on mitigation being successful. As far as is known there are no NatureScot sponsored peer reviewed scientific studies into the effectiveness of renewable energy related mitigation measures in Scottish energy schemes. On the contrary, the experience with projects such as Fallago and Creag Riabhach, is that the reliance on planning controls through conditions has not worked and that environmental harm occurs without subsequent effective enforcement action. Matters have moved forward though. Policy 3 (biodiversity) is key. Policy 3b provides that for, inter alia, national developments, these will only be supported where it can be demonstrated that the proposal will conserve, restore and enhance biodiversity, including nature networks so that they are in a demonstrably better state than without intervention. The application Supporting Statement does not provide any metric based assessment or related specific proposals and guaranteed delivery mechanisms to deliver on the policy requirement for betterment. Without either metrics or a long term guaranteed delivery mechanism it is simply not plausible to rely on say an outline Habitat Management Plan as a basis for asserting compliance with this NPF4 policy. 26. In terms of the criteria set out in Policy 3b) it is concluded as below for the proposed battery storage application: i. It is unclear if the context is properly understood ii. It is not clear that all feasible opportunities have been taken to integrate and make best use of nature based solutions iii. In terms of the mitigation hierarchy the first principle, avoidance, should have led to a more detailed consideration of alternatives on other sites or the use of other technologies iv. There is no evidence of significant biodiversity enhancements of the types mentioned in the Policy text, nor of the required certainty of delivery, nor of binding provisions for the long term management, retention and monitoring that is required to deliver the benefits envisaged by this Policy 27. In conclusion, the proposal fails in respect of this policy test having regard to the general principles and to the related criteria (bar criterion 1 which relates to the understanding of the existing characteristics). The proposal, therefore, fails in terms of this key policy test. 28. Policy 4 (natural places) is another key policy. In relation to this Policy and applying the test in Policy 4a, the proposal’s unacceptable impact on the natural environment means that the proposal should not be supported. In terms of the effects on the landscape, the significant adverse effects are not clearly outweighed by the benefits of at least local importance. In terms of protected species, policy 4f, the proposal has failed to deliver adequate protection in that the likely reduction of effects to a non significant level is again dependent in mitigation whose effectiveness cannot be guaranteed at this stage. The proposal, therefore, fails in terms of this key policy test. 29. Policy 11 (energy) is the key policy in terms of the assessment of the battery storage proposals. In terms of the specific impacts listed in Policy 11e the proposal has not adequately addressed and mitigated: a. Impacts on communities (as seen in the number of local objections and given the concerns in respect of the effects on private water supplies) b. Landscape and visual effects that are not localised c. Impacts on road traffic d. Biodiversity effects including effects on birds e. Cumulative impacts in terms of the known proposals for major OHL related installations 30. The proposal, therefore, fails in terms of this key policy. 31. Some consideration should be given to Policy 14 (design, quality and place). Although not considered to be a key determining issue, the proposal fails the test of Policy 14a in that it has not been designed to improve the quality of the rural locations it affects. It will not contribute towards creating a successful place. 32. In terms of the policy outcomes for Policy 18 (infrastructure first) the applicants have not demonstrated that the existing infrastructure assets can be used sustainably without the need for this proposed new development. 33. Policy 25 (community wealth building) is also considered to be of some relevance. The various factors mentioned in Policy 25a in terms of building local community wealth have not been addressed by the applicants. 34. The consideration of Policy 29 (rural development) follows on from this. It cannot be seen how this project, which is specifically designed and justified (so far as can be assessed at this stage) on the basis of providing support to providing an electricity supply to a distant market and not to a local market, can make a material contribution to helping to create vibrant and sustainable local rural businesses and communities. 35. Therefore, it can be concluded that, overall, the proposal can draw no support from the various NPF4 Policies assessed above. 36. With regard to the [PLACE] Wide Local Development Plan (HWLDP) the policies below provide a further basis for the assessment of the submitted application. The assessment starts by considering the relevant countryside and industrial location policies before considering the renewable energy policy aspects. 37. Policy 36 Development in the Wider Countryside provides a series of considerations which can be applied to this proposal. In terms of the policy the proposed battery storage facility, which is basically a large scale industrial facility located in a field that just happens to be available: a. Is not acceptable in terms of siting and design b. Is not sympathetic to the existing patterns of development in the area c. Is not compatible with the landscape character and capacity d. Creates the incremental expansion of a particular development type – electricity supply infrastructure – into the landscape in a location where other more suitable sites are available 38. The proposal is therefore not acceptable overall in terms of Policy 36. 39. Policy 41 Business and Industrial Land lists and safeguards strategic and local business and industrial sites. The policy provides that, in the first instance, proposals for new business and industrial development should be directed to such sites. The location for the proposed battery storage facility is not an identified business and industrial site. The policy also advises that the Council will support the principle of proposals outwith these sites if it is from an emerging industry with uncertain size and locational characteristics. An example is given of marine renewable energy. However, there are two caveats. Firstly, developers will need to demonstrate that their proposals cannot reasonably be accommodated on existing allocated sites. The applicants, in this case, have not done so. Secondly, proposals still have to be assessed against the other relevant policies in the HWLDP and, when that is done, this proposal is found to be not in accordance with the Plan. 40. The proposal is therefore not acceptable overall in terms of Policy 41. 41. The most directly relevant HWLDP Policy on renewable energy is Policy 67 Renewable Energy Developments. 42. As required by SPP the text of Policy 67 is generally supportive of renewable energy projects, but subject to various caveats. The policy continues by providing that the Council will support proposals “where it is satisfied that they are located, sited and designed such that they will not be significantly detrimental overall, either individually or cumulatively with other developments, having regard in particular to significant effects” on a range of aspects. In terms of this objection, and having regard to the proposed location of the battery storage facility with the consequential adverse effects on the landscape and on the local community, it is considered that the proposal would be significantly detrimental in terms of the adverse effects on: a. Natural, built and cultural heritage features (the locally valued landscape in particular) b. Visual impact and impact on the landscape character of the surrounding area (with the design and location of the proposal being such as to NOT reflect the scale and character of the landscape and NOT seeking to minimise landscape and visual impact) c. Amenity at sensitive locations including residential properties, workplaces and recognised visitor sites d. The amenity of regularly occupied properties (in terms of potential visual impacts, noise impacts and the impact of construction activities on the safe and convenient access to properties) e. The amenity of users of formal and informal walking and cycling routes in the area f. Tourism and recreation interests (in terms of the industrialisation of the countryside) 43. The policy has an “internal” balancing assessment by way of reference to other material considerations. For this assessment a key material consideration is the benefits of the proposal. In that regard it is clear that this battery storage facility will produce only very limited, if any, public economic benefit whilst there is no evidence of any verifiable environmental benefit directly associated with the proposal. 44. It can be safely concluded that, given the failure to comply with the above policy criteria from Policy 67, the proposed battery storage facility, assessed within the terms of renewable energy policy, would not be in accord with the energy topic specific and relevant policy in the HWLDP. 45. However, as would be normal with all energy related applications, it is considered that it is appropriate to briefly address some of the other policies in the HWLDP especially as this is the approach that is normally taken by the Council. 46. In terms of Policy 28 on Sustainable Design it is considered that the planning application proposal for the battery storage development: a. Does not make use of a brownfield site, existing buildings or recycled materials b. Is significantly detrimental to habitats in terms of impacts on landscape and scenery c. Does not demonstrate sensitive siting and high quality design d. Has not demonstrated that it has minimised environmental impact and enhanced the viability of the community e. Does not conserve and enhance the character of the [PLACE] Area nor minimised the environmental impact of the development f. Has significant adverse effects, has not demonstrated that there are no reasonable alternatives, and therefore it is a development that should not be supported by the Council 47. In terms of Policy 61 on Landscape, the proposed development has not been designed to reflect the landscape characteristics and special qualities of the area having regard to the scale, form and pattern of the proposed development sited in open countryside near settlements. Therefore, there is a clear breach of the Council’s landscape policy in the HWLDP. 48. The above consideration of the primary and secondary renewable energy policies in the HWLDP supports the conclusion flowing from the earlier consideration of NPF4 and HWLDP Policies 36 and 41 that planning permission should be refused on account of non-compliance with the Development Plan. 49. In terms of the overall Development Plan conclusions, the proposed [PLACE] battery storage facility is considered to be in breach of the provisions in NPF4 and HWLDP Policies 36, 41, 67, 28 and 61. This conclusion arises on account of the proposal’s location, its adverse scheme specific significant landscape and visual effects (including design effects), and its poor design standard. In terms of the primacy of the Development Plan that conclusion should lead to a refusal of planning permission for the proposal unless material considerations indicate otherwise. 50. NPF4 has been considered earlier within the Development Plan assessment. There are no other material considerations that affect the determination of the application. 51. In terms of the planning balance the proposals have been assessed against the Development Plan always seeking to balance any identifiable scheme specific benefits in the equation. 52. Based on the above it is concluded that the proposed battery storage facility is contrary to the provisions of NPF4 and the HWLD Policies 36, 41, 67, 28 and 61. This conclusion arises on account of the proposal’s siting and its adverse effects on important local interests, all of which adverse effects are not outweighed by the generic benefits of the scheme which will almost wholly flow to the applicants. That conclusion should lead to a refusal of planning permission for the proposal unless material considerations indicate otherwise. 53. Therefore, the overall Development Plan based conclusion of this objection on behalf of the [ORGANIZATION] is that the proposal is not in accordance with the Development Plan and that, therefore, the presumption is for the refusal of planning permission for this [PLACE] battery storage application. 54. There are no material considerations that would change the conclusion that arises from the Development Plan assessment. 55. It is, therefore, respectfully submitted that the Council should refuse planning permission for the repeat planning application for the proposed [PLACE] battery storage facility on account of it being contrary to the provisions of the Development Plan all as set out in this objection.
