With respect to this specific planning application, I would give the following comments: - The local roads are single-track and have already been subject to deterioration from construction traffic to the [PLACE] development. Provision should be made for upkeep of the roads during and after construction. - Lighting for the site - both during construction and afterwards during maintenance activities, should be kept to a minimum. Light pollution from the [PLACE] is already of concern, so efforts should be made to utilize lights that are directional, do not emit upwards and are restricted in their hours of use. - Noise from the site during operational running will obviously already have been designed to be within the required limits - however the noise from each site needs to be modelled in conjunction with the expected noise from the other two battery sites, the grid stabilisation site and from the substation itself to provide a cumulative review of the noise levels, with a baseline used that is prior to the substation being installed - this was originally a very quiet area. - Both construction and maintenance activities need to be reviewed in conjunction with the other sites and the substation so that there is not works all being carried out at the same time from a traffic disruption perspective. - Fire safety plans for the lithium-ion batteries needs to have particular attention paid to it as a result of the close proximity of the other battery sites and from the substation - thermal runaway from one of the other sites could also affect any of the other sites - an emergency response plan covering all of the sites is required. Provision also needs to be made for potential toxic clear-up needed in the event of an incident on each site to prevent chemical leakage into the local area, as most residents are on private water supplies. - Alternative battery technology, other than lithium ion, should be considered - there are other less volatile options available on the market. - Landscaping of the site needs to be considered for the local environment. Local shrubs/trees should be used. - Provision for decommissioning and site-restoration at the end of life of each site needs to be made. - Other local renewable projects that have been installed as a capital investments, such as the wind turbines, have set up a community fund to give back some of their profits to local projects, by way of reparation for the inconvenience that the project is to local residents - this would also be appropriate for new proposals. The main concern remains that these projects are not being given due consideration because the technology is new and the regulations have not had time to catch up yet. By allowing so many projects to proceed before necessary regulations are put in place, this is generating significant risk for local residents. [ORGANIZATION] have a requirement to ensure the safety and well-being of its residents. This planning application is the just the latest set of investors looking to make money by buying and selling electricity conveniently located to the substation, without any consideration for the potentially harmful impact on local residents - how many sites will [ORGANIZATION] allow to be situated so closely together without an overarching policy in place?

I would like to lodge my objection to the planning application to build a Battery Energy Storage Facility at the [PLACE]. I cannot believe this would even be considered to be granted at this location. This is a greenbelt site and right beside residential properties. [PLACE] is a conservation village and this sort of development seems ludicrous. I know Government are pressing for these sites to be built. A more obvious location would be on the moors beside the existing windfarm where space is plentiful away from residential properties. Residents have purchased their properties at a valuation reflecting the desirability of the location and to have a industrial development on their doorstep will inevitably have a detrimental effect on house values and ease of sale. Road safety issues The location of the site entrance being right at the exit of a busy roundabout and at the brow of a hill makes it extremely dangerous. The traffic going through [PLACE] down to the [PLACE] has recently increased dramatically due to the large housing development in [PLACE] and traffic making their way to the [PLACE] and motorways beyond. A bus stop is also to be repositioned closer to the roundabout at this difficult area. Fire safety I am sure you will be well aware of the risks surrounding the fire safety of Lithium Batteries and the problematic extinguishing of potential fires and also the harmful gases produced and polluted water run off as a result doesn’t bear thinking about. Again this sort of development should not be located anywhere near residential areas. Local plan This development blatently goes against the promises laid out in the [ORGANIZATION] local development plan which states that should not result in a significant loss of character to the surrounding area and be appropriate to its location. An industrial site full of shipping containers is neither in keeping with the character of the area or appropriate for this location. Visual impact No amount of hedge planting etc will be able to conceal this sort of development. It will be clearly heard and be seen travelling down form [PLACE] or approaching the [PLACE] via the [PLACE]. The character of [PLACE] is not just about the physical elements and features that make up a landscape but also embraces the aesthetics, perceptual and experiential aspects of the landscape that make different places distinctive. It concerns more than simple the appearance. Disruption The amount of congestion that this development will produce will be significant, not only during the building work at the site, but also the connecting cables that will need to be dug along the roadways or pavements towards the [PLACE]. The air conditioning units used to cool the batteries will produce a constant humming noise which again will significantly impact the surrounding residential properties. Concerns over the actual company placing the application When I delve into the structure and finances of the developer, I have significant concerns over their suitability and future accountability if they become insolvent and subsequently would have concerns over the sites future thereafter. As a result, I plead with you to reject this application and adhere to your local plan promises. I Love the conservation village that I am a part of and would hate on behalf of my own family and that of my fellow residents to have an industrial development such as this spoil the tranquillity of the surrounding we are all a part of and to set a precedent whereby future detrimental developments would continue to spoil our landscape.

I wish to object to this proposal. I visit [PLACE] and its locality frequently and greatly appreciate the rural aspect, pleasant countryside and peaceful ambiance. This proposal puts that all at risk and no adequate justification for that appears to have been made. 1 The visual impact and change in nature of an agricultural/rural scene to what would amount to industrialisation of the countryside is not acceptable. What argument has been put forward by the developers to ensure the preservation of the existing visual amenity? 2 This is a potentially hazardous installation. People are concerned about this. What risk assessment has been done and what measures taken to show that any potential risks are kept to an acceptable level? The risk study should be made available. There is particular concern about the fire risk [which is well documented] associated with Lithium-ion batteries. 3 The contamination of water course and ground water is possible. A soak away pond at the top of a hill certainly contributes to this concern. And what would happen in the event of a fire at the facility, what contamination would occur and potentially pollute local water? 4 The facility is claimed to be 'Storm Proof'. Where is the justification for this statement and should a copy of it not be made available? 5 What traffic impact will there be on people closest to the proposed site during and after construction and for the people of [PLACE]? A copy of the Traffic Study should be made available. 6 Sub-station and battery storage works have been going on for five years now. This places undue stress on those directly affected, but no account appears to have been taken of this in the Proposal. What mitigating effects, if any, will the developer take to minimise stress to local people? 7 What studies have been made and what measures will be undertaken to ensure the protection of the local environment and ecology?

Land 410M SW of [PLACE] - [APPLICATION_CODE] I object to this development in the strongest possible terms. I live and work in the area and feel it is a completely inappropriate use/ outright abuse of the landscape and all who live in it. This area is agricultural and residential, not industrial, and the negative impacts in terms of heavy traffic on single track roads (delivery vehicles and lorries frequently get stuck on our narrow, winding roads and are particularly hazardous in winter), noise pollution, the release of dangerous chemicals and toxins and greatly increased fire risk from Lithium batteries would be hugely detrimental and potentially catastrophic to the entire area, for residents, local businesses, visitors, livestock, wildlife and the natural environment, including nearby woodland. This proposed industrial site further weakens the economic recovery of the area post pandemic as a destination and is linked to a wider destruction of the [PLACE] landscape, split into multiple projects with little consultation or transparency. I work in a business that is heavily dependent on UK and international visitors, who come to the area to experience the region's two greatest assets-Nature and Culture. As a nearby resident, I am also acutely aware of the potential impacts on the local economy, housing, health, and wellbeing that previous energy infrastructure has inflicted on the local population and that this proposed development, which is part of a much larger scheme, will exacerbate. There has been no information or evidence put forward so far that validates the 'green' credentials of this development, or the wholesale destruction of our precious environment and way of life in service of it. The way in which these individual proposals form a greater threat has not been adequately communicated or debated. The approach and withholding of information requested by local communities is immoral, unethical, and contributing to ecological collapse. Across [PLACE], residents are being subjected to widespread desecration and clearance, and this proposed development is part of it. My workplace, which took 25 years to establish and draws people from all over the world, together with other local businesses, accommodations and residents, will potentially be sitting in the middle of 4 substations, this battery storage facility and a further network of 60ft plyons. This concentrated network of industry, surrounding residential, agricultural, heritage sites and a burial ground at [PLACE] is unacceptable. For the sake of all who live here and all who come after us, this battery storage development must not go ahead.

target_text: I object to this Planning Application. I whole-heartedly agree with all the comments made, and would like to add a further general point. The development of SSE's Sub-station, is proving, as anticipated, to act like a 'Moth to a Flame'. This proposal would not be extant, were it not for the presence of the Sub-station. The Industrialisation of a small Residential area, thus continues apace, and no doubt this will not be the final scheme to be inflicted on our despairing Community. The estimates of operating noise, both for the Substation and this development are desktop exercises, and are unproven in practice. The [PLACE] Council's craven acquiescence in the Planning Permission for the Sub-station enlargement (161 Documents, and no mention of the Residents!!!!), will no doubt be repeated here. The Planning process is useless if it does not defend local Council Tax Payers from the depredations of large alien Companies, whose sole purpose is Profit.

retrieved_examples.text: This application is another in a barrage of applications flooding this area like a tidal wave off the back of the application for a substation. This whole area will be turned into industrialised wastelands. These battery farms are dangerous and highly flammable, yet another went on fire just this week causing mass damage to the environment, the area and surrounding properties and people causing masses of damage and smoke pollution; not to mention the irreparable damage to wildlife. There is no reason to support such a large land grab for battery storage that is not needed or required for the over production of electricity more than what we need or can produce. The detrimental effects to people's health, both mental and physical, wealth both business and personal and property far outweighs the needs for the many, many applications coming in. Surely the council whilst judging each one case by case can see the vast uprising in the number of applications coming in. This isn't ok and not what the people want. All applications should be halted until the main application of the [PLACE] to [PLACE] substation and Lines is sorted. SSENs refusal to look at other methods had again in todays storm proves why underground cabling is the ONLY way forwards as above line cabling in storms has yet again proved to be full of issues and cuts. Only more damage can be caused when bigger pylons fall. There can be no bigger than sellafield substation for this to link into in the first place if the people who are represented are listened too. I object on the ground ds of safety to the public and environment, the lack of a combined plan of all the applications so the public can see the true extent of them all, the lack of need for one, the lack of proper meaningful and open consultation with the public and many more reasons beside.

I would like to object to this planning application. There is no reason why another industrial style development should be allowed in this area when there is an [ORGANIZATION] sub station so close. The small community in [PLACE] is being asked to put up with the nuisance of construction noise, increased traffic on the single track road and the loss of more amenity and views for a development that is totally unsuited to the area and location. I agree with the other objections regarding potential hazards, noise and visual impact.

I agree with everything that has been said by the two previous comments. I would like to add that as [ORGANIZATION] will adopt the [ORGANIZATION] substation on completion I see no reason why it can not be sited to the north east of the existing sub station on land that is owned by [ORGANIZATION]. I feel it is unfair that the community has to have another substation in such close proximity. Also the work involved. The disturbance from these works will only add to the problems the community face with the on going works at the main substation. I would ask that this planning application be refused.

We strongly object to the planning application [APPLICATION_CODE] on the following grounds: The road infrastructure is totally unsuited for the size of vehicles required to transport the containers and plant to create the site. The potential of fire and explosion at the proposed facility and subsequent release of toxic fumes puts every household in the vicinity at risk and this alone should stop this from going ahead. Noise pollution from the constant running of cooling fans. House price devaluation in the area. Who would choose to live near such a site? The area we live in is one of great natural beauty and should remain so. This proposed facility would spoil our area and is much more suited for an industrial site away from residential housing. A question must arise as to where this energy for storing is going to come from. We hope that sense will prevail and that this ludicrous plan is rejected finally.

I am objecting to this application for the following reasons: This is a completely inappropriate location for a development like this. Industrial developments such as this should be restricted to either brownfield sites or at least built closer to other infrastructure. This BESS could be sited close to the substation to which its being connected. The chosen site make no sense whatsoever. I live very close to the site. The construction work and associated underground cable connection to the substation will cause massive inconvenience to local residents such as myself. we use the road past the site several times a day. Its narrow and unsuitable for the volume of heavy traffic required. I was told at the applicants consultation in [PLACE] that the cable will be buried under the road right past my front door, I can only imagine the stress and inconvenience that will cause my family and other residents while the work is carried out. I also have concerns regarding fire safety. There have been a couple of similar sites suffered fires recently which seem to take a huge amount of time and resources to put out. How does the applicant intent to deal with a fire during severe weather events such as heavy snow which can easily see the site inaccesible for large vehicles like fire engines for many days? Also there is potential for contamination of the burn that runs immediately adjacent to the site despite the mitigation proposed. The screening of trees etc suggested in the plans is totally inadequate. It will take 20 years to establish trees high enough to screen the site by which time it will be nearing the end of its life anyway! As a nearby resident I know how hard it is to get things to grow in this windswept area. I would urge the council to pause all permissions for BESS sites currently in the system until some kind of national strategy is in place to site them in more suitable locations. preferably adjoining the substations they are connected to or within existing windfarm sites and not in the middle of open countryside.

target_text: I urge you to think carefully before placing this in the midst of [PLACE]. At best this is not part of green space, the IFDLP2 plan, or place making for our communities; at worst it presents a severe, huge, unknown, unquantifiable hazard in the midst of our community. I have no objections to Battery Storage Systems in principle, indeed quite the opposite. Nevertheless very few have actually been built in the UK so far, these are usually placed near electricity generation such as wind farms - remotely from houses, schools hospitals etc. and close to the high voltage electricity transmission lines needed to take power from and supply power to the grid. Fewer still are operational. Indeed, the regulations for planning, construction, and operation of such schemes are in their infancy. There is much current debate around this across the UK, in parliament, in the Dept of Net Zero and in [ORGANIZATION] including [ORGANIZATION] of Northern Ireland. I enclose a link for a Battery Storage Health and Safety Gap analysis on the safety aspects in document from 2021 prepared for the UK government- see page 39 onwards as but one example of the current debate regarding safety. [LINK] To be clear a 50 MW proposal is BIG. This involves 100 MWh (100,000 kWh) of batteries, in other words 10,000 x a single 10 kWh batteries that you might put in a house, or 2000 x 50 kWh batteries that you might use in a car. So the [PLACE] proposal is to put 2000 car sized batteries of as yet unspecified chemical construction built within a quarter of a mile of [PLACE] and houses, and within 1.5 miles of the many schools and houses and our main general hospital for [PLACE]. Imagine that on fire. These BSS development projects can be sold on. And indeed this is often a way land owners and project developers seek to make money. Suitable regulations governing their planning, construction, and operation are not yet in place. Together this is an enormous risk for our community. Although car batteries are inherently safe given the decrease in likelihood of fires in electric cars to petrol cars, despite media coverage to the contrary, such fires when they do start are hard to put out, and can cause the surrounding area to become very hot. Thermal runaway can occur. Can you imagine 2000 car batteries alight in [PLACE] - so close to houses, schools and our hospital, our main hospital for [PLACE]. Further there are several kinds of Lithium ion batteries with differing chemical constructions and safety issues - so specifying Lithium ion is not enough. Even during normal operation, the fans needed to keep things cool will resonate in the hillside, potentially causing low frequency noise disruption especially as time progresses, impacting sleep and mental health of those close by (mainly [PLACE], [PLACE]). And if you investigate those already built, none appear (so far) to have been built near a hill side with active water flowing down it from above. Despite the low risk identified by a flood risk team, they have asked for a constraint regarding the final flood management design. Low risk is not minimal or no risk, and how any flood mitigation is built and run will have a huge impact on safety. And this is a minor risk compared to that of its operation. This scheme is not a simple property development. It carries significant risks associated with it, not merely during construction but significantly during operation. This is industrial (resubmitted as not sure it worked first time)

retrieved_examples.text: I am in favour of Energy Storage facilities in principle in view of the severe risks of ongoing climate change and the urgent need I feel to be able to say to youngsters that we are doing our bit; youngsters are angry and only likely to become more so. That being said, Battery Storage is in its infancy; although it is very likely to be part of the Energy Storage we need to address peak lopping and time shifting, so that excess energy can be stored or provided when available or need, and the grid stability can be enhanced. Very sadly indeed, this planning application does not provide sufficient detail nor address the very real concerns that locals have when facing new technology in their midst. How much energy will be stored Whilst 50MW is the 'size' of the proposal; this is its peak power (its oomph if you like) and therefore this does not describe the size of the batteries. We are all getting to grips with cars 40kWh batteries or 60 kWh for longer range but it is the kW (not kWh) that provide the oomph). The size of the battery - the size of the petrol tank if you like 0 is in kWh. So what will be used here? We do not know; we are not told. This should be a key part of the planning consideration that planners should be made aware of, because it is this size, in MWh, that will determine the amount of energy that will be located here. Think of it of the size of the coal pile, 1 ton, the [PERSON] could probably can put it out quite easily; but 10 tons, not so much. The [PERSON] need to know the size (in MWh), and know this now, so that they can advise [ORGANIZATION] if they have the resources to address an incident with this amount of batteries. Further the [PERSON] should be consulted about what kind of access they might need and planning consent should stipulate this is to be made available. Further, SEPA, needs to know this figure (in MWh) so that they can understand if there is a leak or fire and contamination is running in o the sewers, how much and for how long. Ongoing Regulation of Operations and Safety of Operations: I made comments at the consultation in [PLACE] Golf Clubhouse regarding safety and regulation of operation of the battery storage facility and risk of flooding and I left my email - I did not get a response at the time and have not heard anything since. What I said re safety and regulation of operation of the battery storage facility and risk of flooding is not reflected in their report of the public consultation. This is disappointing and my concerns still stand. What laws and government organisation will be regulating the operation of the battery Storage Facility, particularly given its location within a town? They were not able to answer me and have not yet done so. Even an explanation of the voluntary industry standards to which they will seek to hold themselves has not been explained. I suspect because there isn't one. If I am right, this means that, very sadly, this will be an unregulated facility of, currently, unknown operational size. Also, should an incident occur, where will the smoke go- probably east towards the hospital; where will the water go, into the surface drains of Scottish water and into the burns, to the [PLACE] and [PLACE]. Flooding: From SEPAs flooding map, the area itself is not liable to flood but just below it is, and this is an area which becomes very wet at times, and water drains downhill (to the deep purple on the map). Water and batteries do not mix well. This should be addressed better by the applicant. There is apparently a lack of statutory consultation with other suitable consultees, e.g. [ORGANIZATION] and [PERSON]. Here is a link from UK Govt which proposes extension of statutory consultees for battery storage to [PERSON] and [ORGANIZATION] which is being considered as UK Bill 152 to be read for second time on 24 March 23 - seems like a good idea. [LINK] I suggest [ORGANIZATION] should seek advisory guidance form [ORGANIZATION] and [PERSON]. There are also of course environmental concerns about the Lithium mining. Are the batteries to be recycled car batteries, and what does this do for the safety of facility. To be clear, I support the installation of battery Storage facilities in principle, but [ORGANIZATION] need to be much better at addressing the issue of local communities. We have to get to grips with what is coming for us in the years to come with climate change. But if we are to have this built here (and I suggest we do), we want it to be planned, built and operate to the highest standards of safety, and to the highest standards of ethics.

The proposed site is only 275 metres from the village of [PLACE] (in Fife) and we believe the site isn’t suitable as it’s prone to routine flooding and presents a significant environmental risk should there be a fire. FLOOD RISK 1. The developer flooding report states that the overall flood risk of the site has been found to be ‘low’. This is factually inaccurate. The site is on a narrow strip of land bounded by two water courses, [PLACE] and [PLACE] and both are subject to significant and routine flooding. The report produced by the developer is just a computer model and doesn’t reflect the local reality. The two most recent flooding examples happened on the 18th November 2022 and 30th December 2022 following a normal pattern of winter rain - See photos A-F. 2. The developer is proposing to construct the battery energy storage system and associated infrastructure on 600mm plinths to raise it above any potential flood water, but as seen in the photos, this may not be enough. 3. The regular flooding and drying of the land makes ground stability a concern and unsuitable for surface placed concrete plinths supporting heavy battery storage and electrical equipment that may move and subside as surface conditions change. This may make the site inherently unsafe. The site was also used by ‘Dalgety Skip Hire’ during the late 1970’s and 1980’s, so there’s also the potential that waste was buried onsite, further weakening ground stability. A geotechnical survey may be required. 4. If the developer must construct an entire site on 600mm stilts you know it’s in the wrong place. The site must be resilient and safe. Lithium batteries must not be exposed to water or moisture (Google the consequences!) No reasonable person would deliberately and knowingly construct part of our critical national energy infrastructure on potentially unstable land, in an area that routinely floods and on a site that will be subjected to more extreme flooding events due to climate change. ENVIROMENTAL RISK 1. Most of the time these battery sites in the UK and elsewhere in the world function as designed and deliver as expected. However, all types of Lithium-ion batteries, even the newer versions, have a known weakness of thermal runaway (“battery fire”) and when this occurs at an energy battery storage facility it can result in fire, explosions, toxic run off, and a toxic vapour cloud which, if it reaches an ignition point, will explode as happened at a fire in [PLACE] in 2020. 2. Since 2018, more than 50 fires and explosions have been reported at battery installations such as this - BESS Failure Event Database - EPRI Storage Wiki 3. It is little wonder then that [PERSON] proposed a bill in September 2022 (it is due its second reading in parliament on 24 March 2023), "Lithium-Ion Battery Storage (Fire Safety and Environmental Permits)." Its aim is to ensure that lithium-ion battery storage facilities are correctly categorised as hazardous, so that the Environment Agency, [ORGANIZATION] and Fire and Rescue Service must be statutory consultees when planning applications are considered." (They currently are not). 4. As Dame Miller states, "lithium-ion batteries are innocuous when they function normally, but if they fail, a process called thermal runaway. occurs. The only way to stop a battery fire is to cool it down with a constant stream of water and wait for the fire to go out, which might take days, creating huge quantities of water containing highly corrosive hydrofluoric acid and copper oxide - by-products of battery fires. These toxic chemicals cannot be allowed to seep into watercourses, because they would cause immense environmental damage." 5. Due to the inherent risk of fire and contaminated fire water entering [PLACE] and [PLACE] and therefore the [PLACE] river catchment, there appears to be no mitigation planned such as on-site fire tanks and bunds that would be needed to comply with environmental legislation such as the Water Framework Directive and other environmental legislation. 6. In addition, the field adjacent to the site is in a high-risk area of flooding which potentially further increases toxic run-off risk. 7. The village ([PLACE]) above the site raises questions about the potential for winds blowing a toxic vapor cloud up and around the village.

[ORGANIZATION] have serious and legitimate concerns over the proposed creation of the battery storage system (BSS) on the former golf course at [PLACE]. The two areas of concern relate to: - The potential risk a BSS poses to residents in the area due to historical incidents with other BSS - The area for the BSS is identified as green space on the [PLACE] (IMFLDP) Firstly, there have been serious accidents with other BSS across the globe. One incident took place in [PLACE] in 2020 which resulted in a toxic plume of smoke engulfing the surrounding area and debris being blasted up to 75ft away. This facility had also been built near a residential area and it took the fire service 59 hours to extinguish. Recognising the dangers these systems pose, the [ORGANIZATION] have introduced the following procedures developers should follow: - Procuring components and using construction techniques which comply with all relevant legislation. - The inclusion of Automatic Fire Detection systems in the development design. - Including automatic fire suppression systems in the development design. Various types of suppression systems are available, but the preferred system would be a water misting system as fires involving Lithium-ion batteries have the potential for thermal runaway. Other systems would be less effective in preventing re-ignition. - To include redundancy in the design to provide multiple layers of protection. - Designing the development to contain and restrict the spread of fire using fire-resistant materials, and adequate separation between elements of the BSS - Ensuring the BSS is located with due considerations of impact on communities, sites and infrastructure. Prevailing wind directions should be factored into the location of the BSS to minimise the impact of a fire involving lithium-ion batteries due to the toxic fumes produced. - Developing an emergency response plan with the local fire service to minimise the impact of an incident during construction, operation and decommissioning of the facility. - The emergency response plan should include details of the hazards associated with lithium-ion batteries, isolation of electrical sources to enable fire-fighting activities, measures to extinguish or cool batteries involved in fire, management of toxic or flammable gases, minimise the environmental impact of an incident, containment of fire water run-off, handling and responsibility for disposal of damaged batteries, establishment of regular onsite training exercises. - Environmental impact should include the prevention of ground contamination, water course pollution, and the release of toxic gases. We would add that each site needs particularly careful thought as regards risk of flooding from above which appear a significant risk here. Further, a paper produced for the [ORGANIZATION] of Northern Ireland held by the UK Infrastructure Planning Inspectorate explains the TNT equivalence of BSS. For the proposed 100MWh of storage, the amount to deliver 50MW for 2h, the equivalent is 86 tons of TNT. Putting this in this locality seems simply nonsensical. The proposed site is close to both residential and retail properties, is upwind of residential districts of [PLACE], [PLACE], and [PLACE], as well as [PLACE], [PLACE], and [PLACE], placing these at risk from a toxic cloud in the event of an explosion and fire. The proposed site is totally inappropriate. The facility should be situated either in open country or on an industrial site where any thermal runaway and fumes from a fire would be isolated. As the body that represents the local community, our responsibility to our community is to advocate that such facilities are planned, built and operated to the highest standards of safety, and to comply with all current and expected future recommendations regarding construction and safety. It is the Community Council’s opinion that the proposed area would not allow for the safety mitigations that are required. Secondly and equally importantly, the Community Council are seriously concerned about the use of this land in contravention of its clear identification as green space on the IMFLDP. This plan identifies this area as “.the green network connections and undeveloped green backcloth that help to define the setting and character of the City and provide the entrance to more open countryside to the south.” By allowing a planning application for development of this green space land makes a mockery of all the time and work gone into developing this IMFLDP plan and provides little confidence that this plan, which takes into account the needs of our whole community, will be followed. The Community Council understands the need for and importance of BSS in helping to reduce our impact on the environment. However, this should not come at the expense of a dedicated green space and the health and safety of those who live and work in the area. This system poses a real threat to the safety of everyone nearby and therefore should not go ahead in this location so close to residential areas. The Community Council understands the potential positive impact this would have for [ORGANIZATION], even though this should not factor in anyone’s decision for what is a planning application. We propose that land is identified in a more suitable and safe location that would allow for all the safety requirements to be met. There could be potential for land near the [PLACE] i.e. INC11: Former [PLACE] as identified on the IMFLDP. [PLACE] values highly the 9-hole golf course, driving range, pro-golf shop, restaurant, coffee house, sports bar, indoor bowling stadium, kart raceway and Travelodge already at [PLACE]. The IMFLDP must be respected and other options for the BSS and any other proposed development i.e. 800 houses proposed by [ORGANIZATION], must look for other suitable options. At this time with a new golf course being completed at [PLACE] and other areas in [PLACE] considering new courses, why is the 18-hole [PLACE] not being brought back to life. Considerable finance was spent on its development in the last twenty-five years. If not golf, at a minimum there should be an entrance of character of the city providing paths/cycle tracks to more open countryside to the south.

The need for battery storage facilities, such as this, results from the inherent intermittency of wind energy. It is not clear whether the further roll out of wind energy infrastructure is needed and many are now projecting that there will be a surplus of wind energy which cannot be used or exported. Battery storage facilities only provide power for one or two hours which is of little use during cold spells when there may be little or no wind for days. The proposal should be considered on its merits, not the perceived generic benefits of renewable energy. There are currently numerous proposals for the area including wind farms, pylons, substations and batteries. When added to the existing wind farms and infrastructure there will be a significant cumulative visual impact. There does not seem to be any overall plan for the siting of BESS facilities but rather it depends on the existence of a willing landowner. Siting a further potentially hazardous industrial plant near [PLACE] and next to the river doesn’t make any sense to me and I wonder whether alternative locations have really been considered. My main concern is in relation to health and safety. The Outline Battery Safety Plan (section 3) only refers to reported fires relating to BESS facilities in the UK whereas there have been many incidents in other parts of the World, including the USA. The major hazard with BESS facilities is the risk of “thermal runaway”, not just “fires”. The applicant refers to the BESS that exploded in [PLACE] in September 2020 but fails to distinguish it from their proposal. In the [PLACE] case the fire took 59 hours to extinguish. In September 2022, a bill was introduced in the House of Commons which sought to categorise lithium-ion battery storage units as “hazardous” and to “ensure that the Environment Agency and the [ORGANIZATION] were consulted during planning applications”. It was noted that “the only way to stop a battery fire is to cool it down with a constant stream of water and wait for the fire to go out, which might take days, creating huge quantities of water containing highly corrosive hydrofluoric acid and copper oxide – by products of battery fires. These toxic chemicals cannot be allowed to seep into watercourses, because they would cause immense environmental damage” (Hansard). In March 2023, the fire chief for Hampshire is reported to have said in respect to a BESS scheme “in the event of a fire, our teams would face an impossible choice between protecting the community from potentially toxic or explosive gas plume or applying water that could pollute the water course for many years”. The proposed site is very close to [PLACE], the river and nearby homes. The Applicant seems to be saying that they would let any fire run its course, with a “controlled burn”, rather than cool it with huge quantities of water which might pollute the river. But what about toxic fumes spreading to nearby towns and homes? Residents of [PLACE] have had a recent reminder of what can happen when fires get out of control. In that case, the cause was a camping stove; not an explosion involving hazardous industrial materials. How is our overstretched rural fire service supposed to cope with huge industrial scale fire and thermal runaway incidents? Furthermore, guidance on these matters seems to be fluid at present; the applicant is dispensing with the current 6m rule for container separation based on new material yet to be approved. I have seen at least one large commercial insurance company recommending concrete walls between battery containers. Like most other people, I use Lithium batteries in various consumer products. However, I have become increasing concerned about the reported human rights abuses associated with the mining of these minerals in developing countries. There is also the issue of pollution caused by chemicals used in the mining process and associated high water consumption in what are usually arid areas. Furthermore, the World Bank predicts that the demand for such minerals will eventually outstrip known reserves. In this case, is battery storage truly sustainable? I would ask you to refuse this application due to the cumulative impact with other similar and related proposals, and because I do not believe the applicant has properly addressed the legitimate health & safety concerns associated with battery technology and battery storage facilities of this type.

[APPLICATION_CODE] I object to the above planning application for the following reasons: 1. Location in a Green Belt zone - when other more appropriate sites are available: The proposed development would sit in a Green Belt zone. Development can be permitted in Green Belt land if there is an overriding environmental need and there is no other suitable option. That is not the case here as there are many other possible and more appropriate sites. The use of 2.1 hectares of natural protected space in a predominantly residential zone, for heavy industrial purpose, is highly inappropriate and cannot be justified by a bogus claim that this is the only possible space for this development. 2. Impact on a nearby conservation area: The site is not only located in an environmentally valuable area of ever decreasing [PLACE] land but it is in close proximity to [PLACE] which is rich in bio diversity. Developments of the boundaries of such a rich bio diverse area will be impacted by any inappropriate and damaging development on the boundary area. Further loss of trees will add to the damaging impact. 3. Health and Safety risk during transport of battery units to site: Transport of the battery units to the site will pose risks to people and the environment as they would have to be transported through numerous residential areas in the city and they are classified as 'dangerous goods'. This is not a one-off risk since the batteries have a limited life (5-15 years) and would need to be replaced with ongoing risks to people and the environment during transport of replacement units. 4. Health and Safety risk to nearby residents during operation of the facility: Further Health and Safety concerns include the risk of 'thermal runaway' which has been identified by the UK government as a key failure of these storage systems and which, they caution, can lead to significant hazard to the surrounding environment. Thermal runaway can lead to fire, explosion and release of toxic gasses or water run-off. This is not a risk which the nearby residents should be exposed to, and for which [ORGANIZATION] has a duty to ensure they are not exposed to. (Risk cited in Gov UK guidance published 18th April 2024). The aftermath of any leakage or fire at such a site and cleanup costs, which could extend beyond the site and incur cost for the local authority, is very considerable. 5. Noise and disturbance during the construction phase of the facility and during the operational phase: Although the developer states sound proofing will be provided there is no assurances or guarantee that this will not have an impact on residents and wildlife. am writing to formally object to the proposed large-scale battery storage development at [PLACE]. While I recognise the importance of renewable energy and grid resilience, I believe this particular proposal raises serious concerns that have not been adequately addressed and would result in unacceptable harm to the local area and its residents. 1. Fire and Safety Risks Large battery storage facilities carry a well-documented risk of thermal runaway, fire, and toxic smoke. Given the scale of the proposed installation, any incident could pose a significant danger to nearby homes, businesses, emergency responders, and the wider environment. It is unclear whether sufficient fire suppression measures, emergency response plans, and access routes have been fully assessed or agreed with local fire authorities. 2. Proximity to Residential Properties The proposed development is in close proximity to residential areas. This raises concerns regarding public safety, constant industrial presence, visual dominance, and long-term health impacts. Residents should not be exposed to increased risk or anxiety due to the siting of a high- risk industrial facility near their homes. 3. Noise and Disturbance Battery storage sites operate continuously and rely on cooling systems, transformers, and inverters that generate noise both day and night. This would adversely affect residential amenity, particularly during night-time hours, and may exceed acceptable background noise levels. 4. Visual Impact and Character of the Area The scale, height, and industrial nature of the development would significantly harm the visual character of the area. The site would be out of keeping with its surroundings and would negatively affect landscape quality, local views, and potentially property values. 5. Environmental and Ecological Concerns The development may result in habitat loss, increased surface water runoff, and pollution risks from battery chemicals in the event of leakage or fire. The long-term environmental consequences, including decommissioning and disposal of batteries, have not been convincingly addressed. 6. Lack of Demonstrated Local Benefit There appears to be limited direct benefit to the local community, while the risks and negative impacts are borne almost entirely by nearby residents. This imbalance weighs heavily against the proposal. For the reasons outlined above, I respectfully request that this application be refused or, at the very least, subject to significantly more rigorous scrutiny, including independent safety assessments, greater separation distances from housing, and meaningful community consultation. Thank you for considering my objection.

I am deeply concerned about the lack of a cumulative impact assessment, especially given that there are now six BESS sites proposed for this localized area. Despite [PLACE] Council's recommendation for an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA), one has not been conducted. My primary objections are detailed below: 1. Unsuitable Topography and Ground Conditions The site is fundamentally unsuitable due to its significant sloping topography with a 25m vertical relief. Our research has found no other site in the UK or globally, either in operation or planning, with such a degree of relief. The development plan, which includes 470 shipping containers, 4608 Solar PV Panels, and three 12m-tall transformers, will require reshaping the land through terracing to six levels. This will involve an estimated 500,000 to 1 million tonnes of groundworks. Crucially, the developer's reports contain insufficient data to support this plan, with no boreholes or geophysical surveys conducted within the project area. This absence of data on depth to bedrock, soil thickness, and groundwater movement makes it impossible to accurately assess slope stability or the potential impact on nearby private water supplies. 2. Significant and Unmitigated Visual and Acoustic Impact The scale of this development, at 16.3 hectares (the size of 23 professional football fields), coupled with its sloping nature, makes it impossible to effectively screen. Proposed mitigation, such as 8m high earth bunds, will be completely ineffective on a site that varies in elevation by 25 meters and would introduce an unnatural feature into the landscape. This development is in direct conflict with the area's landscape character, which Scottish Natural Heritage describes as having a "high degree of integrity" and being "unsuitable for turbines due to its medium scale, valley landform, quality, pattern, high value, and visual sensitivity." Furthermore, the developer's LVIA report is flawed as it omits key natural features like the wide views towards [PLACE] and [PLACE], inaccurately describing the landscape solely by its existing infrastructure. The acoustic report submitted by the developers is also lacking significant detail and fails to provide a comprehensive assessment of the cumulative noise impact. The sloping site will make noise containment very difficult, and two noise experts have advised that while it may be possible to make changes, it currently seems unlikely that sound emissions will be acceptable. 3. Incomplete and Unsafe Fire and Water Management The submitted reports contain critical deficiencies related to safety and environmental protection. The developer has not consulted with the Scottish Fire & Rescue Service ([ORGANIZATION]) on the plans, and they have not fully adhered to all National Fire Chiefs Council guidance. The Fire Assessment report lacks a contingency plan for the numerous adjacent residences, some of which have single-track access roads that would force residents to travel toward a fire to escape. Lithium-ion battery fires are very difficult to manage and almost impossible to extinguish, and having such a high density of batteries could potentially lead to a catastrophic and uncontrollable fire. Regarding firewater, the Surface Water Drainage Strategy report is incomplete. It fails to specify the capacity and location of the firewater detention tanks and states that they will be "designed by others." There is also no indication as to where water will be sourced from for the firewater. These crucial omissions leave fundamental questions unanswered. The plan's reliance on an impermeable membrane creates a high-risk scenario: if the system fails, contaminated firewater could escape into the ground, polluting the groundwater that feeds private water supplies for homes, livestock, and flows into the [PLACE] and ultimately [PLACE] River. 4. Flawed Traffic and Construction Plans The traffic report is severely flawed as it bases its traffic numbers on significantly smaller BESS sites. The document fails to account for a vast number of required vehicle movements, including those for welfare units, solar panels, the impermeable layer, and waste removal. Based on data from similar projects, it is anticipated that there will be more than 155,870 vehicle movements during the 24-month construction phase, averaging 270 journeys per day on our single-track roads. The plans do not address how the affected roads will be maintained or how the expected traffic congestion will be managed. The roads are not currently able to accommodate at least 22,232 HGV and articulated lorry deliveries, and the report makes no indication of how the three Abnormal Load deliveries will be made. The plans also make no provision for the construction area, which needs to be approximately double the final asset size for temporary offices, facilities, and parking. 5. Environmental and Community Deficiencies The developer has not conducted an Environmental Impact Assessment, meaning the effect on a known badger colony, bats, and ground-nesting birds in the adjacent Ancient Woodland has not been properly identified or mitigated. There is no consideration in the plans for the effect the disruption from construction and subsequent presence of the site will have on biodiversity, nor any planning to mitigate an ecological disaster should a fire occur and resulting contamination occur. There is also no plan or guarantees for how the site will be rehabilitated at the end of its life, including the removal of the impermeable membrane, concrete slabs, and the earth berm. The "Community Wealth Building Plan" offers no concrete commitment to local employment or community benefits. There are no guarantees of engagement with local community with respect to the development. The developer has ignored the Scottish Government's "Good Practice Principles," which promote a community benefit of £5,000 per installed megawatt per annum, equating to a significant £2.5 million annually. In conclusion, the proposed project fails to meet the requirements of the National Planning Framework 4. The planning documents contain critical omissions and are based on incomplete data, demonstrating that this development is fundamentally unsuitable for its proposed location. It will have a significant impact on the landscape; there is no commitment for local opportunities and no defined plan for community benefit. As a concerned member of the wider community, I have serious reservations about the impacts this project would have on our shared landscape, local infrastructure, and overall safety. I am particularly concerned for the well-being of those living near the development, as the developer's failure to provide a comprehensive, scientifically sound plan for fire safety, water contamination, traffic management, noise abatement, and ecological damage is unacceptable. I urge you to consider the collective well-being of all residents and to reject this application.

The situation is exemplified by projects such as the Hill of Fare wind farm and the [PLACE] battery storage facility, where local opposition has been significant due to concerns over visual intrusion, noise pollution, and the industrialisation of our countryside. This is unacceptable in a time of increasing food insecurity. -Cumulative effect of not just one structure but many others in nearby locations. - Property Devaluation: The proximity of large-scale energy infrastructure has already led to a downturn in property values, with long-term implications for families and communities. - Lack of Strategic Planning: The piecemeal nature of applications from various developers creates a fragmented and overwhelming planning environment, making it difficult for communities to respond effectively. - Failure to Consider Alternatives: There has been insufficient exploration of alternative sites, such as already industrialised areas or decommissioned offshore oil platforms, which could host such infrastructure without encroaching on valuable rural land. Provide a framework of responsibility for Health and Safety, Fire Services to protect residents in locality We are opposed to being excluded from decisions that profoundly affect our homes, health, and heritage. A just transition must be one that listens to and respects the voices of those most affected.

Despite the applicant's assertion of "limited visibility," the location on a ridge would make it prominently visible from various vantage points, including roads frequented by locals and visitors. The current serene, agricultural, and tourist-focused ambiance of the area would be irreversibly disrupted by this project. The BESS is being put forward without a clear local or national strategic framework dictating suitable locations for such developments. The lack of justification for choosing this rural site over brownfield or industrial alternatives raises concerns about the arbitrary nature of such decisions. The absence of strategic siting criteria leaves rural communities in Scotland vulnerable to unsystematic industrial proposals that erode landscape quality and cohesiveness. Moreover, the potential risks to local residents and the broader community from incidents such as fires at the site have been downplayed. Of utmost concern is the impact on the setting and ambiance of [PLACE], a significant and emblematic heritage asset in Scotland. This historic castle, once the cherished retreat of the late Queen Mother, holds a special place in the Commonwealth's heritage. Its meticulously preserved surroundings are integral to its historical significance. Allowing the construction of a BESS facility in close proximity risks commercializing and devaluing the legacy of this royal site. This decision carries international visibility and could have long-term repercussions on Scotland's planning credibility and tourism appeal. Landscape and Visual Impacts The proposed site is situated in a vast, open landscape with expansive views across [PLACE]. Even with the addition of vegetation, this location is not conducive to accommodating large-scale energy infrastructure without significantly altering its natural character. The proposed BESS, with its 50MW of containerised battery modules, switchgear, access roads, fencing, and substations, will destroy this setting with industrial clutter, noise, and security lighting—24/7. No amount of planting or bunding will mitigate this unnatural industrial form. 4. Public Safety and Fire Risk: A Catastrophic Blind Spot BESS systems are known to pose serious fire and explosion risks. Lithium-ion battery fires are toxic, uncontrollable, and extremely difficult to extinguish. Incidents around the world ([PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE]) have demonstrated the risks of thermal runaway, vapour cloud explosions, and first responder incapacitation. Social Injustice and Community Exploitation This development has been imposed on a tiny rural community of fewer than 100 people, with no genuine consultation, no community buy-in, and no benefit-sharing mechanism. It does not serve Scotland’s people. It damages Scotland’s heritage, landscape, and communities. Conclusion: Refuse [PLACE], Defend Rural Scotland I urge the Reporter and Scottish Ministers to reject this application in full. [PLACE] is the wrong development in the wrong place at the wrong time. Refuse this application. Defend our heritage. Stand up for [PLACE].

[PLACE] would not afford access from the public road to the ‘party’ access road without adjustments being permitted and carried out. The site of the proposed battery facility is located between 2 electricity transformers, both of which were struck by lightning in 2021 causing emergency situations with danger of explosion. The solar array that is proposed as Stage 2 makes a nonsense of the applicants claim that Phase 1, the battery Storage Facility is a ‘stand-alone’ development. Solar arrays are ‘the poor relative’ in terms of energy production in Scotland given it’s climate and terrain and technology in terms of production of green energy is evolving rapidly. target_text: OBJECT to the proposals to construct and operate a Battery Energy Storage Site (BESS) on prime grade 1 arable land between the two residential communities of [PLACE] and [PLACE] (Refs [APPLICATION_CODE] and [APPLICATION_CODE]). We understand that this proposal would be one of the largest BESS in the British Isles, at 342MW in total, more than three times the size of the current largest active BESS site. Although smaller than some consented, the specifics of the proposed site between [PLACE] and [PLACE] are marked and cause our Community Council some considerable concerns about the chosen location’s suitability. These include: Loss of prime grade 1 arable land National Planning Framework 4 sets out that greenfield land should only be considered for development where brownfield land is unavailable. That is not the case here, therefore the brownfield site should be preferred. Safety concerns, lack of relevant information or untested data assumptions From a safety perspective, the proposed location squeezed between two residential communities could hardly be less suitable. Given that the current widely acknowledged policy with regards to BESS fires is to leave them to burn, in the event of an emergency this could result in an extensive evacuation of most of the community, as well as nearby community centres, businesses, surgeries, schools and other facilities. Despite National Fire Chiefs Council guidance that information on emergency planning and evacuation should be available ahead of any consultation on this sort of development, no such material has been provided by the developer. Given the volatile nature of the proposed development, using novel technology that has not had sufficient years of testing behind it, local residents are left to assume the worst-case scenarios that could occur in the event of an accident on a packed site between two residential communities. This is simply unacceptable and makes consent at this stage impossible. Furthermore, the applicant seeks to make use of provisions within the Electricity Act (1989) to install this facility. Provision 29.1.b of the Act requires that electricity suppliers and operators conduct their operations in a manner that avoids danger to the public. The proposed battery storage facility quite clearly poses potential risks related to fire hazards, thermal runaway and toxic emissions in the event of a disaster. These risks would endanger public safety in a heavily populated residential area. Negative impacts on amenity The close proximity of the air-cooled air conditioning units required by this technology to residential homes in [PLACE] and [PLACE] will inevitably present a noise nuisance. The Acoustic Design Specification summarises the night time operation at 33dB(A) (precisely the Target Noise Level set by [ORGANIZATION]), +5dB compared to the background noise level, with an uncertainty of +/-3dB (i.e. as much as +8dB due to uncertainty). The report also notes, that under the guidance “A difference of around +5 dB is likely to be an indication of an adverse impact, depending on the context”, while also that “A difference of around +10 dB or more is likely to be an indication of a significant adverse impact, depending on the context.” The proposed facility would also detract from the residential area's aesthetic value, potentially reducing property values and the overall quality of life for residents and adversely impinge on their quality of life. We do not consider such a negative impacts on residential amenity to be acceptable for the hundreds of nearby homes in earshot of this activity. Future of the site and long-term impacts We can see no assurances in the proposal that will guarantee that this site can be returned to prime arable land in the future. Also, in the event of an emergency, we can identify no mitigation measures that have been put in place to prevent contamination of the nearby [PLACE], groundwater or adjacent communities. For all of the above reasons and more, [PLACE] Community Council OBJECTS to the proposed siting of this Battery Energy Storage Site (BESS) between [PLACE] and [PLACE].

retrieved_examples.text: Battery Energy Storage Site (BESS) proposal on prime grade 1 arable land at [PLACE] (Refs [APPLICATION_CODE] and [APPLICATION_CODE]) While I understand the need for energy storage, I am writing to: note my objections to the above proposal; raise concerns about the handling of the case so far, as well as the gaps in policy it has exposed; and to ask that you take supportive action. My concerns are particularly: 1. Safety Government guidance and well-documented global incidents confirm that BESS facilities pose a risk of thermal runaway events, which can lead to uncontrollable fires, explosions and toxic gas releases. The current location is the worst possible from a safety perspective in the event of a fire. It is just too close to people, including housing, a playpark, a [PLACE], a [PLACE] and the primary routes into and out of our community. I understand that no other sites in the UK are located so near to residences and local amenities. Local firefighters have confirmed that current policy with BESS fires is to leave it to burn. A prevailing wind fire at this site would mean a huge evacuation of most of the community, including the main shelter at the Community Centre. I understand that there would be a possibility of the production of a range of harmful and toxic fumes. All of this means huge risks to the local area, including the [PLACE] and the primary [PLACE]. This is simply unacceptable - exposing the community to needless risk while better options exist elsewhere. An incident would also pose unacceptable risks to wildlife habitats and farmland, because there would be no way to prevent harmful liquid or gases entering [PLACE] or wider local environment. 2. Lack of key information in the application The documentation relating to this site is worryingly lacking in adequate safety procedures. For example, there is no Emergency Plan and no Evacuation Plan, as recommended in Fire UK National Fire Chief’s guidance. Also, it refers to different types of batteries which require differing solutions and management. We have to assume the worst scenario which would be that an accident would trigger a plume of Hydrofluoric acid. Therefore, the ECU is being asked to give consent to a half- complete plan whose underlying assumptions may be incorrect by the time of construction. I do not find this acceptable. 3. Ongoing impact on community, locals, health, local environment and amenities The proximity of the site will lead to constant noise for nearby residents. The application’s Acoustic Design Specification notes this will be at least an ‘adverse impact’ at night – and potentially worse. Long-term exposure to this would undoubtedly cause sleep and mental/emotional health problems. I am aware that developers such as [ORGANIZATION] recommend no closer than 200m to residences – almost three times further than this proposal. The likely negative impact on house values, and on the ability to obtain insurance, would also have knock-on effects on mental and emotional health. 4. Community distrust and developer transparency The beneficiary of this development is London-based [ORGANIZATION] financial investment company. Meanwhile [ORGANIZATION] has several roles: as a landowner, with opportunity to profit from land-leasing, and as a planning authority, with responsibilities to the local community (in addition a statutory role in monitoring of noise and air pollution). These are unacceptable conflicts of interest, and I am aware that the Council has recently refused a Freedom of Information request for the expected annual profit from the leasing arrangement. This land was purchased to create economic development opportunities and create local jobs, but it is my understanding that the BESS will create no jobs. 5. Loss of prime grade 1 arable greenfield land National Planning Framework 4 sets out that greenfield land should only be considered for development where brownfield land is unavailable. That is not the case here, therefore the nearby brownfield site should be preferred. Action requested I request urgent consideration of the following: · There must be clear national guidance developed around the proximity of BESS to residences; no communities should be faced with the risks being proposed at [PLACE]. · There should be a properly independent body to oversee the planning process. The fact that local authorities to act as both landowners and planning authorities is a conflict of interest which needs to be addressed urgently. · BESS sites should never be sited on greenfield land where appropriate brownfield sites exist, and careful consideration must be given to permanent loss of prime agricultural land for a BESS site which may supply the grid only infrequently and at great benefit to its owners. · Communities’ interests and benefits for land next to residences, amenity and community space must be prioritised over financial gain for landowners. I specifically request that you: · raise my concerns directly with [PERSON] MSP, Acting Cabinet Secretary for Net Zero and Energy; · identify opportunities in parliament (such as questions and debates) to raise the case of the proposed BESS at [PLACE] and the concerns of our communities; · work with other MSPs, including through Committees and Cross-Party Groups, to explore how regulation in relation BESS sites could be tightened, and the interests of communities could be better represented, as suggested above.

I am writing to express my objection with regards to the proposals to site a Battery Energy Storage Site (BESS) on prime grade 1 arable land at [PLACE] (Refs [APPLICATION_CODE] and [APPLICATION_CODE]) both as a local resident and long serving Firefighter. -This is one of the largest active BESS in Scotland and is also much closer to residential buildings than any other existing site in the country (including a doctor's surgery and primary [PLACE]). I feel that this proposal unnecessarily risks the safety and wellbeing of the families in close proximity to the site and the community as a whole. It lowers multiple standards and protections and sets a race to the bottom. After sharing and collating our knowledge as a community, the main concerns of note are as follows: - High grade farmland will needlessly be lost with multiple brownfield sites available in similar proximity. The land in it's current state is a source of homegrown food and supports local wildlife. Current excavation in proximity of the proposed site have already correlated with instances of disrupted deer and fox activity in the area. - After meeting with my community and community council, and following multiple Q&A sessions with planning representatives (the few willing or able to speak to us), there was an alarming lack of key information relation to this development, including Emergency Plans, an Evacuation Plan, and nobody involved in the discussions could confirm the type of battery to be used in the development. It is either the current technology with all of it's documented risks or a new emerging battery technology with a reduced knowledge of real-world performance. Either way, there can be little confidence in a proposal (or the proposers) that doesn't include such a key piece of information. - The noise impact from the completed running BESS runs a high risk of being significantly, and near constantly, adverse. This is totally unacceptable to both close-living residents and the community as a whole. -The proximity to residential houses, [PLACE] and [PLACE] pose a significant risk to a great number of people in the event of a fire situation. It is widely documented that, despite fire detection and suppression systems being in place, BESS sites have suffered thermal runaway, resulting in fires, explosions and the release of toxic gases. Often over a protracted period of time. At present, and to the best of my knowledge, our policy covering BESS fires puts emphasis on defensive firefighting. Due to a number of factors including the environmental impact of contamination from water application, the dangers of explosion and sudden reignition, and where there is no immediate life risk (assuming the successful and confident evacuation of nearby houses), consideration is to be given to defensive firefighting, allowing batteries to burn themselves out. The long duration of a fire event, and given the prevailing westerly wind, could in turn lead to a large-scale evacuation of the aforementioned GP, primary [PLACE] and a significant number of houses. There is little doubt that people will be exposed to the toxic fumes, including hydrofluoric acid, and smoke to varying degrees and that this will lead to both short- and long-term health complications. - Future of the site and impact wider ecosystem Especially in the event of accident what assurances exist that the site can be returned to prime arable land? What drainage exists for emergencies other than dumping contaminated water in [PLACE]? Is there any information about the acoustic impacts on protected species such as bats? None of this is clear from the application and unless these questions are answered the longer term impact of this development on the environment of our community may be tremendous. As will be quite obvious, I do not support these applications by [ORGANIZATION] on behalf of [ORGANIZATION] and [ORGANIZATION]. Please take account of my concerns and objections in your consideration of this application.
