retrieved_examples.text: 1. The applicant has stated that there will be 12 months of road disruption while the area is prepared and these units are installed. This not only will impact on [PLACE] residents for a prolonged period of time (the queues at the [PLACE] at rush hour frequently extend up the [PLACE] towards [PLACE]) but due to the access roads vicinity to the [PLACE] is likely to impact on the [PLACE] (where the queues at rush hour can extend back 3⁄4 mile directly along this sites northernmost border). 2. The proposed access road entrance is just over the brow of the hill on exiting from the [PLACE] and will not be visible to traffic until almost upon the entrance, thus creating a blind summit. 3. It is important to note that a planning application for a church dwelling diagonally opposite this proposed development on the other side of the roundabout was recently declined in part because of concerns over road safety. In that instance the plan for the entrance had been moved closer to [PLACE] by not much less than what is proposed here. 4. The applicant states that following the public consultations "the issues raised are addressed in full in the technical reports". One such issue that was raised continually and noted by them in section 4.2 in their public consultation documentation was the fire safety risk and therefore it's disappointing that the planners have made no such attempt to involve the fire and rescue service in Scotland at this stage. The "Health and safety in Grid Scale Electrical Storage Systems" guidance published by the UK government online on the 18th April 2024 states that as a stakeholder the fire service should be consulted at the design and planning stage. 5. The applicant makes no note of the type of lithium ion batteries (e.g lithium ion phosphate (LFP); Lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide (NMC)) that they plan to place on the site. They state that they could use a "variety of battery solutions". However, the "Health and Safety in Grid scale electrical energy storage systems" published in April 2024 by the UK government state it is important at the design stage to know which type of lithium battery is proposed as this will impact on the fire and rescue services fire fighting strategy and therefore the applicant should be stating what they intend to use so the correct risk mitigations can be included at the design phase. 6. [ORGANIZATION], the national fire chiefs council and most recently the UK government in April 2024 has stated that there should be at least two access roads to battery energy storage systems so chemical fires can be targeted no matter what the wind direction and in case one becomes obstructed or inaccessible. This is clearly not within these plans. 7. The applicant states that "where water based suppression systems are installed, firewater containment facilities will be provided to ensure firewater run off does not leave the site.such as directing firewater to an appropriate retention facility.which may include collection for off site treatment". However when BESS fires have occur they are protracted events ([PLACE], [PLACE] 2020 required defensive fire fighting for 59 hours). If there was a fire at this development, assuming that 1900 litres of water was being delivered per minute for this time period that would create a total of 6.7 million litres of water. This is enough to fill 2.5 Olympic sized swimming pools. There is no space on this site to house this size of a containment facility. The alternate is that the firewater run off would be directed immediately into the [PLACE] leading to irreparable damage to a major river in [PLACE]. 8. Policy D1: Placemaking and design states that the development "should not result in a significant loss of character to the surrounding area" and "be appropriate to its location". An industrial site full of shipping containers is neither in keeping with the character of the area or appropriate for this location. 9. Strategic policy 1 (development strategy) of ERC's local development plan 2 states that the councils approach is to protect and enhance the green belt and landscape. This project does not do this - it will have negative impacts on the unique identity of [PLACE]. This policy also states that features of historic interest (such as a listed building which is directly opposite the large opening of the access road) should not be adversely impacted upon. A development such as this would negatively impact on this. 10. The applicant states in their full planning application that "the green belt location is essential due to its location within a viable radius of the grid connection point at [PLACE] and the lack of availability of suitable sites within the intervening land area" but what they don't mention is that this site is almost 4 miles away from the [PLACE]. I find it hard to believe that there is no brownfield site (or closer greenfield that is within the [ORGANIZATION] development plan) within a 4 mile radius of [PLACE]. They mention that "higher land values in urban areas can make this type of development. unviable and undeliverable" - essentially they do not wish to eat into profits by paying the prices of what more appropriate land is worth. 11. [PLACE] descends from [PLACE] towards [PLACE]. I have concerns that this means this industrial installation encompassing will be highly visible from the road for every [PLACE] resident that travels down the [PLACE] every day. 12. The units being placed are shipping containers and painting them green or grey is going to have minimal impact on hiding them. 13. The visualisations provided are frankly misleading. The water tank is incorrectly sized - its plan states it is 4 metres tall therefore should be one of the highest buildings on site - yet it is shown on the visualisations as smaller than the BESS units at 2.9 metres. For example a picture taken at [PLACE] at [PLACE] is not representative of the majority of the communities view and has been taken behind a hill. In one case they have specifically stood behind a tree to take a photo (VP01). The picture at the underpass has been taken through the trees - move 10 metres uphill beyond this point and this creates an entirely different vista - with direct views over the hedgerow onto the installation. There is no picture that demonstrates the vast majority of the communities view point on a daily basis- just above the mid Borland turn off where you descend from [PLACE]. 14. The hedgerows planned are double root stock being planted in two rows. The applicant has stated it will take 15 years for these to reach the height of the perimeter fencing of 2.4 metres (no mention of reaching the 2.9m height) 15. There is also a water tank planned for the closest aspect to [PLACE] road which on the plans will measure 4 metres tall by 5 metres wide. This is not adequately represented on the visual impact (viewpoint 7 - year 1). In addition the CCTV poles with security lighting will never be obscured. This will be a massive eyesore for anyone travelling down [PLACE] towards [PLACE] 16. The plans are for the batteries to be raised up on concrete pads on top of a permeable underlayer and the area needs to be flat and high enough due to the fact that they have admitted that this is waterlogged site (which will be compounded by the heavy plants compacting the soil on the site.) By the time the permeable road and the concrete pads are installed it seems highly likely that a degree of land raising will have occurred. 17. The applicants are not taking into consideration any form of shielding the appearances from the [PLACE] side, relying on the existing tress that are not on the land that they will be leasing. There are two large gaps that view into the field from the [PLACE] in a location where slow/standstill traffic is often present. In the winter the existing trees offer no shielding and even in summer there would be a direct line of sight towards the BESS units and their ancillary structures through the gaps. 18. The applicant plans to put the access road directly opposite a [PLACE] which is so listed because it is an example of a late 18th or early 19th century farmhouse. Part of the charm of any listed building is the setting within which it resides. An access road to an industrial unit directly opposite this markedly changes this setting. 19. The European landscape convention in there document Guidelines for landscape and visual impact assessment (GLVIA3), as quoted in the landscape and visual appraisal report state that "landscape is an area, as perceived by people, whose character is the result of the action and interaction of natural and/or human factors" they go on to say "character is not just about the physical elements and features that make up a landscape, but also embraces the aesthetic, perceptual and experiential aspects of the landscape that make different places distinctive. it concerns more than simply the appearance". Essentially in applying this statement to the [PLACE] community who pride themselves on being a conservation village, the impact of this very visible development to the community, will be sorely felt. 20. At the second public consultation the attendees were told that there would be 16 BESS units in the form of standardised shipping containers. It is therefore disappointing to note that along with the 16 6.06 x 2.9 m standard shipping containers there will also be 8 larger 12.16 x 2.44m shipping containers marked as 'PVC'. They have been disingenuous regarding this. 21. The applicant has asked for permission to undertake 'micrositing' by up to 25 metres from the original position. This means that, because they are limited by the pylons and high pressure gas pipeline that converge on the east border of the site, the realistic position change they can make is to move the containers closer to [PLACE]. 22. The flow of the water run off travels from the middle of the western border of the site directly under the proposed placement of the batteries to the north-eastern most tip and then drains into the [PLACE]. In the event of a fire if any water was applied due to the permeable underlayer the water, now contaminated with hydrofluoric acid, would drain into one of Glasgow's major rivers causing significant environmental impact. There is a large site of special scientific interest ([PLACE]) of ancient woodland on the eastern side of the river at [PLACE]. 23. Bats roost in the tress in the surrounding area. The ecological report confirms that this is likely in 4 of the trees surrounding the site and residents have confirmed that bats reside within the area. I would have concerns that this project would impact on their habitat as well as the security lights disturbing their natural behaviours 24. The access road once the site is operational appears to have no gate planned at [PLACE]. As this is an unmanned site, and with no gate barring access I believe that it will be very easy for fly tipping to occur on this road especially in relation to the ease of access from the [PLACE] and the fact that the design of the access road will allow easy access for large vehicles. 25. The applicant plans to use lithium-ion batteries. It should be noted that there are other types of batteries infinitely safer to use in grid systems. Vanadium redox batteries can remain discharged indefinitely without any damage, they have no noise or emissions, have a longer discharge/charge cycle life so would not need to be replaced as frequently as 7 years like these lithium-ion batteries and are non-flammable. They are of course more expensive. 26. The applicant states that they are not putting in any noise mitigation. The batteries omit a continual humming noise due to the need for air conditioning units to cool them. [PLACE] is used heavily by people walking between [PLACE] as well as cyclists using the road to head primarily towards the windfarm. These developments will be audible for these area users. When the council are trying to encourage the use of walking and cycling a development that will deter this goes against ERC's policies. 27. The applicant plans to put in put in three 4 metre tall posts that will house CCTV and security lighting. They state that "it will not be illuminated at night time other than by intruder activated security lighting. The ecological report states that a 10cm gap should be left on the perimeter fence so that badgers can get onto the site. This space would allow relatively large sized animals onto the site which could trigger the lights. In addition bats and owls fly in the area and I would be concerned that they would trigger the security lights frequently.

Hazardous operations I have seen, with frightening regularity, instances of battery plants and electric vehicles burning out of control. Given that the nature of these modern batteries means that they must be left to burn out, rather than the 'normal' fire suppression measures being successful. As the batteries contain hazardous materials, where combustion occurs the contaminants can be carried some significant distances in the air thereby potentially adversely impacting farmland and associated livelihoods of those affected. Furthermore any contamination of water courses and/or the water table could have long lasting consequences for residents and their livestock. Insufficient consideration and information is recorded in relation to emergency response planning particularly if the worst occurs during bad winter weather. Industrialisation of agricultural landscape The visual impact and the change of use from agriculture to industry will be evident to local residents, visitors and people from the village who use the area recreationally. There is nothing in the application that relates to decommissioning and site restitution at end of life. There needs to be a decommissioning fund with security agreement (equivalent to those required for Oil & Gas) to ensure the permanent reinstatement of the land to its pre-development state prior to any site works commencing. Residential amenity impacts Noise The noise level will vary (level and type of noise e.g. whistle or a hum), depending on the configuration and set-up, as well as the time of day- e.g. if all battery sites are offloading to the gird at the same peak time. Acoustic impact needs to be measured against pre-sub-station levels, not against current levels, which have already been elevated by the sub-station, the grid stability facility. Consideration of all sites operating together (combined noise from air conditioning units = cumulative effect). n much the same way as many communities and homes have been impacted by the noise from turbines, whether that be infrasound, air pressure changes due to blade rotation, wind shear or topography, there will be a change in the noise profile for local communities. Consideration needs to be given to the impact on residential amenity before rather than after the site is approved and the Council must apply the precautionary principles to protect residents first and foremost so as not to repeat the mistakes made when industrialisation by turbines was allowed. Residential amenity and recreation will also be impacted during construction due to increased traffic and site work potentially increasing the risks to local road users. Health & Safety Residents in the surrounding areas will have construction noise and traffic. Development will contribute to anxiety, stress and be detrimental to the general wellbeing of residents in the area. With the loss of residential amenity, any increase in risk to the health and safety of the residents needs to be offset by an increase in General Practitioner cover and associated referral services within a reasonable distance of the projects. As noted earlier in objection, there may be a risk to residents health from the water courses and supplies from contaminants from site works, construction, operation as well as from any emergency such as uncontrolled fire at the premises. Ecology It has become apparent from many developer applications over the past several years, that many of the ecological assessments are not worth the paper they're written on and that the Council does not have the resources to effectively identify and challenge false assumptions and negligent (at best)/fraudulent (at worst) claims with regard to the minimal impact on existing flora and fauna of the area. Rather than allowing the applicant to commission the ecological survey from their own choice of supplier, the Council should be commissioning an independent report at the applicant's cost. Only by doing so will all parties be able to rely on the objectivity, independence and validity of the report. Whilst not in the immediate vicinity of the proposed development, and therefore unlikely to be directly affected by the issues of visual and acoustic amenity, my own croft, which is maintained according to organic principles, is only 5 miles away. This development gives me significant concerns for the likelihood of pollution in the event of a fire. I'm concerned for the health of myself, my family members, my neighbours, my livestock and pets, and the wider biodiversity of the area both in relation to any immediate release of toxic and poisonous airborne gases or particulates and in relation to any persistent "fallout" from an event at the site that could have long-lasting or ongoing consequences for our communities. As we've seen with so many of the recent planning applications for 'green technologies' in the area; the developers are not performing in good faith and with appropriate due diligence and are relying on a combination of 'swamping the system' and the elected members failing to act in accordance with precautionary principles due to a combination of urgency to act and insufficient resource to enable due diligence on their own side in order to drive through ill thought through developments for the enrichment of private individuals at the cost to the communities in which the developments are made. I would urge you to consider the views of the local communities and to ensure that before determining any applications you ensure that complete, accurate and valid information is available to enable a balanced cost benefit analysis of the proposal and to ensure that there is transparency over who "wins" and who "loses" as a result of the proposed development. I have no doubt that there will be an impact on me in terms of using the road network around the proposed development site if the application is granted.

Cumulative Impact: There are now six BESS sites in proposal to be constructed in this localised area, including this one, without any overview of the cumulative effects of these projects. There has been no Environmental Impact Assessment carried out, despite [ORGANIZATION] recommending that this be done because of the cumulative effects. Concerns were raised when the original [ORGANIZATION] Transmission's [PLACE] for grid connectivity was established, closely followed by the small BESS facility, and a multiplicity of further proposals, because of the lack of any strategic overview of the cumulative effects that residents felt might be inevitable once these original facilities were established. So it has proved. An area that is historically rural, given over to agriculture - crops and grazing - with small pockets of residential properties, has recently begun to be transformed by stealth - each subsequent proposed facility falling within the parameters that would require such a strategic overview. Thus, one facility has attracted an agglomeration of others, transforming the locality from its former character into a semi-industrial complex. With this enormous proposal will come a major change of use for the land, a significant change in the character of the landscape, a far-reaching environmental impact - and all without any strategic oversight or Environmental Impact Assessment. Landscape and Visual Impact: This site is 16.3Ha (equivalent to 23 football fields) and has a 25m drop across it – it is steeply sloped. The developers propose 6 terraces to deal with the height difference. There will be 470 20-foot shipping containers (332 battery containers and 138 power converters), 4608 Solar PV Panels and three 12m tall Super Grid Transformers, plus other associated equipment. Despite the 4m high fences and 8m high earth bunds proposed – this scale of equipment will be highly visible on the sloping site. Noise: The noise report submitted by the developers is missing significant amounts of detailed information on sound sources, site layout, and receptors. The proposal is likely to increase background noise levels by 3 times the current levels. Two noise experts have reviewed this and advise that whilst it may be possible to make changes to the design of the site to make the sound emissions acceptable, this currently seems unlikely. The sloping nature of the site will make it very difficult to stop noise pollution escaping from the site, both during construction and operation. The lack of detail regarding the specific equipment and the lack of comprehensive assessment for the cumulative impact means that it is more likely that the noise level will have a significant adverse local impact. Fire: It is not possible to extinguish a lithium-ion battery fire. Scottish Fire & Rescue have not been consulted on the plans for this site. The developer has not followed all the National Fire Chiefs Council guidance for BESS sites. An emergency response plan is required for the site and for the area as a whole – including evacuation of residential properties and livestock. The nearby village of [PLACE] has a population of over 1000 residents, with a junior [PLACE]. Currently, some residents would have to drive towards the site as their only evacuation route. Water source for fire containment: Huge volumes of water are required to be stored on site for potential fire suppression. Where will this water be sourced? Will it be trucked in? (adding to the construction traffic). What chemicals will be used to prevent stagnation and freezing? Drainage, Private Water Supply, Fire water run-off and containment: The terracing of the slope and introduction of an impermeable membrane have not been properly modelled with respect to drainage, infiltration from SuDS to the environment, potential impact on private water supplies in terms of contamination and volume and potential pollution of river courses. There simply has not been sufficient, peer reviewed work undertaken on the impact of this project on groundwater. Infrastructure: During construction, there will be major disruption on single track roads from both construction workers arriving and leaving each day, along with the heavy goods vehicle deliveries for all the concrete and the equipment. The table of vehicle movements provided within their CMTP document only accounts for a very limited amount of required traffic that would need to access the site. The welfare units; the solar panels and related housing; the water tanks; the impermeable layer; the removal of waste from the 100+ workers; the water required on site; the fencing panels both palisade deer fencing and acoustic fencing; the landscaping to be planted; all these vehicle movements have not been accounted for in the planning document. Access to the site is via single track road, as are the roads in the vicinity leading to the access road. They are constructed to facilitate farm vehicles and local residential access and are completely unsuitable for wide, heavy construction / emergency services vehicle use. The road surfaces are already suffering considerably from the increase in heavy goods vehicles servicing the current sites (themselves constructed without any assessment of their cumulative impact on the local area.) Large potholes, subsidence and road edge/surface erosion are being tackled piecemeal at present. Biodiversity: As there has been no Environmental Impact Assessment carried out, then there is no proper oversight into the effect on habitats for the known badgers and bats in the adjoining designated Ancient Woodland, or for the other protected species such as the ground nesting birds. Disruption from construction, huge groundworks and 100’s of meters of 4m high fencing are going to impact wildlife. If there is a fire, then the contamination of local habitat, and the contamination of water flowing into the [PLACE] and [PLACE] will have a significant effect. Rehabilitation: Where are the guarantees that the land will be restored at the end of the 25-years of the project – for example, how is the impermeable membrane and the concrete going to be removed from the ground? What are the plans to demolish the 8m high berm that has been planted with the, by then, mature shrubs and trees? Community Wealth: The 'Community Wealth Building Plan' gives absolutely no commitment to the use of local workforce and offers zero community benefit. The document says that there are opportunities for local companies but does not set out any obligation that they will give preference to local companies. The Scottish Governments “Good Practice Principles for Community Benefits from Onshore Renewable Energy Developments” document promotes community benefits of the value equivalent to £5,000 per installed megawatt per annum, index linked for the operational lifetime of the project. £5000 x 500 would equate to £2.5million annually to the community – this has been ignored by the developer. National Planning Framework 4 Policy 11: This encourages renewable energy projects - and I fully support this policy - but only where the landscape, the environment - both built and natural, the health and safety of residents, and visual impact is fully considered and properly safeguarded, and where there are local and community benefits. This site will have a significant impact on the entire locality, and there is no commitment for local opportunities, or community benefit. The proposed project does not meet the policy requirement and therefore should be rejected.

The application is not competent. The application is a major application in terms of the hierarchy and, as a consequence, the requirements of Section 36B of the Town and Country Planning (Scotland) Act 1997 apply. We note from the Pre-Application Consultation Report submitted by the Applicant with the application that a number of Pre-Application Notices have been submitted to [ORGANIZATION]. This is consistent with the Applicant altering the proposals and, as a consequence, further notifications of the Council being required. There is no provision within the legislation for amendment and therefore each Notice needs to be treated on its own merits. It is understood that the third notification to the Council arose from a change in the site proposed for development. This in effect constitutes a new notification to the Council and a new requirement to carry out consultation. Appendix C of the Pre-Application Consultation Report contains the further Pre-Application Notice from the representatives on behalf of the Applicant and is dated 07/04/2025. Appendix F of the Pre-Application Consultation Report includes the Council’s response which is dated 8 April 2025. The 8 April response by the Council confirms that 12 weeks must elapse from the submission of the proposal application notice and the submission of the application. The planning application was submitted on 20 June 2025. This means that the planning application was submitted before the 12 week period had expired in terms of the response to notice of 7 April 2025. In terms of Section 39(1A) of the 1997 Act, a planning authority “must decline to determine an application for planning permission for the development of any land” if, in their opinion, there was a requirement for compliance with Section 35B and there has not been such compliance. The terms of the legislation are absolute and in those circumstances it would not be competent for the planning authority to determine this planning application.

This correspondence serves as a formal objection to the planning application pertaining to the [PLACE] Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), as referenced by the Energy Consents Unit Ref: [APPLICATION_CODE] and [ORGANIZATION] Ref: [APPLICATION_CODE]. The proposed project aims to establish a lithium-ion battery storage facility, alongside its associated infrastructure, in close proximity to residential zones, agricultural land, and environmentally delicate areas. The objection is rooted in evidenced concerns that are of both factual and legal significance, with a particular focus on matters related to public safety, environmental hazards, adherence to planning regulations, and procedural shortcomings within the consultation process. In light of the substantial risks associated with large-scale battery storage operations and their potential implications, it is imperative that the application undergoes a comprehensive review and assessment. Visual Intrusion and Landscape Impact The [PLACE] Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) project proposes the establishment of an industrial-scale facility within a primarily rural and picturesque setting, resulting in a permanent transformation of the landscape. Situated in close proximity to the [PLACE] and [PLACE], the development will be visible from public thoroughfares, walking paths, and residential zones, impacting both local inhabitants and tourists. The installation of necessary security fencing, acoustic shields, and high-voltage infrastructure will further contribute to the visual alteration of the area. While acoustic barriers may aid in noise reduction, they do not address the loss of unobstructed countryside vistas, which are fundamental to the region's's identity and tourism allure. Additionally, the implementation of artificial lighting for security and upkeep purposes will lead to light pollution, affecting residents as well as nocturnal wildlife. Notably, the absence of a comprehensive assessment on light pollution exacerbates concerns regarding excessive light spillage. This significant disturbance to the landscape runs counter to the guidelines outlined in NPF4 Policy 4 (Natural Assets and Landscape Protection), which emphasises the safeguarding of Scotland's natural beauty. Moreover, it fails to align with HWLDP Policy 61 (Landscape), which mandates that developments harmonise with and show consideration for their surroundings. Environmental and Ecological Impact The proposed [PLACE] Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) development poses significant environmental risks, particularly in relation to air and water contamination, biodiversity loss, and landscape disruption. The site's proximity to the [PLACE], a designated Special Area of Conservation ([PLACE]) for Atlantic salmon, places it within an ecologically sensitive area that encompasses multiple Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSIs) and the [PLACE], recognised for its internationally significant wetland habitats. Any potential contamination or disruption to this delicate ecosystem could have far-reaching and detrimental consequences. In the event of a thermal runaway incident in a lithium-ion battery storage system, a variety of toxic gases and airborne pollutants would be released, posing a serious threat to public health and the environment. Such incidents could result in the emission of hydrogen fluoride (HF), carbon monoxide (CO), and sulfur dioxide (SO2) in significant quantities. HF is particularly hazardous due to its highly corrosive nature, capable of causing severe respiratory damage and chemical burns. CO, an odourless gas, can be fatal in high concentrations, while SO2 is a known trigger for asthma and lung diseases. Additionally, particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10) and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) would be released, further exacerbating air quality issues and increasing the risk of long-term cardiovascular and respiratory complications. Given the prevailing wind patterns in [PLACE], these toxic emissions could easily spread into residential areas, agricultural land, and water sources, posing a direct threat to the health of local communities. The potential risk to water quality is equally concerning, particularly in the event of a fire at the BESS facility and subsequent firefighting activities. Lithium-ion battery fires necessitate significant amounts of water for suppression, resulting in toxic runoff contaminated with heavy metals, lithium, and acidic compounds. This contaminated water could potentially infiltrate the [PLACE], endangering its [PLACE]-designated Atlantic salmon population and other aquatic species. Furthermore, SEPA flood risk mapping indicates that the proposed site is situated within or adjacent to a floodplain, heightening the risk of pollutants spreading over a wider area during periods of heavy rainfall or flooding. Despite these risks, the application lacks a comprehensive containment strategy to prevent such contamination. The development also poses a threat to local biodiversity, which includes protected species such as ospreys, buzzards, curlews, red squirrels, pine martens, otters, and great crested newts. Activities such as construction, noise pollution, and artificial lighting could disrupt migration patterns, breeding cycles, and natural behaviours of these species, while habitat destruction and potential chemical contamination present long-term risks to wildlife. The proposal falls short of compliance with key planning policies aimed at safeguarding the environment. NPF4 Policy 3 (Biodiversity Enhancement) stipulates that new developments should deliver net environmental benefits rather than merely avoiding harm; however, this application lacks a clear mitigation strategy for habitat loss. NPF4 Policies 22 and 23 require developments to steer clear of negative impacts on protected conservation areas, while HWLDP Policies 28, 36, 58, 59, 61, 63, 72, and 73 focus on preserving the landscape and natural environment, all of which are evidently compromised by this proposal. In the absence of robust environmental protections, effective mitigation measures, and a well-defined risk management plan, the [PLACE] BESS development poses an unacceptable environmental risk. The potential for airborne and waterborne contamination, destruction of protected habitats, and non-compliance with planning policies render this proposal fundamentally flawed and incompatible with its environmentally sensitive location. Safety and Well-being Challenges for Communities The [PLACE] Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) proposal raises significant concerns regarding fire safety, primarily due to the well-documented potential for thermal runaway in lithium-ion battery storage systems. Instances of thermal runaway can lead to unmanageable fires, explosions, and the emission of hazardous substances such as hydrofluoric acid, dioxins, and heavy metals. Notable incidents at facilities like the [PLACE] in the USA have underscored these risks, with contamination levels in the surrounding environment found to be significantly elevated compared to normal levels. Addressing such incidents requires substantial firefighting resources, as outlined in guidance from the National Fire Chiefs Council ([ORGANIZATION]), which states that even small fires involving BESS installations may necessitate 1,900 litres of water per minute for a minimum of two hours. Real-world scenarios have seen usage exceeding one million gallons of water. Despite this, the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service ([ORGANIZATION]) has not disclosed its readiness to handle such emergencies. A Freedom of Information (FOI) request made in January 2025 regarding emergency response plans remains unanswered, prompting concerns regarding the local authorities' ability to respond effectively. The risks associated with the proposal extend beyond fire incidents, as the runoff from firefighting activities could potentially contaminate the [PLACE], designated as a Special Area of Conservation ([PLACE]) for Atlantic salmon, posing a threat to biodiversity and water quality. The application lacks a clear strategy for containing such risks. The [ORGANIZATION] strongly advises against siting BESS facilities in close proximity to populated areas, a recommendation that this proposal fails to adhere to, contravening National Planning Framework 4 (NPF4) Policies 2, 4, 22, and 29, which stress the importance of prioritising health, safety, and environmental protection in energy developments. Given the absence of a robust fire safety plan, the unresolved nature of the emergency response strategy, and the environmental hazards associated with potential toxic contamination, the current application cannot be deemed safe or acceptable. Cumulative Impact The [PLACE] area has witnessed significant industrialisation as a result of various energy infrastructure projects. The potential addition of a large-scale Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) would further impact local communities, landscapes, and public services. It is imperative to evaluate the collective effects of these developments rather than considering them in isolation to fully comprehend the extent of disruption they may cause. The region has seen a rapid proliferation of energy-related infrastructure, such as substations, battery storage facilities, wind farms, and high-voltage power lines. Some of these projects have already had adverse effects on residents. For instance, SSEN’s [PLACE] Expansion has prompted numerous noise complaints. The proposed [PLACE] BESS would introduce another industrial-scale energy storage site, compounding the risks associated with lithium-ion battery storage. The replacement of the [PLACE] and [PLACE] Substations, along with the planned [PLACE] development spanning an 868-acre site, further concentrates energy infrastructure in the area. The construction of multiple 400kV overhead power lines and pylons, some towering up to 70 metres, is altering the rural landscape significantly. The cumulative impact of wind farm developments must also be taken into account. Projects like the [PLACE], featuring 36 turbines at 230 metres each, and the [PLACE], adding 14 turbines at 200 metres, contribute to the industrialisation of the area. These projects, in conjunction with the proposed [PLACE] BESS, would irreversibly affect the natural environment and visual appeal of the region. Moreover, the planned closure of [PLACE] for up to a year is expected to divert all traffic, including heavy goods vehicles carrying construction materials, through [PLACE]. This will lead to substantial congestion and pose road safety hazards for residents, schoolchildren, and local businesses. The proliferation of energy developments in [PLACE] has placed an unsustainable burden on rural infrastructure, including narrow country roads, emergency services, and public health resources. Introducing another industrial project would only exacerbate these pressures, making it challenging for residents to uphold their quality of life. Both national and local planning policies mandate the consideration of cumulative effects when evaluating new applications. NPF4 Policy 29 stipulates that energy infrastructure projects must demonstrate they will not have unacceptable combined impacts on local communities or the environment. Given the existing level of industrialisation in [PLACE], the continued expansion of large-scale energy developments is no longer viable. NPF4 Policy 3 requires that developments contribute to a net enhancement of biodiversity, a principle contradicted by the cumulative loss of natural landscapes and habitats. Similarly, HWLDP Policy 36 asserts that developments should not disproportionately burden rural communities, a criterion that is evidently unmet given the current strain on local infrastructure and services. Summary The [PLACE] BESS proposal presents considerable hazards to public safety, the environment, and local communities. Critical fire risks associated with lithium-ion batteries have not been adequately addressed, with no definitive emergency response strategy or evidence that the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service can effectively manage a thermal runaway scenario. The potential release of toxic gases coupled with contaminated firefighting runoff poses substantial risks to public health and to the safeguarded ecosystem of the [PLACE]. Furthermore, the project's proximity to conservation areas raises pressing environmental concerns. Potential pollution, habitat degradation, and loss of biodiversity stand in stark opposition to both national and local planning policies. An increase in noise, traffic, and visual intrusion is also anticipated, which would adversely affect residents, tourism, and general road safety. Compounding these issues is a lack of transparency throughout the consultation process. Essential details, including fire safety measures, emergency response procedures, and comprehensive information on the battery technology, are conspicuously absent. There has also been an insufficient level of consultation with emergency services and local authorities. Considering that existing energy developments already strain the local infrastructure and services, this project is likely to further intensify these pressures. In light of the unresolved safety challenges, environmental risks, and failure to align with established planning policies, it is recommended that the [PLACE] BESS proposal be rejected. Environmental and Ecological Impact The proposed [PLACE] Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) development poses significant environmental risks, particularly in relation to air and water contamination, biodiversity loss, and landscape disruption. The site's proximity to the [PLACE], a Special Area of Conservation ([PLACE]) for Atlantic salmon, places it within an ecologically sensitive area that encompasses multiple Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSIs) and the [PLACE], renowned for its internationally significant wetland habitats. Any potential contamination or disruption to this fragile ecosystem could have wide-ranging repercussions. In the event of a thermal runaway incident in a lithium-ion battery storage system, a variety of toxic gases and airborne pollutants would be released, presenting a serious hazard to public health and the environment. Such occurrences could result in the emission of hydrogen fluoride (HF), carbon monoxide (CO), and sulfur dioxide (SO2) in substantial quantities. HF is particularly hazardous due to its highly corrosive nature, capable of causing severe respiratory damage and chemical burns. CO, an odourless gas, can be fatal in high concentrations, while SO2 is a known trigger for asthma and lung conditions. Furthermore, the release of particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10) and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) would exacerbate air quality issues, heightening the risk of long-term cardiovascular and respiratory complications. Lithium-ion battery fires necessitate significant water volumes for suppression, leading to the production of toxic runoff contaminated with heavy metals, lithium, and acidic substances. This contaminated water could potentially seep into the [PLACE], endangering its [PLACE]-designated Atlantic salmon population and other aquatic species. Moreover, SEPA flood risk mapping indicates that the proposed site is situated within or near a floodplain, heightening the risk of pollutants spreading across a wider area during periods of heavy rainfall or flooding.
