Impact on people – whilst these developments are being targeted in rural locations with low populations, the reality is that people living in the vicinity are suffering a high level of mental anguish and worry regarding how such a development will affect their health and wellbeing. It is stated that there will be 5.1m lights that not only will be seen from great distances but will have a negative impact on the dark skies that are enjoyed locally. How much noise will be produced? How thorough are the surveys conducted on the impact all this will actually have on the local residents? Access / traffic – the amount of traffic, noise, pollution and disturbance this development will generate will have a significant impact on local residents during the 2 years of construction and the [PLACE] has become busier in recent years with the promotion of the [PLACE] route. They state in their application that this access has been used previously during wind farm construction – this is completely untrue! When E-ON applied for planning permission to build [PLACE] they had intended to use the [PLACE] for access to the site but the [ORGANIZATION] insisted that access be via the more appropriate [PLACE] instead, NOT at [PLACE]. No contribution to the climate emergency – the majority of the public “believe” this development will store renewable energy from the neighbouring wind farms and therefore make a contribution to net zero targets and saving the planet. However, these batteries will be charged when energy is at it’s cheapest, usually in the middle of the night when the wind isn’t blowing and the sun isn’t shining, directly from the grid, therefore having a high percentage of fossil fuels, NOT renewables. This stored energy will then be sold back to the grid at peak demand when the prices are at their highest. This is PURELY about the applicant making profits through arbitrage as they are energy traders. Planning policy – whilst NPF4 supports the development of renewable energy generation, this is NOT energy production, but storage, and NOT storage of renewables but simply energy trading using the grid. NPF4 policy 11 Energy does support battery storage but ONLY where they maximise net economic impact, and in this case, with no direct benefit to the local community, this development does not meet the aims of NPF4. In addition, it does not demonstrate the enhancement of biodiversity stated in policy 3 of NPF4. It appears that the land they intend to regenerate would be replanted anyway as part of the tree management plan already in place, and this would therefore NOT constitute enhancement and should not be supported on this basis. Benefit vs environmental damage – stating the size of a battery storage facility in MW is very misleading and should be MWh. This development will result in tree removal, damage and removal of carbon storing peat, destruction of wet heathland, wildlife (including protected species) and habitats, permanent and irreversible affect on visual amenity and for what gain? This facility, as confirmed by the applicant, will store energy that will last for a maximum of just 2 hours!! Does the gain outweigh the destruction? Mitigation measures – the developer plans to use existing trees for screening and also do compensatory planting. However, it is unclear whether they intend planting trees further up the hill, which is unlikely to produce good quality woodland due to the poor soil quality, or on the land where felling has already taken place, and will therefore be due for replanting anyway, so will NOT be compensatory. Any compensatory planting and existing trees being used for screening should either be under developer ownership or managed by a 3rd party to ensure they are maintained for their intended purpose. As mentioned above, it looks like existing trees planned to be used for screening are under threat from other renewable developments so should not be relied upon. Adverse impact on landscape – the sheer number of energy developments in this small community has had a huge affect on the landscape of this beautiful glen which in turn affects tourism and the local business that depend on it. This HUGE industrial development with fencing and floodlighting will have a significant visual impact on the surrounding landscape. Flooding – the landslip scars on the hillside above the proposed development are lasting evidence of the horrific flooding of 2017 and the impact potential flooding would have on this project does not seem to have been fully investigated or addressed. How “Green” is this development? – whilst the obsession to hit net zero targets continues the environmental impact during the manufacture of these lithium-ion batteries seems to be ignored – what about the mining of the rare metals? The significant emissions during the manufacturing process? The use of forced labour and abuse of human rights? The hazardous processes and chemical used in manufacture and the inability to recycle? Just because these do not occur on our shores does not mean they are not negatively contributing to the very climate crisis we are supposed to be tackling. There are significant environmental impacts arising throughout the lifecycle of battery storage systems, from raw material extraction to end-of-life disposal. Key issues include resource depletion, greenhouse gas emissions, and pollution from mining activities. The applicant – whilst the history of the developer is not taken as a material consideration, morally and for due diligence their background should be! [PERSON] (a former banker energy trader) was the co. founder of Bulb that went bust leaving a taxpayer bailout of £6.5bn. He then set up a holding company [ORGANIZATION] in Dec 2020. Under this holding company each of the [ORGANIZATION] sites have been set up as separate limited companies. [ORGANIZATION] was only incorporated in Nov 23 so no Companies House filing to date. The company does not have a long history of battery storage expertise and R&D, but energy trading. I am EXTREMELY concerned about the impact and safety of this proposed development in such close proximity of my home for all the reasons listed above and therefore request that permission be refused.

target_text: We are writing to inform you of our objection to the above named proposed battery storage facility along with the proposed facility at the water treatment works. The initial construction of both sites will cause disturbance to the community but will bring constant low level noise once operating. Our main concern is that the site at the sewage plant will be based alongside a major gas pipe and the [PLACE] which is a main artery to the [PLACE] and surrounding area, it will also be in close proximity to a petrol station and should the plant have a fire causing toxic fumes this may result in a major catastrophe in the area which due to the close proximity to housing could see many fatalities. There is an abundance of sites in this area - mainly disused warehouses that have been abandoned due to the downturn in the oil industry. These sites could be used for this type of facility without putting lives at risk, as they do not sit within densely populated areas. There is also the benefit of having the road infrastructure already in place along with services in situ. It does seem to appear that the 2 sites being considered are sites where the landowners will gain, hence their reason to push planning approval though. Would it not be more environmentally friendly to repurpose a redundant industrial site as opposed to destroying 2 sites that have an abundance of wildlife which has flourished over many years. We regularly see Badgers, Deer, Hawks and many varieties of birds and butterflies along with various insects such as Bees which will now have their habitat destroyed.

retrieved_examples.text: I object to the construction of the battery storage facility for a number of reasons: The construction of the battery storage facility will cause distruption to the wildlife and environment. Badger sets and ground nesting birds are known to the area and will be disrupted. Due to a large number of trees being cut down to create access roads to local battery storage sites, many birds will also have lost/will lose their habitats. Construction of the battery storage facility will alter the land that previously absorbed rainfall, increasing surface runoff and potentially divert water to nearby properties and roads. [PLACE] and surrounding properties have existing flooding issues and this will exacerbate the issue. There are already visible issues with the road conditions on local roads due to the heavy construction traffic on another nearby battery storage site, much smaller than that of the proposed site. Many potholes have formed with no sign of any repairs being made. Verges are being damaged due to vehicles turning and inadequate passing places leading to further water drainage issues, on top of the flooding concerns noted above. Road safety is also a concern for cyclists, pedestrians and other road users. The minor roads leading to the site are narrow and the use of heavy construction traffic is a hazard to oncoming road users. The battery storage site will produce a persistent noise in what is currently a very peaceful residential area and will be very disruptive to nearby residents, affecting sleep quality and overall well-being. Lithium batteries have been known to cause fires and explosions. These cannot be extinguished and are left to burn out, wasting local fire resources time whilst they are on standby on site. Not only is there a major fire risk to nearby residents, live stock and wildlife but also the release of toxic gases/chemicals into the environment is a real concern. There also appears to be a lack of clear emergency evacuation procedures for nearby homes in place. Property values will be reduced due to the uncertainty of fire risks, noise pollution and visual effects. This has caused worry and stress to local residents, some who have lived in the area for decades and many would consider it to be a very desirable area to live currently.

I wish to register my objection to the proposed battery storage facility near [PLACE]. As someone who lives in [PLACE] and values its natural environment, I find this development deeply concerning. The site lies within a landscape described in the planning application itself as 'well-settled, wooded and diverse'. It's currently used for agriculture and as a recreational area by people from [PLACE], [PLACE], and beyond. Transforming it into an industrial zone adjacent to the substation will cause significant visual and acoustic disruption. Ecologically, the area is rich in biodiversity. There are at least four badger setts within the [PLACE] and known populations of bats and ground-nesting birds. Has the Badger Trust, [ORGANIZATION], or a qualified ecologist been properly consulted? When was the last independent ecological survey carried out? Noise from air conditioning units and battery discharging-especially if all sites operate simultaneously-will further degrade the environment and people's mental wellbeing, which has already been impacted by years of nearby energy developments. [PLACE] should not become a dumping ground for poorly planned industrial sites. This proposal is inappropriate, incomplete, and ecologically risky.

I wish to give comment of my strong objection to this planning. The infrastructure around such a small village, is already needing addressed without the need for this site. There are many other remote locations in and around the [PLACE] and [PLACE] areas which do not have residential and commercial areas in such close proximity. There are many reasons for my objection: - The environment would be negatively impacted whilst also being an eyesore in the countryside charm of the village. There are many different types of wildlife that would be affected for example swans, deer and bee hives which all live in the same space as this proposed facility. - There are many safety and potential health risks such as the potential of battery chemical leakage into soil which would be nearby residential areas. Many people have animals dogs, cats and horses which are walking around the area regularly due to the wooded area and fishing pond. Battery storage is a high risk storage facility. With residents living near by, if such a major incident occurred (explosion or fire) this could be detrimental to their health due to the chemicals exposed. There is not enough research into long term health and with having young children how would their health be affected long term with this? - With the village being small there is not the infrastructure for increased traffic. The roads around are already narrow and many vehicles pass through to reach other locations. With having young children living nearby this would be a risk for them also. Please review these comments seriously.

I am writing to vehemently oppose the proposed battery energy storage facility. While acknowledging the imperative shift towards renewable energy, the selected site for this project raises profound environmental concerns that cannot be overlooked. First and foremost, the construction and operation of the facility would disrupt delicate ecosystems and wildlife habitats in our area. Our village is surrounded by pristine natural landscapes, home to diverse flora and fauna. Introducing a large-scale industrial facility threatens to fragment these habitats, disturb migratory patterns, and potentially endanger local wildlife populations. Moreover, the increased traffic and industrial activity associated with the facility's construction and ongoing operation would exacerbate air and noise pollution in our already serene environment. The idyllic atmosphere that draws residents and visitors alike would be compromised, impacting not only our quality of life but also our physical and mental well-being. Additionally, the visual intrusion of such a facility contradicts the principles of conservation that our village holds dear. Our community has worked tirelessly to preserve its historic charm and rural character, and the presence of towering battery storage units would starkly contrast with our scenic surroundings, detracting from the beauty that defines our village. Furthermore, the long-term implications of the facility on our local environment are deeply troubling. The disposal of battery components, potential leaks or spills, and the risk of fire pose significant environmental hazards that could irreversibly damage our ecosystem and compromise the health of our residents. In light of these profound environmental concerns, I urge the Planning Committee to reconsider the proposed location of the battery energy storage facility and explore alternative sites that minimize harm to our natural surroundings

I am writing to formally object to the proposed development of a battery storage facility near [PLACE]. While I recognize the importance of renewable energy and the transition to more sustainable energy solutions, I have significant concerns about the potential environmental and tourism impacts of this project on our community. Environmental Concerns: 1. Disruption of Local Wildlife and Ecosystems: the area is home to a diverse range of wildlife and natural habitats. The construction and ongoing operation of a large battery storage facility could severely disrupt local ecosystems, displacing native species and harming the delicate balance of our environment. The proposed site is located in a region where wildlife conservation is vital, and the impact of such a development could be long-lasting. 2. Pollution Risks: Battery storage facilities involve the use of potentially hazardous materials, including chemicals that could pose risks to both the land and surrounding water sources. In the event of an accident, such as a fire or leakage, there could be significant contamination of local soil and water, endangering both human and animal health. We are deeply concerned about the environmental footprint this facility could leave behind. 3. Aesthetic Degradation: The natural beauty of [PLACE] is one of its defining features and is vital to its identity. The construction of a battery storage facility would introduce large, industrial structures into what is currently a peaceful, scenic landscape. This could spoil the aesthetic value of the area, leading to long-term environmental degradation and a loss of visual appeal. Impact on Tourism: 1. Visual Pollution: The construction and operation of the battery storage facility would introduce large-scale infrastructure into an otherwise picturesque area. This could significantly diminish the visual appeal of the landscape, which is a key attraction for tourists who visit to enjoy the natural beauty of [PLACE] 2. Potential Economic Harm: Tourism is an essential part of our local economy, with many businesses relying on visitors who come for the natural scenery, outdoor activities, and local heritage. The proposed facility could deter tourists from visiting the area, leading to a reduction in foot traffic and a potential downturn in revenue for small businesses, hotels, and local restaurants. 3. Noise and Traffic: During construction and the ongoing operation of the facility, there is a risk of increased noise pollution, which could disturb the peaceful environment tourists come to enjoy. Additionally, the increased traffic from construction vehicles and the facility's operations could result in congestion, further detracting from the area's appeal. We strongly urge you to reconsider the approval of this project in its current location and to take into account the long-term consequences for both our environment and economy. Thank you for your consideration.

target_text: 1. This holding objection has been prepared in respect of the proposed [ORGANIZATION] [PLACE] BESS application, ECU reference: [APPLICATION_CODE] and [ORGANIZATION] ePlanning reference [APPLICATION_CODE]. 2. The response has been prepared by [PERSON] (a planning consultant with 48 years’ experience and specialising for the last 20 years in the assessment of renewable energy projects and the related expert witness advice). It has been prepared on behalf of Ms [PERSON], [PLACE], [PLACE] who has significant concerns around the scheme specific and cumulative adverse significant environmental and risk effects that will arise as a result of this proposed development. 3. Given the wide range of large scale renewable energy developments being progressed in the wider area comprising an arc to the west, east, and south of [PLACE], the likely wide range and nature of cumulative effects is of particular concern in the circumstances of there being no single forum that assesses, considers and determines what is happening to this locality as a whole. Instead, there is only uncoordinated multiple single project decisions. 4. It is considered that the application material does not adequately describe the emerging cumulative position in this locality. Therefore, two up to date cumulative maps, prepared by Ms Haltiner, will be submitted as an appendix to this holding objection and should be loaded up to the case file alongside the objection. 5. The instructions in this case have been issued by Ms Haltiner. The objection is being submitted to the ECU representations email address and to the Council via the ePlanning portal. 6. The application, in its current form, is for a battery storage facility of a maximum output of 300MW, located in a randomly selected field near the village of [PLACE] in [PLACE]. The application documentation freely admits that the proposal is part of an attempt to address intermittency and constraints payments, two serious consequences of current energy policy. However, although the proposed development is large scale in its appearance, its ability to contribute to grid management is tiny compared with the scale of the problem. Therefore, by way of a preliminary point, it is submitted that rather than litter the countryside with hundreds of these small scale energy storage units much more sustainable solutions, such as colocation of generation and demand, and/or mini nuclear generating stations should be promoted. 7. Using an installed capacity figure, such as that given here, is not a realistic way of considering the ability of the proposed BESS to contribute to the management of electricity supply and transmission from intermittent generation sources. Rather, what matters is the total storage capacity of the batteries (which will presumably decline over time with each discharge and recharge cycle), the rate at which it can supply electricity to the grid, for how long it can supply at that rate (and hence the total amount of electricity transmitted to the grid), and how long it then takes to recharge the BESS facility. 8. The built facilities, as proposed, are described in Table 1.1 of the submitted Planning Statement. The 196 battery units would each be 6.06m (l) by 2.44m (w) by 3.2m (h). the 98 associated MV Skid control units would be 12.19m (l) by 2.44m (w) by 3.61m (h). the high voltage transformer would be 7.65m high. containers and 88 power conditioning units is not given. There would be associated transformer units. There would be switchgear and control buildings. The site would have a screening fence. Overall, the development would have a highly industrialised appearance. 9. There would also be associated infrastructure including fencing, hardstanding areas, parking, security lighting, and the formation of an access to the [PLACE]. 10. The grid connection is not part of the current proposal even although it is clearly and intrinsically part of the overall scheme. The failure to assess its impact as part of the Environmental Information Assessment means that the whole project has not been assessed in accordance with the requirements of the 2017 Environmental Impact Assessment Regulations. The relevant tests are quite clear, and the question is would either of the two elements be implemented without the other, and the obvious answer is that they would not. For this reason alone, the application should be refused. 11. In addition to the plethora of wind farms and wind farm proposals in the wider area it is becoming clearer that the dispersed random pattern of energy production favoured by the Scottish Government is leading to the need for significant grid connections in the form of new OHLs, upgraded OHLs, new and/or expanded substations, and also a considerable number of other BESS proposals (a situation that is being replicated in many locations throughout [PLACE]). In this locality there is a particular focus on the arc around the west, south and east of [PLACE]. The existing substation at [PLACE] is likely to be expanded. There is the [PLACE] Hub substation proposal that has now been submitted. There are at least two additional new substations proposed in that location (with other substations elsewhere). In community consultation events [ORGANIZATION] admitted that [PLACE] was a “suitable location” as there so much room for expansion and building. 12. In this specific locality there are also a range of other potential offshore and onshore renewable energy facilities as recognised in the supporting material for the application. There might also be the need for accommodation camps for the construction stages (as is becoming clear with the [PLACE] renewable energy projects). Such proposals would be visually dominant and would be in addition to wind farms and OHLs and BESS facilities all in the same view or views. 13. These important multi project aspects should all be included in the cumulative visualisations and in the cumulative assessments. If they are not included, then the decision maker has only a partial picture of what the outcome of a consent would be. 14. It should also be made clear in the assessment of BESS applications that the cumulative aspects include cumulative fire risks, cumulative pollution risks, and cumulative noise risks. These are regarded as serious risks that merit careful consideration, and there is the need for the development of new policy and guidance, including requiring quantitative risk assessments. This has been established good practice with other high risk development proposals such as petrochemical plants, nuclear related facilities, shipping and docks proposals and certain MoD related facilities, all of which have full time on site staff unlike BESS facilities which are remotely managed. 15. It has been increasingly realized that the risk of fire from this type of battery storage is a potentially serious hazard that could impact on the local community and the local environment. It is noted that the trains on the Scottish Government owned ScotRail now have warning messages in the carriages advising that lithium battery devices are not allowed on trains. That formal position by a Scottish Government entity confirms that there is an issue. There have also been several press reports of battery fires where the response of the emergency services has been to just let the fire burn out while trying to prevent the fire from spreading by cooling neighbouring units with copious amounts of water. That is unlikely to be an acceptable response in localities around [PLACE] especially if peat is burned out as part of this process. 16. It is generally accepted that the operation of the planning and consenting systems should not seek to replicate or duplicate other regulatory regimes. However, it is also understood that the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service ([ORGANIZATION]) is currently not a statutory consultee in respect of planning applications or S36 applications. That means that there is a potential gap in the consideration of the possible risks involved with BESS applications. 17. An objector for the Fasnakyle BESS planning application ([ORGANIZATION] reference [APPLICATION_CODE]) decided to contact [ORGANIZATION] directly and received the undernoted answer (an extract is provided): 18. a. However, from an operational perspective, there are a couple of pertinent points I would seek clarification on. 19. b. Would the BESS be upwind from any residential housing? These systems can produce toxic gases/smoke. A gas release can occur well before and without the occurrence of a thermal runaway, at temperatures of approximately 90°C. If the emitted gases are mixed with air in a confined or partially confined environment (e.g. the battery box itself), there is a risk of gas overpressure which can cause an explosion. This may result in debris being ejected over a considerable distance. According to the attached document, the minimum safe distance from buildings would be 25 m and 10 m from combustible vegetation. 20. c. To deal and extinguish these types of fires require copious amounts of water. Are there adequate water supplies nearby? This can also lead to environmental considerations from water run-off. 21. d. In terms of response to an incident involving a BESS, this would likely include a HAZMAT response and would include resources from surrounding stations including [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE] and possibly strategic resources from further afield. 22. e. I am unaware if there has been consultation with [ORGANIZATION] on any Risk Management Plans or Emergency Response Plans shared. Like I mentioned, my colleagues in Prevention & Protection may be aware so I have cc'd them into this email. 23. This response clearly articulates the issues and the risks. A few points can be made in further response, drawing on other situations where the planning system has to address risk issues: 24. a. It is agreed that the correct principle is that the planning and consenting systems should not seek to duplicate other regulatory regimes. 25. b. But in the case of nuclear, oil and gas, MoD, railways, and shipping/port related proposals there has always been a protocol for liaison with the relevant safety regulator and, when taking an application to Committee or to Ministers for determination, the relevant officer would be aware of what the Regulator was going to decide. 26. c. However, it appears that there is currently no such protocol for BESS proposals. 27. d. As seen from the [ORGANIZATION] response there could be environmental consequences which are material planning considerations (in addition to the obvious safety issues). 28. e. The recent very extensive wildfire at [PLACE] shows just how quickly a fire can get largely out of control in remote rural woodland and moorland ecosystem locations (forests, heather, peat, especially drying peat, wildlife) with widespread and devastating consequences as well as clearly showing the challenges of responding to a fire in such locations. 29. f. The January 2024 wildfire in [PLACE] shows that wildfires can start and spread very quickly over a wide area even in winter conditions. 30. g. Very recently there have been further reports of e-Bike fires whilst, in [PLACE], SEPA has withdrawn a waste management licence from a site because of safety and pollution concerns arising from battery storage. In addition, there was a recent intensive fire at waste management site at [PLACE] ([PLACE]) that involved battery units, leading to acrid smoke that was seen up to 25 miles away and the attendance on site of SEPA staff to address potentially significant pollution issues. 31. h. And there have been further battery fires at [PLACE] and [PLACE] all as reported in news media. 32. 25. Taking all of these points together the key planning issue is the significant safety, environmental risk, and damage that would follow from a fire at a BESS site and from the fighting of that fire at such locations (assuming that there are [ORGANIZATION] resources nearby). The scale of those risks adds significantly to the case for refusal of this application, as does the consideration of the local geography. Experience suggests that if there was a fire in the area the smoke would tend to travel north towards [PLACE] and then towards [PLACE]. 33. It is also noted, as considered later in this objection, that the Council is actively preparing new guidance on safety issues associated with BESS proposals. 34. There are other health and safety and related environmental risk factors that could be mentioned including: 35. a. The growing number of battery fires in Scotland, the growing concerns and experiences with the related issues of contaminated water runoff and the release of toxic fumes, and 36. b. Specific to this application, the risks that would arise if a vehicle, say a car or a large HGV, left the public road and crashed into any of the multiple BESS and substation sites and the cumulative safety risks and the necessary enhanced responses from having multiple BESS developments adjacent to each other. 37. However, the most critical update is the consultation response to this application from [ORGANIZATION], dated 6th February 2025. That response advises that the [ORGANIZATION] are assessing all BESS applications and that a Working Group has been established to enable the provision of unified responses to all applications. It is submitted that no further BESS applications should be progressed until this Working Group has published its conclusions and responses to applications. 38. The Submitted Supporting Information 39. No formal EIA was required by the Council for this proposal. However, supporting documentation was submitted and some comments on that material are set out below particularly with regard to the LVIA assessment and elevation figures, transportation, biodiversity and safety. 40. The proposal is basically 196 shipping containers, with extensive ancillary equipment, including 98 similarly sized MV Skid containers, set out in two rows in a field. From considering the limited number of submitted visualisations it can be concluded that the standard techniques, especially wide angle views and the rendering of the buildings and other infrastructure, are wholly inadequate for showing the visual effects of such an extremely large scale regimented site layout. Furthermore, the existing woodland which provides some screening is not under the control of the applicants and, therefore, this screening cannot be relied upon as mitigation. 41. In addition, the viewpoint visualisations and the elevational drawings do not show the cumulative effects from the wide range of cumulative schemes from both scenarios 1 and 2 in the LVIA report. The elevations drawings do not even show the whole development proposed for the site. Given the extensive range of these projects it is considered that fully detailed cumulative wirelines and photomontages are needed for each application viewpoints. However, considering the ZTV for this proposed development alongside the ZTVs for the cumulative schemes, it is probable that an additional set of cumulative viewpoints would be needed. Without these cumulative visualisations it is not possible to assert that the landscape and visual effects of the proposal are acceptable. 42. There is no doubt that the transportation effects of this proposed development will include disruption, noise, dust, vibration and the risks of an accident closing the lifeline [PLACE]. However, this is only one of many potential developments off this section of the [PLACE] and that is a serious concern. The Transportation Assessment and Outline Construction Traffic Management Plan does address cumulative effects, but the approach seems to be one of waiting to see what is consented/approved and the start of site works and then discuss matters. Should consent be granted for this proposal the objector would wish to see much firmer proposals to assess the detailed adverse effects of the various cumulative schemes as well as more effective controls that would prevent too multiple developments proceeding at the same time. 43. Additionally, in respect of cumulative transportation issues, this will be but one of several renewable energy related developments seeking a new access to the [PLACE]. The creation of multiple new junctions on what is already a fast and potentially dangerous road is a matter of considerable concern. 44. An Ecological Assessment report has been provided. However, the details of proposed habitat management and enhancement measures are deferred to later stages. Given the complex cumulative position it is considered that more detail should have been required at the application stage. 45. There is an Outline Battery Safety Management Plan for this application. However, its terms are fairly generic, and no further comment is made pending the outcome of the [ORGANIZATION] Working Group. 46. The above short comments are taken into account in the wider concerns that are set out in this objection. 47. Consultee Responses 48. At this stage there are no significant available key consultee responses. Further comment can be made on these at a later stage. 49. However, continuing on the safety aspects, the initial and draft update guidance documents from the English National Fire Chiefs Council ([ORGANIZATION]) are referenced in the application material but the actual documents have not been submitted. The range of issues, information requirements, design guidance and responses in the [ORGANIZATION] guidance appears to be comprehensive. It is noted that the outputs that are sought are a risk management plan, an emergency response plan, and a post incident recovery plan (in addition to environmental information). The objector welcomes the notification, in the consultee responses for other BESS applications, that the Council is preparing guidance based on this English documentation (see above). It is submitted that the required assessments and output plans should be submitted PRIOR to the determination of any BESS application by either the Council or the ECU. 50. The Development Plan Assessment 51. The HWLDP does not contain policies associated with BESS proposals and, therefore, the focus on the Development Plan assessment is on the relevant policies in NPF4. This is considered to be an appropriate approach for what has been submitted as a S36 application. 52. Policy 1 (tackling the climate and nature crises) is an overarching policy that requires that significant weight is given to these two issues when considering development proposals. In relation to this Policy there is ample evidence that this BESS proposal will cause some harm to nature through effects on bird species, and habitat displacement. Furthermore, the applicants can point to no evidence that the project, on its own or in combination with other BESS or transmission projects, will have any verifiable and measurable beneficial effect on global climate. The proposal, therefore, is not supported by any evidence of any beneficial effect on global climate but it will have an adverse effect on nature (that is not offset by net biodiversity gain) and so the proposal fails to demonstrate compliance with the terms of this overarching policy test especially as there are alternative technologies for storing any surplus electricity. 53. In this respect it is noted that, on 18th September 2023, in a response to the BBC about the First Minister attending climate change talks in New York in person, the Cabinet Secretary for Transport, Net Zero, and Just Transition went on to talk about the licence for the Rosebank oil field west of [PLACE]. What she said, as reported by the BBC Scotland web page, was: 54. a. “It is an evidence based approach that we want to see taken by the UK Government including a very strict climate compatibility test, and if Rosebank can’t meet a strict climate compatibility test I see no reason why it should go ahead.” 55. 43. The Scottish Government Depute First Minster repeated the need for an evidence based approach to climate policy compatibility tests when commenting on further rounds of North Sea oil and gas exploration licences. 56. These statements by Ministers are taken to be supportive of the submission above of seeking an evidence based approach to the evaluation of the asserted climate change benefits of renewable energy proposals. 57. In the supporting information the findings for the various effects for the various biodiversity considerations are predicated on mitigation being successful. As far as is known there are no NatureScot sponsored peer reviewed scientific studies into the effectiveness of renewable energy related mitigation measures in Scottish energy schemes. On the contrary, the experience with projects such as the existing Fallago Rig, Creag Riabhach, and Viking wind farms is that the reliance on planning controls through conditions has not worked and that environmental harm occurs without subsequent effective enforcement action. 58. In terms of Policy 1 (Global Climate and Nature Crises) the proposed BESS development will not directly contribute any benefit to addressing climate change. 59. Policy 3 (biodiversity) is key. Policy 3b provides that for, inter alia, national developments, these will only be supported where it can be demonstrated that the proposal will conserve, restore and enhance biodiversity, including nature networks so that they are in a demonstrably better state than without intervention. The supporting material for the application does not provide an appropriate detailed metric based specific proposals and guaranteed delivery mechanisms to deliver on the policy requirement for betterment (having regard to the accepted adverse biodiversity effects of constructing the BESS). It is considered that without either metrics or a long term guaranteed delivery mechanism it is simply not plausible to rely on say an outline Biodiversity Enhancement Plan as a basis for asserting compliance with this NPF4 policy. 60. The very recent Garcrogo wind farm appeal decision ([ORGANIZATION] reference PPA-170-2172) specifically addressed NPF4 Policy 3 in rejecting the appeal. The decision letter should be referred to by the NPAC. The Reporter set out what she saw as the information requirements that would be needed to comply with NPF4 Policy 3 (paras 105 to 112) and in the absence of that information she finds that the proposal does not comply with the Policy. Similar considerations apply in this case and this BESS proposal would also not accord with the Policy given the absence of up to date assessment and enhancement metrics and guaranteed delivery mechanisms. 61. In terms of the criteria set out in Policy 3b) it is concluded as below for the proposed [ORGANIZATION] [PLACE] BESS proposal: 62. a. It is agreed that the context is broadly understood, although the fieldwork had a limited geographic extent. 63. b. It is not clear that all feasible opportunities have been taken to integrate and make best use of nature based solutions. 64. c. In terms of the mitigation hierarchy the first principle, avoidance, should have led to a more detailed consideration of alternatives on other sites or the use of other technologies. 65. d. There is no evidence of significant biodiversity enhancements of the types mentioned in the Policy text, nor of the required certainty of delivery, nor of binding provisions for the long term management, retention and monitoring that is required to deliver the benefits envisaged by this Policy. 66. e. Nor are there firm proposals for delivering and securing local community benefits from biodiversity enhancement. 67. 50. In conclusion, the proposal fails in respect of this policy test having regard to the general principles and to the related criteria (bar criterion 1 which relates to the understanding of the existing characteristics). The proposal, therefore, fails in terms of this key policy test. 68. As an aside, and in respect of NPF4 Policy 3, it is noted from other cases that the [ORGANIZATION] is requesting that management and/or enhancement plans are secured by way of a S75 Agreement so that the terms are legally binding on all current and future parties with an interest in the relevant land. 69. Policy 4 (natural places) is another key policy. In relation to this Policy and applying the test in Policy 4a, the proposal’s unacceptable impact on the natural environment means that the proposal should not be supported. 70. In terms of protected species, Policy 4f, the proposal (having regard to cumulative effects) has failed to deliver adequate protection in that the reduction of effects to the predicted level is again dependent in mitigation whose effectiveness cannot be guaranteed at this stage. The proposal, therefore, fails in terms of this key policy test. 71. Policy 11 (energy) is the key policy in terms of the assessment of renewable energy related proposals. 72. Policy 11b) does not apply as the proposal is not in a National Park or an NSA. 73. Policy 11c) addresses net economic impact. A Socio-economic Impact Report has been submitted. However, there is no assessment of the net effects to take account of social and environmental costs or displacement. The analysis of realistic options for maximising the local benefits is very limited. Therefore, the proposal does not demonstrate that the net economic benefit is maximised and therefore the proposal is in conflict with this Policy. Again, the Garcrogo appeal decision deals with the similar situation and confirms that the Policy expectation is that there should be specific and up to date evidence that addresses the maximisation point. 74. In terms of the specific impacts listed in Policy 11e, the proposed BESS facility has not adequately addressed and mitigated: 75. a. Impacts on communities. 76. b. Landscape and visual effects. Such effects, arising from the extensive scale of the proposed development, are not localised, nor has appropriate design mitigation been applied. The scheme specific and cumulative landscape and visual impacts are potentially under-assessed in the supporting material and are unacceptable overall. 77. c. Impacts on road traffic and on road safety. Road safety is a major concern with this being one of several proposed developments that could affect the [PLACE]. 78. d. Biodiversity effects including adverse effects on bird species. 79. e. A full range of cumulative impacts in terms of the known proposals for major renewable energy projects in the wider locality. 80. 58. Notwithstanding that considerable weight is to be given to the contribution to renewable targets and emissions reduction targets, the adverse impacts are unacceptable. 81. The overall conclusion that is reached is that the proposal, therefore, fails in terms of this key NPF4 policy. 82. Some consideration should be given to Policy 14 (design, quality and place). Although not considered to be a key determining issue, the proposal fails the test of Policy 14a in that it has not been designed to improve the quality of the rural locations it affects. It will not contribute towards creating a successful place. 83. In terms of the policy outcomes for Policy 18 (infrastructure first) the applicants have not demonstrated that the existing infrastructure assets can be used sustainably without the need for this proposed new development. 84. Policy 25 (community wealth building) is also considered to be of some relevance. The various factors mentioned in Policy 25a in terms of building local community wealth have not been addressed by the applicants. A more localised development and use model for renewable energy would be appropriate here following on from the lead given in Policy 15 (local living and 20 minute neighbourhoods) and also reflecting the regulatory updates being progressed by OFGEM. 85. The consideration of Policy 29 (rural development) follows on from this. It cannot be seen how this project, which is specifically designed and justified (so far as can be assessed at this stage) on the basis of providing an electricity supply to a distant market and not to a local market, can make a material contribution to helping to create vibrant and sustainable local rural businesses and communities. 86. Therefore, it can be concluded that, overall, the proposal can draw no support overall from the various NPF4 Policies assessed above. 87. Material Considerations 88. The objector is satisfied that all of the appropriate policy provisions and material considerations for a determination are now captured in the very up to date NPF4 and there is no need to go beyond that other the for the risk related issues. 89. Therefore, there is, at this stage, nothing that would lead to a setting aside of the conclusions that flow from the assessment of the relevant policies as set out above. 90. A Suggested Planning Condition 91. It has been noted that a fairly generic Outline Battery Safety Management Plan has been submitted in support of the application. It can only be assumed that the general approach of the applicants will be to try to defer the necessary detailed assessments to the stage of compliance with a post planning permission “plan” type pre-commencement condition. 92. Following on from the general points made above on risk, this assumed approach is similar to that proposed in respect to the [PLACE] BESS ([ORGANIZATION] ePlanning Ref: [APPLICATION_CODE]). The applicant/agent for that proposal wrote to the Council on 20th May 2023 suggesting that the application could be approved with a planning condition requiring the pre-commencement approval by the Council, in consultation with the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service ([ORGANIZATION]), of a site specific emergency response plan/fire response plan. The letter is 3 pages long and it should be read for its full terms. 93. The suggestion is an interesting concept drawn from the applicant’s experience in England. In Scotland, and despite repeated requests to the Scottish Government from various Planning Authorities, the [ORGANIZATION] is not a statutory consultee for development management purposes. However, as noted earlier, the [ORGANIZATION] has set up a Working Group to assess BESS applications and the related issues. 94. However, setting that [ORGANIZATION] position aside for the moment, it is worth considering the detail of what would be involved. The suggested condition lists 12 issues that would be addressed in the “plan”. These issues include, inter alia, fire access design drawings, details of the substances on site, incident plans, details of the onsite water supply, an environmental assessment associated with the risks, measures to address containment of contaminated water (which might well have an influence on site design and so should be addressed just now), a site recovery plan, and any other information required by [ORGANIZATION]. 95. The list of issues is fairly comprehensive, representing a very considerable quantity of technical, risk, and consequence information. However, in the format proposed the application would have already been approved before this documentation was produced, meaning that there would be pressure for the material submitted in compliance with the pre-commencement condition to be approved. 96. Nonetheless, there is value to be taken from the suggestion but applying it at a different stage in the process. It is submitted that the Council, for this [ORGANIZATION] [PLACE] BESS proposal and for every other BESS application that comes before it, should urgently complete the preparation of its own guidance. It should also require that the resultant sets of information envisaged by the suggested condition mentioned earlier, and the [ORGANIZATION] guidance should be submitted for evaluation and consideration PRIOR to the consideration and/or determination of any application by the Council. 97. The ECU, for its part, should be pausing the progressing of all BESS applications until the [ORGANIZATION] Working Group has reported. 98. Summary and Conclusions 99. Having considered the issues raised earlier and having reviewed the submitted supporting information it is concluded that the application is not in accordance with the Development Plan on account of the scheme specific and cumulative adverse effects and risks not being outweighed by the asserted benefits of the scheme such that the proposal in not in accordance with the provisions of the Development Plan, especially NPF4 Policies 1, 3, 4 and 11. 100. There are no material considerations that would change that Development Plan conclusion. 101. As this is being proposed as an Electricity Act application (but see the legal point made at the start of this holding objection) it is concluded that insufficient mitigation has been provided and, therefore, the requirements of the Act have not been met. 102. There are a number of other considerations that the NPAC is asked to take into account in the formulation of the Council’s response to the ECU on this application. 103. If the various risk related assessments and the associated outputs have not been prepared and considered as part of the evaluation of the proposal, then the application should be the subject of an objection on the grounds of insufficient information. 104. As noted earlier, it is appreciated that the Committee members might find it difficult to visualise the complexity and variety of cumulative effects arising from a range of renewable energy projects comprising existing, consented, and proposed elements. This cumulative aspect of a considerable number of renewable energy related projects coming forward in a short time frame is a very major concern to the client. 105. Therefore, as noted earlier, up to date cumulative plans, prepared by the objector, will be submitted as an appendix to this objection. 106. Also as noted earlier, it is clear that BESS applications have scheme specific and cumulative risks including cumulative fire and cumulative pollution risks all of which could adversely affect both local populations and the local environment. These are regarded as serious risks that merit careful consideration. 107. It is submitted that, in addition to lodging an objection for this proposed BESS, the Council should pause the consideration of all BESS applications pending the development and implementation of their own new guidance taking account of the [ORGANIZATION] Working Group outputs, and the issuing of a requirement that all BESS applications must be accompanied by: 108. a. A full EIA-R that follows on from a scoping assessment. 109. b. A quantified mathematical risk assessment report based on a review of known events, a listing of the design lessons learned, and the risks designed out, and then the evaluation of probability and consequence for the remaining risks. 110. c. The full range of assessments and response/recovery plans as referenced earlier in this objection and as envisaged in the suggested condition for the [PLACE] BESS application, the Glengolly BESS application supporting information, the English [ORGANIZATION] document, and the expected [ORGANIZATION] advice. 111. The objective of this approach is to ensure that the Planning Officer, and then the NPAC, has all of the relevant environmental and safety information before them at the same time and in advance of the determination of the Council’s position on any BESS application. It will also ensure that the ECU has this relevant information. 112. Recommendations 113. Having regard to the terms of this holding objection it is recommended that Scottish Ministers should: 114. a. Consider whether it is lawful to progress such applications, which are not electricity generating stations, as Electricity Act S36 applications 115. b. If, contrary to the position taken by the [ORGANIZATION], they do consider the application to be lawful then they should refuse S36 consent and deemed planning permission on account of insufficient mitigation being secured and on account of non compliance with the relevant Policies in NPF4.

retrieved_examples.text: Introduction 1. This holding objection has been prepared in respect of the proposed [PLACE] application, ECU reference: [APPLICATION_CODE] and [ORGANIZATION] ePlanning reference [APPLICATION_CODE]. If the application continues to be processed then further submissions will be made at later stages. The Legal Position 2. There has been recent correspondence with the [ORGANIZATION] in connection with Reporters sustaining renewable energy appeals and granting planning permissions to proposals where the combined installed capacities of the proposed turbines and the proposed BESS were well in excess of the 50MW threshold (PPA-17-2179 and 2178). 3. In their response to the suggestion that a procedural error had been made, the [ORGANIZATION] advised on 23rd July 2024, that: “Section 36 of the Electricity Act 1989 relates to the consent required for construction etc of generating stations. Based on the definition of “stored energy” in section 4(3ZB) of the Electricity Act 1989, battery energy storage systems store electricity that is already generated rather than generating electricity themselves.” 4. The clear implication was that the Reporters were not counting the BESS element as contributing to the installed capacity in either case. 5. Drawing on this position, as set out by a Scottish Government Agency, the above application is for the storage of electricity and not for the generation of electricity and, therefore, it cannot lawfully be progressed as an Electricity Act S36 application. 6. However, pending a response from the ECU on this matter, a response to the application has been prepared. Background 7. The response has been prepared by [PERSON] (a planning consultant with 47 years’ experience and specialising for the last 20 years in the assessment of renewable energy projects and the related expert witness advice). It has been prepared on behalf of Ms [PERSON], [PLACE], [PLACE] who has significant concerns around the scheme specific and cumulative adverse significant environmental and risk effects that will arise as a result of this proposed development. 8. Given the wide range of large scale renewable energy developments being progressed in the wider area comprising an arc to the west, east, and south of [PLACE], the likely wide range and nature of cumulative effects is of particular concern in the circumstances of there being no single forum that assesses, considers and determines what is happening to this locality as a whole. Instead, there is only uncoordinated multiple single project decisions. 9. The instructions in this case have been issued by Ms Haltiner. The objection is being submitted to the ECU representations email address, to the ECU administration team, and to the Council via the ePlanning portal. 10. It is noted that at their April meeting the NPAC continued their consideration of the [PLACE] BESS application in order to consider the requested response from the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service ([ORGANIZATION]). This aspect is material to the consideration of all sizes of BESS proposals in the whole of the [ORGANIZATION] area (and is addressed later in the context of a consultee responses and a proposed planning condition). The Application Proposals 11. The application, in its current form, is for a battery storage facility of a maximum output of 300MW, located in a randomly selected field near the village of [PLACE] in [PLACE] (near the proposed but not yet built [PLACE] switching station). Indeed there appears to be two substations proposed – [ORGANIZATION] references [APPLICATION_CODE] and [APPLICATION_CODE]. 12. Using a figure such as that given is not a realistic way of considering the ability of the proposed BESS to contribute to the management of electricity supply and transmission from intermittent generation sources. Rather, what matters is the total storage capacity of the batteries (which will presumably decline over time with each discharge and recharge cycle), the rate at which it can supply electricity to the grid, for how long it can supply at that rate (and hence the total amount of electricity transmitted to the grid), and how long it then takes to recharge the BESS facility. 13. The built facilities, as proposed, are described in para 4.1 of the submitted Environmental Information Report but the dimensions of the 352 containers and 88 power conditioning units are not given. However, based on figures in the SEI these battery containers will have dimensions of 2.9m high, 2.4m wide, and 12.1m length. There would be associated transformer units. There would be switchgear and control buildings. The site would have a screening fence and surveillance equipment. 14. There would also be associated infrastructure including fencing, hardstanding areas, parking, and the formation of an access to the public road (the minor [PLACE] which is a single track road). Development traffic would also use the [PLACE] and [PLACE] and these roads are part of the [PLACE] route (and the [PLACE] runs alongside the site). 15. The grid connection (including any OHLs) is not part of the current proposal even although it is clearly and intrinsically part of the overall scheme. The failure to assess its impact as part of the Environmental Information Assessment means that the whole project has not been assessed in accordance with the requirements of the 2017 Environmental Impact Assessment Regulations. The relevant tests are quite clear, and the question is would either of the two elements be implemented without the other, and the obvious answer is that they would not. For this reason alone, the application should be refused. The Emerging Cumulative Position 16. In addition to the plethora of wind farms and wind farm proposals in the wider area it is becoming clearer that the dispersed random pattern of energy production favoured by the Scottish Government is leading to the need for significant grid connections in the form of new OHLs, upgraded OHLs, new and/or expanded substations, and also a considerable number of other BESS proposals (a situation that is being replicated in many locations throughout [PLACE]). In this locality there is a particular focus on the arc around the west, south and east of [PLACE]. The existing substation at [PLACE] is likely to be expanded and at least one additional new substation proposed in that location (with other substations elsewhere). In community consultation events [ORGANIZATION] admitted that [PLACE] was a suitable location as there so much room for expansion and building. 17. In this specific locality there are also a range of other potential offshore and onshore renewable energy facilities as recognised in the supporting material for the application. There might also be the need for accommodation camps for the construction stages (as is becoming clear with the [PLACE] renewable energy projects). Such proposals would be visually dominant and would be in addition to wind farms and OHLs and BESS facilities all in the same view or views. 18. These important multi project aspects should all be included in the cumulative visualisations and in the cumulative assessments. If they are not included, then the decision maker has only a partial picture of what the outcome of a consent would be. 19. It should also be made clear in the assessment of BESS applications that the cumulative aspects include cumulative fire risks, cumulative pollution risks, and cumulative noise risks. These are regarded as serious risks that merit careful consideration, and there is the need for the development of new policy and guidance (as has been provided to Planning Authorities in England) including requiring quantitative risk assessments (this has been established good practice with other high risk development proposals such as petrochemical plants, nuclear related facilities, shipping and docks proposals and certain MoD related facilities, all of which have full time on site staff unlike BESS facilities which are remotely managed). These risks have led to additional documentation being submitted in support of the Glengolly BESS planning application but with no similar assessment for this application. These aspects are addressed later in this holding objection. 20. As another overarching issue, it is appreciated that NPAC Members might find it difficult to visualise the geographic intensity, complexity, and variety of cumulative effects arising from an almost overwhelming range of renewable energy projects comprising existing, consented, and proposed elements. Therefore, it is submitted that, prior to considering any further renewable energy related projects, including this application, NPAC Members instruct Officers to prepare and submit to the Committee an OS based plan, for an area comprising a radius of 25km centred on [PLACE], on which should be shown (site boundary) and labelled (project/site name) every known existing and proposed renewable energy related projects. That plan can then be forwarded to the ECU as part of the Council’s consultation response. Community Safety Concerns 21. In recent years it has been increasingly realized that the risk of fire from this type of battery storage is a potentially serious hazard that could impact on the local community and the local environment. It is noted that the trains on the Scottish Government owned ScotRail now have warning messages in the carriages advising that lithium battery devices are not allowed on trains. That formal position by a Scottish Government entity confirms that there is an issue. There have also been several press reports of battery fires in England where the response of the emergency services has been to just let the fire burn out. That is unlikely to be an acceptable response in localities around [PLACE] especially if peat is burned out as part of this process. 22. It is generally accepted that the operation of the planning and consenting systems should not seek to replicate or duplicate other regulatory regimes. However, it is also understood that the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service ([ORGANIZATION]) is not a statutory consultee in respect of planning applications or S36 applications. That means that there is a potential gap in the consideration of the possible risks involved with BESS applications. 23. An objector for the Fasnakyle BESS planning application ([ORGANIZATION] reference [APPLICATION_CODE]) decided to contact [ORGANIZATION] directly and received the undernoted answer (an extract is provided): a. However, from an operational perspective, there are a couple of pertinent points I would seek clarification on. b. Would the BESS be upwind from any residential housing? These systems can produce toxic gases/smoke. A gas release can occur well before and without the occurrence of a thermal runaway, at temperatures of approximately 90°C. If the emitted gases are mixed with air in a confined or partially confined environment (e.g. the battery box itself), there is a risk of gas overpressure which can cause an explosion. This may result in debris being ejected over a considerable distance. According to the attached document, the minimum safe distance from buildings would be 25 m and 10 m from combustible vegetation. c. To deal and extinguish these types of fires require copious amounts of water. Are there adequate water supplies nearby? This can also lead to environmental considerations from water run-off. d. In terms of response to an incident involving a BESS, this would likely include a HAZMAT response and would include resources from surrounding stations including [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE] and possibly strategic resources from further afield. e. I am unaware if there has been consultation with [ORGANIZATION] on any Risk Management Plans or Emergency Response Plans shared. Like I mentioned, my colleagues in Prevention & Protection may be aware so I have cc'd them into this email. 24. This response clearly articulates the issues and the risks. A few points can be made in further response, drawing on other situations where the planning system has to address risk issues: a. It is agreed that the correct principle is that the planning and consenting systems should not seek to duplicate other regulatory regimes. b. But in the case of nuclear, oil and gas, MoD, railways, and shipping/port related proposals there has always been a protocol for liaison with the relevant safety regulator and, when taking an application to Committee or to Ministers for determination, the relevant officer would be aware of what the Regulator was going to decide. c. However, it appears that there is currently no such protocol for BESS proposals. d. As seen from the [ORGANIZATION] response there could be environmental consequences which are material planning considerations (in addition to the obvious safety issues). e. The recent very extensive wildfire at [PLACE] shows just how quickly a fire can get largely out of control in remote rural woodland and moorland ecosystem locations (forests, heather, peat, especially drying peat, wildlife) with widespread and devastating consequences as well as clearly showing the challenges of responding to a fire in such locations. f. The January 2024 wildfire in [PLACE] shows that wildfires can start and spread very quickly over a wide area even in winter conditions. g. Very recently there have been further reports of e-Bike fires whilst, in [PLACE], SEPA has withdrawn a waste management licence from a site because of safety and pollution concerns arising from battery storage. In addition, there was a recent intensive fire at waste management site at [PLACE] ([PLACE]) that involved battery units leading to acrid smoke that was seen up to 25 miles away and the attendance on site of SEPA staff to address potentially significant pollution issues. 25. Taking all of these points together the key planning issue is the significant safety, environmental risk, and damage that would follow from a fire at a BESS site and from the fighting of that fire at such locations (assuming that there are [ORGANIZATION] resources nearby). The scale of those risks adds significantly to the case for refusal of this application, as does the consideration of the local geography. Experience suggests that if there was a fire in the area the smoke would tend to travel east towards [PLACE] and north over [PLACE]. 26. As noted above there is no safety related documentation associated with the application and this is addressed when consultee responses and a suggested planning condition (from another BESS planning application) are considered. 27. It is also noted, as considered later in this objection, that the Council is actively preparing new guidance on safety issues associated with BESS proposals, although it would be ideal if there was national level guidance in Scotland. 28. It cannot be stressed enough that there is a need for a consistent approach for all BESS proposals to have in place a rigorous hazard identification system with detailed descriptions and responses. The BEES proposals present a classic risk assessment case of a low probability (at a site level) but with serious consequences. Indeed, it would not be unreasonable to suggest that the [ORGANIZATION] needs to be involved in the provision of advice on such applications or even to be required to assess and issue or refuse a licence for such proposals. The Submitted Supporting Information 29. No formal EIA was required by the Council for this proposal. However, supporting documentation was submitted and some comments on that material are set out below particularly with regard to the LVIA assessment and figures set out in Appendix 3. 30. Five relatively close viewpoints were assessed, although the visibility of the proposal does extend much further west. a. VP 1 Minor Road near Philips Main – the photomontages show that the very extensive length of the development site along with the repetitive pattern of green boxes, totally changes the view from the existing. This is a significant adverse effect. b. VP 2 NCR1 Near [PLACE] – although there is a backdrop of existing trees the same significant adverse effect arises because of the sheer scale of the proposal. c. VP 3 [PLACE] at [PLACE] – there is virtually no visibility from this viewpoint and another viewpoint should have been chosen. d. VP 4 [PLACE] GDL – it is likely that the real life visibility would be greater than shown in the photomontage. e. VP 5 [PLACE] at [PLACE] – the same conclusion is reached as for VP 4. 31. The proposal is basically 352 shipping containers set out in long lines in a field. From considering the submitted visualisations it can be concluded that the standard techniques are wholly inadequate for showing the visual effects of such an extremely large scale regimented site layout. 32. An Outline Biodiversity Enhancement and Management Plan has been submitted but the approach is to defer detailed work, including the necessary metrics, until the post consent stage. 33. There is no Outline Battery Safety Management Plan for this application. This is considered to be unacceptable in comparison with the suite of safety related material that has been lodged in respect of Glengolly BESS ([APPLICATION_CODE]) and also as referenced in Ms Haltiner’s objection to that Glengolly BESS. That material should be referenced in connection with the assessment of this application, especially given the scale of this proposed development. 34. The above short comments are reflective of wider concerns that are set out in this objection. Consultee Responses 35. At this stage there are no significant available key consultee responses. Further comment can be made on these at a later stage. 36. However, continuing on the safety aspects, the guidance document from the English National Fire Chiefs Council ([ORGANIZATION]) that had been submitted for the Glengolly BESS has not been submitted for this application. The range of issues, information requirements, design guidance and responses appear to be comprehensive. It is noted that the outputs that are sought are a risk management plan, an emergency response plan, and a post incident recovery plan (in addition to environmental information). The objector welcomes the notification, in the consultee responses for other BESS applications, that the Council is preparing guidance based on this document (see above). It is submitted that the required assessments and output plans should be submitted PRIOR to the determination of any BESS application by either the Council or the ECU. 37. The above comments have been taken into account in the following section considering the Development Plan. Development Plan Assessment 38. The HWLDP does not contain policies associated with BESS proposals and, therefore, the focus on the Development Plan assessment is on the relevant policies in NPF4. This is considered to be an appropriate approach for what has been submitted as a S36 application. 39. Policy 1 (tackling the climate and nature crises) is an overarching policy that requires that significant weight is given to these two issues when considering development proposals. In relation to this Policy there is ample evidence that this BESS proposal will cause some harm to nature through effects on bird species, and habitat displacement. Furthermore, the applicants can point to no evidence that the project, on its own or in combination with other BESS or transmission projects, will have any verifiable and measurable beneficial effect on global climate. The proposal, therefore, is not supported by any evidence of any beneficial effect on global climate but it will have an adverse effect on nature (that is not offset by net biodiversity gain) and so the proposal fails to demonstrate compliance with the terms of this overarching policy test especially as there are alternative technologies for storing any surplus electricity. 40. In this respect it is noted that, on 18th September 2023, in a response to the BBC about the First Minister attending climate change talks in New York in person, the Cabinet Secretary for Transport, Net Zero, and Just Transition went on to talk about the licence for the Rosebank oil field west of [PLACE]. What she said, as reported by the BBC Scotland web page, was: a. “It is an evidence based approach that we want to see taken by the UK Government including a very strict climate compatibility test, and if Rosebank can’t meet a strict climate compatibility test I see no reason why it should go ahead.” 41. The Scottish Government Depute First Minster repeated the need for an evidence based approach to climate policy compatibility tests when commenting on further rounds of North Sea oil and gas exploration licences. 42. These statements by Ministers are taken to be supportive of the submission above of seeking an evidence based approach to the evaluation of the asserted climate change benefits of renewable energy proposals. 43. In the supporting information the findings for the various effects for the various biodiversity considerations are predicated on mitigation being successful. As far as is known there are no NatureScot sponsored peer reviewed scientific studies into the effectiveness of renewable energy related mitigation measures in Scottish energy schemes. On the contrary, the experience with projects such as the existing Fallago Rig, Creag Riabhach, and Viking wind farms is that the reliance on planning controls through conditions has not worked and that environmental harm occurs without subsequent effective enforcement action. 44. In terms of Policy 1 (Global Climate and Nature Crises) the proposed BESS development will not directly contribute any benefit to addressing climate change. 45. Policy 3 (biodiversity) is key. Policy 3b provides that for, inter alia, national developments, these will only be supported where it can be demonstrated that the proposal will conserve, restore and enhance biodiversity, including nature networks so that they are in a demonstrably better state than without intervention. The supporting material for the application does not provide an appropriate detailed metric based assessment or related specific proposals and guaranteed delivery mechanisms to deliver on the policy requirement for betterment (having regard to the accepted adverse biodiversity effects of constructing the BESS). It is considered that without either metrics or a long term guaranteed delivery mechanism it is simply not plausible to rely on say an outline Biodiversity Enhancement Plan as a basis for asserting compliance with this NPF4 policy. 46. The very recent Garcrogo wind farm appeal decision ([ORGANIZATION] reference PPA-170- 2172) specifically addressed NPF4 Policy 3 in rejecting the appeal. The decision letter should be referred to by the NPAC. The Reporter set out what she saw as the information requirements that would be needed to comply with NPF4 Policy 3 (paras 105 to 112) and in the absence of that information she finds that the proposal does not comply with the Policy. Similar considerations apply in this case and this BESS proposal would also not accord with the Policy given the absence of up to date assessment and enhancement metrics and guaranteed delivery mechanisms. 47. In terms of the criteria set out in Policy 3b) it is concluded as below for the proposed [PLACE] proposal: a. It is agreed that the context is broadly understood, although the fieldwork had a limited geographic extent. b. It is not clear that all feasible opportunities have been taken to integrate and make best use of nature based solutions. c. In terms of the mitigation hierarchy the first principle, avoidance, should have led to a more detailed consideration of alternatives on other sites or the use of other technologies. d. There is no evidence of significant biodiversity enhancements of the types mentioned in the Policy text, nor of the required certainty of delivery, nor of binding provisions for the long term management, retention and monitoring that is required to deliver the benefits envisaged by this Policy. e. Nor are there firm proposals for delivering and securing local community benefits from biodiversity enhancement. 48. In conclusion, the proposal fails in respect of this policy test having regard to the general principles and to the related criteria (bar criterion 1 which relates to the understanding of the existing characteristics). The proposal, therefore, fails in terms of this key policy test. 49. As an aside, and in respect of NPF4 Policy 3, it is noted from other cases that the [ORGANIZATION] is requesting that management and/or enhancement plans are secured by way of a S75 Agreement so that the terms are legally binding on all current and future parties with an interest in the relevant land. 50. Policy 4 (natural places) is another key policy.
