Having considered the issues raised earlier and having reviewed the submitted supporting information it is concluded that the application is not in accordance with the Development Plan on account of the scheme specific and cumulative adverse effects and risks not being outweighed by the asserted benefits of the scheme such that the proposal in not in accordance with the provisions of NPF4 Policies 3, 4 and 11. 93. There are no material considerations that would change that Development Plan conclusion. As this is a planning application and not a S36 application, the presumption in law, therefore, is for refusal of planning permission. 94. There are a number of other considerations that the Committee is asked to take into account in the determination of this application. 95. If the various risk related assessments and the associated outputs have not been prepared and considered as part of the evaluation of the proposal then the application should be rejected on the grounds of insufficient information. 96. As noted earlier, it is appreciated that the Committee members might find it difficult to visualise the complexity and variety of cumulative effects arising from a range of renewable energy projects comprising existing, consented, and proposed elements. A full EIA-R that follows on from a scoping assessment. 101. A quantified mathematical risk assessment report based on a review of known events, a listing of the design lessons learned, and the risks designed out, and then the evaluation of probability and consequence for the remaining risks. 102. The full range of assessments and response/recovery plans as referenced earlier in this objection and as envisaged in the suggested condition for the [PLACE] BESS application and the English [ORGANIZATION] document. 103. This objection has been prepared on behalf ‘The [PLACE] Fishing Syndicate’ who have significant concerns around the scheme’s specific and cumulative adverse environmental and risk effects that will arise as a result of the proposed [PLACE] BESS. The site is Class 2 Agricultural Land surrounded by greenfield land on the north, east, and west boundaries. The southern boundary runs along and is adjacent to the [PLACE], which is owned by the [PLACE] Fishing Syndicate. The [PLACE] is home to the IUCN red listed Atlantic salmon, along with numerous other protected and valued species. e.g. the European eel, Freshwater Pearl mussel etc. Examination of SEPAs classifications for the [PLACE] catchment suggests that water quality is generally of a high standard. The Proposed Development The Applicant has been in contact with [ORGANIZATION] who have indicated that the [PLACE] has the operational capacity to accommodate the Proposed Development. Consequently, they have deemed it unnecessary to explore further grid connection points beyond the secured connection point at [PLACE] Substation. It is understood that the connection to the substation from the Proposed Development is proposed to be achieved utilising underground cabling which would have to be routed underneath the [PLACE]. No discussions have occurred with the [PLACE] Fishing Syndicate relating to such a cable. Rights to lay such a cable are dependent upon the Syndicate as owner of the riverbed and salmon fishing. [ORGANIZATION] is opposed to any such cables either under or above the river. The application is for a BESS with a storage capacity of up to 100MW with associated infrastructure, earthworks, drainage, accesses and ancillary works (including landscaping, biodiversity enhancements). This equipment would be sited on a levelled and stoned platform with appropriate surface water drainage, with the compound enclosed by suitable security fencing. The Proposed Development would have a built compound that has a development footprint of approximately 1.5 hectares (ha) across the 18.51 ha site. The Emerging Cumulative Position The following renewable developments and infrastructure exist within a 5km radius of the application site: - Existing overhead power lines (OHL), including two 132kV OHL extending east-west through the Site; - Existing [PLACE], located 1.4km to the west of the Site; - Existing [PLACE], located 2.8km to the west; - Proposed [PLACE] Quary BESS (ref: [APPLICATION_CODE]) located 1.1km to the west; - Proposed [PLACE] (ref: [APPLICATION_CODE]) located 2.7km to the west; - Proposed [PLACE] BESS (ref: [APPLICATION_CODE]) located 2.9km to the west. Additional proposals at EIA scoping stage include: - A 400kV [PLACE] located 3.7km to the southwest (planning ref: [APPLICATION_CODE]). - A 400kV OHL would extend from this substation in an easterly direction towards [PLACE] (ref: [APPLICATION_CODE]). As part of this proposal, the existing OHL network would be rationalised, and the proposed 400kV alignment would replace one of the two existing 132kV OHLs that extend east-west across the Site. In addition to the above it is becoming apparent that the dispersed random pattern of energy production favoured by the Scottish Government is leading to the need for significant grid connections in the form of new OHLs, upgraded OHLs, new and/or expanded substations, and also a considerable number of other BESS proposals throughout [PLACE]. There might also be the need for accommodation camps for the construction stages. Such proposals would be visually dominant and would be in addition to wind farms and OHLs and BESS facilities all in the same view or views. These important multi project aspects should all be included in the cumulative visualisations and in the cumulative assessments. If they are not included, then the decision maker has only a partial picture of what the outcome of a consent would be. It should also be made clear in the assessment of BESS applications that the cumulative aspects include cumulative fire risks, cumulative pollution risks, and cumulative noise risks. Legislative Context Electricity Act 1989: Section 36 of the Electricity Act 1989 relates to the consent required for construction etc of generating stations. Based on the definition of “stored energy” in section 4(3ZB) of the Electricity Act 1989, battery energy storage systems store electricity that is already generated rather than generating electricity themselves. The proposed application is for the storage of electricity and not for the generation of electricity and, therefore, it cannot lawfully be progressed as an Electricity Act S36 application. Planning Policy Context The statutory Development Plan in the case of the Proposed Development consists of NPF4, the [PLACE]-Wide Local Development Plan (HwLDP), [PLACE] (2024) and any related Supplementary Guidance. This objection focuses on the incompatibility of the proposed development with the following NPF4 polices: - Policy 3: Biodiversity; - Policy 4: Natural Places; - Policy 5: Soils; - Policy 11: Energy; - Policy 14: Design, quality and place; - Policy 23: Health and Safety; - Policy 25: Community Wealth Building; - Policy 29: Rural Development. Policy 3 (Biodiversity) is a key policy. Part a) applies to all scales of development and states that proposals will contribute to the enhancement of biodiversity including, building and strengthening nature networks and the connections between them. The Preliminary Ecological Appraisal and HRA submitted with the planning application highlight the [PLACE] [PLACE], RAMSAR site and SPA that exist downstream from [PLACE] (1km from the site), and species on site but there has been no assessment made in relation to [PLACE] or relevant protected species which are directly adjacent to the site, approximately 10m away. NPF4 Policy 3b states that national and major developments will only be supported where it can be shown that they will conserve, restore and enhance biodiversity, including nature networks, so they are in a demonstrably better state than without intervention. The policy requires that such proposals demonstrate significant biodiversity enhancement, in addition to any proposed mitigation. The application does not provide guaranteed delivery mechanisms to deliver on the policy requirement for betterment (having regard to the accepted adverse biodiversity effects of constructing the BESS). It is therefore considered that without a long term guaranteed delivery mechanism it is simply not plausible to rely on a ‘recommended’ Habitat Management and Monitoring plan as a basis for asserting compliance with this NPF4 policy. It notes the effects associated with the Proposed Development would coalesce with the effects exerted by the existing pylons and notwithstanding mitigation planting, it accepts the proposed BESS would lead to additional effects which would be noticeable. As such, a cumulative effect on landscape character would arise and have a worsened cumulative effect on the landscape. These are regarded as serious risks that merit careful consideration in the assessment of the proposed BESS development. Policy 14 (design, quality and place). Policy 25 (community wealth building). The various factors mentioned in Policy 25a in terms of building local community wealth have not all been addressed by the applicants. Policy 29 (rural development). It cannot be seen how this project, which would also contribute to the provision of long-term sustainable and competitive energy supplies, assisting the UK renewables industry to become competitive in home and export markets can make a material contribution to helping to create vibrant and sustainable local rural businesses and communities. Conclusion It is concluded that the application is not fully in accordance with the Development Plan on account of the scheme specific and cumulative adverse effects and risks not being outweighed by the asserted benefits of the scheme, especially NPF4 Policies 4 and 11. While the proposed BESS would make a meaningful contribution to renewable energy and greenhouse gas emission reduction targets, it would entail development on Class 2 prime agricultural and have an unacceptable adverse effect on the environment. Recommendations Having regard to the terms of this objection it is recommended that Scottish Ministers should: a. Consider whether it is lawful to consent this application, which is not an electricity generating station, as Electricity Act S36 applications b. Or, Scottish Ministers should refuse S36 consent and deemed planning permission on account of insufficient mitigation being secured and on account of non-compliance with the relevant Policies in NPF4. c. Given the overwhelming range of renewable energy projects comprising existing, consented, and proposed elements. I think we have enough! Why do we need another massive battery storage plant in this small rural community when 3 have already been approved?! In addition, whilst the planning policies support renewable developments, this is ONLY when there is direct benefit to the community and this development contributes absolutely nothing, so should be refused. This facility would NOT store renewable energy, but instead be used to generate huge profits for the developer through arbitrage and not have any positive impact on climate change. Only a maximum of 2 hours of electricity could be provided by this massive industrial development, that would be more appropriately located on an industrial site and not in the heart of our rural community. I am a nature lover and during my walks on the hills looking down on this site, I regularly see black grouse and red kites plus occasionally our local ospreys and a golden eagle plus there is an abundance of mountain hare. I am extremely concerned that the planning policy’s push for net zero targets will adversely affect legally protecting species when we are supposed to be actively protecting them. There are also the environmental risks of chemical seepage into land and waterways, potential toxic fumes coming over my house in the event of a fire and how exactly a major incident would be dealt with when we have no mains water and our nearest fire station is 16 miles away and is only a retained service? This raises serious concerns for the safety, health and well-being of those living near this development. Yet another industrial scale development will also have adverse effects on our stunning landscape and residents will be unfairly subjected to noise and light pollution once the facility is in operation. We need to address the climate crisis but the contribution of battery storage is questionable when the rare metal mining, hazardous processes, human rights issues, manufacturing emissions and lack of recycling are added in when calculating their contribution to net zero. The benefits do NOT outweigh the environmental damage they cause. PLEASE reject this application as it is totally inappropriate for this area. We should be protecting our trees, wildlife and natural places, not destroying them with no benefit to our communities or any real contribution to the climate crisis.

We live in very close proximity of this proposed development (under 1km) and I wish to raise my very serious concerns: We live in a former hunting lodge ([PLACE]) have ancient woodland and protected bird and mammal species on our land. Our area has been bombarded over the last few years with energy infrastructure – 2 wind farms, 1 wind farm extension, a pylon line and a substation. ALREADY consented are [PLACE] Battery Storage ref: [APPLICATION_CODE], [PLACE] Wind Farm Extension 11 including battery storage ref: [APPLICATION_CODE], and [PLACE] including battery storage ref: [APPLICATION_CODE]. These are all within a few miles of this proposed development. We do not need yet another 200MW facility in such a small, rural community as we have 3 consented here already! This development should be refused on the grounds of cumulative impact NPF4 Policy 11.3 and the lack of proven need. If it is felt a development on this scale is needed, it should be built in a more appropriate brown field site, not within our rural community. Fire Safety – It would appear that the developer has failed to submit a full and thorough fire safety plan for this development despite the well-publicised risks of catastrophic thermal runaway fires! This should result in this application being refused. There is no mains water supply at the site, no pressurised hydrant, and the nearest fire stations are at [PLACE], (a reserved service 16 miles away) and [PLACE] (30 miles). The applicant has said that fires will simply be left to burn out BUT a huge amount of water is still required to cool the reaction to prevent fires spreading and containers exploding – The [ORGANIZATION] 2023 Guidance advises that sites should be capable of delivering no less than 1,900 litres per minute for at least 2 hours – where will all this water come from? In addition, any emergency response vehicles will only have one main road access point. How will toxic fumes be contained when our prevailing winds come from the west, sending them directly over our house and then on towards [PLACE] and [PLACE]? This proposal therefore does not align with NPF4 policy 5 Community Well-being, and policy 22 Environmental risk. Threat to protected species – There has been no Environmental Impact Assessment and the developer says that surveys “will” be carried out before construction commences. This is wholly unacceptable and should be grounds alone for refusal. Previous surveys for other developments, including by [ORGANIZATION], have highlighted the presence of otters, badgers and pine martens as well as mountain hare and red squirrels. Local birdlife too includes osprey, golden and sea eagles and red kites that could also be at risk from this development and should be protected according to NPF4 policy 1 tackling the nature crisis and policy 4 protecting natural places. Damage to trees, peat and wet heathland – NPF4 supports the protection and enhancement of woodland yet the developer has little evidence of plans to manage ancient woodland at the site or for true biodiversity enhancement. Replanting a felled area already due to be done anyway under standard woodland management would not constitute compensatory planting. Scale of this industrial development - at 18.3 hectares with 66 x 20ft battery containers this is completely disproportionate to the size of our surrounding area. If approved, what would come next? This development would continue the domino effect of the industrialisation of this rural area. We have already done our bit for renewable energy. Effect on residents – our home is approx. 700 m from the site with other properties even closer. NPF4 policy 5 health and wellbeing is about ensuring developments enhance community wellbeing and minimize harm. Yet this proposal will have residents subjected to construction traffic and disruption during the construction phase and noise and light pollution once complete, together with the toxic fume risk in the event of a fire – we are being put at risk! No local Socio-Economic Benefits - The developer mentions working with local schools to promote STEM careers which is primarily a public relations exercise with no tangible benefit to the community. There are no plans for community benefit funds, local employment opportunities, or any positive economic contribution to the area in contradiction of NPF4 policy that states that renewable energy projects will be supported ONLY if they provide local economic benefits, which this does not. Need – this MASSIVE battery storage facility will be charging batteries from the grid i.e. NOT storing renewable energy at all. They will be charged when prices are low (middle of the night with minimal renewables in the grid energy mix) and released / sold back at premium prices for maximum profit for the developer – a financial benefit through energy trading NOT a benefit towards tackling the climate crisis or net zero targets. In addition, the 200MW plant (should state MWh) will only be able to supply energy for a maximum of 2 hours! A totally ridiculous amount of destruction for such little gain. This together with the fact that 3 BESS developments have ALREADY been CONSENTED in this area confirms there is NO NEED for this development. Flooding - NPF4 Policy 22 addresses flood risk management and after the dreadful floods in this area in 2017, the developer has not fully addressed or have plans in place to manage this significant risk. Environmental Impact of Battery Production – the production of lithium-ion batteries in other countries that includes rare metal mining, human rights issues, hazardous chemical processes including Co2 emissions are not counter-balanced by their ability to store energy here in Scotland. Instead, their manufacture contributes directly to the climate crisis we are supposed to be tackling. In respect of planning policy NPF4, this proposal fails against enhancing biodiversity, benefiting local communities, safeguarding our well-being and tackling the nature crisis. The burdens far outweigh the gains and the scale of this development in inappropriate for this location and this application should be refused.

I am writing to formally raise objections to the Section 36 planning application put forward by [ORGANIZATION] ([ORGANIZATION]) for the proposed Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) development situated to the north of [PLACE], near [PLACE]. The project aims to establish a 100 MW lithium-ion battery facility on currently unused agricultural land, along with associated transformers, fencing, lighting, fire infrastructure, and drainage. My objection is centred on the significant risks that the development presents to public safety, the local environment, and community welfare. These risks encompass fire and contamination hazards, potential harm to biodiversity, degradation of the landscape, disruption to traffic flow, and inadequate emergency preparedness. The planning documentation provided by the developer lacks the necessary technical specifications, safety measures, and compliance with policies essential for the responsible implementation of an energy project of this magnitude. Each part of this objection articulates specific reasons why the application falls short of meeting the criteria outlined in the National Planning Framework 4 (NPF4) and the [PLACE] Local Development Plan. These reasons include deficiencies in consultation, the absence of ecological protections, a lack of assessment of cumulative impacts, and a failure to address the entire lifecycle of hazardous infrastructure. I strongly recommend that the planning authority rejects this application in its entirety. Environmental and Ecological Impact The development site is located in a rural farmland area surrounded by hedgerows, marshy grassland, and drainage features that provide support to wildlife and contribute to the local ecological network. It is in close proximity to the [PLACE] and encompasses habitats recognised for their biodiversity value, including waterlogged ground and species-rich grass margins. However, the ecological assessments that have been submitted are incomplete and crucial seasonal survey data has been omitted. Key assessments such as bat roost evaluations, dusk or dawn emergence surveys, monitoring of badger activity, and studies on amphibians have not been carried out during the appropriate seasons. These assessments are standard requirements under the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 and the Nature Conservation (Scotland) Act 2004 when potential habitats are impacted by development. The absence of this data means that the developer cannot accurately claim to comprehend or address the ecological risks associated with the proposal. The site is set to be significantly covered with containerised battery units, impermeable roads, fencing, firewater tanks, and related infrastructure, leading to the permanent loss of semi-natural grassland and the fragmentation of hedgerow corridors. This will eliminate foraging and commuting paths for protected species like bats and birds. While the planting of replacement hedgerows is presented as a biodiversity enhancement, no Biodiversity Net Gain (BNG) calculation has been provided, and there is no proposed habitat management or monitoring plan. According to National Planning Framework 4 Policy 3, developments must enhance biodiversity and prevent harm to existing natural assets. [PLACE] Local Development Plan Policy PV7 mandates the protection and mitigation of priority habitats and species. Unfortunately, this proposal fails to meet either standard. The lack of comprehensive survey work, habitat destruction, and inadequate mitigation measures render it environmentally unsound. There is a risk of long-term ecological deterioration in an area that supports farmland species and local biodiversity. Cumulative Impact The [PLACE] area has emerged as a significant hub for energy infrastructure projects, encompassing large substations, overhead transmission lines, solar developments, and various proposals for Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS). The addition of a 17-acre BESS to the existing cluster of industrial energy assets is expected to intensify the physical, environmental, and psychological pressures on the local community. Despite the presence of other approved or pending developments within a 1 km radius, the current application lacks a cumulative impact assessment. There is no consideration given to how the simultaneous construction, noise emissions, lighting, fire risk, and traffic volumes from multiple projects will be managed. This fragmented approach to development neglects to address the overall impact of infrastructure saturation on the land, wildlife, and residents of [PLACE]. Concerned residents have highlighted issues regarding the industrialisation of the area and the combined effects of these proposals on mental well-being, safety, and environmental standards. It is imperative for the planning authority to evaluate not only the repercussions of this individual development but also its contribution to a broader trend of encroachment and disruption. Policy 29 of the National Planning Framework 4 stipulates the necessity of considering cumulative effects in decision-making processes. The absence of such an assessment represents a significant oversight. Approving this development without a comprehensive overview would further exacerbate the disproportionate and unsustainable strain on this rural community. Increased Traffic and Infrastructure Strain The construction of the Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) would entail almost 900 Heavy Goods Vehicle (HGV) movements over a 12-month period, with peak daily traffic reaching up to 1 large vehicles. These vehicles will navigate narrow rural roads not originally intended for heavy industrial traffic, such as [PLACE] and the surrounding local road network, which are currently shared by [PLACE] transport, agricultural vehicles, cyclists, and pedestrians. Despite the presence of multiple other energy projects proposed or already in progress in the vicinity, there has been no comprehensive assessment of the cumulative traffic impact. The planning application lacks any proposed mitigation measures, such as road reinforcement, visibility enhancements, or traffic diversion plans. Additionally, there is no specified construction delivery schedule to avoid peak traffic hours, and no road safety assessment has been provided. The proposed BESS construction also poses a threat to [PLACE], a popular walking and cycling route that passes near the site. The establishment of the construction compound and access roads is anticipated to cause disruption, visual obstructions, and potential safety risks for path users. No temporary diversion or strategy to safeguard the path has been outlined. According to NPF4 Policy 13, infrastructure should be designed to minimise impacts on local networks and ensure safety for all users, a criterion that this application fails to meet. Without adequate transport planning, this development could lead to road deterioration, heightened collision risks, and prolonged disruption to the community and local access rights. Community Wellbeing, Mental Health, and EMF Concerns The proposed development in the vicinity of [PLACE] raises significant concerns beyond physical risks and environmental impacts, particularly regarding community wellbeing and mental health. The area is already facing pressure from various energy projects, and the introduction of another large-scale, high-risk facility is causing considerable stress and anxiety among residents. Concerns about potential battery fires, pollution, explosions, and toxic smoke are not merely hypothetical, as similar risks have been observed at comparable sites globally. Local residents have voiced worries about the psychological impact of residing near such infrastructure, especially when it is inadequately understood and regulated. The sense of being surrounded by hazardous industrial developments can lead to enduring fear, disrupted sleep patterns, and diminished trust in public decision-making processes. The absence of a Health Impact Assessment accompanying the application is troubling. There is a failure to acknowledge the psychological strain that prolonged proximity to a high-risk site can impose, particularly in rural areas where quality of life hinges on peace, safety, and environmental stability. This oversight is particularly concerning for families, elderly residents, and individuals already grappling with mental health conditions. Furthermore, concerns have been raised about potential exposure to electromagnetic fields (EMFs) emanating from the site's electrical infrastructure, such as transformers and underground cabling. While EMF levels may comply with accepted thresholds, the lack of transparent monitoring or public information contributes to local unease. Perceived risk can be as detrimental to wellbeing as physical exposure, especially when residents feel excluded from the planning process. National Planning Framework 4 Policy 23 mandates that developments safeguard health, wellbeing, and safety, encompassing mental health and quality of life, not solely physical risk. The absence of any wellbeing assessment or mitigation strategy further highlights the applicant's disregard for the local population. Summary The application is fundamentally flawed as it does not address or mitigate the serious risks linked to large-scale lithium-ion battery storage. The planning documents lack essential information concerning fire safety, pollution control, waste management, biodiversity, and community health. The consultation process was insufficient, and the proposal does not adhere to the standards set out in National Planning Framework 4 or the [PLACE] Local Development Plan. If approved, this development would industrialise a rural landscape, compromise local wellbeing, strain emergency services, and create lasting environmental issues. It does not exemplify responsible energy infrastructure and does not serve the public interest. Therefore, it should be rejected.

I am writing as a neighbouring resident to strongly object to the proposed Battery Storage Facility in [PLACE]. My house sits at the top of [PLACE] and is mentioned in the planning document as being 220m from the proposed development. Given the proximity and mention of our property I have been surprised to have not been notified directly as a neighbour to this project. After finding out about the planning application myself I have studied the full application and all the additional resources and I also attended the consultation last May. I am extremely concerned at the impact this will have on the surrounding area, and I believe the planning application severely downplays and fails to consider several key points. Whilst I'm sure everyone is in agreement that this kind of infrastructure is key to meeting climate targets, I feel this is a shortsighted lazy attempt by the applicant to situate a facility only to reap the benefits of existing (poorly situated) electrical infrastructure, instead of putting in the required investment into a suitable futureproofed site capable of housing and scaling up battery storage to meet the growing need of renewables. It is clear there will be no direct benefit to the people of [PLACE] (confirmed to me by [PERSON] staff during the consultation in May), the development will create no jobs or opportunities for business development. Presumably the only parties to financially benefit will be the applicant and the private landowner. All at the expense of local residents and the environment. I am objecting on several grounds which I will cover in detail below: Firstly the visual impact of the facility on the surrounding area. This is something I feel has not been well detailed in the submitted drawings and plans. We are talking about a field containing 53 metal containers (with dimensions of 13m x 2.5m x 2.8m) terraced down a steeply sloping incline toward the [PLACE]. Whilst I appreciate the proposed measures to shield the view of the infrastructure, there is no avoiding that this development is being placed on a hill, the bund at the bottom of the hill and trees would need to be of a great size to actually mask it's view. The relief of the area doesn't appear to have been mentioned or considered in the application. Whilst mention has been made to the old toll house on [PLACE] who's view will be impacted, the applicants downplay the impact this will have on residents and visitors as you drive down the [PLACE] toward [PLACE] past [PLACE]. Drivers and pedestrians will be met with an unavoidable view of the 53 containers as you proceed along the route. The [PLACE] is a popular walking route, and the view from the currently scenic peaceful cemetery will also be blighted by the view. I also believe the development will be visible from farther up the [PLACE] beyond [PLACE], as I can often see the top of our house on the horizon as I drive toward [PLACE]. From my own point of view, from our house we will have some view of the development from upstairs and the top of our garden. Many people walk their dogs along the path at the rear of our property between [PLACE] and [PLACE] and the proposed view from this path looks nothing short of a prison camp with barb wire topping high fencing. As the environment team note in their consultation document, the proposed planting to mask the development is not fit for purpose given the exposed coastal nature of the site. My own garden and the existing landscape can attest to the fact that not much survives beyond the native gorse which does not grow high enough to mask the development. I am not confident the proposed measures can go very far in mitigating the impact of local residents from a visual perspective. During the consultation I was provided with a photo of a similar battery storage site, which were quite eye opening. I would advise the planners request some more detailed images of the proposed development, photos /3D mockups and such like, as in its current form the drawings are not very representative of the reality. Secondly what is the potential impact on nature and the environment? There is a lot of wildlife often seen in these fields, I routinely see deer, birds, rabbits, foxes and have seen badgers in the past. There is little in the way of information on safety of the battery infrastructure, these are lithium batteries - in the consultation there was notes about the risk from fire and possible pollution that I don't see considered in the application, further details should be sought on this. Next I have concerns about the construction of the site, the proposed access is via the top of [PLACE]. Can the streets of [PLACE] cope with high quantities of plant and lorries weaving along the tight roads to access the site? What will be the impact on local residents in terms of noise and pollution from this activity? Also the noise of the construction concerns me personally, we can clearly hear tractors ploughing and working in the same field. How long will the construction take and what will be the noise impact? This is not addressed in the application. My children and others also walk along the path to the primary [PLACE], what safety measures will be in place to ensure they come to no harm? Lastly the noise pollution report is not well detailed, which is also noted by the environmental health team. I was surprised to read my property is named in this section as being a closed neighbour at 220m, however is not covered in the table along with other houses of a similar distance where a predicted dB level is attributed to their position. I would kindly ask for Environmental Health to request this in addition the added information they have asked for. Lastly the area in question is already blighted by electricity infrastructure, 2 mobile phone masts and a water reservoir. I personally think this is more than enough given the proximity to residential properties and in an area of outstanding natural beauty enjoyed by many locals for walking and recreation. I am also concerned how this could potentially devalue both our own and other nearby resident's properties. Any application should weigh up the positives against the negative for the community. Here it seems there are no direct benefits to the local community but there is the potential to irreparably damage a beautiful area, impacting nearby residents significantly, with the wider community fairly unaware of the blight that could be soon built on their landscape. Whilst I appreciate my comments are quite long, I trust they are fully considered and taken on board by those considering this application.

Given the industrial nature of the proposal and the requirement for lighting, vehicle access, and continuous energy storage infrastructure, the habitat fragmentation and long-term ecological degradation may be substantial and irreversible. 3. Residents in the area have already endured years of disturbance from the substation, the grid stability facility, and other associated projects. Visual mitigation measures, such as planting or paint colour, do not address the underlying loss of open space and the displacement of the ecosystems that depend on it. target_text: This correspondence constitutes a formal objection to the planning application concerning the [PLACE] Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), designated under Energy Consents Unit Ref: [APPLICATION_CODE] and [ORGANIZATION] Ref: [APPLICATION_CODE]. The proposed project aims to establish a lithium-ion battery storage facility, inclusive of pertinent infrastructure, in close proximity to residential zones, agricultural lands, and environmentally delicate sites. The objection is founded upon factual and legally pertinent concerns pertaining to public safety, environmental hazards, adherence to planning regulations, and procedural deficiencies within the consultation process. Given the inherently high-risk nature of large-scale battery storage and its associated potential ramifications, it is imperative that the application undergoes meticulous evaluation. Transportation Disruptions and Road Network Issues The establishment and continuous operation of the BESS facility are projected to lead to a notable rise in traffic flow, exerting additional pressure on rural roads ill-suited for heavy industrial transport. During the construction phase, a substantial number of Heavy Goods Vehicles (HGVs) will be engaged in transporting materials to the site, while routine maintenance and emergency response activities will contribute to a regular influx of vehicles. The rural roads in the vicinity are frequently utilised by schoolchildren, pedestrians, and cyclists, raising legitimate concerns regarding road safety. Furthermore, the [PLACE] region is already contending with various large-scale infrastructure endeavours, such as [PLACE], overhead power line installations, and wind farm projects. The proposed closure of [PLACE] for a potential duration of up to one year will necessitate redirected traffic through [PLACE], exacerbating congestion and heightening risks for local residents. Regrettably, the application fails to furnish a comprehensive evaluation of the impact on local road networks or present any strategies for mitigating safety apprehensions. This oversight directly contravenes NPF4 Policy 1 (Infrastructure and Transport), which stipulates that developments must not unduly strain local transport systems. Correspondingly, HWLDP Policy 56 (Traffic and Transport) mandates that developments must safeguard public safety by ensuring that augmented traffic does not have adverse effects. Cumulative Impact The [PLACE] area has undergone significant industrialisation due to various energy infrastructure projects, and the proposed installation of a large-scale Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) would further impact local communities, landscapes, and public services. It is essential to evaluate the collective effects of these developments to fully comprehend the extent of disruption they may cause. The region has seen a rapid increase in energy-related infrastructure, such as substations, battery storage facilities, wind farms, and high-voltage power lines, which have already negatively affected residents. For instance, noise complaints have arisen from SSEN’s [PLACE] Expansion, and the proposed [PLACE] BESS would introduce another industrial-scale energy storage site, amplifying the risks associated with lithium-ion battery storage. Additionally, the replacement of [PLACE] and [PLACE] Substations, along with the planned [PLACE] development covering an 868-acre site, further concentrates energy infrastructure in the area. The construction of multiple 400kV overhead power lines and pylons, some towering up to 70 metres, is altering the rural landscape significantly. The cumulative impact of wind farm projects, such as the [PLACE] with 36 turbines at 230 metres each and the [PLACE] adding 14 turbines at 200 metres, contributes to the industrialisation of the area. These projects, combined with the proposed [PLACE] BESS, would irreversibly affect the natural environment and visual appeal of the region. Moreover, the planned closure of [PLACE] for up to a year is expected to divert all traffic, including heavy goods vehicles carrying construction materials, through [PLACE], leading to congestion and road safety concerns for residents, schoolchildren, and local businesses. The proliferation of energy developments in [PLACE] has strained rural infrastructure, including narrow roads, emergency services, and public health resources beyond sustainable levels. Introducing another industrial project would exacerbate these pressures, making it challenging for residents to uphold their quality of life. National and local planning policies mandate the consideration of cumulative effects when evaluating new applications. NPF4 Policy 29 stipulates that energy infrastructure projects must demonstrate they will not result in unacceptable combined impacts on local communities or the environment. Given the current level of industrialisation in [PLACE], the continuous expansion of large-scale energy developments is no longer viable. NPF4 Policy 3 requires developments to enhance biodiversity, a principle contradicted by the cumulative loss of natural landscapes and habitats. Similarly, HWLDP Policy 36 states that developments should not place undue burdens on rural communities, a requirement not met due to the existing strain on local infrastructure and services. Environmental and Ecological Impact The proposed [PLACE] Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) development poses significant environmental risks, particularly in relation to air and water contamination, loss of biodiversity, and disruption of the landscape. The site's proximity to the [PLACE], designated as a Special Area of Conservation ([PLACE]) for Atlantic salmon, places it within an ecologically sensitive area that includes multiple Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSIs) and the [PLACE], recognised for its internationally significant wetland habitats. Any potential contamination or disruption to this fragile ecosystem could have wide-ranging consequences. In the event of a thermal runaway incident in a lithium-ion battery storage system, a variety of toxic gases and airborne pollutants would be released, posing a serious risk to public health and the environment. Such incidents could result in the emission of hydrogen fluoride (HF), carbon monoxide (CO), and sulfur dioxide (SO2) in significant quantities. HF is particularly hazardous due to its highly corrosive nature, capable of causing severe respiratory damage and chemical burns. CO, an odourless gas, can be fatal in high concentrations, while SO2 is a known trigger for asthma and lung diseases. Additionally, particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10) and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) would be released, further exacerbating air quality issues and increasing the risk of long-term cardiovascular and respiratory complications. Given the prevailing wind patterns in the [PLACE] region, these toxic emissions could easily spread into residential areas, agricultural land, and water sources, posing a direct threat to local communities' health. The potential impact on water quality is equally concerning, particularly in the event of a BESS fire and subsequent firefighting activities. Lithium-ion battery fires necessitate large quantities of water for suppression, resulting in toxic runoff contaminated with heavy metals, lithium, and acidic compounds. This contaminated water could infiltrate the [PLACE], endangering its [PLACE]-designated Atlantic salmon population and other aquatic species. Moreover, SEPA flood risk mapping indicates that the proposed site is situated within or adjacent to a floodplain, heightening the risk of pollutants spreading over a wider area during periods of heavy rainfall or flooding. Despite these risks, the application lacks a comprehensive containment strategy to prevent such contamination. Furthermore, the development poses a threat to local biodiversity, which includes protected species such as ospreys, buzzards, curlews, red squirrels, pine martens, otters, and great crested newts. Construction activities, noise, and artificial lighting could disrupt migration patterns, breeding cycles, and natural behaviours, while habitat destruction and potential chemical contamination present long-term risks to wildlife. The proposal fails to adhere to key planning policies aimed at safeguarding the environment. NPF4 Policy 3 (Biodiversity Enhancement) stipulates that new developments should deliver net environmental benefits, rather than merely avoiding harm. However, this application lacks a clear mitigation strategy for habitat loss. NPF4 Policies 22 and 23 require developments to prevent negative impacts on protected conservation areas, while HWLDP Policies 28, 36, 58, 59, 61, 63, 72, and 73 focus on safeguarding the landscape and natural environment, all of which are compromised by this proposal. Without robust environmental safeguards, effective mitigation measures, and a well-defined risk management plan, the [PLACE] BESS development represents an unacceptable environmental hazard. The potential for airborne and waterborne contamination, destruction of protected habitats, and non-compliance with planning policies render this proposal fundamentally flawed and incompatible with its environmentally sensitive location. Well-being and Safety Risks for the Public The [PLACE] Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) proposal raises significant concerns regarding fire safety, primarily stemming from the well-documented hazard of thermal runaway in lithium-ion battery storage systems. Instances of thermal runaway can lead to unmanageable fires, explosions, and the emission of harmful substances such as hydrofluoric acid, dioxins, and heavy metals. Considering that the local infrastructure is already strained by existing energy projects, the addition of this scheme would further tax local services and resources. Dismissal of Alternative Sites: The applicant has dismissed several alternatives, citing reasons such as visibility, proximity to residential areas, the use of Grade 2 agricultural land, proximity to ancient woodland, flooding concerns, and distance from the substation. However, the proposed site contradicts many of these criteria and raises additional concerns related to the disturbance of protected wildlife, such as nesting birds including Ospreys, which have regularly nested within 1km of the site. Furthermore, the proposal fails to consider the potential impact on the migration of the Atlantic salmon (classified as an endangered species in the UK), sea trout and other river species native to the [PLACE]. In addition there is no mention of the short- and long-term impact of installing the connecting cable through the [PLACE]. The applicant’s selection criteria seem to place little weight on the preservation of river-related wildlife, which should be reconsidered. 2. Location Considerations: The applicant appears to have overlooked a highly suitable location for the proposed facility, which is the quarry immediately west of the substation site. This alternative location offers several advantages: - it is a brownfield site, thus avoiding the use of agricultural land; - it can be constructed at a lower elevation which would naturally reduce noise impact; - it would not be visible to any external occupiers; - it would minimize the length of connection to the substation; - it would not disturb beavers or otters; - it would provide excellent vehicular access. It is noted that in multiple instances the applicant refers to alternative sites being "unavailable at the time of their survey", which is inadequate as justification for not giving apt consideration. All alternative sites must be investigated with due rigour applied, upon completion of which a fact-based recommendation for the most suitable project site may be made. If this project qualifies as a National Infrastructure Project of National Importance, compulsory purchase may be an option. While I am not an expert in this area, I question whether a 100MW facility qualifies for such designation. 3. Inadequate Ecological Survey: The river margins host a wide variety of bird species with the adjacent woodland providing a key nesting and foraging habitat. Having spent approximately 30 years fishing the river, I have first hand experience of the rich biodiversity of flora, fauna and bird life; even otters - considered to be a Bio Indicator species - have been observed on quite a few occasions over the years. The ecological survey conducted is insufficient, consisting of only two field trips. The primary survey, carried out on August 8th, can only be deemed partial at best. By this time of the year, many birds would have completed their nesting phases, and some migratory species would have already moved on. The potential impact on these species therefore cannot have been taken into account and the long-standing nesting presence of Ospreys in the vicinity finds only only a brief mention in the second report. The acoustic report indicates that noise levels exceeding 35dB will affect significant areas of the adjacent woodland, yet no consideration is given to the potential negative impact on wildlife. These shortcomings in the Ecological Survey should be addressed. 4. Fire Prevention and Safety: As a non-expert in fire safety, I note concerns regarding the proximity of the development to woodland. The applicant’s strategy of allowing any potential fires to burn out raises concerns, especially given the site's close proximity to, and downwind location from, the woodland. The proposed mitigation plan mentions the use of local water supplies for firefighting. More detail is needed as to which local water supplies are intended for use in a fire emergency and the potential impact that extinguishing water running off a burning site with presumably toxic elements would have for the [PLACE]? What measures are to be put in place to ensure no negative or even detrimental effects on the [PLACE] and its biodiversity in the even of a fire? 5. Acoustic Report Concerns: Certain sections of the Acoustic Report have been redacted in the application. The conclusions presented in the WSP report seem marginal and should be further examination by an expert, particularly regarding sensitivity and variation around ambient temperature. It would appear logical to assume that higher ambient temperatures would need increased mechanical ventilation, which would result in higher noise levels. This noise would coincide with periods when local residents are likely to have their windows open and in turn making them more vulnerable to the increased noise levels. Suggested mitigation methods include a 4m barrier which would at a level not only require planning consent but which would constitute a significant visual intrusion on this sensitive rural location. Considerably more thought must be given to here. In conclusion, I believe the applicant has chosen an inappropriate site, one that conflicts with many of the criteria they themselves have used to deem other sites unsuitable. Furthermore, the site raises other significant concerns that should be carefully considered. I therefore strongly urge that the application be rejected.

I am concerned about the precedent that this application would set if alternative applications were included for the same use and the surrounding area of the substation would be littered with multiple battery sites. Does the next application use the 2nd best site in the study and repeat until all sites are developed? Just because this is the best / recommended site for battery storage in the study doesn't mean it is appropriate for this use in this location. I would raise concerns that an application on this site for any other use than the one presented (green infrastructure) would be outrightly rejected due to the location / characteristics of the subject site so why do we not hold the standards for the proposed use. I have concern for the impact this site could have on tourism to the wider area. This is a particularly popular part of the country for tourism for the fact that it is the countryside and people use it to get away from the towns / cities. Over developing this site and the surrounding area would affect this enormously. I am concerned about how close this site is to the river, why can't the site be included at the front of the field adjacent to the road? Is this due to visual amenity, well I would argue if it is not suitable there, it is not suitable in its current location. Do we know what effect this development could have on the river and its users? I am concerned that the noise during construction and operational noise would be significant. They appear to be required to be cooled etc. so there will need to be some sort of air conditioning unit or similar so this will no doubt create noise which would affect users of the river / walkers / local housing etc. I would argue that locals have already taken on the brunt of national green infrastructure with hydroelectric dams, the new pylon lines developed a number of years ago, and the vastly increased size of the [PLACE]. Does this area really need another development which harms locals both in terms of visual amenity, construction disruption while it benefits those who live hundreds of miles away.

In general, I am in favour of developing Energy Storage and consider there to be considerable potential benefits for energy generation in terms of decarbonisation, efficiency and maintaining supply. However, energy developments should still be located, sited and designed appropriately. The application states that the site was selected as it adjacent to an existing business park and it is an available site, however beyond that there is no justification provided as to why this proposal is the right development in the right place and as such I object for the following reasons: Impact on Greenspace: In the adopted [PLACE] the site is shown on the settlement map as Open Space and states that there should be continued protection of active greenspace at [PLACE]. Equally the [PLACE] Proposed Local Development Plan 2, whilst not the adopted Plan, is at an advanced stage and is considered the 'settled view' of the Council. Within the [PLACE] Map, the site of this proposal is shown as greenspace. Under Policy 4 Greenspace, land identified as greenspace on the maps is safeguarded from development. Land is identified as greenspace as it contributes to the character and setting of a place and provide amenity, biodiversity and recreation benefits. The site is used as an informal area for recreation and provides access towards a larger greenspace in the former golf course and Core Paths. At present the site is completely permeable but this proposal would introduce barriers to this permeability for both people and wildlife. The southern side of [PLACE] has experienced considerable development in the last decade and this wider greenspace which includes this site, provides a welcome area for recreation, amenity and biodiversity. Noise: There is no information provided on the expected level of noise from the site. It is to be expected that there would be some background noise from the operational site. Without knowing this detail it is impossible to determine if this would be a problem for nearby residential areas and the adjacent hotel. Amenity and Visual Impacts: The proposals include a grid layout of 'containers' and, whilst not very tall, will be extensive and industrial in appearance. The site would also be surrounded by security fencing (some of it up to 4 metres high) with barbed wire along the top. The location of the proposal is adjacent to [PLACE], a Supermarket and housing areas. [PLACE] consists of a variety of uses - [PLACE], Golf Course/Club building, retail units, bowling club, Kart Track and office units. This proposal would introduce an industrial use to an area with no current industrial uses and as such is not sympathetic to the local area and existing pattern of development. Information provided in the Supporting Statement for the application sets out that the proposal needs to be sited close to a substation. This site is not in proximity to a substation, and neither is it in proximity of 'first time' generators, e.g. renewable energy sources. A substation does not form part of this application however within the supporting statement at paragraph 2.4 it is noted that part of the groundworks is to prepare a substation base. It is not clear if a subsequent application would be submitted for a substation on site and if this was the case a substation would add an extra element of visual and amenity impact. Health and Safety: The site is a potential fire hazard which is a safety concern as it is located in close proximity to many buildings. Battery fires can burn for days and any water run off can contain toxic elements which could run into nearby watercourses. No mention is made of consultation with the Fire and Rescue Service or the [ORGANIZATION]. Whilst this is not a statutory requirement, given the close proximity to busy commercial properties and adjacent housing, this would appear prudent. There is also no information in the application about decommissioning of the site when the batteries reach their end of life.

I would like to object to the above project. Please find my below my concerns and reasons as to why I think this project needs to be re-thought out before the planning permission is approved. 1) The location plan for the proposed site in [APPLICATION_CODE] application clearly shows access coming from the West, [PLACE] direction. However, at the second consultation held on the 18th March 2025, ‘Field’ staff were proud to tell attendees that they had listened to the locals and would take access from the East past ‘Mains of Greens’. This would avoid heavy construction and other site traffic going through the village of [PLACE]. This should NOT have reverted again without further consultation. (please see site location plan 2.1) The area outlined in red on the location plan also includes most of the land holding at [PLACE] next door. This land has already been included in a planning application from [ORGANIZATION] for ‘[PLACE] 2 substation’. Is there a mistake here? The residents of the local are need an explanation and a halt to proceedings at the very least. 2) The application states that the site is to be in an area of ‘felled forestry’ the 9.9ha site is not felled, it is newly re-planted woodland. 3) The [PLACE] and the [PLACE] both begin on or adjacent to [PLACE], they in turn feed into the ‘[PLACE] priority catchment drinking water area’. On the East side of [PLACE], the water course of ‘Burn of Asleid’ and ‘Little Water’ run south feeding the ‘[PLACE] priority catchment’ area. As the proposed ‘[ORGANIZATION] BES 400MW’ site is at the top of [PLACE] is on the water shed for both the ‘[PLACE] priority’ catchment area and the ‘[PLACE] priority’ catchment area. Contaminants from the site have the potential to enter BOTH the [PLACE] and [PLACE] priority catchments. No reference is given in the entire application to the [PLACE] or [PLACE]? These rivers are both priority rivers and should NOT be put at risk by large industrial developments. 4) The application mentions surface water and low risk of flooding, however there is no reference to ground water. Existing ditches and ponds at [PLACE] are evidence that there is an all-year-round source of water from [PLACE]. Private wells in the area are further evidence of this. 5) The Fire water tank and the 1900l attenuation pond for site run off are both located to the North of the only access to the site. Therefore, in the event of a fire, firefighting appliances would have to drive along the only access route through potentially burning Battery compounds on either side, to reach the water source, to cool the other batteries! This is highly dangerous and ill thought out! This application should not go ahead. 6) The underlying soil type on the site is ‘Peat’ a valuable Carbon sink, the ‘Environmental Impact assessment’ states that the depth of peat is no greater than 50cm. This requires further investigation. 7) The single-track roads leading to the site in both directions are inadequate for the large construction traffic, there is high risk of subsidence on both sides of the road in both directions. Resulting in dangerous operating conditions for the project and even worse dangers for local people living and working in the area. 8) No consideration has been given to the condition of the roads in the planning application at all. The single-track road leading past the site at [PLACE] was designed for horses and carts 100 years ago. Another reason that the application should not proceed.

While I appreciate some of the aims behind this project, I am very concerned about the project's location, particularly its close proximity to the [PLACE] and the location of the attenuation pond. The land in question is a greenfield site, and it appears no consideration has been given to the potential of using brownfield sites when assessing alternative options. As a result, significantly less invasive project designs on brownfield sites were not even considered. The development of a greenfield site, as opposed to a brownfield site, can lead to unnecessary environmental degradation, loss of biodiversity, and disruption of local ecosystems. [PLACE] is a highly popular destination for national and international visitors and tourists. Their motivation to visit [PLACE] is precisely its pristine natural surroundings and fishing opportunities. Granting the application will have an obvious detrimental impact in this regard, endangering Beauly's essence. The construction and operation of the project could lead to visual pollution, noise, and other disturbances that would detract from the natural beauty and tranquility that attract visitors. This, in turn, could have a negative impact on the local economy, which relies heavily on tourism. The project appears to increase flood risk from the [PLACE], with the sadly well-known and long-term effects on the resident community. The construction activities and changes in land use could alter the natural drainage patterns, leading to increased surface runoff and potential flooding. This is particularly concerning given the existing flood risks in the area. The long-term consequences of increased flood risk include damage to property, displacement of residents, and potential loss of life. Finally, the fire risks and noise pollution from the project seriously call into question the wisdom of choosing this particular site as the best location. The storage and management of energy in battery systems inherently carry fire risks, which could be exacerbated by the site's proximity to residential areas and natural habitats. Additionally, the noise generated during both the construction and operational phases of the project could disrupt the peace and quiet of the local community, affecting the quality of life for residents. In light of these concerns, I urge that consent under Section 36 of the Electricity Act 1989 in relation to this project be denied. The potential environmental impact, threat to the local economy, increased flood risk, and safety concerns make this project unsuitable for the proposed location. I strongly recommend that alternative sites, particularly brownfield sites, be considered to mitigate these issues.

I object most strongly to these very large substations as I feel they are inappropriate for a rural setting - the cumulative impact is detrimental to visual amenity as well as to habitats and ecology and sets a precedent for further industrial development outwith more appropriate areas allocated in our local development plan. As well as insufficient analysis of the socioeconomic impact on the community making it impossible to come to an informed decision. The fire risks and subsequent risk to people and local watercourses have not been adequately assessed and our local fire service are unable to respond adequately to any incident that may occur. The proximity to local homes means noise will have an impact and location is low lying boggy ground with watercourses surrounding. Risk of ground water pollution is high and the impact on species is not adequately assessed. No more projects of this nature please. More research needed into viable alternatives which have much less impact on biodiversity and the well being of people.

target_text: I am writing to formally object to the application submitted by [ORGANIZATION] for consent under Section 36 of the Electricity Act 1989 in relation to the proposed Battery Energy Storage Site (BESS) near [PLACE]. This proposal, located diagonally across from the [PLACE], raises significant concerns which I believe need thorough consideration before any approval is granted. Firstly, the site proposed for development is a greenfield area, and there appears to have been no serious consideration of alternative brownfield sites in the site appraisal. As such, the proposal fails to prioritise the use of land that could be repurposed, resulting in unnecessary harm to open, undeveloped landscapes. Secondly, the potential for industrialisation of the surrounding landscape due to the saturation of similar proposals in the region is highly concerning. The increasing presence of such large-scale developments risks changing the character of the area irreparably, impacting the quality of life for residents and visitors alike. The potential impact on tourism and local businesses, particularly those associated with fishing, must also be given serious consideration. The [PLACE] is an important resource for fishing and consequently local tourism. The introduction of a large industrial facility in close proximity could significantly deter visitors and therefore also damage the local economy. There are various environmental risks associated with the site’s location, including the proximity of the development to the [PLACE] which heightens concerns regarding flood risks. The proposal also presents concerns related to fire safety, given the nature of battery storage technology. The risks posed by fires in such facilities need to be carefully evaluated, and measures to mitigate these risks must be transparent and robust. Finally, noise pollution from the BESS site, both during construction and operation, could be detrimental to the wellbeing of local residents and wildlife. A comprehensive noise impact assessment should be conducted to assess the full extent of this concern. In conclusion, the proposed BESS site near [PLACE] poses significant environmental, safety, and economic risks that have not been adequately addressed in the application. I urge the Scottish Ministers to consider these concerns thoroughly and to reject the proposal in its current form.

retrieved_examples.text: I am writing to express my objection with regards to the proposals to site a Battery Energy Storage Site (BESS) on prime grade 1 arable land at [PLACE] (Refs [APPLICATION_CODE] and [APPLICATION_CODE]) both as a local resident and long serving Firefighter. -This is one of the largest active BESS in Scotland and is also much closer to residential buildings than any other existing site in the country (including a doctor's surgery and primary [PLACE]). I feel that this proposal unnecessarily risks the safety and wellbeing of the families in close proximity to the site and the community as a whole. It lowers multiple standards and protections and sets a race to the bottom. After sharing and collating our knowledge as a community, the main concerns of note are as follows: - High grade farmland will needlessly be lost with multiple brownfield sites available in similar proximity. The land in it's current state is a source of homegrown food and supports local wildlife. Current excavation in proximity of the proposed site have already correlated with instances of disrupted deer and fox activity in the area. - After meeting with my community and community council, and following multiple Q&A sessions with planning representatives (the few willing or able to speak to us), there was an alarming lack of key information relation to this development, including Emergency Plans, an Evacuation Plan, and nobody involved in the discussions could confirm the type of battery to be used in the development. It is either the current technology with all of it's documented risks or a new emerging battery technology with a reduced knowledge of real-world performance. Either way, there can be little confidence in a proposal (or the proposers) that doesn't include such a key piece of information. - The noise impact from the completed running BESS runs a high risk of being significantly, and near constantly, adverse. This is totally unacceptable to both close-living residents and the community as a whole. -The proximity to residential houses, [PLACE] and [PLACE] pose a significant risk to a great number of people in the event of a fire situation. It is widely documented that, despite fire detection and suppression systems being in place, BESS sites have suffered thermal runaway, resulting in fires, explosions and the release of toxic gases. Often over a protracted period of time. At present, and to the best of my knowledge, our policy covering BESS fires puts emphasis on defensive firefighting. Due to a number of factors including the environmental impact of contamination from water application, the dangers of explosion and sudden reignition, and where there is no immediate life risk (assuming the successful and confident evacuation of nearby houses), consideration is to be given to defensive firefighting, allowing batteries to burn themselves out. The long duration of a fire event, and given the prevailing westerly wind, could in turn lead to a large-scale evacuation of the aforementioned GP, primary [PLACE] and a significant number of houses. There is little doubt that people will be exposed to the toxic fumes, including hydrofluoric acid, and smoke to varying degrees and that this will lead to both short- and long-term health complications. - Future of the site and impact wider ecosystem Especially in the event of accident what assurances exist that the site can be returned to prime arable land? What drainage exists for emergencies other than dumping contaminated water in [PLACE]? Is there any information about the acoustic impacts on protected species such as bats? None of this is clear from the application and unless these questions are answered the longer term impact of this development on the environment of our community may be tremendous. As will be quite obvious, I do not support these applications by [ORGANIZATION] on behalf of [ORGANIZATION] and [ORGANIZATION]. Please take account of my concerns and objections in your consideration of this application.

This formal objection is lodged in response to planning application [APPLICATION_CODE] (Council Ref: [APPLICATION_CODE]) submitted by [ORGANIZATION] for the establishment of a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) at [PLACE] within the jurisdiction of the [ORGANIZATION]. I am a parent to young children and we live nearby the proposed development site. I am particularly concerned for their health and safety given the potential for fires with battery storage systems. Water used to attempt to control the fire will also be contaminated and while there is an attenuation basin, it's risky that it could overflow if the thermal events coincides with a rainfall event (capacity for 1 day of 1-in-30 rain event plus 14 hours of fire-fighting water is not enough). Another key concern is placing a high-security industrial development in this beautiful part of [PLACE]. The road the development is planned for is a popular route for my family and others in the community - for walking, cycling and driving. To consider that a massive industrial complex is planned for development with high-security, bright lights and CCTV towers is shocking. This will entirely change the landscape of the area. The development should be on a brownfield site instead. The surrounding area is grassland, shrub and conifer plantation. A truly green Scotland would be vastly reducing its energy use, farming the land regeneratively and restoring poor agricultural ground to native woodland once the plantations are harvested. This is a unique part of Scotland which greatly benefits from being near conservation areas like [PLACE] and [PLACE]. That's what we should be building upon here. The [PLACE] development is not a step forward and is another development that's having a galvanising effect on the population to reject the trend.

This formal objection is hereby submitted in response to planning application [APPLICATION_CODE] (Council Ref: [APPLICATION_CODE]) put forth by [ORGANIZATION] for the establishment of a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) at [PLACE] within the jurisdiction of the [ORGANIZATION]. The proposed industrial development poses a threat to the historical landscape and rural ambiance of the area. Despite the applicant's assertion of "limited visibility," the BESS's location on a ridge would render it prominently visible from various vantage points, including roads frequented by locals and tourists. The current serene, agricultural, and tourism-focused character of the area stands to be irreversibly disrupted. The lack of a clear local or national strategic framework for the placement of such developments raises concerns. The rationale behind selecting this rural site over available brownfield or industrial alternatives remains unexplained. In the absence of strategic siting guidelines, rural communities in Scotland are left susceptible to arbitrary industrial proposals that erode landscape quality and cohesion. Furthermore, the potential risks to local residents and the wider community from incidents such as fires at the site have been downplayed. Of utmost concern is the impact on the setting and ambiance of [PLACE], a significant and emblematic heritage asset in Scotland. The [PLACE], once a cherished retreat of the late Queen Mother, holds a prominent place in the Commonwealth's landmarks. Its meticulously preserved surroundings have been safeguarded for generations. Allowing a BESS facility in close proximity risks commercializing and devaluing the legacy of this royal site. Such a decision carries international visibility and could have long-term repercussions on Scotland's planning credibility and tourism appeal. Landscape and Visual Impacts The proposed site is situated in a vast, open landscape with expansive views over [PLACE]. Even with the addition of vegetation, this location is ill-suited for accommodating large-scale energy infrastructure without significantly altering its current character. The project would introduce harsh elements such as metal fencing and 6-metre structures into a tranquil rural environment, with many residents residing just a short distance from the entrance. The resulting impact is not adequately justified or mitigated in any substantial manner. Summary This project is being situated in close proximity to a small rural village without demonstrating a clear public benefit, thereby contravening the principles of environmental justice and democratic planning. The Council's own guidance acknowledges "particular sensitivities in this location" that remain unaddressed. Despite its industrial scale, the project does not offer any discernible community advantages such as local employment opportunities, infrastructure enhancements, or revenue sharing. Consequently, it falls short of the criteria outlined in the Scottish Planning Policy (SPP) and [PLACE] Council's Community Benefit Policy for Renewables. There has been no community referendum, vote, or widespread support for this development. Consultation has been superficial, lacking meaningful engagement with local residents. Despite evident opposition from the community, their concerns have been consistently disregarded. A project with significant implications for daily life, health, heritage, and the environment should not be imposed without genuine, positive, and locally-driven consent. This development is incongruent with the core values of sustainability, place-based decision-making, heritage preservation, and rural fairness as outlined in the National Planning Framework 4 (NPF4). Its scale and location are fundamentally inappropriate, posing a threat to the local landscape and the historic rural setting of [PLACE], a site of national significance. Approving an industrial battery installation in such close proximity to a Royal heritage site based on speculation, inadequate evidence, and flawed policy implementation is unacceptable.

The absence of an EIA hampers a comprehensive evaluation, erodes public trust, and raises doubts about the legal integrity of the application process. This oversight represents a substantial procedural deficiency and undermines the credibility of any decision taken without a complete and transparent environmental assessment. Summary This proposal is of industrial scale and lacks a solid justification. It is fundamentally incompatible with the setting of a protected royal heritage site, local land use, and the planning principles outlined in NPF4 and HEPS. There is no proven national need for this facility at this particular location, and it would have significant negative impacts visually, ecologically, and socially. Approving this development would mean sacrificing a valued rural community to unplanned infrastructure expansion. It would harm the integrity of one of Scotland’s most iconic landscapes and go against national policies on heritage, nature, and rural sustainability. This large-scale project offers no clear community benefits, such as local employment opportunities, infrastructure improvements, or revenue sharing.
