target_text: I am writing to comment on the proposed project detailed above - namely [PLACE] 2 BESS, to be operated by [ORGANIZATION]. I live very close to the proposed site and I am very familiar with the site and the surrounding minor roads proposed for access to the site. The area surrounding the proposed BESS site is extremely rural. Any form of industrial development is therefore disruptive - and because the ambient noise level is so low, noise from construction, and ongoing ‘hum’ from transformers and fans will be particularly noticeable and distressing. Residents in rural areas are adversely affected to a much greater extent by these industrial infrastructure projects as the surrounding area is completely undeveloped and there is no real way to disguise or mitigate the appearance of such enormous infrastructure projects within the environment. Consultation Events I attended both Consultation Events for [PLACE] 2 Bess and, along with others, expressed my concerns regarding excessively large and overwhelming infrastructure, loss of public access to the woodland area, potential damage to private water supplies, concerns about suitability of the site and the risk of fire on a site which is to remain at least partially forested. At the first Consultation Event, maps were on display which showed the proposed access to the BESS site via [PLACE], ‘Teuchar Road’ also known as [PLACE] and a very minor road which runs through part of the [PLACE] to the proposed site. Considerable effort was expended explaining how unsuitable this access route would be. At the second Consultation Event, staff members seemed very pleased to confirm that the access to the site had changed and would instead be from the East, avoiding [PLACE] and the very narrow and low quality road through the forest. Maps were on display which showed the modified access arrangements and improved public access routes within the forest to the periphery of the BESS installation. Staff members assured me that the new plans would be available on the project website - however I have not been able to view them there and unfortunately I don’t have any photographs. The site plan presented on the Energy Consents Unit is not the version displayed at the second Consultation Event but instead from the first - the proposed access route to the site clearly shows ‘Teuchar Road’ ([PLACE]) and access from the west. This ‘error’ serves to make the Consultation Events invalid. Private Drinking Water Supply Concerns The great majority of properties in the area surrounding the proposed site have no access to mains drinking water. We have to drink locally occurring ground water, either from shallow-ish wells, or deeper boreholes. The warnings, recently issued by SEPA and [ORGANIZATION], advising residents that many private water supplies would be reaching critically low levels following a dry Spring indicate just how vulnerable this drinking water resource is. The fact that a few days of recent heavy rain ( rainfall in the first week of June) has added considerably to the water table and the previous warnings have been downgraded indicates how rapidly surface water is translocated into groundwater. This fact makes our drinking water supply extremely vulnerable to contamination from the super-industrial amount of toxic constituents contained within the structures of a proposed BESS. Even if more modern types of battery are utilised, with a reduced risk of fire, the potential for ground water contamination remains. Massive excavation into the ground and placement of potentially toxic components at the same altitude as neighbours are obliged to drink groundwater seems absurd. Supporting documentation for the proposed [PLACE] 2 BESS clearly shows water lying on the ground surface within the site. As the past week’s rainfall has proven, water above ground is in continuous contact with our drinking water supply, risking widespread contamination. The proposed [PLACE] 2 Bess site sits on the watershed of two of Aberdeenshire’s largest rivers - namely the [PLACE] and [PLACE]. Accidental contamination from the site - either silt run off or chemical contamination has the unfortunate potential to cause widespread and catastrophic damage to two separate aquatic ecosystems. The Nature of The Proposed Site The proposed site is currently fully planted with commercial forestry. It has been fully replanted within the last couple of years following a clear fell - so it is not as described in the provided documentation ‘felled forestry’ but a growing forest. Should this project be given the go- ahead, it will involve early felling of many acres of semi mature trees, partially paid for, I believe, with the assistance of public funds via Forest and Land Scotland. Although the ground is not a pristine peat habitat, it is still a considerably peat based soil. Removal of such a large amount of peat based soil as well as the considerable amount of timber ‘trash’ from previous felling operations which is on site, in pursuit of a supposedly ‘green energy’ industrial development seems ridiculous. There will be a large release of stored carbon during site clearance, defeating the supposed purpose of a ‘green energy’ project. This forestry site has also been earmarked for at least 2 different wind turbine proposals which did not go ahead for reasons unknown. The site owner therefore has a habit of initiating, then cancelling projects without obvious cause. Another topic which was a major point of discussion at the first consultation event was the high degree of public access which is enjoyed within the proposed BESS site. The land owner has previously promoted public access to the woodland ( for example, he provided a pedestrian access gate when the woodland was deer-fenced in recent years), and industrialisation of the site will be a significant loss to the local community engaged in SOAC compliant leisure pursuits. Having read the submitted documentation, I disagree that the site is of low ecological value. Red List bird species are routinely to be seen, and the fenced forestry area provides a haven, especially for ground nesting bird species. However, even casual observation of the fencing line indicates that badgers routinely enter and leave the woodland area, especially on the Western boundary. Fire Safety and [ORGANIZATION] Attendance at the Proposed Bess Site The other main topics of discussion at the first public consultation was the very narrow and poorly constructed nature of the access road to the proposed BESS site and how exactly the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service would attend any emergencies. The vast majority of fire fighters in this area are volunteers and are expected to cover very large areas of countryside from each station. Such large industrial installations as the proposed Bess and adjacent proposed Substation will by definition require the attendance of numerous Fire Appliances and personnel from several stations if any type of emergency ( or false alarm) occurs. As well as the risk of a toxic fire or other emergency at the proposed [PLACE] 2 BESS, this also means that large areas of [PLACE] will be left without [ORGANIZATION] cover for more ‘ordinary’ fires and routine accidents. It is already a sad reality that the majority of house or building fires in this area result in total distraction of the building. This is due to a combination of how long it takes crews to attend a rural location, lack of water (no water hydrants for refilling the water bowser vehicle) and difficulty of access due to narrow roads and tracks. The proposed site of the [PLACE] 2 Bess suffers from all three of these problems. In addition the proposal is to site a potentially flammable industrial installation amongst an even more flammable forest with a very high organic matter and flammable soil type - and then expect volunteer firefighters to manage any fire at this site, and simultaneously any other fire or emergency within their (very large) operational area. Problems with the Site Plan and Project Documentation submitted to the Energy Consents Unit The site plans presented vastly over estimate the area of land owned by the site owner ( which is solely the replanted or existing forestry area). The site plan as submitted here includes agricultural land which is not under the control of [ORGANIZATION] or the owner of the proposed [PLACE] 2 BESS site. In fact, a large part of the ‘site plan’ includes land which has already been identified as required for the proposed [ORGANIZATION] [PLACE] 2 Substation, which is awaiting planning decision. The land cannot be simultaneously under the control of two separate organisations, for 2 different planning applications, particularly when this one ( [PLACE] 2 Bess) is entirely dependent on the other, larger, proposed development for its very existence. In particular, a substantial area of land shown is under the control of a third party associated neither with [ORGANIZATION] or [ORGANIZATION]. That landowner is himself pursuing a BESS project, so it is extremely unlikely he will co-operate with any aspect of the [ORGANIZATION] [PLACE] 2 BESS in preference to his own project. I believe this misrepresentation of the extent of the proposed [PLACE] 2 BESS site is deliberate, to mislead readers of the submitted documents to believe that permissions, particularly regarding cable connection between the proposed BESS and the proposed [ORGANIZATION] Substation, have already been agreed over intervening agricultural land. In fact the proposed cable route is down the verge of an exceptionally narrow single track road which will be significantly damaged by such excavations. Being such a rural area, one of the very few amenities local properties possess is cable broadband - buried in the very narrow verge which is supposed to also accommodate the BESS- Substation cable connection and a cattle-proof fence. The Broadband cable is certain to be damaged during cable burying or proposed road widening activities. In this area we have already experienced the effects of the Moray East Wind Farm cable-lay - and so we are aware how much damage widespread roadside excavations cause to utilities, the road surface and adjacent land. The other significant misrepresentation on the supplied site mapping, is the enclosure of the adjacent public road within the site boundary. This implies that the applicant has automatic rights over the public road, which they do not. The public road should not be enclosed within the red line of the ‘site boundary’ but indicated in a different way to highlight the proposed access route for machinery/ personnel/BESS components. Information regarding the proposed access route is confusing - in fact two access routes are illustrated. The site plan clearly shows the use of ‘Teuchar Road’ which is the local name for the C26S [PLACE] - [PLACE] road, which would involve components being transported through [PLACE]. Attendees at the second public event were informed this option had been abandoned - but it still appears on the site plan submitted to the Energy Consents Unit. Other documentation describes transport through (by passing) the villages of [PLACE] and Auchnagatt but not [PLACE]. Both cannot be correct. At this stage, surely a definite transport plan must have been decided apon? I believe that there is deliberate ambiguity regarding the proposed route because the developers know that neither the western or eastern access routes to the proposed site are sensibly viable or safe. Continued inclusion in the site map of the western approach to the BESS site, despite the clear description in the transport plan of an approach from the East, raises the suspicion that options are being kept open to appeal for a change of route when the first access route becomes unusable due to overuse - with the result that a much greater length of road is permanently damaged and even more local lives disrupted. Concerns Regarding the Proposed Access Route in the Immediate Vicinity of the Site of [PLACE] 2 Bess The intended use of the extremely narrow road adjacent to the proposed BESS site is the most alarming and badly considered part of the submitted plans. This route is continually incorrectly referred to as the C1S in all documentation and by all parties when discussing the proposed access route to the site. The ‘Planning, Design and Access Statement by TNEI Group, ‘Transport Statement and Construction Traffic Management Plan by Pell Frischmann and the Consultation Response by [ORGANIZATION]) all erroneously refer to the road as the C1S - which is a road in Dumfries and Galloway running between Castle Douglas and Dumfries. The road which the proposed [PLACE] 2 BESS is located on is definitely [PLACE] Council’s [PLACE]. [ I have attached a freedom of information request, from [ORGANIZATION], confirming this. The Information Officer has also included a description of the [PLACE] ( wrongly referred to as [PLACE]) as ‘These types of roads are evolved tracks that have been surfaced over many years. as such they have not been designed to any standard.’] Such a basic error as incorrectly identifying the access road to the proposed site indicates a woefully poor standard of preparation for this application or a deliberate attempt to hide the very minor nature and unsuitability of the UNCLASSIFIED access road. It is impossible not to imagine that this low standard of attention to detail will not be duplicated throughout the project. How can we be reassured that our safety as residents and the viability of our homes ( drinking water) is dependent on an organisation which cannot correctly identify the alpha numeric designation of a road essential to their project? The road which is adjacent to the proposed BESS site and must be used for access is extremely narrow - no more than 3 to 3.5m wide. There are only informal passing places in field or house gateways. FOI information from [ORGANIZATION] confirms the presence of a bridge/ raised culvert of ‘only 2.8m’ ( their description). This is very much less than the required road width for the massively sized HGV vehicles required to deliver the largest BESS components. Despite description of road widening which ‘will’ (according to project documentation) take place over the length of the [PLACE] ( wrongly referred to as the [PLACE]), this can only take place with the agreement of other landowners, which might not be granted. It will be impossible to widen the road in some locations due to housing immediately adjacent to the road. The site owner does not own any additional land adjacent to the road along the Eastern end of the [PLACE] access road to offer up for this road widening scheme. The unsuitability of the [PLACE] ( or as described, [PLACE]) as an access road for industrial electricity development has already been indicated by SSEN’s proposal to avoid its use altogether for their proposed [PLACE] 2/ [PLACE] Substation. [ORGANIZATION] are planning to build their own parallel access road within their site because of the narrowness and hazards of this very minor road. However, this same road is now proposed as access to this proposed BESS site and its proposed loads of 140 Tonnes, 16 axle trailer, 3.5m wide vehicles. Despite discussion in the developers documentation regarding forestry vehicles and agricultural tractor and trailer combinations, these types of vehicles are much smaller in weight than the loads proposed for delivery of BESS components. For example the maximum permitted combined weight for agricultural tractors and trailers is 31 Tonnes and for HGVs involved in timber transportation is 41 Tonnes. Supplied documentation indicates a weight of 140 Tonnes for transformers to be delivered to the proposed site of [PLACE] 2 Bess, vastly more than the normal ‘heavy’ traffic. The western end of the [PLACE] road ( referred in documentation as [PLACE]) has been damaged in the past by timber wagons exiting the other parts [PLACE] ( proposed BESS site) at felling time. As confirmed by [ORGANIZATION] in the FOI response, the very thin tarmac layer on top of the historic stone underlying has cracked in several places. There is also more than one persistent water spring which breaches the surface tarmac and a culvert carrying a small burn ( tributary of the [PLACE]) which is not recorded on [ORGANIZATION] roads data base. I believe that there is deliberate ambiguity regarding the proposed route because the developers know that neither the western or eastern access routes to the proposed site are sensibly viable or safe. Continued inclusion in the site map of the western approach to the BESS site, despite the clear description in the transport plan of an approach from the East, raises the suspicion that options are being kept open to appeal for a change of route when the first access route becomes unusable due to overuse - with the result that a much greater length of road is permanently damaged and even more local lives disrupted. The western end of the [PLACE] ( also referred to as [PLACE]) is a particularly valuable route locally as it allows the most direct pedestrian access to the amenities of [PLACE] ( shop, sporting facilities, village hall, public transport). Public transport options are very limited in the area but there is a popular service bus to a nearby town which travels down the [PLACE] accessible via the western end of the [PLACE] ( [PLACE] in documentation). Because of the rough nature of some private tracks to houses in the area, the western area of the [PLACE] ( called by [ORGANIZATION] etc the [PLACE]) is a popular pick up point for local dial-a-bus and taxi clients. Damage, blockage or closure of this part of the proposed unclassified access road will cause considerable harm to local residents who do not have other transport options. A diversion of even a few miles, as is inevitable in a very rural area, is unsuitable for pedestrian or cyclist travellers. The comments in the Transport Plan of the absence of, or distance from, [PLACE] 1 and core paths is simply invalid. Local people are not required to travel only on recognised National Cycle Routes. Minor roads such as this road, proposed to provide access to a massive infrastructure project, are the back bone of safe, low traffic active travel in rural areas. Even if the proposed movements of very heavy components are directed via the eastern access route as described in the supporting documentation, I remain concerned that the required personnel - scores of excess journeys per day - will be instructed to access the site via the Western approach in order to reduce congestion for movement of very large components. Road quality will still deteriorate due to excess vehicle journeys and the road will become more dangerous for local people who wish to, or require to walk or cycle on it. Considering the expenditure which the project has already enjoyed, there must be a reason that the wrong access route is displayed so prominently on the site mapping and documentation. My strong suggestion is that it represents an early attempt at evading agreed transport plans, in the knowledge that the road proposed for access is highly unsuitable in both directions, and an application to change the preferred direction of access will have to be made partway through the project, should it gain approval. Or at the very least, that contrary to the written proposals, personnel movements to and from the site will be directed in a different direction to equipment and infrastructure transport because the road quality and width is insufficient to support all the journeys required. Reinstatement of damage to the roadway still means that the roadway has been damaged and local people will be forced to suffer the consequences until repairs can be instigated. It’s common knowledge that patch repairs to minor roads, particularly those which were constructed originally as ‘tracks’, as in this case are never fully successful. There are many reasons why this proposed project, [PLACE] 2 Bess, [APPLICATION_CODE], is badly considered and clearly already badly planned. Because of the very unsuitable nature of the proposed access road to the site of [PLACE] 2 Bess, I would urge you not to allow this project to proceed further within the planning system.

retrieved_examples.text: One of my major concerns relating to this development is the road access. - The proposed site is along a single-track narrow road with very little opportunity to create suitable passing places. - The developer themselves refer to this road as a “lane” (fig 1). This is wholly inappropriate for any large-scale development. - The road leading to the development “C1S” has been deemed inappropriate for HGV traffic by [ORGANIZATION] who are also proposing a substation in the locality. The road is so unsuitable that [ORGANIZATION] are creating their own access road which avoids using this access route and small bridge. - The small bridge over “[PLACE]” burn is not strong enough to cope with the increased HGV traffic this development will bring. I don’t see in any of the submitted documentation by the applicant that they have conducted any structural survey work to ensure this bridge is strong enough to withstand the increased HGV traffic. - The applicant refers to previous HGV traffic for the forestry operations, but they did not access the site over this small, old and fragile bridge. - Please see Fig 2, Fig 3 & Fig 4 for map and photographs of single-track road and mentioned bridge. A full structural survey is required before any large-scale developer is granted permission to use this road. Additional concern is that the developer has failed to conduct a breeding bird survey due to their rush to submit their application. - Having visited the location in June 2025 I can confirm the presence of Corn Bunting. - The Corn Bunting is a red list species, and this development will be detrimental to the species and its survival in our rural farmland habitat. 1. Location and Land Use Concerns The proposed BESS site is situated in close proximity to residential dwellings, schools, and recreational areas. The selection of this particular site raises several issues: - Proximity to Homes: The planned facility is less than 500 metres from the nearest residential properties, exposing inhabitants to potential risks associated with noise, air pollution, and possible catastrophic failures. - Impact on Community Character: BESS installations are industrial in nature. Their presence in a rural environment fundamentally alters the character of the area, undermining its aesthetic and amenity value. - Future Development Restrictions: The establishment of a large-scale, high- voltage facility may restrict future residential or commercial development in the area. 2. Safety and Fire Risk Battery energy storage systems can pose significant safety hazards, especially in the event of malfunction or fire. Lithium-ion batteries, in particular, are known for their volatility under certain conditions. - Thermal Runaway: Industry records from similar installations globally have recorded incidents of thermal runaway, leading to fires that are extremely difficult to extinguish, sometimes requiring days to fully control. - Lack of Emergency Preparedness: The application does not provide sufficient details regarding emergency response protocols, coordination with local fire services, or the provision of specialised equipment and training necessary to manage BESS incidents. - Public Health and Safety: The proximity to [PLACE] raises significant concern for the wellbeing of children. In the event of a fire or chemical release, evacuation and containment may be challenging. - The location of the fire water tank to the north of the site proposes a serious fire safety risk. In the event of any fire, any emergency vehicles will have to access this tank via the only access route which will be through burning battery compounds on either side to reach the only water source on site. Another flaw in the design which is extremely dangerous to those attending and another reason for this development to be refused planning. 3. Environmental Impact The environmental assessment presented in the application appears insufficient in several respects: - Potential for Soil and Water Contamination: In the event of battery leakage or fire, hazardous substances could seep into the soil or local waterways, posing long- term risks to ecosystems and human health. - Noise and Air Pollution: The operation of cooling fans, inverters, and other ancillary equipment may result in unacceptable noise levels, especially during periods of peak operation or emergency venting events. Chemical off-gassing and emissions during normal operation or, worse, during thermal incidents are also a concern. - Insufficient Mitigation Measures: The application does not provide robust or verifiable measures to mitigate these environmental risks, nor does it propose ongoing monitoring beyond the construction phase. - Potential disruption to private water supplies and water contamination. o [PLACE] and the [PLACE] which originate on or adjacent to [PLACE]. These feed into the [PLACE] priority catchment drinking water area. o “[PLACE]” and “[PLACE]” both run into the [PLACE] area. o Contaminants from this development have the potential to enter both [PLACE] and [PLACE]. o The developer has not referenced the potential of this or any mitigation matters, they seem to have completely ignored these watercourses and omitted any reference of them from their application in its entirety. If they have missed these obvious water courses visible on any map, what else have they omitted in their rushed application? 4. Inadequate Community Consultation A critical aspect of any major infrastructure project is meaningful engagement with the affected community. - Lack of Transparency: Many local residents became aware of the BESS proposal only after the formal application was submitted, signalling a lack of early-stage consultation. - Insufficient Information: Public information sessions, where they have occurred, have not addressed fundamental questions about risk, mitigation, or alternative siting. - 2 Public Consultations were held on 25th February and 18th March 2025. Even though the applicant has held the required 2 consultations these were held extremely close together with very little difference in the 2 sessions. This felt like a very rushed process simply to “tick the box”. 5. Alternatives and Site Selection The application does not adequately demonstrate why this specific location was chosen over others that may present fewer risks to the community. - Lack of Alternatives Analysis: No comprehensive site assessment has been shared that weighs the risks and benefits of this site versus more remote or industrial settings. - Potential for Co-location: Opportunities to co-locate the BESS with existing infrastructure or within industrial zones have not been explored in detail. This site is neighbouring the proposed [ORGANIZATION] [PLACE] 2 substation development. 6. Economic and Property Impacts Beyond the immediate health and safety risks, the presence of a BESS facility may have a profound effect on local property values and the economic well-being of current residents. - Devaluation of Property: Evidence from similar projects suggests that nearby property values may decrease due to perceived risks and reduced desirability of the area. - Lack of Compensation: The application does not identify any plan for compensating affected property owners or for contributing to community benefit funds. - A transparent and meaningful community benefit fund has not been provided by the applicant. 7. Regulatory and Planning Policy Issues The proposal appears to be inconsistent with existing local planning policies that prioritise the welfare of residents, the protection of green spaces, and the sustainable development of infrastructure. - Non-Compliance with Planning Guidelines: Local development frameworks often stipulate the need for buffer zones, robust environmental assessments, and clear justification for siting major infrastructure near sensitive receptors. The BESS application, as it stands, falls short of these requirements. - Precedent Setting: Approval of this application may set a worrying precedent, opening the door for further industrial encroachment into residential and environmentally sensitive areas. Conclusion and Request While the integration of advanced energy storage solutions is a commendable goal, the current application for the BESS facility fails to address, in a satisfactory manner, the considerable risks it poses to health, safety, the environment, and the character of our community. The lack of meaningful consultation, inadequate safety measures, insufficient environmental protection, and disregard for local planning frameworks demand that this application be denied or, at the very least, substantially revised. I respectfully urge the planning authority to reject the current application for the BESS facility at the proposed location. Should the applicant wish to proceed, I request that they be required to undertake a thorough review of alternative sites, perform a detailed risk assessment in collaboration with local emergency services, and enter into sincere and transparent consultation with the community. Only through such a robust and inclusive process can the legitimate concerns of residents be addressed and the best interests of all stakeholders safeguarded.

I am writing to object the Installation of Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) at land to North East of [PLACE], [APPLICATION_CODE]. Firstly, my objection in general terms is the further industrialisation of rural areas and the impact on an agricultural area that already has significant Energy infrastructure. Currently it is not possible to look in any direction from this area without seeing excessive amounts of windmills and pylons (both at land and at Sea). By approving this BESS within this area it will present a further huge impact on our natural countryside, wildlife, and prime agricultural land. If approved it will be adding more industrial infrastructure to an already industrially congested rural area and potentially setting precedence for even more future industrial development of a rural setting. This is wholly unacceptable to anyone who values our countryside and the well-being of its residents and inhabitants. Below I lay out more pointed reasons that I object this development. Each of these objections has merit individually and collectively. NON-ESSENTIAL INFASTRUCTURE We are already 3x above the 2045 target for net zero in the area so this is not a required facility. Within the [PLACE] catchment area there is currently 102MW of intermittent renewable energy generation online or awaiting construction, that could benefit from energy storage backup. Within the same area code, there is currently 130MW of BESS approved and awaiting construction; that leaves 28MW of excess energy storage capacity already due to come online. This local overcapacity (combined with national capacity well on the way to far exceed 2045 targets), demonstrates that no further BESS sites are necessary and should not be considered as 'essential infrastructure' within this area. As non-essential infrastructure, building this BESS will in fact be in conflict with any Green Agenda or Policy as we will be destroying natural land and expending resource and creating pollution on a scheme that provides Zero benefit due to overcapacity in supply. The environmental impact of manufacturing all items that would be installed at this site must be considered along with the destruction of agricultural land. Also, the civil engineering work utilising plant and equipment, transportation, construction of access roads, installation of foundations, and all building activities associated with the placement of these units which is not required. Where this BESS would connect to the grid, and the distance between this site and the grid connection, also has to be considered in the context of Non-Essential Infrastructure (See INADEQUATE LOCATION below) FLOOD CONCERNS The land is in a flood prone area as advised by SEPA. It has a high likelihood (10%) of annual surface flooding. Severe flooding and run off can regularly be witnessed in the area of the proposed BESS (as anyone who uses this road can confirm). The run off from [PLACE] and its natural reservoirs is significant, especially after periods of sustained rain, significant down pours, or during winter when the ground is frozen and impermeable. It is generally understood and accepted that these conditions will only get worse due to climate change and predicted weather patterns - so we can anticipate that flooding will be worse than historically experienced. When flooding does happen then any contamination will leak into the [PLACE] which will damage our wildlife, pollute the water and cause significant negative effects. Further consideration should also be made of the nearby area that these waters discharge into the sea: [PLACE] is an [ORGANIZATION] [PLACE] and any potential contamination could have a significant detrimental effect on the birdlife. Thermal runaway is a major health risk for our local community and wildlife. Current policies do not permit development in flood risk areas unless for essential infastructure. As previously noted, this is not essential due to the overcapacity of BESS. However, taking this out of the equation, there has been no valid points raised as to why this location is the most appropriate for linking to a substation that is miles away, taking up prime agricultural land, invading an area thriving with wildlife and surrounded by residential properties. There is also no clarity provided for this development on how this BESS would be connected to the substation - several miles of ditches and cabling adding to the Net Positive impact of a site that simply is not required? There are two main areas relating to my flood concerns. The first is natural flooding (which already occurs on a regular basis), and the second is flooding in a fire scenario where, as has been experienced elsewhere, substantial amounts of water have to be used over extended periods of time to control battery fires. INADEQUATE LOCATION It is understood the location of this application is a considerable distance from the substation that it is being connected to. Although nothing in the application states where this is actually being connected to? Therefore, a report should be commissioned into where this is being connected to and how they propose to do this without causing unjustifiable disruption and damage. At the initial consultation it was advised that it is due to be connected to [PLACE] and this location was carefully considered due to the close proximity to [PLACE]. The location of [PLACE] substation, which is now the presumed substation due to initial plans with [PLACE] not going ahead, is between 7.4 miles and 11 miles away depending on the route they take. Therefore, requiring major disruption to our local community during the digging to allow the cables to be placed in the ground. This road is a [PLACE] bus route and if closed is going to impact our children getting to [PLACE], along with locals getting to work and going about their daily routine. This route would need to cross the [PLACE] and would cause significant disruption to place significant quantities of cabling all this way along single track roads. It is hard to justify that this scheme and location has any logical or reasonable benefit in reaching net zero. Common sense determines that if this development is absolutely necessary, then a location near the substation is the right thing to avoid disruption to roads, noise pollution from diggers, air pollution and emissions from construction plant running in excess due to the distance required to be dug up, disruption to countryside digging up verges and therefore disturbing wildlife which may inhabit these areas. There is simply no logic that can reasonably support this as a reasonable chosen location for a BESS. I would request that a report is commissioned into why this is even considered an appropriate location, and seek clarity on the connection point to the grid which appears to be a substantial distance away? ACCESS ROAD CONCERNS Another major concern is that having the stated 21 vehicles and one HGV per day accessing the site on multiple occasions for an extended duration. Plus the cranes etc that will inevitably be involved with construction activity and loading and offloading of battery and associated units. The road is already in very poor condition (probably due to the flooding mentioned above). It has significant pot holes which get very deep very quickly due to wash out. What measures would be taken to ensure the condition of this road is not worsened by the increased volume of traffic during construction, and what will be done to ensure the road is returned to its current condition (or better) after construction There is no slip off from the [PLACE] to turn onto the single carriageway road and this is extremely dangerous for a car, having more and larger vehicles turning off is definitely going to increase the risk of a road traffic accident HGV type vehicles will need to come to an almost complete stop on the duel carriageway before turning off due to the tightness of the turn off. Knowing the behaviours of drivers on this fast stretch of road will most definitely cause accidents. Equally heading North and turning onto the [PLACE], the middle area at the intersection, that does not even fit a car comfortably, will be so dangerous for a HGV. Heading South will be HGVs turning into a Major Road without the benefit of any slip road to gain speed. CLOSE PROXIMITY TO HOMES & NATURAL RESOURCE This proposed area is encircled by properties who will all be directly impacted by the building of this BESS. The noise and light pollution emitted from it will be significant due to how open this area is. If it was to go on fire this would be a major concern for loss of property, loss of woodland, loss of protected wildlife, and health complications. Situated right next to woodland which is currently being replanted, and being in such a windy spot, this could get out of control very quickly. Recent fires of battery storage have proven that they will burn for days. The toxic chemicals leaked from this are a massive health concern for nearby residents and wildlife and these concerns also need to be considered as part of the Planning consideration. FIRE RISK As well established by media reports BESS carry significant risk of substantial fire. The fumes from a thermal runaway can be fatal to anyone present, including first responders. Via the Media we are also advised that such fires burn for at least a few days until it has burnt out. Given the proximity to houses this is not an acceptable scenario. The proposed plan states that there will be a pond, however, this only has enough to provide initial firefighting for 2 hours. The [ORGANIZATION] guidance states that there is no way to extinguish a BESS fire so it is difficult to understand how the pond is deemed adequate and simply increases the concern of local residents of an uncontrolled fire scenario. NOISE IMPACT The noise impact assessment needs to be reviewed and reconsidered as it appears to be inadequate and contains anomalies which are neither explained nor understood. Within the Report itself it states that the findings were considered unusual. It is also understood that the noise surveys were not carried out at all property locations adjacent to the site (i.e. [PLACE]). With these anomalies and omissions it is clear that a proper noise assessment has not been conducted and the proposer has not determined any level of suitability and acceptability. FLAWS IN DESIGN/LAND OWNERSHIP ERROR On the Planning application there is a proposed cut off ditch at the opposite site of the field to the access road. It is not clear what this entails? Clarity is required to determine what the intent is here. Also for your info and consideration it appears there are more than one land owners in this area, which conflicts with the proposal. The corner of the field closest to [PLACE] (approx. 0.5 acre in size) is actually not owned by the current landowner, as presented on the documentation, who is proposing to lease land for the BESS development. Therefore the proposer is misrepresenting the ownership and right to lease the land. It is likely that if this development is given the go ahead, and that area above is impacted, then legal issues could arise as ownership of lands has not been truly represented in the application? PRIME AGRICULTURAL LAND This field is currently farmed and is prime agricultural land. Once this site is changed to cater for a BESS, it is stated it will be returned to its natural farming state after use. Consideration needs to be taken as to the validity of this statement as it is not understood, or explained, how they would get this back to it's natural farming state once un-natural and harmful chemicals and construction materials had been present (especially in the aftermath of a fire scenario). VISUAL IMPACT As stated in the application the development will present a moderate to major visual impact on [PLACE]. That is not an acceptable situation for the residents, nor should it be for the decision makers within the Planning Dept. This rural area is already heavily congested with large amounts of Masts and windmills. RISK TO SPECIES The local area is home to pine marten, common toad, European water vole, and two species of owl. By allowing this BESS we would be disturbing and damaging the natural habitat of species that we should be trying to protect. OTHER SIGNIFICANT CONSIDERATION Although the following may not be wholly relevant to this particular Planning Application it cannot go un-noted that the entire concept of BESS Development is very poorly considered, fundamentally flawed, and wholly inadequate to the best interest of the country as a whole. There appears to be no consolidated Plan or consideration as to where and how many BESS are being built, and these things are becoming so numerous that they are having a detrimental impact on rural areas. I have no doubt that at a point in the future this whole topic will become a source of National shame and scandal in the way it is being handled by both National Government and Local Councils. BESS developments are not adequately controlled and are being allowed to be developed in existing agricultural areas and destroying the natural footprint of this land, industrialising rural areas. The huge and unrealistic money being paid for the BESS developers to lease this land is many many times more than the actual value of the land. The BESS sites are often located miles from the asset they will connect to, thus introducing further excessive infrastructure and destruction to achieve connection to the Network and generating significant costs that would not normally be regarded as economical. All these costs will have to be recovered and it will be the consumers who have to face the bill. Once the general public realise what is going on and are faced with large bills to pay for the excessive expenditure of these developments I imagine the roof will come off, and the decision makers such as yourselves who facilitated and approved this will be held accountable. Why can BESS units not be located at existing sites, such as within the footprint of existing windmills, where infrastructure has already been installed and exists - thus significantly reducing the cost and the damage to existing green spaces. I would appreciate these points to be put forward for objection.

I am writing to formally object to the proposed development of a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) facility near [PLACE]. As a resident with a connection to the area, I have serious concerns regarding the environmental, safety, economic, and procedural implications of this proposal. My objections are as follows: 1. Visual and Landscape Impact The proposed site is situated on the skyline near to [PLACE], making it highly visible from numerous public viewpoints. The construction of “landscape berms” and the planting of shrubbery will not mitigate the visual impact of this installation. The industrial nature of the proposed development is incompatible with the rural character of the surrounding landscape. 2. Risk to Private Water Supplies There is a significant risk of contamination to private water sources in the area, including springs, burns, wells, and aquifers. I formally request that a comprehensive hydrogeological assessment be undertaken by an independent body at the expense of [ORGANIZATION] to ensure that not only my private water supply, but also those of neighbouring properties, are fully protected even in the event of a catastrophic incident. An example of the area's vulnerability, excavation work previously conducted at [PLACE] resulted in the disruption and failure of a local resident's water supply at a property known as [PLACE] located in close proximity to the proposed BESS site, highlighting the risk of disruption and contamination and demonstrating just how fragile and interconnected these water sources can be. This assessment must be overseen by the appropriate regulatory bodies, including the Drinking Water Quality Regulator for Scotland (DWQR). At present, [ORGANIZATION] appears to lack a clear understanding of the locations and interconnections of private water supplies, springs, wells, and the associated inlets and outlets within the area. [ORGANIZATION] must therefore commission an independent and qualified body to conduct a detailed survey and analysis to map and clarify how all private water sources and aquifers are interlinked. Water samples should be collected, and the results recorded for future reference. It may be necessary for legislation to be put in place to ensure that the quality of private water supplies is monitored on a six-monthly or annual basis. This monitoring should include testing for any signs of cross-contamination affecting private water sources and associated infrastructure. The responsibility and accountability for funding this ongoing monitoring must lie with [ORGANIZATION]. 3. Hazardous Emissions and Wildlife Impact While BESS are presented as safe during normal operation, accidents will and do happen, and continuous toxic fumes can be released during a catastrophic failure and cannot be completely mitigated. The continuous venting of hazardous fumes from battery units poses a significant risk to both human health, livestock, and local wildlife. The adjacent [PLACE] supports a range of protected species, and no development should proceed without a full comprehensive Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) and an Ecological Survey must be part of the planning process to ensure that developments do not harm protected species, habitats, or biodiversity. A comprehensive plume dispersion study should be conducted as part of the planning and risk assessment process for the proposed Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) development. Given the known risks associated with lithium-ion battery systems, particularly the potential for thermal runaway events that can release toxic and flammable gases such as hydrogen fluoride, carbon monoxide, and hydrogen gas, it is essential that the potential impacts of such emissions are fully understood and transparently assessed. This study should model a range of worst-case scenarios, including: 1. Full and partial battery cell failure. 2. Fire events involving multiple units. 3. Seasonal and directional wind variations. 4. Proximity to residential properties and sensitive receptors. The modelling should use recognised tools (e.g., CFD or ADMS) and include: 1. Gas dispersion patterns. 2. Thermal radiation zones. 3. Emergency response implications. 4. Potential health impacts on nearby residents. Given the proposed site proximity to residential areas and private water sources, this study is critical to ensuring public safety, environmental protection, and informed decision-making by the planning authority. I also request that the findings of these studies be made publicly available and submitted as part of the planning application documentation. 4. Proximity to Critical Gas Pipeline Infrastructure: It is deeply concerning that part of the proposed infrastructure is planned to be constructed directly above a live underground gas pipeline. This appears to be in direct contravention of established safety guidance, including the Health and Safety Executive’s publication HSG47: Avoiding Danger from Underground Services, which outlines strict precautions for any construction or excavation near such critical infrastructure. While the Pipelines Safety Regulations 1996 do not specify a fixed exclusion zone, industry best practice and [ORGANIZATION] guidance strongly discourage any construction directly over or within close proximity to high-pressure gas pipelines without thorough risk assessment, stakeholder consultation, and mitigation measures. In many cases, a minimum clearance distance of up to 100 metres is observed, depending on the pipeline’s pressure and classification. I presume that the pipeline stakeholders will require a comprehensive risk assessment and third-party engineering review before this application proceeds any further. This alone should be grounds for immediate refusal of the application. 5. Emergency Response & Fire Safety The proposed development raises serious concerns regarding emergency response capabilities and fire safety, particularly in relation to lithium-ion battery fires. These types of fires are highly complex and hazardous, often involving thermal runaway, toxic gas emissions, and the potential for rapid escalation. They require specialist firefighting techniques, including prolonged cooling with large volumes of water and the use of specific suppression agents. Does [ORGANIZATION] currently have this specialist training, equipment, and resources necessary to manage lithium-ion battery fires effectively? These incidents are not comparable to conventional fires and demand a coordinated response involving hazardous materials, teams, and continuous access to a high-capacity water supply - something that is not available on-site, regardless of the size of the proposed BESS water storage system. Furthermore, is the proposed catchment pond adequate for managing runoff from a major fire event? Of even greater concern is its proposed location, on the side of a hilltop (skyline), which would significantly increase the velocity of water runoff during an emergency, reducing the effectiveness of containment and increasing the risk of uncontrolled discharge. In the event of overflow, the runoff could carry contaminated water containing heavy metals, electrolytes, and toxic combustion by-products into nearby watercourses. This poses a serious threat to groundwater quality, local ecosystems, and marine environments. The presence of a burn on the opposite side of the road provides a direct hydrological pathway for these pollutants to reach the sea, thereby compounding the environmental risk. Given the topography and the nature of potential contaminants, a comprehensive hydrological and environmental risk assessment must be conducted. This should include detailed modelling of runoff scenarios, containment capacity, and mitigation measures to prevent pollution of surrounding land and water bodies. Given these factors, it is essential that a comprehensive Fire Safety and Emergency Response Plan be developed in consultation with local fire services, environmental agencies, and hazardous materials experts and shared with local residents. This plan must include a full risk assessment of fire scenarios, specialist training and equipment for local responders, on-site infrastructure capable of supporting extended firefighting operations, and a containment system to prevent environmental contamination. Without these critical safeguards, the proposed development poses an unacceptable risk to residents, public safety, and the environment. 6. Economic Viability and Transparency It was unclear as to how this site will be connected to the grid, either a distance of approximately 7 to 9 miles to the [PLACE] or the [PLACE] and either under or above ground. This lack of transparency raises serious concerns about the overall viability of the proposal and whether alternative or additional infrastructure potentially not yet disclosed is being considered behind the scenes. It is difficult to understand the logic being applied by [ORGANIZATION], independent bodies, [ORGANIZATION], and the relevant local authorities in supporting this approach. Based on the information currently available, the proposal does not appear to be practical, viable, or economically sound. The financial case simply does not stack up, and the absence of clear justification only adds to the growing uncertainty surrounding this development. In particular, there is growing concern that overhead pylons may ultimately be used in place of underground cabling, contrary to current representations. This would be wholly unacceptable, especially given that the proposed pylon alignment route has already been met with strong local opposition and is subject to ongoing refusal. This raises serious questions about the practicality and environmental justification of situating a BESS facility so far from its grid connection point. It is unclear what rationale supports the notion that constructing such infrastructure over this distance is either economically viable or environmentally responsible. There is no precise information on how and where the proposed underground cable route will be installed, including maps, construction methods, and any land or environmental impacts. There needs to be clarification on whether any further infrastructure is being planned or considered that has not yet been disclosed to the public or included in the current planning documentation and the cumulative impact on the infrastructure and area. How many of these BESS sites are needed and will there be a maximum limit? There is already another site earmarked at [PLACE] that appears to be connecting to the [PLACE], but this is not yet even gone to public exhibition yet. Clear and honest communication on these matters is essential to maintain public trust and support informed decision-making. I have no confidence in the transparency or integrity of this planning process. It appears that the proposal is being rushed forward prematurely, without all necessary details being compiled, risks properly assessed, or meaningful discussions held with key stakeholders such as [ORGANIZATION] and the cumulative impact on our area. How are we, as residents, supposed to protect our area when there are so many proposals, by different agencies, companies, overlapping and confusing applications, supposed to monitor and comment on so many different applications? This in itself is overwhelming! 7. Disproportionate Legal Protections of Wildlife v Human Rights It is increasingly concerning that, in some planning decisions, protected wildlife species such as badgers appear to receive stronger legal safeguards than the residents whose homes, health, and livelihoods may be directly affected by proposed developments. While the protection of biodiversity is vital and legally mandated, this must be balanced with the rights and well-being of local communities. Planning authorities must ensure that human and environmental interests are considered equitably, and that the voices of residents are not overshadowed by procedural obligations related to wildlife alone. This imbalance should be addressed through a more integrated and transparent planning process that respects both ecological and human rights. 8. Premature & Illogical Planning Application The submission of this application is premature and speculative, given that the primary infrastructure it depends on - the [PLACE] at [PLACE] - has not yet received approval. Proceeding at this stage is not only illogical, but also risks unnecessary environmental harm, financial waste, and contributes to heightened distress and anxiety among local residents. It is essential that foundational infrastructure is approved and in place before dependent developments are even considered. 9. Noise, Frequency, and Digital Interference While [ORGANIZATION] asserts that noise impacts from the proposed BESS site will be minimal based solely on computer modelling, there is no certainty as to how residents and neighbouring properties will be affected in reality. The assessments provided to date appear incomplete, lacking both comprehensive research and supporting data, particularly in relation to all potential sources of noise and electromagnetic interference (transformers) within the BESS site. It is essential that [ORGANIZATION] conducts thorough, real-world acoustic testing using transmitters and receivers placed across the [PLACE] valley and in proximity to surrounding residences to verify there will be no disruption to residents, rather than relying solely on theoretical model projections. If the BESS site was to be approved and acoustic noise at my property or any neighbouring residence is later found to be excessive or disruptive, [ORGANIZATION] must be held fully responsible and accountable. In such a case, the site should be immediately shut down, and operations must not resume until noise levels are independently verified to be within acceptable and legally compliant thresholds. Furthermore, if BESS was to be approved, the site must operate to conditions that reflect the original acoustic environment prior to development. Additionally, the impact on quality of life must be considered. During warm summer months, residents expect to enjoy the outdoors, gardens, opening windows, and appreciating the tranquillity of the countryside. Any persistent industrial noise would significantly diminish this experience and impact their mental health and welfare. It is also unclear whether transformer noise has been fully accounted for, or whether site-generated frequencies could interfere with 4G/5G signals. Many residents in [PLACE] rely on mobile broadband networks for internet and digital communications due to the lack of landline or fibre broadband infrastructure. Any disruption to these services would be unacceptable and [ORGANIZATION] will be held accountable. These are legitimate and pressing concerns for those living in close proximity to the proposed development. I therefore request the immediate release of all acoustic and electromagnetic frequency studies, including those conducted across seasonal and weather variations, to ensure a full understanding of potential impacts as soon as the analysis has been performed and conclusions can be shared with all parties, including local authorities. If such studies have not yet been completed, they must be undertaken prior to the submission of any planning application. On calm days, sound travels easily in this area, especially at night, and any additional industrial noise would be highly intrusive. Should any adverse effects be identified, appropriate mitigation measures must be implemented at Flexpower’s expense imminently. These should include installation of triple-glazing or other soundproofing measures for affected homes. Consideration should be given to the implementation of enhanced acoustic barriers or other noise mitigation measures around the BESS site to effectively contain and minimize operational noise emissions. 10. Road Infrastructure The local B-class roads surrounding the proposed BESS site are not designed to accommodate the volume, frequency, or weight of heavy construction traffic associated with such a development. These roads are typically narrow, with limited structural capacity, and are often subject to wear and degradation under normal rural use. I would hope that Flexipower would undertake road upgrades to accommodate heavy goods vehicles (HGVs), undertake ongoing maintenance during the construction phase, and undertake post-construction repairs to address damage caused by construction traffic. The roads around this site are not rated for the maximum axle loads of construction lorries, which can exceed 32 to 44 tonnes depending on configuration. Using such vehicles on unsuitable roads can lead to structural damage, increased safety risks, and long-term degradation of the local transport network. This would lead to disruption to local residents, emergency access, and agricultural operations. A comprehensive transport and logistics plan must be submitted, including a full road condition survey before and after construction, traffic impact assessments, mitigation measures such as designated haul routes, vehicle weight restrictions, and scheduled maintenance. Until such plans are provided and approved, the proposal remains incompatible with the existing road infrastructure and should not proceed. 11. Evacuation and Insurance To date, no evacuation plan has been provided for residents, livestock, or wildlife in the event of a catastrophic failure at the proposed BESS site. This is a serious oversight, particularly given the known risks associated with lithium-ion battery systems, including fire, toxic gas release, and potential explosion. Our community demands clear, detailed information on evacuation procedures for residents, including vulnerable individuals, emergency relocation plans for farm animals and domestic livestock, strategies for wildlife protection and habitat management in the event of an incident, an emergency notification system to alert residents in real time, insurance coverage for property damage, health impacts, livestock loss, and business interruption, temporary housing arrangements for displaced residents, and support for affected farms. Clarification is required regarding who will be financially responsible for the associated costs. Will these be borne by the landowner, the developer, or ultimately passed on to the taxpayer? This was not addressed at the initial consultation by [ORGANIZATION]. This is unacceptable and must be addressed before any planning application is considered. Given the rural nature of the area and the presence of working farms, it is essential that a comprehensive Emergency Response and Evacuation Plan be developed in consultation with local authorities, emergency services, environmental and animal welfare agencies, and affected residents and landowners. Without such a plan, the proposal poses an unacceptable risk to public safety, animal welfare, and environmental integrity. 12. Decommissioning and Financial Security Given the 14-year operational lifespan of the batteries and the 25-year term of the land leases, I have serious concerns regarding the long-term viability and sustainability of the site. I therefore request formal documentation confirming the existence of a secured financial mechanism such as a bond or insurance policy that ensures full site reinstatement in the event of operator default or insolvency. It must be made clear who will ultimately bear this responsibility. Will it be the landowner or the taxpayer? 13. Material Sourcing and Peatland Disturbance The proposed site is situated on a hillside skyline, with limited availability of natural materials suitable for visual or acoustic screening. As a result, the importation of external materials would likely be required, which raises significant concerns regarding additional environmental degradation, increased carbon emissions, and potential damage to local road infrastructure due to heavy vehicle traffic. Furthermore, any disturbance to peatland within or adjacent to the site must be strictly avoided. Peatlands are ecologically critical due to their role in carbon sequestration, biodiversity support, and water regulation. Their disruption could result in irreversible environmental harm and the release of stored carbon, undermining broader climate objectives. 14. Inaccuracies and Misrepresentations in Public Materials The applicant’s public materials referenced an incorrect location. In the [PLACE] [ORGANIZATION] 500 MW BESS pamphlet under the site drainage and water supply section, there is a plan referencing [PLACE], which has nothing to do with [PLACE]. [PLACE] is located near [PLACE], and when questioned, they said this was just an indicative image used. If this was correct or not, it does not instill confidence that information is not just “copy pasted” from other applications and demonstrates a lack of accuracy and undermines my confidence in the proposal. 15. Lack of MOD Consultation There appears to have been no formal consultation with the Ministry of Defence (MOD) regarding the proposed development, particularly given its close proximity to sensitive or strategic infrastructure that’s based behind [PLACE] Wood. The MOD plays a critical role in assessing potential risks to national security, operational integrity, and airspace management. I presume the MOD will be consulted on this application, and whether the MOD has any objections, concerns, or recommended actions in relation to the proposed Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) will be taken into consideration. In light of the above, I will respectfully urge [ORGANIZATION] to seriously reconsider their proposed application. The planning authority should reject it and never allow this location to be used for a BESS. I truly find it very disappointing that company investors ([ORGANIZATION]) are clearly simply trying to cash in and take advantage of another government scheme. I request that all points raised be formally acknowledged and addressed in full.
