The applicant plans to put the access road directly opposite a [PLACE] which is so listed because it is an example of a late 18th or early 19th century farmhouse. Part of the charm of any listed building is the setting within which it resides. An access road to an industrial unit directly opposite this markedly changes this setting. The European landscape convention in there document Guidelines for landscape and visual impact assessment (GLVIA3), as quoted in the landscape and visual appraisal report state that “landscape is an area, as perceived by people, whose character is the result of the action and interaction of natural and/or human factors” they go on to say “character is not just about the physical elements and features that make up a landscape, but also embraces the aesthetic, perceptual and experiential aspects of the landscape that make different places distinctive. it concerns more than simply the appearance”. Essentially in applying this statement to the [PLACE] community who pride themselves on being a conservation village, the impact of this very visible development to the community, will be sorely felt. At the second public consultation the attendees were told that there would be 16 BESS units in the form of standardized shipping containers. It is therefore disappointing to note that along with the 16 6.06 x 2.9 m standard shipping containers there will also be 8 larger 12.16 x 2.44m shipping containers marked as ‘PVC’. They have been disingenuous regarding this. The applicant has asked for permission to undertake ‘micrositing’ by up to 25 metres from the original position. This means, because they are limited by the pylons and high pressure gas pipeline that converge on the east border of the site, the realistic position change they can make is to move the containers closer to [PLACE]. Concerns over this Type of Company I have major concerns about allowing a limited company with no liability to construct a BESS. The public consultations were done on behalf of [ORGANIZATION] by [ORGANIZATION] (as detailed in the newspaper article on page 6 of the [ORGANIZATION] public consultation report). All three of these companies have the same director. It concerns me that this current organisation is a limited company. Unless they have personal guarantees they are able to walk away from any venture at any stage with no comeback. Bearing in mind the equipment being placed is potentially dangerous, if they did choose to abandon the site at any stage after the ground was dug who would take responsibility for a now brownfield site that may require decommissioning of hazardous materials, would it be the Scottish government, [ORGANIZATION] themselves or the land owner? NPF4 policy 11 states that project design and mitigation will demonstrate that they can “guarantee availability of finances” around site restoration plans. As this would in 40 years time I would be keen to know how this could be guaranteed with such a volatile group of companies. [ORGANIZATION] has no experience in the installation of BESS developments and neither does [ORGANIZATION]. Excess Noise Levels The applicant states that they are not putting in any noise mitigation. The batteries omit a continual humming noise due to the need for air conditioning units to cool them. [PLACE] is used heavily by people walking between [PLACE] as well as cyclists using the road to head primarily towards the windfarm. These developments will be audible for these area users. When the council are trying to encourage the use of walking and cycling a development that will deter this goes against ERC’s policies. Environmental Considerations The flow of the water run off travels from the middle of the western border of the site directly under the proposed placement of the batteries to the north-eastern most tip and then drains into the [PLACE]. In the event of a fire if any water was applied due to the permeable underlayer the water, now contaminated with hydrofluoric acid, would drain into one of Glasgow’s major rivers causing significant environmental impact. There is a large site of special scientific interest ([PLACE]) of ancient woodland on the eastern side of the river at [PLACE]. Bats roost in the tress in the surrounding area. The ecological report confirms that this is likely in 4 of the trees surrounding the site and residents have confirmed that bats reside within the area. I would have concerns that this project would impact on their habitat as well as the security lights disturbing their natural behaviours. The preliminary ecological appraisal states that the current landscape is of low ecological value but could recommended three measures to enhance the biodiversity. The three recommendations (development of a SUDS pond, creation of a herptile hibernaculum and creation of species rich native grassland that have been suggested) have not been taken on by the applicant and therefore what they are proposing reduces the ecological value of the site rather than adding to it. The access road once the site is operational appears to have no gate planned at [PLACE]. As this is an unmanned site, and with no gate barring access I believe that it will be very easy for fly tipping to occur on this road especially in relation to the ease of access form the [PLACE] and the fact that that design of the access road will allow easy access for large vehicles. Light Pollution The applicant plans to put in put in three 4 metre tall posts that will house CCTV and security lighting. They state that “it will not be illuminated at night time other than by intruder activated security lighting. The ecological report states that a 10cm gap should be left on the perimeter fence so that badgers can get onto the site. This space would allow relatively large sized animal onto the site which could trigger the lights. In addition bats and owls fly in the area and I would be concerned that they would trigger the security lights frequently. Community Benefits In there statement of community involvement the applicant states that a Community Wealth Building Plan accompanies the planning application – I have not seen any attached document to this effect to this planning application. This community has already taken on its fair share of energy related infrastructure in the area with [PLACE], the largest onshore windfarm in Europe, being on our doorstep NPF4 (Scotland’s fourth national planning framework) states that community benefits should be put in place for developments such as this. From the applicant’s proposal they seem to think that offering jobs in the local area is sufficient to say that the community is being benefited. In conclusion, please take the above objection points into consideration, as part of your duty of care responsibility for myself as a local resident to the proposed application site.

target_text: I object to this application. As a local resident & one who attended the 1st of the 2 consultations that took place in [PLACE] in March I feel I should make comment on the quality of the information being used by this applicant. At the consultation the staff members were delighted to boast how all those living within a certain distance of the proposed development had been contacted directly. The distance was 3 or 5 miles. When we commented that we had had not information at all about this development they were perplexed. We live less than a mile from the area. It appeared that because we live on the [PLACE] side of the boundary we may have missed out on the notifications. In which case so must many others as this site is very close to the boundary between [PLACE] & [PLACE]. Surely a company intending constructing & running a BESS facility should be able to cope with district boundaries. It also suggests that the consultation exercise was badly flawed. The consultation itself was full of staff trying hard to persuade us all how wonderful this development would be. However there was a lack of detail to much of what was being displayed. The maps were confusing with areas for this application overlapping the [ORGANIZATION] substation being planned for [PLACE]. Even the names of these various applications have changed as the applicants realise that the original names were not accurate. In the case of [ORGANIZATION] they started by naming this substation as [PLACE] 2 but when it was pointed out that technically it is not in the [PLACE] district they then amended it to [PLACE]. There is also some confusion about whether the area proposed is clear of felled timber or is actually recently planted. Surely those drawing up the plans must have visited it & would realise trees are growing there. It is strange that the proposal does not appear to mention either the rivers [PLACE] or [PLACE] & yet it is actually on the watershed between these 2 priority rivers. This is a sensitive area & any spills would affect 2 important rivers & their ecosystems. This must be recognised & addressed by anyone working in this area. In fact it is questionable whether such large scale industrial activity is appropriate in this area. Although the application refers to flooding & surface water no mention is made of ground water. This is highly important for local residents as most of us rely on private water supplies. What effect will these large industrial activities have on our supplies? Safety is another area of concern to locals & we are aware of how many battery storage units have gone up in flames recently. In addition to the fire hazard there is also the release of toxic fumes. The design of the layout of this site seems strange with the water tank & pond being sited at the far end meaning emergency workers would have to pass through the site in order to reach the water. Access is another area of concern. The roads here are barely satisfactory for the local traffic but now we have the prospect of all the additional traffic to construct these sites. Certainly the roads leading directly to this site are single track which could not be deemed suitable for this sort of transport. Whether they propose to access from the east or west none of the roads are suitable in their current state. If improvements are required who pays? Previously talking to [ORGANIZATION] about their decision to site a substation in this area one reason they mentioned was that the chosen site was not on peat. Other possible sites nearer the coast had been considered but rejected due to them being peatland. Does the same not apply with BESS?

retrieved_examples.text: Firstly – I would ask if there is a need for this particular BESS - various national reports are highlighting over-subscription of planning applications for such storage units and that the national picture for infrastructure shows that there are many more bids in the system than required. My family members attended all of the public meetings held by [ORGANIZATION] plus those with the Community Council. I feel that information was poorly presented and lack of knowledge of the area by the company undermined confidence in any appropriate approach and research for the siting. I felt that community members were not fully respected for their local knowledge and information. - Areas of specific concern Safety and fire risk Answers to questions at the open meeting around risk from fire, chemicals, smoke and ground leakage were far from detailed or clear leading those present to be very concerned. There remains lack of clarity about management of accident response at the proposed site making me feel the arrangements are not in place. no residents should be subjected to this or expected to support such a development. Impact on value of properties I have undertaken some research and expect properties in the surrounding area of the proposed BESS to suffer considerable devaluation. This is an extremely negative factor which is inescapable for many of us in the area. I assume local elected members are aware of this. Location should always be selected with minimum impact on local households. Impact on the environment The site is right next to a waterway. Local people know that this provides a haven for wildlife and could well be at risk from this development. Has this been taken into consideration adequately? Is there research to create any confidence that disturbance will be very minimal or non-existent. Inappropriate use of good agricultural land One of the arguments against the siting of the [ORGANIZATION] recent proposed large substation was the use of good agricultural land in an area of importance to farming. The same argument stands with this application even though it is smaller in scale. There is land at [PLACE] and in other places which are not designated for agriculture which should be considered before this use of good farmland. Impact on Tourism This area benefits from the tourism created around the history and culture of [PLACE] and in particular the land associated with James Leslie Mitchell – one of Scotland’s best regarded authors. This BESS will endanger the experience of tourists and affect local businesses and the wider world of tourism. This was a huge factor in the consultation with [ORGANIZATION] and many academics, historians, tourist managers and lovers of literature pointed to the danger of undermining the “Sunset Song” story. Impact on culture and heritage Following on from the issue highlighted above – this area has many sites of ancient historic interest which the University of [PLACE] are currently working with. There are neolithic sites, a stone circle and burial cairns overlooking the very area affected by this application, even if not directly. Noise and light pollution No-one from [ORGANIZATION] has been able to reassure residents about potential noise and light pollution. Research shows both of these to be factors affecting local people when such sites are up and running. The impact on wildlife is likely to be a challenge also. Danger of flooding and snow closures of roads impeding access Flooding and snow road closure is an annual issue at [PLACE], This does not seem to have been adequately allowed for. In any health and safety incident there is no mitigation against weather impeding access to the BESS. Those who live here know this. Conflicting underground cabling proposed The BESS proposal does not seem to be planned in conjunction with the likely underground cabling from the coast to [PLACE] which means local residents may be disturbed twice with considerable road closures. This lack of co-ordination does not build confidence in local people. - Final comments I would point out that the recent proposal for the substation by [ORGANIZATION] in the same area as the BESS was withdrawn and an alternative with less impact was eventually selected. I hope for the same here. If Battery Energy Storage Systems are to be agreed by planning authorities then it should be clear that the proposed sitings are appropriate – in the case of [PLACE] BESS there must be better places for such a development than in this location. Other sites should be explored – we were told that this site was not the ideal location but that the landowner concerned was the only one offering up his land. This should not be a prime aspect of any such development – it should surely be about a strategic plan and locations based on more than a single landowner being offered a sum of money. This is a very good way to destroy neighbour relations and community wellbeing. In consultation the community to be affected should be awarded the highest of status in terms of consideration and process – I definitely feel this is not the case here. I personally have felt aggrieved at the way information was shared with the public for this [PLACE] development and in particular I was offended by the declaration that the development would be going ahead as agreement was already in place with [ORGANIZATION] for access to the [PLACE] and there was no going back. This is entirely inappropriate to say at an event which is declared a consultation. This makes me feel that the information sharing and consultation was a waste of time as it was a done deal in the eyes of the developer. The impact of a sense of low status of the community in any process results in disengagement from the public and failure of the developer to build any relationship with those ultimately concerned and lessons seem not to be learned. I very much hope this development is not approved for the reasons shared above. The area is too valuable to be lost to such an inappropriately located piece of infrastructure.

One of my major concerns relating to this development is the road access. - The proposed site is along a single-track narrow road with very little opportunity to create suitable passing places. - The developer themselves refer to this road as a “lane” (fig 1). This is wholly inappropriate for any large-scale development. - The road leading to the development “C1S” has been deemed inappropriate for HGV traffic by [ORGANIZATION] who are also proposing a substation in the locality. The road is so unsuitable that [ORGANIZATION] are creating their own access road which avoids using this access route and small bridge. - The small bridge over “[PLACE]” burn is not strong enough to cope with the increased HGV traffic this development will bring. I don’t see in any of the submitted documentation by the applicant that they have conducted any structural survey work to ensure this bridge is strong enough to withstand the increased HGV traffic. - The applicant refers to previous HGV traffic for the forestry operations, but they did not access the site over this small, old and fragile bridge. - Please see Fig 2, Fig 3 & Fig 4 for map and photographs of single-track road and mentioned bridge. A full structural survey is required before any large-scale developer is granted permission to use this road. Additional concern is that the developer has failed to conduct a breeding bird survey due to their rush to submit their application. - Having visited the location in June 2025 I can confirm the presence of Corn Bunting. - The Corn Bunting is a red list species, and this development will be detrimental to the species and its survival in our rural farmland habitat. 1. Location and Land Use Concerns The proposed BESS site is situated in close proximity to residential dwellings, schools, and recreational areas. The selection of this particular site raises several issues: - Proximity to Homes: The planned facility is less than 500 metres from the nearest residential properties, exposing inhabitants to potential risks associated with noise, air pollution, and possible catastrophic failures. - Impact on Community Character: BESS installations are industrial in nature. Their presence in a rural environment fundamentally alters the character of the area, undermining its aesthetic and amenity value. - Future Development Restrictions: The establishment of a large-scale, high- voltage facility may restrict future residential or commercial development in the area. 2. Safety and Fire Risk Battery energy storage systems can pose significant safety hazards, especially in the event of malfunction or fire. Lithium-ion batteries, in particular, are known for their volatility under certain conditions. - Thermal Runaway: Industry records from similar installations globally have recorded incidents of thermal runaway, leading to fires that are extremely difficult to extinguish, sometimes requiring days to fully control. - Lack of Emergency Preparedness: The application does not provide sufficient details regarding emergency response protocols, coordination with local fire services, or the provision of specialised equipment and training necessary to manage BESS incidents. - Public Health and Safety: The proximity to [PLACE] raises significant concern for the wellbeing of children. In the event of a fire or chemical release, evacuation and containment may be challenging. - The location of the fire water tank to the north of the site proposes a serious fire safety risk. In the event of any fire, any emergency vehicles will have to access this tank via the only access route which will be through burning battery compounds on either side to reach the only water source on site. Another flaw in the design which is extremely dangerous to those attending and another reason for this development to be refused planning. 3. Environmental Impact The environmental assessment presented in the application appears insufficient in several respects: - Potential for Soil and Water Contamination: In the event of battery leakage or fire, hazardous substances could seep into the soil or local waterways, posing long- term risks to ecosystems and human health. - Noise and Air Pollution: The operation of cooling fans, inverters, and other ancillary equipment may result in unacceptable noise levels, especially during periods of peak operation or emergency venting events. Chemical off-gassing and emissions during normal operation or, worse, during thermal incidents are also a concern. - Insufficient Mitigation Measures: The application does not provide robust or verifiable measures to mitigate these environmental risks, nor does it propose ongoing monitoring beyond the construction phase. - Potential disruption to private water supplies and water contamination. o [PLACE] and the [PLACE] which originate on or adjacent to [PLACE]. These feed into the [PLACE] priority catchment drinking water area. o “[PLACE]” and “[PLACE]” both run into the [PLACE] area. o Contaminants from this development have the potential to enter both [PLACE] and [PLACE]. o The developer has not referenced the potential of this or any mitigation matters, they seem to have completely ignored these watercourses and omitted any reference of them from their application in its entirety. If they have missed these obvious water courses visible on any map, what else have they omitted in their rushed application? 4. Inadequate Community Consultation A critical aspect of any major infrastructure project is meaningful engagement with the affected community. - Lack of Transparency: Many local residents became aware of the BESS proposal only after the formal application was submitted, signalling a lack of early-stage consultation. - Insufficient Information: Public information sessions, where they have occurred, have not addressed fundamental questions about risk, mitigation, or alternative siting. - 2 Public Consultations were held on 25th February and 18th March 2025. Even though the applicant has held the required 2 consultations these were held extremely close together with very little difference in the 2 sessions. This felt like a very rushed process simply to “tick the box”. 5. Alternatives and Site Selection The application does not adequately demonstrate why this specific location was chosen over others that may present fewer risks to the community. - Lack of Alternatives Analysis: No comprehensive site assessment has been shared that weighs the risks and benefits of this site versus more remote or industrial settings. - Potential for Co-location: Opportunities to co-locate the BESS with existing infrastructure or within industrial zones have not been explored in detail. This site is neighbouring the proposed [ORGANIZATION] [PLACE] 2 substation development. 6. Economic and Property Impacts Beyond the immediate health and safety risks, the presence of a BESS facility may have a profound effect on local property values and the economic well-being of current residents. - Devaluation of Property: Evidence from similar projects suggests that nearby property values may decrease due to perceived risks and reduced desirability of the area. - Lack of Compensation: The application does not identify any plan for compensating affected property owners or for contributing to community benefit funds. - A transparent and meaningful community benefit fund has not been provided by the applicant. 7. Regulatory and Planning Policy Issues The proposal appears to be inconsistent with existing local planning policies that prioritise the welfare of residents, the protection of green spaces, and the sustainable development of infrastructure. - Non-Compliance with Planning Guidelines: Local development frameworks often stipulate the need for buffer zones, robust environmental assessments, and clear justification for siting major infrastructure near sensitive receptors. The BESS application, as it stands, falls short of these requirements. - Precedent Setting: Approval of this application may set a worrying precedent, opening the door for further industrial encroachment into residential and environmentally sensitive areas. Conclusion and Request While the integration of advanced energy storage solutions is a commendable goal, the current application for the BESS facility fails to address, in a satisfactory manner, the considerable risks it poses to health, safety, the environment, and the character of our community. The lack of meaningful consultation, inadequate safety measures, insufficient environmental protection, and disregard for local planning frameworks demand that this application be denied or, at the very least, substantially revised. I respectfully urge the planning authority to reject the current application for the BESS facility at the proposed location. Should the applicant wish to proceed, I request that they be required to undertake a thorough review of alternative sites, perform a detailed risk assessment in collaboration with local emergency services, and enter into sincere and transparent consultation with the community. Only through such a robust and inclusive process can the legitimate concerns of residents be addressed and the best interests of all stakeholders safeguarded.

Firstly I see that this planning application has been submitted prior to the 12 week notice period passing since the submission of the notice of this application, which I believe makes the application invalid. Secondly, the site of this proposal is wrong, inappropriate and unnecessary. I will note why for each reason below. Wrong The site is next door to an [PLACE] and is situated on what can be described as a nature/wildlife corridor. I do not believe that other sites were considered for this project despite this site’s complete lack of suitability. There are many other sites that would be much more suitable due to the distance from homes (physically and visually), already being shielded from view by established trees, would not require trees to be felled to gain access, would not destroy the visual impact of countryside that can be seen and enjoyed by so many. When applying for planning to build a dwelling or other building in the countryside there are so many criteria such as how the building must look to fit into the surrounding landscape, how local materials should be used etc. Why then is it OK to build an industrial site on a site right next to the main road, in the view of established and new homes and in an area of natural beauty? Why is this different to other planning applications? Inappropriate The unnecessary change to the natural landscape at this site would be wholly inappropriate. The photo examples in your application have not shown the catastrophic effect to the natural view from the houses that sit above the site, nor do they show the further disruption of the tree felling which is also proposed. In fact the photos have been taken from points where nobody will ever be viewing from. The visual impact of this proposed site will be devastating to the homes on the hill and no amount of bunding will block the visibility of the storage containers when looking from above, from these properties. Unnecessary Looking at other applications for BESS units near [PLACE] you can see that all others are in the surrounding area to the substation but this application is further away for no understandable reason other than because the land has been offered. This site is causing unnecessary disturbance and upset that could be avoided. Surely when there are so many battery storage sites in for planning applications it makes sense to proceed with the sites that are in the right locations i.e. away from homes, out of sight and in closer proximity to the substation. Surely you should only proceed with sites where these issues do not apply – these sites do exist and are available. This site is not one of them. The [PLACE] is a 60mph road and the proposed access is on a straight stretch of this road where cars have the opportunity to overtake or to sit at/exceed the speed limit. This is dangerous but so is the visibility of vehicles leaving the proposed site. Felling healthy trees to make this access visible could be avoided if another more appropriate site were chosen. Felling these trees is only going to open up the negative visual impact of the proposed site to more homes and more of the passing public. Personal Impact I live next door to my parents who built a house 3 years ago – two fields away from the proposed site, up the hill. This is a house for my mother who is housebound much of the time due to having and the quiet location and the view was why this site was chosen. The proposed BESS will not only destroy the view (see attached photos from their home) but it will bring noise and unnatural activity to their extended front garden too. Not only this but the value of their house (and neighbours’ homes) will decrease significantly because of the eye sore of an industrial site that could potentially sit below their home. This application is causing significant distress that could be avoided if an appropriate site could be chosen instead. Please reject this planning application.

I would hereby like to OBJECT to the building of a BESS at the [PLACE]. My main objection is that this location is completely unsuitable for the BESS. The BESS would be located right next to and upstream from a Site of Special Scientific Interest which is the moss. Any runoff from the site would flow into the moss which would affect the [PLACE] situated there. Any runoff from this BESS is likely to contain some hazardous matter even without a fire event or battery leakage incident. The site contains concrete, plastics and other materials that would naturally give off some form of hazardous waste into the environment and direct runoff into the moss is completely unacceptable. This [PLACE] needs protection. There is a compete lack of discharge and drainage agreements in the planning application and this requires urgent review. The project should not be allowed to go into any sort of construction phase until a connection agreement has been established. The site is several kilometres away from the nearest substation and no agreements are in place as yet. If construction went ahead and agreements were then not agreed, unnecessary construction waste and damage would have been caused to the area. There is no clear decommissioning plan for the end of the project's life and this is unacceptable. These sites are going to completely alter a rural landscape and should have a very clear decommissioning plan that leaves all involved parties responsible for the return of the land back to its original rural, agricultural landscape. We do not want to leave a legacy of constructed wastelands for our children and granchildren across what should be arable, agricultural, rural land. There are already 5 other sites in their construction phase, approved or in planning in the immediate area. This is a quiet, rural area where the cumulative impact of industrial creep should be considered. The local residents have already tolerated 6 years of building electrical infrastructure here: the substation, grid stability facility, laying of various cables to connect wind farms to the substation. This continuous construction should be more planned in a considered manner. Some local residents have chosen to live here because it is a quiet, rural area and subjecting them to endless construction has a very real adverse affect on their mental health. We have come to realise that the developers who are submitting plans to construct BESS sites in our local area are submitting documents that are incomplete and inadequate and without the full knowledge of what the construction of their sites will entail and they are being economical with the truth. I am trusting the council's planning departments to ensure that these sites are properly assessed and that all the plans are checked rigorously so that the best decisions can be made as to whether the projects should go ahead or not. I understand that supporting the environmental project plans for the country is necessary but we need to be sure that shortcuts and incorrect information does not leave us regretting these decisions in the future when communities and individuals are hurt and damaged forever.

I am writing to formally object to the above planning application. I am a long-term resident of the area, having lived at [PLACE] with my family since 1991. My parents, now elderly, continue to live here, and I am deeply concerned about the risks this development poses to their health, safety, and quality of life. This proposal is one of six separate BESS applications currently under consideration within a small area around [PLACE]. Yet there appears to be no assessment of the cumulative effects on our community. That in itself is deeply troubling. My objections are as follows: 1. Fire Risk and Emergency Response Lithium-ion battery fires are notoriously difficult to control, as seen in the recent incidents at [PLACE] and [PLACE]. These fires are capable of reigniting, producing toxic smoke, and burning for days. The proposal fails to explain how such an incident would be managed on this rural site, which lacks the infrastructure and proximity to emergency services. Most importantly, there is no public evacuation plan - yet residents like my elderly parents may have limited mobility. We need clarity on how people in their position would be safely informed, assisted, and protected in an emergency. 2. Water Supply for Firefighting The village of [PLACE] does not have a mains water supply, raising serious concerns over how a fire could be effectively tackled. The application does not provide any detail on water storage volumes, sourcing, or whether boreholes could compromise local private water supplies, which my family relies on. 3. Environmental Pollution from Fire Water Run-Off Fire suppression water is often contaminated with harmful chemicals. Without proper containment, this could easily enter the local water table or the burn that flows into [PLACE], putting both human and environmental health at risk. This is particularly serious for homes with private wells. 4. Noise Impacts Cooling units, inverters, and transformers produce continuous operational noise. As a quiet rural area, any new noise sources must be assessed against baseline levels before the substation was built - and must also factor in the noise from the five other proposed BESS facilities. Living close by, this noise will affect our daily lives and long-term well-being. 5. Construction Traffic and Access Concerns This development would lead to significant disruption during construction, especially from heavy goods vehicles and daily movements of large construction crews. Our roads are narrow and not designed for this level of industrial traffic. As a resident of [PLACE] Avenue, I worry about the safety of my elderly parents and other vulnerable people walking or driving on these single lane roads, especially given limited visibility and lack of pavements. 6. Decommissioning and Land Restoration There are no guarantees in the proposal for how the site will be properly decommissioned after the 25-year operational period. Concrete bases, cables, and other infrastructure may remain unless a fully costed restoration plan and secured fund are in place. Without this, the land could be left permanently damaged. In conclusion, this development is completely unsuitable for a rural residential area. The lack of emergency planning, the risks to water and air quality, and the unacceptable disruption to residents - particularly to vulnerable people like my elderly parents - make this proposal deeply inappropriate. I strongly urge [ORGANIZATION] to reject application [APPLICATION_CODE] in the interest of protecting residents, safeguarding our environment, and preserving the character of our community.

target_text: I wish to OBJECT to the above application. I read an article recently in the Press & Journal, 2nd May 2025 - which stated 1305 applications on [PLACE] Renewable map, I wonder what that equates to as per 1,000 of population, you can bet it is one of the highest in the UK. I feel that it is my duty not only as a resident but also as a guardian of the county to protect our once beautiful countryside for future generations, who wish to remain living locally. This application is yet another large scale BESS for the [PLACE] area (I understand a 5 acre site) and once again the cumulative impact is not properly assessed. BESS are also very concerning because of safety aspects. Reading in the news of fires in [PLACE] and [PLACE] highlight how problematic such fires are. Also, we are reliant on a retained fire service, over 10 miles away. Often batteries are advertised as a solution to windless days - when in fact all they offer are short term storage. [PLACE] BESS is planned next to existing and planned substations, and should not therefore be reviewed in isolation. Please no more industrialisation - I hope you refuse this application.

retrieved_examples.text: I am writing to formally object to the [PLACE] Battery Energy Storage Project No. [APPLICATION_CODE]. As a community we have accepted the need for some development in our area as part of the transition to renewable energy. We did not object to the extension of [PLACE], nor to the first three applications for BESS development namely [ORGANIZATION], [ORGANIZATION] and [ORGANIZATION]. These three applications have now been granted whereby over 80 acres of our prime agricultural land will be lost and the environment around [PLACE] industrialised from rural countryside. My understanding is that National Planning Framework 4 addresses the need for Cumulative Impact to be considered. This development, if approved, would be in a field adjacent to the [ORGANIZATION] development which has already been approved and close to the other developments mentioned above. Further development in this area will change our environment out of all recognition. I object to the development on the basis that it would not be for essential infrastructure and as such would not be permitted by NPF4 on prime agricultural land. [ORGANIZATION] has identified the total requirement for battery storage across the UK and divided this into regions. The region concerned in this development is [PLACE] where the quota is 3.9GW. At this time there is 1.6GW in operation with a further 7.6GW with planning consent. There is therefore no justification for further planning permissions to be granted for BESS in our area. Our community has provided a clear mandate to our Community Council to oppose all further BESS development in our area. That mandate is reflected in our Place Plan which has been registered with [ORGANIZATION]. I have lived and worked in this area for over 24 years and during that time I have enjoyed the peace, tranquility and unspoilt countryside in this beautiful part of the Scottish Borders. I have no wish to live near to an industrial site and this development will totally destroy my lifestyle, cause my family and I much stress, worry and anxiety for not only our future health, wellbeing and safety but also for that of our community. The light and noise level of the development is also of major concern. I am extremely concerned about the environmental impact as well as the risks due to fire pollution. Having this development within our local community will detract from the future marketability of our properties. Our community should not be paying a higher price in terms of local amenity than other communities across Scotland. There should be no further developments within this locality other than the three BESS developments that have already been approved immediately adjacent to [PLACE] Sub-Station.

I understand there has been an application by [ORGANIZATION] for a BESS on the energy consents Unit. I wish to raise my concerns about this application, this is a rural but well populated area and the dangers of thermal runaway from any fire in a BESS are truly terrifying. I don't think enough notice is taken of the potential dangers of such incidents. Lithium batteries burn at an extremely high temperature and are almost impossible to extinguish. The advice from the fire service for such an occurrence for even ONE small battery is to immediately evacuate due to the toxic fumes. I can't even begin to imagine how horrific the consequences would be to the local area when scaled up to the proposed BESS size. Scotland is being inundated with infrastructure applications for energy storage and transfer without any need for it in the local area. Someone somewhere has to take a stand and say enough is enough, help protect our beautiful countryside and clean air. This is being pushed forward as part of the 'so called' Green Energy. which is in no way shape nor form Green, the infrastructure for the proposed wind farms and substations will decimate our beautiful countryside with tons of concrete, steel and access roads. The minerals needed for the horrific number of batteries in the proposed BESS are mined FAR from Scotland in less than acceptable conditions and it takes significant amounts of non - green energy to transport them. This and any other BESS application should be investigated much more thoroughly into what it costs environmentally to produce them and the harm their failure can cause, instead of being whitewashed as part of the Green Revolution and ushered in without thought for consequence. I would like you to take into consideration the growing worry and concern of the local population at the potential harm to the environment and local communities of such monstrosities being constructed.

I write to strongly object to the above application. I am co-owner of the adjacent fields to the East of this proposed Battery Storage Site - land known as [PLACE]. I have never at any point received neighbour notification regarding this project and was not aware of the public consultations held back in 2024. The first I knew about it, was reading about the planning application in our local newspaper! My grave concerns are that, as there are reports almost on a daily basis of fires breaking out from BESS installations, though the industry wants to play this down, the poisonous smoke and fumes will seriously affect those living close by and depending on the direction and speed of the wind, could be carried for miles! The toxic particles in the smoke will most definably, be detrimental to human health and these particles will also contaminate waterways and fields for miles around. Who will compensate us if we can no longer grow crops in our fields or graze livestock? If these Battery units catch fire, is there provision to contain run off? I can see no mention of this in their website. How can this be classed as environmentally friendly and green energy? Minerals used to construct the batteries is mined in foreign countries, with no regard to pollution caused by their extraction, then shipped half way round the world to get here. A huge carbon footprint has already been created getting the materials into this country! It is of little benefit to our community, as it will not create local jobs. The workforce employed for the construction will be from other parts of the country. I find it very hard to believe, that [ORGANIZATION] have not had to complete an environmental risk assessment given the wildlife that reside in the gully between our land and [PLACE]! How many hours will the BESS hold power for? Is the environmental impact and carbon footprint caused by this project going to be offset by the benefits? There is no mention of any of this on their website! There is also no mention of how the site will be maintained, secured or what measures will be in place to prevent unauthorised access. There is no mention of how long this BESS will be in place. Surely these are all points that should be stated before any planning application is considered! It is criminal what the Scottish Government is allowing to happen to Scotland - desecrating the beautiful countryside with Wind Turbines, BESS, Solar Panels and Power Stations. The one thing we can't make any more of on this island is land. If you continue allowing permission for all of these projects to develop, and all of the tree planting that is taking place on good agricultural land, there will be a food shortage! I find it particularly concerning that the area around [PLACE] has been picked on for so much infrastructure and the above application is just the first of many that are in the pipeline for our area. [ORGANIZATION] want to construct 3 rows of Pylons through our farm, which is going to totally devalue our land not to mention the privately owned houses in close proximity, but no-one seems to care as long as it's not in their backyard! Scotland is responsible for just 0.3% of the Global Emissions yet you are going to allow the destruction of our beautiful country to meet Net Zero, when all of the biggest polluting countries in the world don't care!

target_text: This letter constitutes my objection to the proposed 500MW battery energy storage system (BESS) at [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE], ref: [APPLICATION_CODE]. The main points of objection are: 1. Landscape and Visual Impact: This site is 16.3Ha (equivalent to 23 football fields) and has a 25m drop in elevation across its steep slope. The developers propose 6 terraces to deal with the height difference. There will be 470 20-foot shipping containers (332 battery containers and 138 power converters), 4608 Solar PV Panels and three 12m tall Super Grid Transformers, plus other associated equipment. Despite the 4m high fences and 8m high earth bunds proposed – this scale of equipment will be highly visible on the sloping site. 2. Noise: The noise report submitted by the developers is missing significant amounts of detailed information on sound sources, site layout, and receptors. The proposal is likely to increase background noise levels by 3 times the current levels. Two noise experts have reviewed this and advise that whilst it may be possible to make changes to the design of the site to make the sound emissions acceptable, this currently seems unlikely. The sloping nature of the site will make it very difficult to stop noise pollution escaping from the site, both during the construction and operation. The lack of detail regarding the specific equipment and the lack of comprehensive assessment for the cumulative impact means that it is more likely that the noise level would have a significant adverse impact on the locality. 3. Fire: It is not possible to extinguish a lithium-ion battery fire. Scottish Fire & Rescue have not been consulted on the plans for this site. The developer has not followed all of the National Fire Chiefs Council guidance for BESS sites. An emergency response plan is required for the site and for the area as a whole. This should include evacuation of residential properties and livestock, currently some residents would have to drive towards the site as their only evacuation route. 4. Water source, for fire containment: Huge volumes of water are required to be stored on site for potential fire suppression. There are no details where this water will be sourced or stored. 5. Drainage, Private Water Supply, Fire water run-off and containment: The terracing of the slope and introduction of an impermeable membrane have not been properly modelled with respect to drainage, infiltration from SuDS to the environment, potential impact on private water supplies in terms of contamination and volume and potential pollution of river courses. There simply has not been sufficient, peer reviewed work undertaken on the impact of this project on groundwater. 6. Infrastructure: During construction, there will be major disruption on single track roads from both the 100+ construction workers arriving and leaving each day, along with the heavy goods vehicle deliveries for all of the concrete and the equipment. The table of vehicle movements provided within their CMTP document only accounts for a very limited amount of required traffic that would need to access the site. The welfare units; the solar panels and related housing; the water tanks; the impermeable layer; the removal of waste from the 100+ workers; the water required on site; the fencing panels both palisade deer fencing and acoustic fencing; the landscaping to be planted; all of these vehicle movements have not been accounted for in the planning document. 7. Biodiversity: As there has been no Environmental Impact Assessment carried out, then there is no proper oversight into the effect on habitats for the known badgers and bats in the adjoining designated Ancient Woodland, or for the other protected species such as the ground nesting birds. Disruption from construction, huge groundworks and 100’s of meters of 4m high fencing are going to impact the wildlife. If there is a fire, then the contamination of local habitat, and the contamination of water flowing into the [PLACE] and into [PLACE] will have a significant effect. 8. Rehabilitation: Where are the guarantees that the land will be restored at the end of the 25-years of the project – for example, how is the impermeable membrane and the concrete going to be removed from the ground? What are the plans to demolish the 8m high berm that has been planted with the by then mature shrubs and trees? 9. Community Wealth: The 'Community Wealth Building Plan' gives absolutely no commitment to the use of local workforce and offers zero community benefit. The document says that there are opportunities for local companies, but does not set out any obligation that they will give preference or a minimum percentage of work. The Scottish Government “Good Practice Principles for Community Benefits from Onshore Renewable Energy Developments” document promotes community benefits of the value equivalent to £5,000 per installed megawatt per annum, index linked for the operational lifetime of the project. £5000 x 500 would equate to £2.5million annually to the community – this has been ignored by the developer. National Planning Framework 4 Policy 11 encourages renewable energy projects, but only where the landscape and visual impact is minimised and where there are local and community benefits – this site will have a significant visual impact on the landscape, and there is no commitment for local opportunities, nor community benefit. The proposed project does not meet the policy requirement, and therefore should be rejected. The proposed BESS will be sited close to people's homes and will severely impact on the residential and visual amenity provided by this area of rural countryside. The construction and operation of these facilities results in traffic congestion on single track roads, noise impact, visual impact and light pollution. Previous development plans have unfortunately been ineffectively deployed in this regard to mitigate these impacts. The risks associated with battery fire in BES facilities are significant and not yet fully understood. Potential water pollution from any fire containment would rapidly enter the [PLACE] which flows to [PLACE] and into the [PLACE]. Similarly, any fumes from such fire would impact adjacent properties and could very rapidly affect the local population of [PLACE] and [PLACE]. The recent (Q1/2025) battery unit fire at [PLACE] BESS demonstrates that BES units are prone to fire which is difficult to manage. The proposal does not comply with the principles of [ORGANIZATION] Local Development Plan; particularly in relation to this being a hazardous and potentially polluting development which will have negative environmental impact on prime green belt agricultural land, negative impact on traffic and transportation and negative impact on noise and pollution. The proposal will become part of an incremental plan to develop large scale industrial facilities on green belt / prime agricultural land. The existing recent adjacent developments ([PLACE] Sub- station, Grid Stability facility and [PLACE] BESS) are extremely prominent in relation to the surroundings. Long term damage to the landscape character and the environment has already been evident and will be added to by further developments. Should approval be granted, this and the four or five more potential BESS development proposals in very close proximity to this location will constitute an excessive number of BESS within a very small area of significant population. The cumulative impact of this rapid and ill-considered industrial development of the countryside is already too great. Any further BES development on this scale is unacceptable.

[PERSON] [PLACE] [EMAIL] [PHONE] 08.02.2025 [APPLICATION_CODE] Installation of Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) with installed capacity of [PLACE] and Associated Infrastructure. I am writing to object to the planning application submitted for the Installation of Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) with installed capacity of [PLACE] and Asociated Infrastructure to land north east of the [PLACE]. The proposed project poses a risk of irreversibly changing the character of the area while also placing unjustifiable burdens on the community. This objection articulates why the application should be declined, drawing upon its inconsistencies with planning regulations, environmental standards, and community welfare. 1: Loss of Landscape Character and Visual Amenity: The proposed BESS presents a significant encroachment upon the landscape of the area of [PLACE], known for its expanses of farmland. The industrial aesthetic of this development is poised to dominate the surrounding setting, resulting in irreversible harm to its visual charm. Noteworthy aspects regarding the visual impact encompass: - Prominence on the Horizon: The BESS's visual presence will be pronounced from houses nearby and from the busy road. The proposed alleviation strategies like tree plantations and bundling fall short in adequately concealing the development. The inadequacies in the proposed screening measures serve to compound apprehensions, as they neglect to comprehensively mitigate the extent of the visual encroachment. The proposed bund is 3m high to the front and only 1m high at the side. As the field is at an angle then the 1m high bund will not screen the facility from people travelling east on the road or from houses at [PLACE] or [PLACE] as the field cuts in front of the house and so It should therefore be at least 3m on both sides. The report states that the visual impact from [PLACE] will be Moderate to Major which is a great concern and by saying that planting some trees, which stated in the report "should in 15 years screen the BESS from people living nearby" is just not good enough. The National Planning Framework4 (NPF4) states in Policy 4 that "Development proposals which by virtue of type, location or scale will have an unacceptable impact on the natural environment will not be supported". I feel that it has been well documented that this would have an unacceptable impact on the environment. [PLACE] Local Development Plan 2023. Policy C2. Renewable Energy. This policy states that [ORGANIZATION] "Will support renewable energy developments including energy storage, which are in appropriate sites". I do not feel that this is in an appropriate site. Policy R2 The sub policy states that "siting and design of any new development will be a primary consideration. The re use of brownfield land will always be preferred over greenfield land. There is no evidence that any brownfield sites have been looked into. - Accumulative Visual Impact: The BESS, will give rise to an industrialised environment that starkly contrasts with the rural surroundings. 2: Significant Noise Pollution for Local Residents The operation and construction of the BESS are expected to generate significant noise levels, thereby disrupting the peace and tranquillity of the rural area. The current low noise levels will be compromised by the additional noise produced by the BESS, which is likely to be particularly intrusive. Specific concerns to the projected noise disturbances are as follows: - Operational Noise: The transformers and cooling systems of the BESS are anticipated to emit continuous background noise, which will be most noticeable during the quieter periods of the day and night. - Construction Noise: The construction phase is expected to involve the use of heavy machinery, excavation activities, and increased vehicle traffic, all of which will contribute to temporary yet considerable noise pollution. - Proximity to Residences: The proximity of several residential properties to the proposed site implies that the noise pollution will directly and materially impact the quality of life for these residents. The proposal suggests that local waste disposal companies would be employed to cope with the level of contaminated runoff in the event of a larger fire, as if such vehicles could even approach a lithium ion fire site considering the level of heat, toxicity and danger to life, makes a complete mockery of this strategy. The reality is, that in the event of a larger fire, contaminated runoff would inevitably flow into the local watercourse, poisoning the adjacent marshland and streams all the way down to the coast with devastating effect. - There exists a real danger of any fire to spread to adjacent forestry, woodland and hedgerows, with potential to escalate risking local properties and life. - [ORGANIZATION] states in their brochure that a Fire Risk Management Plan would be prepared in consultation with Regional Fire and Rescue Services but I see no evidence of this. 5. The application does not consider the full extents of the BESS through to grid connection, with excessively large site footprint: - This application is only for the BESS site, excluding the grid connection from roadside to the substation, raising the question as to how this further energy infrastructure will be routed, above or below ground and following what route. This piecemeal approach, means that the cumulative impact of this development alone, cannot be properly considered. - Where is the proposed site of connection to be? We were under the impression it was to be connected to the planned new substation at [PLACE], [PLACE] but it was scraped with a new site being proposed at [PLACE], [PLACE]. If it is now to be connected to the proposed Hurly substation at [PLACE] then this would be between 7 -11 miles away depending on the route. If it is to be connected to the existing small substation at [PLACE] then this is still about 2 miles away! - The site boundary 'Option Plan' under application is also excessively large considering the BESS footprint, leaving opportunity for the developer to push the BESS closer to local residence and / or apply for future extensions. 6. Road Safety and Construction Logistics - Raises significant safety and logistic concerns for local roads and the very busy [PLACE]. - From the south transporting materials will require the use of the central reservation which is too narrow to safely accommodate large vehicles. For vehicles approaching from the north, there is no slip road, creating high risk of accidents on an already hazardous turn as the lorries would need to come to a complete stop on the [PLACE] to take the turn off - Tight corners and the narrow busy single track road off the [PLACE] are unsuitable for heavy goods vehicles. - 20 vans and 1 HGV travelling on that road every day for around 6 months until construction ends is a lot of extra traffic on an already busy single track road with no dedicated passing places, 7. The proposed development will have a damaging impact on the landscape, character of the area and community, especially considering the cumulative impact of all other power generating facilities in the Community area: This proposed BESS site, is situated on a quiet greenfield site, on rural farmland that is encircled by residential properties and is placed at a significant distance from the substation which would result in roads being dug up for miles. Also, the landowner lives nowhere near the site. On the other hand 2 x BESS have already been approved at the [PLACE] Site: [APPLICATION_CODE] (NW of West Bendings) approved 29/06.23 and [APPLICATION_CODE] ([PLACE]) approved 19/09/23 and a further 2 storage facilities being subject of proposal of applications notice: [APPLICATION_CODE] and [APPLICATION_CODE] also very close to the [PLACE]. In these cases it makes sense to have them here as they are close to the [PLACE] so very easy to connect without digging up field and roads and there is only one house close by at [PLACE], the home owner has a financial interest in the BESS and therefore he is reaping the financial rewards but not inflicting noise, visual impact, stress and worry about potential fires giving off toxic fumes and impacting on their everyday lives on anybody else. There is also one already approved Northwest of [PLACE], [PLACE] ([APPLICATION_CODE]. A further BESS in the area should therefore not be considered as essential infrastructure within this area. If this should go ahead it will set a precedent for individuals, who do not live in an area, to buy up land and offer to the energy companies for financial gain with no thought to the changes in the rural landscape or the people they are inflicting this on. There is no evidence of a site suitability assessment against alternative sites in the area to demonstrate why such greenfield land development is justified, especially considering potential for brownfield development in this area. According to the Department for Energy Security & Net Zero database at end of October 2024, there are already 304 energy storage applications under construction or in the planning system, totalling approximately 21GW excluding those co-located with renewable energy generation; approximately Three (3) times the 2045 target. Within the [PLACE] catchment area and including the CKD community, there is currently 102MW of intermittent renewable energy generation online or awaiting construction, that could benefit from energy storage backup. Within the same area code, there is currently 130MW of BESS approved and awaiting construction; that leaves 28MW of excess energy storage capacity already due to come online. This local overcapacity (combined with national capacity well on the way to far exceed 2045 targets), demonstrates that no further BESS sites are necessary and should not be considered as 'essential infrastructure' within this area - The proposed development will be visually imposing and will cause constant noise pollution during construction and the lifetime of the BESS; bringing detrimental social impact for the community and risking impact on local protected wildlife species. - From an economic standpoint, the development offers minimal benefits to the local community. The short-term nature of construction jobs, coupled with potential losses in agricultural land, underscore the disproportionate burden imposed on the local area. ¿ In terms of policy compliance, the application deviates from [ORGANIZATION] Local Development Plan and does not align with the principles of the National Planning Framework 4 (NPF4). It prioritises industrial expansion over sustainability, community well-being, and environmental conservation. These shortcomings are exacerbated by a lack of robust mitigation measures, casting doubt on the project's ability to operate without causing lasting harm. This BESS project establishes a risky precedent for rural industrialisation, jeopardising not only this area but also other rural communities in Scotland. Approving this development would suggest that community needs and rights can be overlooked in favour of industrial ventures, contrary to the principles of a Just Transition and equitable energy development. The approval of this application would set a precedent, that will result in BESS applications being installed throughout this area, regardless of site suitability and the negative impact they have on the community. 9. Selecting the Site The process of selecting the substation site has been marred by fundamental flaws, including a lack of transparency and a failure to consider alternative locations that could mitigate environmental and social impacts. [ORGANIZATION] states that "proximity to grid connection sites are chosen near substations for easy grid connectivity with minimal environmental disruption" and " use of brownfield or previously developed land is the preference to minimise the impact on undeveloped or agricultural land". I feel they have not followed their own ethos in this case as do not seem to have considered other suitable land. 10. Flood Prone Risk - The application site is situated on flood prone ground, demonstrated by SEPA as having High Likelihood (10%) of annual surface flooding, with severe flooding and run off from this site being evidenced and recorded with the past two years alone; The developer dismisses this flood risk along with accuracy of SEPA data, their proposal could increase flood vulnerability in this area, and alternative lower risk locations have not been considered. Flooding run off goes into the local watercourse as well as neighbouring marshland with underlying carbon rich peat bog, then onwards to [PLACE] and [PLACE]; this is important to note when considering pollution risks. - National and local Planning Policies do not permit development in flood risk areas, unless this is for Essential Infrastructure where location is required for Operational Reasons. Even if the above over capacity of BESS in this area is ignored, there has been no demonstration as to why this site location is required for Operational Reasons, neither can there be such justification considering its remoteness from the connecting Substation at [PLACE], together with further arguments against its suitability for BESS siting. 11. Protected Species The NESBREC Report confirms Common Toad, Pine Martens, Water Vole, Brambling and Barn Owls in very close proximity to the site. [ORGANIZATION] states "sites near areas with environmental protections are often avoided" but not in this case it seems! This report is very important but has been totally ignored. SUMMARY: The proposed development is anticipated to have severe and widespread consequences for the area. These repercussions encompass adverse effects on the environment, and community well-being. The combined impacts of this project, alongside existing and planned infrastructure developments, would fundamentally alter the rural landscape, resulting in an undesirable level of industrialisation and visual degradation. The loss of agricultural land is particularly troubling, as it signifies a permanent reduction in the region's capacity to support sustainable agriculture and food production. Key issues like visual impact, noise pollution, traffic disruptions, and safety risks during construction and operation remain insufficiently resolved, leaving residents exposed to significant and prolonged disturbances. I strongly urge [ORGANIZATION] to reject this proposal outright. By doing so, the Council can safeguard the rural character of the area, preserve its economic and social foundations, and advocate for a more sustainable, community approach to energy infrastructure development. Only by rejecting this proposal can we ensure that Scotland's renewable energy future is grounded in fairness, sustainability, and respect for local communities Yours sincerely, MRS KAY KING

target_text: I am writing to register my formal objection to the application [APPLICATION_CODE] for a 500MW battery energy storage system (BESS) and associated infrastructure at [PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE]. This proposal represents one of six BESS projects in the same locality, yet no Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) has been carried out to consider the cumulative effects, despite [ORGANIZATION] recommending such an assessment. The absence of this work is a fundamental flaw in the application. My specific objections are as follows: 1. Landscape and Visual Impact - The proposed site covers 16.3 hectares (23 football fields) on a steep slope with a 25m elevation change. Developers propose six terraced platforms to manage this relief, an unprecedented scale for a BESS project. There is no other BESS site in the world that we can find that is placed on this level of slope! - The development would introduce 470 shipping containers (332 battery units and 138 power converters), 4,608 solar panels, and three 13m high transformers on the highest Terrace. - Screening proposals (4m fences, 8m x 39m bunds with planting) are wholly inadequate given the elevated nature of the site. - The site lies within NatureScot Landscape Character Type 32: Farmed and Wooded River Valleys, recognised as attractive, settled, and diverse agricultural heartland with high visual sensitivity. - National Planning Framework 4, Policy 11, requires visual and landscape impacts to be minimised; this development would dominate the valley and fundamentally alter its character. The proposed 16.3 hectare site will introduce: - Significant visual clutter from high-security fencing, industrial structures, and PV arrays; - Loss of open views and visual containment due to tree removal and earthworks; - Disruption to landscape character as a result of terracing, new road construction, and artificial screening bunds, which in themselves are visual intrusions; - Night-time visual intrusion, with likely light pollution from security and operational lighting. - Moreover, the landscape and visual assessments submitted by the applicant fail to address seasonal effects (e.g. deciduous tree cover loss in winter), visibility from nearby residences, and cumulative impact with other BESS developments in the vicinity— further undermining their reliability and compliance with NPF4 standards. - NO work has been completed to assess the geology of the ground and if the terraces on the slope will be stable with the additional weight of the batteries and power converters, this contravenes BS 6031:2009 (Code of Practice for Earthworks) and BS 5930:2015+[PLACE]:2020 (Code of Practice for Ground Investigations) as mentioned above there is no other BESS site in the world that we can find that is placed on this level of slope. - This site runs contrary to NPF4 Policy 6: Design, Quality and Place, which states that developments must be "designed to be of high quality, contribute to local identity and sense of place, and be compatible with their surroundings." The [PLACE] proposal is wholly incompatible with the surrounding rural landform, introducing an expansive, artificial, and heavily engineered facility into a tranquil and low-intensity farming environment. 2. Noise Pollution - The developer’s acoustic assessment (by [ORGANIZATION]) lacks detail on sound sources, receptor locations, and equipment specifications. - Independent experts have confirmed that background noise could triple compared to current levels. - The sloping site will act as a natural amplifier, allowing construction and operational noise to escape into the wider landscape. - Cumulative noise from six BESS sites has not been assessed. 3. Fire Safety and Emergency Planning - Lithium-ion battery fires are effectively impossible to extinguish once thermal runaway begins. - Scottish Fire & Rescue Service ([ORGANIZATION]) have not been consulted, and no fire response strategy has been presented. - [ORGANIZATION] (National Fire Chiefs Council) guidance has not been followed in full. - There is no community evacuation plan despite homes directly adjoining the site. Some residents have only evacuation routes leading toward the site, exposing them to fumes and smoke in the event of an incident. - Town and Country Planning (Environmental Impact Assessment) (Scotland) Regulations 2017 — identify and assess significant effects on "population and human health", including vulnerability to major accidents/disasters, before permission is granted (Regs 4(2)–(5); Schedule 4). - National Planning Framework 4 (NPF4), Policy 23 — Health & Safety — decisions must protect people and places and mitigate safety hazards; a layout compelling evacuation into a credible hazard sector conflicts with this policy. - Scottish Office Circular 4/1998 — Use of Conditions — conditions cannot defer fundamental uncertainties or where delivery is not reasonably certain; life-safety is not a "condition later" matter. - Winter access issues (drifting snow, impassable rural roads) further compromise emergency response. 4. Water Supply, Drainage and Contamination - The design relies on impermeable membranes across large areas, diverting all rainfall into a SuDS pond. The infiltration modelling is based on test pits located 500m away and not on-site. - The modelling is fundamentally flawed as it does not consider the slope in the design of the suds ponds - which due to varying levels of the water table throughout the year will mean that for half the year it will be full regardless of the run-off water. - SEPA/Local Plan policy makes clear that development must not increase flood risk or contaminate watercourses (NPF4 Policy 22; [PLACE] SG LSD8) - No boreholes or geophysical surveys have been conducted. The absence of subsurface data undermines confidence in groundwater, drainage, and slope stability assessments. - Private water supplies for local homes and farms are at risk of contamination or depletion. - In the event of a fire, contaminated firewater would be stored in unspecified tanks with no design detail. Any failure would result in polluted water entering the [PLACE] and [PLACE], with severe ecological and public health consequences. 5. Construction Traffic and Infrastructure - The CTMP (by [ORGANIZATION]) is based on 20–50MW projects, not a 500MW facility. - Independent analysis suggests: - 100,000+ vehicle movements during construction. - 22,000+ HGV deliveries. - Average of 265 daily journeys, including abnormal loads. - Rural single-track roads are unsuitable for this volume and size of traffic. Several bends cannot accommodate abnormal loads without overrunning third-party land, yet there is no evidence of landowner consent. - No provision has been made for laydown areas, welfare facilities, parking, or waste management for an average of 100–200 workers on site daily. Best practice is to have a laydown area at least the same size as the proposed design site. - Road damage is already evident from smaller projects and is falling on the public purse to repair. - They don’t even include the battery movements in their plan! 6. Biodiversity and Ecology - No Environmental Impact Assessment has been carried out, despite [ORGANIZATION] recommending such an assessment be completed. - The site borders Ancient Woodland, home to badgers, bats, and ground-nesting birds. - Construction disturbance, heavy groundworks, and fencing will fragment habitats. - In the event of fire or water contamination, run-off into the [PLACE] and [PLACE] will severely damage aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems. 7. Rehabilitation and Decommissioning - No credible plan has been provided for restoring the land after the 40-year operational period. - Issues include: - Removal of impermeable membranes. - Breaking up of extensive concrete foundations. - Dismantling of 8m high by 39m wide earth bunds with established vegetation. - Without a legally binding restoration guarantee, there is a serious risk of long-term landscape degradation. 8. Community Wealth and Benefit - The "Community Wealth Building Plan" contains no firm commitments to local employment or contractors. - It ignores the Scottish Government’s Good Practice Principles, which recommend community benefits of £5,000 per installed MW per year. - For a 500MW project, this would equate to £2.5m annually to the local community, yet nothing is being offered. - This represents a failure to deliver meaningful socio-economic benefit to those most affected. 9. Accuracy and Feasibility of Application - Many documents use generic specifications for batteries and equipment. The developer does not yet know the suppliers or models. - This undermines the validity of noise, fire, and safety assessments. - Approval cannot reasonably be granted based on incomplete, speculative data. 10. Scotland does not need another BESS site - The Clean Power 2030 UK action plan states we need between 23-27GW of battery storage nationally, and according to the Renewable Energy Planning database, as of April 2025 Scottish Government and local planning combined have given approval for 13.85GW - so more than half of the UK's BESS sites are already approved and are in Scotland, when only 7% of the UK's population lives in Scotland. - There would be less losses from electricity transmission if the BESS were located where the energy was going to be used – not in remote rural areas. Conclusion This application is flawed in evidence, disproportionate in scale, and inappropriate for this sensitive rural setting. It: - Fails to minimise visual and landscape impacts. - Presents unacceptable risks of noise, fire, flooding, and water contamination. - Disregards biodiversity and ecological protections. - Provides no meaningful community benefit. - Relies on inadequate, incomplete, and in some cases inaccurate documentation. On these grounds, and in line with National Planning Framework 4 Policy 6, 11 and 23, I strongly urge the Energy Consents Unit to reject this application.
