I am deeply concerned about the lack of a cumulative impact assessment, especially given that there are now six BESS sites proposed for this localized area. Despite [PLACE] Council's recommendation for an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA), one has not been conducted. My primary objections are detailed below: 1. Unsuitable Topography and Ground Conditions The site is fundamentally unsuitable due to its significant sloping topography with a 25m vertical relief. Our research has found no other site in the UK or globally, either in operation or planning, with such a degree of relief. The development plan, which includes 470 shipping containers, 4608 Solar PV Panels, and three 12m-tall transformers, will require reshaping the land through terracing to six levels. This will involve an estimated 500,000 to 1 million tonnes of groundworks. Crucially, the developer's reports contain insufficient data to support this plan, with no boreholes or geophysical surveys conducted within the project area. This absence of data on depth to bedrock, soil thickness, and groundwater movement makes it impossible to accurately assess slope stability or the potential impact on nearby private water supplies. 2. Significant and Unmitigated Visual and Acoustic Impact The scale of this development, at 16.3 hectares (the size of 23 professional football fields), coupled with its sloping nature, makes it impossible to effectively screen. Proposed mitigation, such as 8m high earth bunds, will be completely ineffective on a site that varies in elevation by 25 meters and would introduce an unnatural feature into the landscape. This development is in direct conflict with the area's landscape character, which Scottish Natural Heritage describes as having a "high degree of integrity" and being "unsuitable for turbines due to its medium scale, valley landform, quality, pattern, high value, and visual sensitivity." Furthermore, the developer's LVIA report is flawed as it omits key natural features like the wide views towards [PLACE] and [PLACE], inaccurately describing the landscape solely by its existing infrastructure. The acoustic report submitted by the developers is also lacking significant detail and fails to provide a comprehensive assessment of the cumulative noise impact. The sloping site will make noise containment very difficult, and two noise experts have advised that while it may be possible to make changes, it currently seems unlikely that sound emissions will be acceptable. 3. Incomplete and Unsafe Fire and Water Management The submitted reports contain critical deficiencies related to safety and environmental protection. The developer has not consulted with the Scottish Fire & Rescue Service ([ORGANIZATION]) on the plans, and they have not fully adhered to all National Fire Chiefs Council guidance. The Fire Assessment report lacks a contingency plan for the numerous adjacent residences, some of which have single-track access roads that would force residents to travel toward a fire to escape. Lithium-ion battery fires are very difficult to manage and almost impossible to extinguish, and having such a high density of batteries could potentially lead to a catastrophic and uncontrollable fire. Regarding firewater, the Surface Water Drainage Strategy report is incomplete. It fails to specify the capacity and location of the firewater detention tanks and states that they will be "designed by others." There is also no indication as to where water will be sourced from for the firewater. These crucial omissions leave fundamental questions unanswered. The plan's reliance on an impermeable membrane creates a high-risk scenario: if the system fails, contaminated firewater could escape into the ground, polluting the groundwater that feeds private water supplies for homes, livestock, and flows into the [PLACE] and ultimately [PLACE] River. 4. Flawed Traffic and Construction Plans The traffic report is severely flawed as it bases its traffic numbers on significantly smaller BESS sites. The document fails to account for a vast number of required vehicle movements, including those for welfare units, solar panels, the impermeable layer, and waste removal. Based on data from similar projects, it is anticipated that there will be more than 155,870 vehicle movements during the 24-month construction phase, averaging 270 journeys per day on our single-track roads. The plans do not address how the affected roads will be maintained or how the expected traffic congestion will be managed. The roads are not currently able to accommodate at least 22,232 HGV and articulated lorry deliveries, and the report makes no indication of how the three Abnormal Load deliveries will be made. The plans also make no provision for the construction area, which needs to be approximately double the final asset size for temporary offices, facilities, and parking. 5. Environmental and Community Deficiencies The developer has not conducted an Environmental Impact Assessment, meaning the effect on a known badger colony, bats, and ground-nesting birds in the adjacent Ancient Woodland has not been properly identified or mitigated. There is no consideration in the plans for the effect the disruption from construction and subsequent presence of the site will have on biodiversity, nor any planning to mitigate an ecological disaster should a fire occur and resulting contamination occur. There is also no plan or guarantees for how the site will be rehabilitated at the end of its life, including the removal of the impermeable membrane, concrete slabs, and the earth berm. The "Community Wealth Building Plan" offers no concrete commitment to local employment or community benefits. There are no guarantees of engagement with local community with respect to the development. The developer has ignored the Scottish Government's "Good Practice Principles," which promote a community benefit of £5,000 per installed megawatt per annum, equating to a significant £2.5 million annually. In conclusion, the proposed project fails to meet the requirements of the National Planning Framework 4. The planning documents contain critical omissions and are based on incomplete data, demonstrating that this development is fundamentally unsuitable for its proposed location. It will have a significant impact on the landscape; there is no commitment for local opportunities and no defined plan for community benefit. As a concerned member of the wider community, I have serious reservations about the impacts this project would have on our shared landscape, local infrastructure, and overall safety. I am particularly concerned for the well-being of those living near the development, as the developer's failure to provide a comprehensive, scientifically sound plan for fire safety, water contamination, traffic management, noise abatement, and ecological damage is unacceptable. I urge you to consider the collective well-being of all residents and to reject this application.

This formal objection is hereby lodged in response to planning application [APPLICATION_CODE] (Council Ref: [APPLICATION_CODE]) submitted by [ORGANIZATION] for the establishment of a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) at [PLACE] within the jurisdiction of the [ORGANIZATION]. The proposed industrial development poses a threat to the historic landscape and rural character of the area. Despite the applicant's claim of "limited visibility," the location on a ridge would make it clearly visible from various points, including roads frequented by locals and visitors. The current tranquil, agricultural, and tourist-oriented character of the area would be irreversibly altered by this development. The BESS is being put forward without a clear local or national strategic framework dictating the appropriate siting of such facilities. The lack of justification for selecting this rural location over brownfield or industrial alternatives raises concerns about the potential for ad hoc industrial proposals to erode landscape quality and cohesion in rural communities across Scotland. Furthermore, the inadequate assessment of risks to local residents and the wider community from potential incidents at the site is troubling. Of utmost concern is the impact on the setting and experience of [PLACE], a significant and symbolic heritage asset in Scotland. The [PLACE], formerly a cherished retreat of the late Queen Mother, holds a prominent place in the Commonwealth's heritage. Its carefully preserved setting is integral to its historical significance. Allowing a BESS facility in close proximity risks commercializing and devaluing the legacy of this royal site. This decision carries international visibility and could have long-term reputational implications for Scotland's planning integrity and tourism image. Summary This project is being situated on the outskirts of a small rural village without a clear public benefit, contravening the principles of environmental justice and democratic planning. The Council's own guidance acknowledges "particular sensitivities in this location" that remain unaddressed. This large-scale industrial project offers no discernible community advantages, such as local employment guarantees, infrastructure improvements, or revenue sharing, thus falling short of the requirements outlined in the Scottish Planning Policy (SPP) and [PLACE] Council's Community Benefit Policy for Renewables. There has been no community referendum, vote, or significant public support for this development. Consultation has been merely perfunctory, lacking in effectiveness. Despite clear local opposition, it has been consistently disregarded. A project with such significant implications for daily life, health, heritage, and land should not be imposed without genuine, positive, and locally driven consent. This development lacks such consent. It goes against the core principles of sustainability, place-based decision-making, heritage preservation, and rural fairness as outlined in the National Planning Framework 4 (NPF4). The project is clearly disproportionate and unsuitable for the area. It would irrevocably change the local landscape and the historic rural surroundings of [PLACE], a site of national and symbolic significance. Approving an industrial battery installation in such close proximity to a Royal heritage site based on speculation, insufficient evidence, and flawed policy implementation is unacceptable. Personal Comments FULL OBJECTION TO MEY BESS ([APPLICATION_CODE]) Submitted by [PERSON] 26/05/2025 Introduction I am writing to lodge my strongest and unequivocal objection to the proposed [PLACE] Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) development, located just 1.3 km from [PLACE] in [PLACE]. This development is wholly incompatible with the character, values, and future of our rural community. It fails across every relevant policy test, represents a gross abuse of the planning system, and threatens to irreversibly damage the heritage, landscape, safety, and social cohesion of the area. It must be refused. 1. Violation of National Planning Framework 4 (NPF4) NPF4 Policy 11(e)(ii) explicitly states that energy proposals must “not have significant adverse effects on the integrity or special qualities of national or international designations.” The proximity of [PLACE] to [PLACE], a Category A-listed building and internationally significant tourist destination, violates this requirement. The applicant’s attempt to sidestep this is disingenuous. The Castle is not merely a visual asset—it is a cultural anchor for [PLACE], attracting thousands of visitors annually and forming part of Scotland’s Royal and historic identity. Any development that industrialises the surrounding countryside irrevocably damages the integrity of this national treasure. 2. Heritage Impact: Irreparable Harm to [PLACE] and Its Setting The [PLACE] is a unique, irreplaceable asset. Its value lies not just in its architecture, but in its setting: a vast, open, rural coastal landscape with uninterrupted views to the north and west. The proposed BESS, with its 50MW of containerised battery modules, switchgear, access roads, fencing, and substations, will destroy this setting with industrial clutter, noise, and security lighting—24/7. The applicant’s Heritage Impact Assessment is fatally flawed. It grossly underestimates visibility, ignores seasonal variation, and dismisses experiential and cumulative harm. [ORGANIZATION] has failed to defend the setting of this vital heritage asset, despite receiving robust objections and FOI evidence of concerns. 3. Landscape and Visual Impact: Industrialisation of Unspoiled Countryside [PLACE] is under siege. [PLACE] is not an isolated project—it forms part of a coordinated wave of industrialisation, including: - [PLACE] and Switching Station - [PLACE] Tidal Project - [PLACE] - RIGIFA Substation - [PLACE] (proposed turbines and BESS) These projects combine to devastate the open, farmed, coastal landscape. The developer’s Planning Statement Addendum attempts to downplay this cumulative impact, despite clear guidance from NatureScot and NPF4 that such development must not result in significant visual or experiential harm. The “low-lying” claim is misleading. Even at 3–4m height, the BESS containers, substations, palisade fencing, and CCTV masts will break the visual line of the landscape and permanently scar its character. No amount of planting or bunding will mitigate this unnatural industrial form. 4. Public Safety and Fire Risk: A Catastrophic Blind Spot BESS systems are known to pose serious fire and explosion risks. Lithium-ion battery fires are toxic, uncontrollable, and extremely difficult to extinguish. Incidents around the world ([PLACE], [PLACE], [PLACE]) have demonstrated the risks of thermal runaway, vapour cloud explosions, and first responder incapacitation. No credible plan has been provided to demonstrate how [PLACE]—with no full-time fire service, no nearby HAZMAT-trained crews, and no large-volume firefighting foam resources—would respond to such an incident. [PLACE] Council’s failure to demand a full Fire Risk Assessment or statutory Fire Safety consultation is negligent. 5. Policy Non-Compliance Across the Board This application fails every relevant test in NPF4 and [PLACE] policy, including: - Policy 1: Tackling the Climate and Nature Crises – No evidence of biodiversity net gain, ecological enhancement, or protection of prime agricultural land. - Policy 2: Climate Mitigation and Adaptation – No life-cycle emissions analysis; the project may worsen rather than reduce emissions. - Policy 4: Natural Places – Total disregard for rural amenity, wildland characteristics, and high-quality farmland. - Policy 6: Design, Quality, and Place – A functional industrial site with no design merit or community benefit. - Policy 16: Quality Homes – Nearby residents will suffer noise, light, and visual pollution, undermining quality of life. 6. Social Injustice and Community Exploitation This development has been imposed on a tiny rural community of fewer than 100 people, with no genuine consultation, no community buy-in, and no benefit-sharing mechanism. Local residents—many elderly—were blindsided by a stealth planning process that relied on a centralised Energy Consents Unit system, bypassing meaningful local scrutiny. The Scottish Government’s much-touted Social Values Charter is exposed as toothless. No health impact assessment, no local socio-economic study, no rural equality analysis. This is extractive development at its worst: profit for developers and investors; risk and loss for residents. 7. The Precedent: If This Is Approved, Nothing Is Safe If [PLACE] is approved—despite proximity to a royal castle, a Category A listed building, open agricultural land, and a fragile community—then no rural area in Scotland is safe from speculative industrialisation. The Reporter must take a stand. The Scottish Ministers must draw the line. This development is not green energy—it is greenwashed infrastructure driven by grid balancing speculation, not public need. It does not serve Scotland’s people. It damages Scotland’s heritage, landscape, and communities. Conclusion: Refuse [PLACE], Defend Rural Scotland I urge the Reporter and Scottish Ministers to reject this application in full. [PLACE] is the wrong development in the wrong place at the wrong time. It fails national policy, threatens lives and landscapes, and tears at the very fabric of rural Scotland. We cannot let this become the model for the future of energy planning. Refuse this application. Defend our heritage. Stand up for [PLACE].

Approving an industrial battery facility in such close proximity to a Royal heritage site based on speculation, inadequate evidence, and flawed policy implementation is unacceptable. Furthermore, the BESS is being put forward without a defined local or national strategic framework dictating suitable locations for such developments. The rationale behind selecting this rural site over brownfield or industrial alternatives remains unexplained. The absence of strategic siting criteria leaves rural communities in Scotland susceptible to unplanned industrial proposals that erode landscape quality and cohesion. Concerns are also raised regarding the understated risks to local residents and the wider community in the event of a fire or other incident at the site. Of utmost concern is the potential impact on the setting and experience of [PLACE], a significant and symbolic heritage asset in Scotland. The [PLACE], a cherished retreat of the late Queen Mother and a landmark recognized across the Commonwealth, has had its setting meticulously preserved for generations. Allowing a BESS facility in close proximity risks commercializing and devaluing the legacy of this royal site. Such a decision carries international visibility and could have lasting repercussions on Scotland's planning credibility and tourism appeal. Landscape and Visual Impacts The proposed location is situated in a vast, open landscape with expansive views over [PLACE]. Even with the addition of vegetation, this area is not suited for accommodating large-scale energy infrastructure without significantly altering its natural character. The project would introduce industrial elements such as hard boundaries, metal fencing, and 6-metre structures into a serene rural environment, with numerous residents living just a short distance from the entrance. The resulting impact is neither justified nor adequately mitigated. Community Consultation and Consent Process The BESS proposal advanced to the consent stage without affording local residents and community groups a meaningful opportunity to influence or raise objections. Consultation efforts were inadequate, poorly publicized, and disconnected from other developments in the area. The community affected by this proposal deserves a fair chance to voice their opinions on whether industrial energy infrastructure is suitable for their surroundings. By sidestepping local planning procedures and directly approaching the Scottish Government’s Energy Consents Unit, the application has marginalized the community's ability to influence the decision-making process. Residents, who will bear the consequences of this development, have been left with minimal opportunity to impact the final outcome. Projects of such significant local consequence should involve genuine community engagement in decision-making, rather than being relegated to mere footnotes in the realm of energy infrastructure. Harm to Tourism and Rural Economy [PLACE] is renowned for its expansive horizons, tranquillity, and unspoiled rural charm, qualities that are becoming increasingly scarce and precious. These scenic vistas appeal to hikers, cyclists, artists, and eco-tourists. The large-scale energy industrialization plans, which include battery storage facilities, jeopardize the distinct allure of the area and threaten the future of the local economy reliant on sustainable, rural tourism. Fire and Safety Risks From Battery Infrastructure Large lithium-ion battery storage systems pose well-documented fire hazards. Although rare, these incidents can be severe, challenging to put out, and dangerous to nearby individuals, animals, and emergency services. The developer has not provided a comprehensive emergency response plan or addressed how rural firefighting resources would handle a battery fire. Given the site's proximity to woodlands and peat, a fire in the Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) could potentially lead to a rural wildfire disaster. The rural location implies a delayed emergency response time and insufficient firefighting capabilities. The potential risks to life, property, and the environment should not be ignored for the sake of convenience. Impacts from Noise: Flooding and Site Hazards Serious concerns have been raised regarding the adequacy of the noise impact assessment that has been submitted for the proposed [PLACE] Battery Energy Storage System (BESS). The assessment has been criticized for its lack of transparency, failure to consider the specific site conditions, and the absence of the necessary level of independent scrutiny required for a development of this scale in a rural and heritage-sensitive location. The current assessment is deemed inadequate, and the proposal is deemed unsuitable for the site due to the inevitable acoustic impacts it would bring. Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) facilities are known to produce continuous operational noise from various equipment such as cooling fans, HVAC systems, transformers, inverters, and fire suppression systems. Experts in the industry have pointed out that these systems can generate tonal noise and persistent background hums that are more intrusive than indicated by their decibel ratings, especially in quiet rural environments with minimal background noise. Tonal noise, recognized under BS4142:2014 ([PLACE]:2019), is considered a "penalized" noise type due to its heightened impact on residential amenity. In tranquil settings like [PLACE], even moderate industrial noise can cause significant disruption. The submitted report appears to overlook the importance of the area's auditory tranquillity, which is as crucial as its visual appeal. Moreover, the application fails to adequately address historical surface flooding issues. The construction of impermeable infrastructure like container bases and access roads is expected to increase surface runoff, potentially elevating the risk to nearby properties. This raises serious concerns about local water management and flood resilience. Road Network and Inadequate Access Infrastructure The location is accessed via narrow, unclassified rural roads that are currently under pressure from agricultural and residential activities. The introduction of construction traffic, heavy machinery, and ongoing maintenance vehicles would lead to congestion, road surface deterioration, and potential risks to local residents and livestock. The applicant has not provided sufficient evidence of how they plan to effectively handle the higher volume of traffic on roads that were not intended for industrial purposes. Threat to Local Wildlife and Habitats The area forms a diverse landscape of pasture, hedgerows, and woodland edges that provide habitats for various bird species, small mammals, and invertebrates. However, there has been no comprehensive ecological evaluation released for the BESS project, only a superficial assessment influenced by the developer's perspective. The introduction of concrete surfacing, fencing, artificial lighting, and vegetation removal would result in an ecological void within the surrounding ecosystem. This goes against the nature-positive planning principle outlined in NPF4. Grid Expansion and Landscape Fragmentation The proposed Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) would solidify the presence of high-voltage energy infrastructure in this area of [PLACE]. With the establishment of a battery installation, switching station, and turbines, it establishes a precedent that simplifies the case for more pylons, substations, and transmission lines. This gradual process of industrial expansion progressively breaks up a previously cohesive rural environment, eroding its distinctive qualities, compromising its environmental and cultural heritage, and reducing its worth for generations to come. Absence of Environmental Impact Assessment Despite the size and characteristics of the proposed BESS, a comprehensive Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) has not been conducted. Considering the potential for substantial effects on the landscape, heritage, biodiversity, noise levels, and overall infrastructure, an EIA would typically be required for a project of this nature. The lack of a mandatory EIA is a significant deficiency in environmental assessment and compromises the transparency and effectiveness of the planning procedure. No Long Term Decommissioning or Restoration Plan The candidate has not presented a definitive long-term plan for the decommissioning, restoration, or safety measures of the site once the BESS reaches the end of its operational lifespan. In the absence of concrete restoration guidelines and financial guarantees, there is a potential for the site to be abandoned with deteriorating infrastructure, environmental contamination, or perpetual maintenance responsibilities long after the energy benefits have ceased. Industrialisation of Prime Agricultural Land The proposed BESS would be constructed on land that has historically been utilized for productive agriculture, cultivating crops such as oats for an extended period. The establishment of the BESS, involving structures, fencing, roadways, and related infrastructure, would result in the permanent conversion of valuable farmland. This conflicts with national planning goals aimed at promoting sustainable rural land utilization. Once the development is completed, the land will no longer be available for future agricultural purposes or to contribute to food security. NPF4 Policy 1 emphasizes the importance of sustainable land use and climate resilience. Therefore, the conversion of prime agricultural land for industrial purposes contradicts these objectives and jeopardizes local food security. Summary This project is situated in close proximity to a small rural village without any evident public benefit, thereby contravening the principles of environmental justice and democratic planning. The Council's own guidance acknowledges the "particular sensitivities in this location," which remain unaddressed. Despite its industrial scale, the project offers no discernible advantages to the community, such as local employment opportunities, infrastructure enhancements, or revenue sharing. Consequently, it falls short of the standards outlined in the Scottish Planning Policy (SPP) and the [PLACE] Council's Community Benefit Policy for Renewables. The absence of a community vote, referendum, or popular petition in support of this development raises concerns about the legitimacy of the decision-making process. Consultation efforts have been minimal and largely ineffective, disregarding clear opposition from local residents. A project with significant implications for daily life, health, heritage, and land should not be imposed without genuine, proactive, and locally endorsed consent. This development lacks such consent. It contradicts the core values of sustainability, place-based decision-making, heritage preservation, and rural fairness outlined in NPF4. The project is clearly disproportionate and unsuitable for its surroundings, posing a permanent threat to the local landscape and the historic rural character of [PLACE], a site of national significance. Approving an industrial battery installation in such close proximity to a Royal heritage site based on speculation, inadequate evidence, and flawed policy implementation is unacceptable.

Cumulative Impact: There are now six BESS sites in proposal to be constructed in this localised area, including this one, without any overview of the cumulative effects of these projects. There has been no Environmental Impact Assessment carried out, despite [ORGANIZATION] recommending that this be done because of the cumulative effects. Concerns were raised when the original [ORGANIZATION] Transmission's [PLACE] for grid connectivity was established, closely followed by the small BESS facility, and a multiplicity of further proposals, because of the lack of any strategic overview of the cumulative effects that residents felt might be inevitable once these original facilities were established. So it has proved. An area that is historically rural, given over to agriculture - crops and grazing - with small pockets of residential properties, has recently begun to be transformed by stealth - each subsequent proposed facility falling within the parameters that would require such a strategic overview. Thus, one facility has attracted an agglomeration of others, transforming the locality from its former character into a semi-industrial complex. With this enormous proposal will come a major change of use for the land, a significant change in the character of the landscape, a far-reaching environmental impact - and all without any strategic oversight or Environmental Impact Assessment. Landscape and Visual Impact: This site is 16.3Ha (equivalent to 23 football fields) and has a 25m drop across it – it is steeply sloped. The developers propose 6 terraces to deal with the height difference. There will be 470 20-foot shipping containers (332 battery containers and 138 power converters), 4608 Solar PV Panels and three 12m tall Super Grid Transformers, plus other associated equipment. Despite the 4m high fences and 8m high earth bunds proposed – this scale of equipment will be highly visible on the sloping site. Noise: The noise report submitted by the developers is missing significant amounts of detailed information on sound sources, site layout, and receptors. The proposal is likely to increase background noise levels by 3 times the current levels. Two noise experts have reviewed this and advise that whilst it may be possible to make changes to the design of the site to make the sound emissions acceptable, this currently seems unlikely. The sloping nature of the site will make it very difficult to stop noise pollution escaping from the site, both during construction and operation. The lack of detail regarding the specific equipment and the lack of comprehensive assessment for the cumulative impact means that it is more likely that the noise level will have a significant adverse local impact. Fire: It is not possible to extinguish a lithium-ion battery fire. Scottish Fire & Rescue have not been consulted on the plans for this site. The developer has not followed all the National Fire Chiefs Council guidance for BESS sites. An emergency response plan is required for the site and for the area as a whole – including evacuation of residential properties and livestock. The nearby village of [PLACE] has a population of over 1000 residents, with a junior [PLACE]. Currently, some residents would have to drive towards the site as their only evacuation route. Water source for fire containment: Huge volumes of water are required to be stored on site for potential fire suppression. Where will this water be sourced? Will it be trucked in? (adding to the construction traffic). What chemicals will be used to prevent stagnation and freezing? Drainage, Private Water Supply, Fire water run-off and containment: The terracing of the slope and introduction of an impermeable membrane have not been properly modelled with respect to drainage, infiltration from SuDS to the environment, potential impact on private water supplies in terms of contamination and volume and potential pollution of river courses. There simply has not been sufficient, peer reviewed work undertaken on the impact of this project on groundwater. Infrastructure: During construction, there will be major disruption on single track roads from both construction workers arriving and leaving each day, along with the heavy goods vehicle deliveries for all the concrete and the equipment. The table of vehicle movements provided within their CMTP document only accounts for a very limited amount of required traffic that would need to access the site. The welfare units; the solar panels and related housing; the water tanks; the impermeable layer; the removal of waste from the 100+ workers; the water required on site; the fencing panels both palisade deer fencing and acoustic fencing; the landscaping to be planted; all these vehicle movements have not been accounted for in the planning document. Access to the site is via single track road, as are the roads in the vicinity leading to the access road. They are constructed to facilitate farm vehicles and local residential access and are completely unsuitable for wide, heavy construction / emergency services vehicle use. The road surfaces are already suffering considerably from the increase in heavy goods vehicles servicing the current sites (themselves constructed without any assessment of their cumulative impact on the local area.) Large potholes, subsidence and road edge/surface erosion are being tackled piecemeal at present. Biodiversity: As there has been no Environmental Impact Assessment carried out, then there is no proper oversight into the effect on habitats for the known badgers and bats in the adjoining designated Ancient Woodland, or for the other protected species such as the ground nesting birds. Disruption from construction, huge groundworks and 100’s of meters of 4m high fencing are going to impact wildlife. If there is a fire, then the contamination of local habitat, and the contamination of water flowing into the [PLACE] and [PLACE] will have a significant effect. Rehabilitation: Where are the guarantees that the land will be restored at the end of the 25-years of the project – for example, how is the impermeable membrane and the concrete going to be removed from the ground? What are the plans to demolish the 8m high berm that has been planted with the, by then, mature shrubs and trees? Community Wealth: The 'Community Wealth Building Plan' gives absolutely no commitment to the use of local workforce and offers zero community benefit. The document says that there are opportunities for local companies but does not set out any obligation that they will give preference to local companies. The Scottish Governments “Good Practice Principles for Community Benefits from Onshore Renewable Energy Developments” document promotes community benefits of the value equivalent to £5,000 per installed megawatt per annum, index linked for the operational lifetime of the project. £5000 x 500 would equate to £2.5million annually to the community – this has been ignored by the developer. National Planning Framework 4 Policy 11: This encourages renewable energy projects - and I fully support this policy - but only where the landscape, the environment - both built and natural, the health and safety of residents, and visual impact is fully considered and properly safeguarded, and where there are local and community benefits. This site will have a significant impact on the entire locality, and there is no commitment for local opportunities, or community benefit. The proposed project does not meet the policy requirement and therefore should be rejected.
